context: These four titles (1989, 1991, 1997, 2002) built out de Jasay's distinctive libertarian-classical-liberal position over almost 15 years. His prose was precise, French-influenced, and often mordant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay.

question: One economist argued that many things people think only a state can do -- roads, courts, even money -- could be run by private deals instead. What branch of economics asks whether public workers act for the public or for themselves?
answer: Public choice economics
choices: Public choice economics
Behavioral finance
Monetary theory
Labor economics
context: Boettke is a longtime GMU Austrian economist and a prominent modern advocate for the Austrian and public-choice traditions. His essay helped shift de Jasay from a marginal figure to a widely-read one in libertarian and classical-liberal circles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: Anthony de Jasay was one of the most cited libertarian thinkers of the last century. One fact about his life sets him apart from almost every other big name in that tradition. What is it?
answer: He never held a permanent academic post; he spent his working life at a Normandy wine business
choices: He never held a permanent academic post; he spent his working life at a Normandy wine business
He served as prime minister of Hungary from 1990 to 1994
He co-authored 'Capitalism and Freedom' with Milton Friedman
He founded the Chicago School of Economics
context: De Jasay wrote his books outside the university system entirely. The Liberty Fund began publishing his Collected Works in 2010, and the Anthony de Jasay Institute in Vienna now carries his name. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay.

question: A country has a hundred million voters. Your one vote almost never picks the winner. So how much time should you spend studying each name on the ballot?
answer: Very little -- studying takes real time, and one vote almost never decides
choices: Very little -- studying takes real time, and one vote almost never decides
Hundreds of hours -- every vote is the deciding vote
Zero -- voting is against the law in most countries
About two hours -- the same as watching a movie
context: Anthony Downs's An Economic Theory of Democracy (Harper, 1957) was his Stanford PhD dissertation under Kenneth Arrow. It founded formal public-choice modeling of elections. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Downs.

question: Anthony Downs wrote a famous 1957 book on voting. His top prediction: when voters pick between two sides on one issue, both sides end up chasing one voter in the middle. What is this result called?
answer: The median-voter theorem
choices: The median-voter theorem
The lucky-loser theorem
The consensus principle
The Condorcet convergence
context: The median-voter theorem: under simple-majority voting on a single-issue spectrum, competing platforms converge to the preference of the median voter. Duncan Black had proved the mathematical version in 1948; Downs popularized and applied it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_voter_theorem.

question: The math proof of the median-voter idea came out in 1948, ten years before Downs's book. It was done by a British economist. What was his last name?
answer: Black
choices: Black
Arrow
Vickrey
Robbins
context: Duncan Black's 1948 JPE paper 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making' proved the mathematical version of what became the median-voter theorem. Downs popularized it for political-competition analysis in 1957. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Black.

question: The median-voter theorem says two parties end up sounding alike near the middle. This explains one common pattern people notice in two-party races. Which pattern does it explain?
answer: Two major American parties on many issues look similar at election time
choices: Two major American parties on many issues look similar at election time
The two parties diverge sharply on every issue
The two parties become identical in name
The two parties dissolve after each election
context: The convergence prediction: both parties chase the median voter, ending up close together on many issues. This explains the 'not a dime's worth of difference' complaint often voiced by third-party advocates. Source: Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957).

question: Downs added a second big idea about voters beyond the median theorem. It explains why most voters know very little about most policy issues, even though voting matters. What is this idea called?
answer: Rational ignorance
choices: Rational ignorance
Adaptive expectations
Bounded rationality
Anchoring bias
context: Rational ignorance: studying candidates and issues costs time; the expected influence of any one vote is essentially zero; therefore rational voters minimize the time they spend informing themselves. Most voter ignorance is rational, not stupidity. Source: Downs (1957).

question: Downs argued that one vote almost never swings the outcome. So each voter gets almost no personal payoff from studying the issues. In his model, what are the private returns to informed voting?
answer: Near zero
choices: Near zero
Very high
Highly volatile
Perfectly aligned with public returns
context: The private return to becoming informed as a voter is near zero because the probability that one vote determines the outcome is near zero. The social return may be high, but the individual voter's incentive to learn is not. Source: Downs (1957).

question: Three friends vote on lunch: pizza, tacos, or sushi. Each picks a first, second, and third choice. Is there any voting rule that will always give a fair winner beating every other option one-on-one?
answer: No, math shows some sets of preferences make every rule fail
choices: No, math shows some sets of preferences make every rule fail
Yes, majority rule always gives the fairest answer
Yes, if everyone ranks honestly the answer is obvious
Only if there are exactly two choices on the menu
context: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (1951) showed no voting rule can satisfy a modest set of intuitive fairness axioms across multidimensional preferences. Arrow was Downs's Stanford dissertation advisor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow%27s_impossibility_theorem.

question: Anthony Downs's later career shifted from formal voting theory to a specific applied field. Which area of urban economics did his 1960s-70s work most influence?
answer: Urban traffic and expressway congestion
choices: Urban traffic and expressway congestion
Central-bank monetary policy
International trade theory
Sports economics
context: Downs wrote widely on traffic and urban planning. His 'law of peak-hour expressway congestion' -- that expanding highways induces more driving until the new capacity is filled -- is standard reference in transportation economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Downs.

question: Downs said voters stay uninformed because study takes time and one vote almost never decides. Bryan Caplan pushed that idea further. What did Caplan say voters are, beyond just uninformed?
answer: Systematically irrational because the private cost of holding wrong beliefs is zero
choices: Systematically irrational because the private cost of holding wrong beliefs is zero
Perfectly rational and consistently informed
Manipulated by hidden elites
Guided by strong moral principles
context: Caplan's Myth of the Rational Voter (2007) extended Downs: not just uninformed but systematically wrong, because holding economically incorrect beliefs is privately costless. This is the 'rational irrationality' move. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Myth_of_the_Rational_Voter.

question: A hurricane hits a town. A trucker from far away buys 19 generators and drives them in to sell for double the price. What good did his high prices do the town?
answer: They made it worth his trip -- the town now has generators it would not have had
choices: They made it worth his trip -- the town now has generators it would not have had
Nothing -- he should have given them away for free
They caused the hurricane to last longer
They lowered the price of every other item in town
context: Hurricane Frances hit Florida on September 4-5, 2004. Shepperson brought 19 generators to affected areas to sell at roughly double his cost. Source: Munger, 'They Clapped: Can Price Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' (Cato Unbound, 2007).

question: In 2004, John Shepperson drove to hurricane-hit Florida to sell generators. Florida police stepped in. Using the state's price-gouging law, what did they do to him?
answer: They arrested him, confiscated the generators, and jailed him for four days
choices: They arrested him, confiscated the generators, and jailed him for four days
They cited him with a small fine and let him continue
They escorted him to hurricane shelters as a preferred vendor
They asked him to sell only to registered emergency workers
context: Police arrested Shepperson under Florida's anti-gouging statute, seized his 19 generators, and detained him for four days. The confiscated generators sat unused in police custody while hurricane victims went without power. Source: Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: A man drives a truckload of ice into a town hit by a hurricane, where people are desperate for it. He wants to charge more than normal to cover his gas, time, and risk. Police arrest him for 'price gouging.' What is the hidden cost of stopping him?
answer: Fewer people bring in emergency supplies next time, because the trip does not pay
choices: Fewer people bring in emergency supplies next time, because the trip does not pay
Ice always shows up on its own during disasters
The hurricane damage gets fixed faster
Local stores stop selling ice for good
context: Michael Munger (Duke University, formerly chair of political science) wrote 'They Clapped: Can Price Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' (Cato Unbound, 2007). It is the standard reference for the Shepperson story. Source: cato-unbound.org (Munger 2007).

question: Michael Munger tells the Shepperson story in the language of one famous 1945 article by Friedrich Hayek. What is that article's title?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
The Denationalization of Money
The Fatal Conceit
context: Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (American Economic Review, September 1945), argued that prices coordinate dispersed knowledge no central planner could possess. Munger applies the argument to disaster price controls. Source: jstor.org (Hayek AER 1945).

question: In Hayek's way of thinking, what did John Shepperson's trip really do -- and what did Florida's anti-gouging law block?
answer: He moved scarce capital from a low-value use to a high-value use using the price signal
choices: He moved scarce capital from a low-value use to a high-value use using the price signal
He engaged in fraud against desperate consumers
He violated federal interstate-commerce rules
He operated without a state contractor's license
context: The elevated Florida price told Shepperson that generators were desperately needed there. His willingness to make the 600-mile trip depended on the elevated price making the effort worthwhile. Anti-gouging laws sever the signal and prevent the coordination they claim to enable. Source: Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: Michael Munger wrote a Cato Unbound essay on disaster supplies. He framed the choice as one stark pair. Which pair did he name?
answer: Expensive supply that arrives versus cheap supply that does not exist
choices: Expensive supply that arrives versus cheap supply that does not exist
Fair supply versus unfair supply for the wealthy
State-supplied versus corporation-supplied
Rationed supply versus black-market supply
context: Munger's line reframes the ethical debate: the anti-gouging law does not create abundance; it prevents the arrival of supply. The real trade-off is between expensive arriving supply and cheap nonexistent supply. Source: Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: In the 1970s, US price caps on gasoline caused the same mess at the national level that anti-gouging laws cause at the state level. What familiar symptom did the price caps cause?
answer: Long gas lines at filling stations
choices: Long gas lines at filling stations
Rapid electric-vehicle adoption
Federal gasoline rationing bonds
Voluntary carpooling clubs
context: The 1973-74 oil crisis and its 1970s aftermath saw federal price controls on gasoline. The visible shortage took the form of hours-long lines at filling stations rather than higher prices. Source: eia.gov (oil crisis history); Yergin, The Prize (Simon & Schuster 1991).

question: After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, one big private store chain got food and water to Louisiana faster than FEMA did. Why did the private chain move faster?
answer: Local managers had authority to act without waiting for headquarters
choices: Local managers had authority to act without waiting for headquarters
The chain had a secret contract with the president
The chain owned trucks that could drive on water
The government told the chain exactly what to do
context: Sobel and Leeson documented Walmart's post-Katrina supply-chain response as delivering food, water, and supplies to affected areas faster than federal agencies. Source: Sobel + Leeson, 'The Use of Knowledge in Natural-Disaster Relief Management,' Independent Review (2007).

question: After 2013, Venezuela under Nicolas Maduro became the modern textbook case for the pattern Michael Munger warns about. What did years of price controls produce there?
answer: Chronic and severe shortages of basic goods
choices: Chronic and severe shortages of basic goods
Sudden general abundance of consumer goods
Rapid convergence with US per-capita income
The largest sustained economic boom in South American history
context: Venezuela's price controls under Maduro produced sustained shortages of food, medicine, and household necessities, empty shelves, and mass emigration. It is the extreme modern illustration of the price-control / knowledge-problem link. Source: Grokipedia 'Economic crisis in Venezuela.'

question: The lesson at the heart of the Shepperson case applies across price-control debates. When a rule cuts the price signal in a market where knowledge is spread among many people, what should you expect to happen to the coordination that signal used to make possible?
answer: It disappears
choices: It disappears
It intensifies
It becomes visible for the first time
It moves onto voluntary channels
context: Hayek's 1945 point applied as policy diagnostic: prices coordinate dispersed knowledge. Sever the signal and the coordination goes with it. The seen effect (no one 'gouged') coexists with the unseen cost (thousands in the dark for weeks). Source: Hayek AER 1945; Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: A government pays a small group of farmers extra money for growing certain crops. The cost is spread as a tiny tax hike across everyone in the country. Why does this kind of rule almost never get repealed?
answer: The farmers fight hard to keep it; each taxpayer barely notices the cost
choices: The farmers fight hard to keep it; each taxpayer barely notices the cost
Farmers do not vote in elections
All taxpayers live in the same town
The rule expires by itself every year
context: Roughly 2 million US farms receive federal subsidies funded by about 130 million taxpaying households. The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 created the modern structure; each Farm Bill preserves it. Source: usda.gov farm bill history.

question: US farmers get subsidies -- payments from the government -- for growing certain crops. From a farmer's point of view, what is the main effect of a subsidy for that crop?
answer: Farmers grow more of it than the market would want on its own
choices: Farmers grow more of it than the market would want on its own
Farmers stop growing it entirely
The crop becomes illegal to sell
Nothing changes about how much is grown
context: The Farm Bill is the general term for the periodic reauthorization of USDA programs. Most recent: 2018 Agriculture Improvement Act and its 2024 continuing resolutions. Source: usda.gov farm bill.

question: The US sugar program is often called the purest Olson case. Tariff-rate quotas and price supports raise US sugar prices to roughly what multiple of world prices?
answer: About twice
choices: About twice
About 20 percent higher
About ten times
About the same
context: US sugar prices run roughly 2x world prices as a result of tariff-rate quotas and price supports. About 4,000 US sugar producers benefit; 330 million consumers pay the higher price on anything sweetened. Source: cbo.gov sugar program analysis.

question: The US sugar program helps about 4,000 sugar producers. Together they earn about $1 billion a year from it. It costs each of the 330 million shoppers only a few extra dollars a year. Under Olson's theory, which side is easier to organize?
answer: The 4,000 producers
choices: The 4,000 producers
The 330 million consumers
Both sides equally organized
Neither side ever organizes
context: Olson's mechanism: concentrated benefits attract concentrated lobbying; dispersed costs generate almost no counter-organization. The producers form associations (American Sugar Alliance, US Sugar Corporation); the 330 million consumers do not organize to save $3 each per year. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: In 1950, only about 5 percent of US workers needed a state license to do their job. That share has grown a lot over 70 years, driven by the same Olson pattern. About what share needed a license by 2020?
answer: About 25 percent
choices: About 25 percent
About 5 percent still
About 50 percent
About 75 percent
context: Roughly 25% of US workers needed a state license by 2020, up from 5% in 1950. Barbers, hair braiders, morticians, interior designers, tour guides, florists (in some states). Source: Kleiner + Krueger 2013.

question: Workers already in a licensed job push state boards to make it harder for new people to enter. People who would like to enter that job don't push back much. Why can't they organize a strong counter-push?
answer: They are not yet in the profession and cannot organize as members
choices: They are not yet in the profession and cannot organize as members
They lack the constitutional right to petition
They are barred by antitrust law from lobbying
They earn too little to fund political action
context: The would-be barber, hair braider, or interior designer is not yet in the profession; they have no association to fund the counter-lobby. Olson's classic mechanism: concentrated present interests always outweigh dispersed future ones. Source: Kleiner + Krueger 2013.

question: A state passes a new law. To braid hair for pay, you now need a license that takes months of training and hundreds of dollars. What usually happens to insider wages, and to newcomers trying to enter the trade?
answer: Insider wages rise because competition drops; newcomers find it much harder to start
choices: Insider wages rise because competition drops; newcomers find it much harder to start
Insider wages fall because the license costs eat into their pay
Newcomers flood in because the license is a badge of quality
Nothing changes because the customers set the wages
context: Morris Kleiner's empirical work has documented the wage premium and entry-barrier effect of state licensing across dozens of occupations and states. His work with Alan Krueger is widely cited. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Kleiner.

question: In some states you need a government license to braid hair, arrange flowers, or shampoo customers. Who usually pushes hardest for laws that require these licenses?
answer: Existing workers in the field who want fewer competitors
choices: Existing workers in the field who want fewer competitors
Consumers hoping to pay lower prices at every shop
Newcomers trying to enter the trade for the first time
The federal government looking for extra tax revenue
context: Louisiana licenses roughly 70 occupations including tour guide, florist, and hair braider. Wyoming and other Western states license far fewer. The variation is a natural experiment for the entry-barrier hypothesis. Source: Institute for Justice Occupational Licensing report.

question: The deep move in Olson's applied cases: whenever a policy attracts intense lobbying from one side and indifference from a much larger group on the other, expect the intense side to win. What is the standard shorthand name for this pattern?
answer: Concentrated benefits, dispersed costs
choices: Concentrated benefits, dispersed costs
Median-voter capture
Cantillon distortion
Adverse selection
context: 'Concentrated benefits, dispersed costs' is the standard shorthand for the Olson mechanism. It explains why farm subsidies, sugar tariffs, and occupational licensing all survive despite failing textbook welfare analysis. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action.

question: Olson's fix for a small group winning big while a large group each loses a little: move the choice to a level the small group cannot control. Which tools are the standard set?
answer: Constitutional-level rules, judicial review, sunset clauses
choices: Constitutional-level rules, judicial review, sunset clauses
Executive orders and administrative rulings
Tariff hikes and export subsidies
Referendums and initiative petitions
context: The remedies fit Buchanan's constitutional-political-economy tradition: move the decision from ordinary politics (where the sugar lobby wins) to constitutional-level rules or automatic sunset clauses that force periodic re-litigation with the dispersed group's attention gathered. Source: Buchanan + Wagner, Democracy in Deficit.

question: A law pays 500,000 farmers about $20,000 each per year. It costs each of 100 million taxpayers only about $100 per year. Farmers fight hard to keep the law; most taxpayers don't even notice. What is this pattern called?
answer: Concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
choices: Concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
The knowledge problem
The natural rate of output
Adverse selection in crop insurance
context: The AAA is the archetypal founding case: a relatively small farm sector concentrated benefits; 130 million taxpayers dispersed the costs. Olson would have written The Logic of Collective Action about this if the AAA had come 30 years later. Source: Olson (1965).

question: In June 2020, Argentina passed a national rent-control law. It was called Ley 27,551. What did the law mainly do?
answer: Set three-year minimum leases and indexed rent adjustments
choices: Set three-year minimum leases and indexed rent adjustments
Made rentals free of any regulation
Prohibited foreign ownership of Argentine property
Established a state rental agency
context: Ley 27.551 mandated three-year minimum leases and required annual rent adjustments only via a Central Bank formula tied to wages and inflation. It also imposed other tenant protections. Source: infoleg.gob.ar (Ley 27.551).

question: In 2020, Argentina passed a rent-control law. Within a year, Buenos Aires realtors saw a big change in how many long-term rentals were listed for rent. What happened to the number of new listings?
answer: It fell by roughly 40-50 percent
choices: It fell by roughly 40-50 percent
It rose by about 30 percent
It stayed almost exactly the same
It quadrupled
context: Buenos Aires realtor associations reported new-listing supply falling by 40-50% in the first year of the law. Rents on remaining listings rose sharply -- tripling or more in nominal terms by 2023. Source: CEMA Buenos Aires studies.

question: After Argentina's 2020 rent-control law, landlords pulled units out of the long-term rental market. Where did those units go instead?
answer: Airbnb, unfurnished monthly, or held empty
choices: Airbnb, unfurnished monthly, or held empty
State-owned public housing programs
Government seizures for social housing
New industrial warehousing

question: In 2023, Argentina elected a new president. He ran on cutting spending, ending price caps, and taming inflation. He also promised to scrap a strict rent-control law. What school of thought did he say he followed?

question: On December 29, 2023, Milei signed a huge early decree. It struck down Ley 27,551 along with many other rules. What is that kind of Argentine order called?

question: Within months of Argentina's late-2023 rent-control repeal, Buenos Aires saw a big shift in rental supply. What happened to new listings?

Supply stayed flat while rents doubled
Supply fell further and rents rose sharply
Supply doubled but rents rose faster than incomes

question: Argentina's rent-control cycle lasted about three and a half years. Caps were on from 2020 to 2023, then off from 2024. What plain lesson does the cycle show most clearly?

Interventions raise both supply and demand simultaneously

question: Most rent-control studies only cover the caps-on phase. Argentina's 2020-to-2024 story adds a rare second phase. What made this case such a clean test?

The ceiling was only partially applied

The country simultaneously changed currencies

question: Milei's December 2023 mega-decree was constitutionally challenged in Argentina's courts, but the specific rent-decontrol portion survived. What is the standing status of Ley 27.551 as of 2026?

Reinstated by the Supreme Court
Suspended pending review
Amended to add stronger tenant protections

question: A US president pressures the head of the central bank to keep money cheap so voters feel richer just before the election. What is the hidden cost of that choice?

question: President Nixon pushed the Fed chair to keep interest rates low. He was hoping to help his own timing on one big event. What was that event?

question: Fed chair Arthur Burns kept a private diary about Nixon's pressure. It came out in 2010, long after Burns had died. What is that book called?

question: In the 1970s the US Federal Reserve kept money cheap and easy, while an oil supply shock from Middle Eastern producers pushed fuel prices up. US consumer prices climbed year after year. By 1980, how high did yearly consumer-price inflation reach?

question: In the mid-1970s, both inflation and unemployment shot up at the same time. A leading Keynesian model said this could not happen. It claimed one always fell when the other rose. What is the model called?
answer: The Phillips curve

The Laffer curve
The Solow growth model
context: The Phillips curve, dating to A.W. Phillips's 1958 paper, held that inflation and unemployment traded off. The 1970s showed both could rise together -- 'stagflation' -- which the model could not explain. Source: Grokipedia 'Phillips curve' (2026-09-05).

question: A central bank tries to lower unemployment by printing more money and letting prices rise. It works at first. After a few rounds, workers start expecting the higher prices and demand pay raises to match. What happens to the trade-off?
answer: It breaks: unemployment goes back up, but inflation stays high too

question: Austrian economists like Mises and Rothbard argued that central banks had a built-in flaw. Burns's failure was not just bad luck under one bad president. What flaw did they see?
answer: Any institution empowered to expand credit will be captured by politicians who benefit from short-term stimulus regardless of long-term cost
choices: Any institution empowered to expand credit will be captured by politicians who benefit from short-term stimulus regardless of long-term cost

Any institution empowered to expand credit will refuse to lend during recessions
Any institution empowered to expand credit will always coordinate perfectly with fiscal policy
context: The Austrian point: Burns's tenure is the textbook case. An academically distinguished chairman with proper theoretical training nevertheless caved to a president's re-election needs, and destroyed the dollar's purchasing power over the following decade. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: A retired Federal Reserve chair once gave a famous speech. He said central bankers cannot easily fight inflation. What political pressure was he describing?

Newspapers refuse to print any story about the Fed at all

question: The 2020s parallel to Burns is often drawn by Austrian analysts as a warning about premature rate cuts. If the modern Fed cuts too early -- as Burns did after the first 1970 wave -- what specific 1980s outcome do they warn will recur?

A collapse of the Bretton Woods system in a redux form
An immediate return to gold-standard convertibility

The 2020s warning: if Powell repeats the Burns error, a Volcker-style rescue will be needed, at rates the current 120% debt-to-GDP ratio can barely tolerate. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: The Burns tenure teaches a specific recognition move about the political economy of central-bank appointments. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: An academically distinguished appointee with proper theoretical training can still cave to political pressure and produce the exact inflationary outcome his training warned against
choices: An academically distinguished appointee with proper theoretical training can still cave to political pressure and produce the exact inflationary outcome his training warned against

The problem is not the chair's training but the institutional structure that puts a single reappointable individual under presidential pressure at four-year intervals. Source: Grokipedia 'Arthur Burns' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2009 and 2010, when Bitcoin was new, everyone mined on the same kind of chip. Satoshi did, Hal Finney did, and any regular hobbyist could too. Which common chip did they all use during Bitcoin's first eighteen months?

A dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)

question: In 2010, miners discovered a trick. The chip inside a video-game graphics card could solve Bitcoin's puzzle roughly 50 to 100 times faster than the normal computer chip. Which kind of chip took over Bitcoin mining in 2010 and 2011?

question: Bitcoin mining moved from normal computer chips, to gaming graphics cards, then to reshaping chips, and finally to specialized chips built for just one job. Why did each new step outcompete the last one?
answer: Each step used less energy per calculation, so older miners could not cover their power bill

question: A new kind of computer chip is designed to do only one calculation — the exact math Bitcoin miners need — and nothing else. Compared to a general-purpose chip trying to do the same job, what is the trade-off?
answer: The single-purpose chip is far faster and cheaper per calculation, but useless for anything else
choices: The single-purpose chip is far faster and cheaper per calculation, but useless for anything else

The general-purpose chip is always faster at any specialized task
The two chips perform the same because the math is identical
context: The first Bitcoin ASICs shipped from Butterfly Labs and Avalon in early 2013. Because an ASIC's silicon is committed to one algorithm at fabrication, it cannot be repurposed if the algorithm is abandoned. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Application-specific_integrated_circuit.

question: In Bitcoin's first years, anyone with a home computer could mine coins. By 2015 hobbyists could not compete with a few big factories in China building special-purpose chips. What made home mining stop being profitable?

question: A special Bitcoin-mining chip can only compute one kind of puzzle. It cannot run video games, browse the web, or edit photos. Why does this actually help make Bitcoin more secure?

The chips are impossible for hackers to copy or steal

question: After the June 2021 China mining ban, the world's largest Bitcoin mining farms physically relocated. Which set of destinations absorbed most of the migrating hash power?

question: Modern economies have booms and busts. Growth roars for years, then suddenly crashes. In 1936, John Maynard Keynes blamed swings in mood, from hope to fear. The bust is the market discovering the truth. Keynes's animal-spirits account made the swing psychological; Austrians made it institutional and monetary. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: Ludwig von Mises first laid out what became the Austrian idea of booms and busts in a 1912 book. Friedrich Hayek then wrote two books that built on it, all while he was still in his twenties. In which two decades did the young Hayek publish those two books?

Prices and Production made him world-famous at 32 and launched the great 1930s debate against Keynes. He was 46 when The Road to Serfdom appeared in 1944 and 75 when he won the Nobel in 1974. Source: mises.org/library/book/monetary-theory-and-trade-cycle.

question: In the 1920s a few economists warned that keeping loans too cheap for too long would set off a boom that would crash badly. When the 1929 crash came, they were proven right. What is this line of thinking called?
answer: Austrian Business Cycle Theory
choices: Austrian Business Cycle Theory
Comparative advantage theory
Rational expectations theory
The efficient markets hypothesis
context: Hayek's Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle (1929) and Prices and Production (1931) developed the theory that predicted a major crash was coming; the 1974 Nobel citation reads as retroactive vindication. Comparative advantage is Ricardo 1817; rational expectations is Lucas and Muth 1960s-70s; efficient markets is Fama 1970 -- none of these are Hayek's. Source: iea.org.uk/hayek-and-the-nobel-prize-50-years-on/.

question: In 1929, Ludwig von Mises was offered a top job at Austria's biggest bank, the Kreditanstalt. He turned it down. context: Kreditanstalt collapsed in May 1931, its failure rippling through central European banking and deepening the Great Depression across the continent. Mises had read the ABCT tea leaves correctly. The Wall Street crash was October 1929; the US bank-holiday crisis was 1933; the second-dip Roosevelt Recession was 1937. Source: mises.org/online-book/skyscraper-curse-and-how-austrian-economists-predicted-every-major-economic-crisis-last-century/chapter-13-who-predicted-great-depression.

question: A developer sees very cheap 1% loans and starts a fifteen-year housing project. Others do the same in every long-term industry. Two years later, rates rise to 4% and many of those projects no longer make sense — some get abandoned mid-build. What do Austrian economists call projects like these?
answer: Malinvestments
choices: Malinvestments
Public goods
Positive externalities
Comparative advantages
context: MALINVESTMENT is the core ABCT concept -- resources committed to structures of production that cannot in fact be sustained. Not 'bad investment' in the ordinary sense but investment that would have been correct if the rate signal had been true; the misallocation is traceable to the rate distortion, not to entrepreneurial stupidity. Public goods, positive externalities, and comparative advantages are unrelated concepts from public finance, welfare economics, and trade theory. Source: mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/explaining-malinvestment-and-overinvestment.

question: The Federal Reserve under Alan Greenspan cut the federal funds rate from 6.5% in late 2000 down to 1.0% by mid-2003, and held it at 1% from June 2003 to June 2004. Which market did they identify?

US Treasury bonds
Grocery-store retail
Municipal utilities

Peter Schiff and other Austrian-influenced analysts made the housing-crash call publicly and repeatedly in 2005-2007; the crash arrived in 2007-2008. Treasuries respond to rate cuts in price but do not overbuild; groceries and utilities are short-horizon and rate-insensitive. Source: cato.org/publications/commentary/how-greenspan-bernanke-fed-created-bubbles.

question: Peter Schiff, an American investment adviser trained in Austrian economics by his father Irwin, spent 2005 through 2007 warning of a US housing crash on cable business shows, where the standard reaction was open laughter. The prediction landed exactly. Schiff's 2007 book Crash Proof extended the argument to the dollar and the wider economy. Source: wiki.mises.org/wiki/Austrian_predictions/Housing_bubble.

question: A book on the 1929 stock crash blamed one particular Federal Reserve action during the 1920s. The Federal Reserve pushed interest rates artificially low to help foreign banks. What does Austrian economics say cheap central-bank credit does to an economy?

Rothbard traced the boom to Strong's inflationary credit expansion and the 1929 collapse to its inevitable correction. Marriner Eccles chaired the Fed 1934-1948; Paul Warburg was a founding governor 1914-1918; William McChesney Martin chaired 1951-1970. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America%27s_Great_Depression.

question: A town builds too many empty office towers during a lending boom. When the boom ends, buyers won't touch them at boom-era prices. Austrian-school economists say: if the government now steps in and buys the empty towers at boom prices, what happens to the correction?
answer: The correction drags on, because bad projects are kept alive instead of cleared

The correction ends quickly and demand fully returns
Deflation is prevented and prices stay stable

context: The Austrian argument is that a bust is DIAGNOSTIC as well as painful: the projects that fail are the ones that never should have been started, and liquidating them frees capital and labour for uses that DO reflect real time preferences. Keynesian stimulus -- keeping demand up for the malinvested projects -- protects them from liquidation and stretches the correction. Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) presses this reading of the 1930s: Hoover's and Roosevelt's interventions prolonged the depression they were supposed to cure. Source: mises.org/online-book/skyscraper-curse-and-how-austrian-economists-predicted-every-major-economic-crisis-last-century/chapter-24-what-wrong-abct.

question: Austrian economists say that in a healthy market, interest rates would settle at a level where the amount people want to save equals the amount businesses want to borrow for real projects. What is the name for that reference rate?
answer: The natural rate of interest
choices: The natural rate of interest
The federal funds rate
The prime rate
The Wicksellian target rate
context: Mises and Hayek inherit the 'natural rate' concept from the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell (Interest and Prices, 1898): it is the interest rate at which voluntary saving and voluntary investment would balance in the absence of monetary distortion. When the central-bank rate is BELOW the natural rate, credit expands beyond real saving and malinvestment follows. The federal funds rate is the Fed's actual operating target; the prime rate is a commercial bank benchmark; 'Wicksellian target' is not a standard term. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: John Maynard Keynes wrote a famous 1936 book on the boom-bust cycle. He turned down the monetary story and instead pointed to a mental force at the wheel -- spontaneous urges to invest that swing between confidence and panic. Keynes gave those urges a memorable two-word name. Which name?

choices: Animal spirits
Bounded rationality

Adaptive expectations
context: Keynes: 'Most, probably, of our decisions to do something positive... can only be taken as a result of animal spirits -- of a spontaneous urge to action rather than inaction.' The clash is direct: Austrians say the cycle is a MONETARY event with a specific institutional cause and a specific remedy (stop suppressing the rate); Keynes says it is a PSYCHOLOGICAL event with no simple institutional cause and a specific remedy (stabilise demand). Bounded rationality is Herbert Simon 1955; rational and adaptive expectations are 1960s-70s macro developments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_spirits_(Keynes).

question: In 2000 Thomas Sowell, then 70 years old, published a book aimed at a working adult who had never taken an economics class. Basic Books put it out; by 2015 it had gone through five editions. What was the book called?

question: Sowell's Basic Economics uses real cases instead of math models. It draws on Ghana, US rent control, apartheid South Africa, Ireland, and post-Soviet Europe. How does the book group its chapters?

question: A famous 1932 definition says economics is the study of how people use scarce resources that could serve many different needs. What kind of decision does this force on every person, every day?

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics is often described as a broader version of an older short 1946 book -- Hazlitt in one afternoon, Sowell across a summer. What was the older short book?

question: Since its 2000 first edition, 'Basic Economics' has become the book most often recommended as the first serious economics reading for a high schooler or an adult new to the subject. What is one specific reason for that reach?

question: A country puts a big extra tax on wheat brought in from other countries. The country's own landlords, who own the wheat fields, love the tax. Who is hurt most by it?

Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington
Lord Palmerston and Lord John Russell
context: Cobden (1804-1865) and Bright (1811-1889) led the League from Manchester through seven years of relentless public campaigning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anti-Corn_Law_League.

question: In 1846 a British Prime Minister pushed through a repeal of the 'Corn Laws' — the tariffs on imported grain that kept bread expensive. It split his own party so badly that he had to resign four days later. What did his action show about tariffs?
answer: They can help a small group but hurt millions of ordinary buyers
choices: They can help a small group but hurt millions of ordinary buyers
They always help everyone in the country equally
They never split political parties
They automatically raise wages for workers
context: Peel's repeal of the Corn Laws on June 25, 1846 was the classic case study of a free-trade movement winning against a landed political interest. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Repeal_of_the_Corn_Laws.

question: In the 1840s Frederic Bastiat traveled to England. He watched a huge movement of ordinary people demand an end to grain tariffs so bread would be cheaper. Why did those poor families want the tariffs gone?
answer: The tariffs made bread more expensive than it needed to be
choices: The tariffs made bread more expensive than it needed to be
The tariffs made grain farmers richer worldwide
The tariffs raised wages for factory workers
The tariffs stopped foreign wars
context: The League's headquarters and organizational base was Manchester; Bastiat traveled there in 1845 specifically to study its methods. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: After his 1845 English trip Bastiat wrote a book introducing the League's campaign to French readers, published by Guillaumin in Paris the same year. What is the book's short title?
answer: Cobden et la Ligue
choices: Cobden et la Ligue
Sophismes economiques
Harmonies economiques
La Loi
context: Cobden et la Ligue, ou l'agitation anglaise pour la liberte des echanges (Guillaumin, 1845) translated the League's speeches and pamphlets for French audiences. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In 1846 a French writer, inspired by the British movement against grain tariffs, started his own free-trade league in a French port city. What was the main argument these free-trade leagues made?
answer: Tariffs help a few producers a lot but raise prices for everyone else, so most people are worse off
choices: Tariffs help a few producers a lot but raise prices for everyone else, so most people are worse off
Tariffs make everyone richer because they protect the whole country
Tariffs are free of any hidden costs because the government keeps the money
Tariffs speed up the invention of new machines
context: The French Free Trade Association (Association pour la liberte des echanges) was founded in Bordeaux in February 1846 and expanded to Paris and elsewhere later that year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In the 1840s a group of French writers started a newspaper devoted to arguing that tariffs hurt ordinary buyers. What is the main free-trade argument against a tariff on foreign shoes?
answer: Every family pays more for shoes so a few shoemakers can charge more
choices: Every family pays more for shoes so a few shoemakers can charge more
Tariffs create infinite jobs at no cost to anyone
Foreign shoemakers pay the tariff instead of local shoppers
Tariffs are always undone the next day by the mayor
context: Le Libre-Echange (November 1846 onward) was the movement's official periodical, edited by Bastiat during his most productive years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In the 1840s a group of English factory-city thinkers pushed hard for free trade and against tariffs. They were named after the industrial city they came from. What is their two-word name?
answer: The Manchester School
choices: The Manchester School
The Fabian School
The Chicago School
The Salamanca School
context: The Manchester School was the British counterpart to Bastiat's French free-trade tradition and gave English a shorthand for classical-liberal political economy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Manchester_School.

question: France's Second Republic ended slavery in its colonies. The order came from the new government in April of one year. What was the date of that order?
answer: April 27, 1848
choices: April 27, 1848
August 4, 1789
February 22, 1848
context: The abolition decree of April 27, 1848 covered Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana, and Reunion; it was the second and definitive French colonial abolition after Napoleon had reversed the first (1794) in 1802. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Abolition_of_slavery_in_France.

question: When a country ends slavery, workers become free to pick their own jobs and quit if they want. Compared to forced labor, what does free labor tend to be over time?
answer: More productive -- people work harder when they choose the work and keep the pay
choices: More productive -- people work harder when they choose the work and keep the pay
Exactly the same -- pay and freedom do not affect effort
Less productive -- nobody works without being forced
Impossible -- no country has ever tried it
context: Victor Schoelcher (1804-1893) drafted and championed the April 27, 1848 decree. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Victor_Schoelcher.

question: France had actually ended slavery once before, in 1794. But in 1802 one French leader brought it back. Who reversed that first end?
answer: Napoleon Bonaparte
choices: Napoleon Bonaparte
King Louis XVI
Robespierre
King Louis Philippe
context: Napoleon's 1802 reversal restored slavery in French colonies until Schoelcher's 1848 decree ended it definitively. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Abolition_of_slavery_in_France.

question: In April 1848, right after the February Revolution, France held new elections. Frederic Bastiat won a seat in the new assembly. Which French department elected him?
answer: Landes
choices: Landes
Paris
Bouches-du-Rhone
Nord
context: Bastiat represented Landes, his native southwestern department, in the Constituent Assembly from May 1848. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat used his usual seen-and-unseen method to argue against slavery. Which move did he press against those who defended the slave economy?
answer: The slave has no incentive to be productive and the master's character is corrupted
choices: The slave has no incentive to be productive and the master's character is corrupted
The abolitionist movement had no chance of political success
The Caribbean colonies were unprofitable regardless of the labor system
The moral case for slavery outweighed the economic case against it
context: Bastiat argued that the slave region SEES the free labor and its products but does not see the incentive-destroyed population, the strangled free-labor market, and the corrupted master class. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: The British Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 freed slaves in a way that stirred lasting debate. France later used a version of the same model. What choice did the British Act make?
answer: Compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves
choices: Compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves
Compensating the freed slaves directly for years of unpaid labor
Confiscating the plantations and redistributing them to the freed slaves
Requiring the freed slaves to purchase their freedom over 20 years
context: The 1833 British Act paid GBP 20 million in compensation to former slave owners; freed slaves received an 'apprenticeship' period rather than direct compensation. This became the framework for later 19th-century abolitions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833.

question: In Bastiat's 1850 pamphlet The Law he frames slavery as the maximal case of a specific concept he uses across the pamphlet. Which concept?
answer: Legal plunder
choices: Legal plunder
Natural monopoly
Diminishing returns
The margin of exploitation
context: The Law defines legal plunder as one person's labor or property being taken from them by legal force and given to another; slavery is its purest form. Source: bastiat.org/en/the_law.html.

question: An accuracy note: the slavery abolition decree came on April 27, 1848, but the new National Assembly did not first meet until May 4, 1848. So Bastiat's actual voting record on slavery had a particular shape. Which characterization is correct?
answer: He did not vote on the initial decree; he supported the abolition publicly and voted for its implementation
choices: He did not vote on the initial decree; he supported the abolition publicly and voted for its implementation
He voted against the abolition decree because he opposed the Provisional Government
He drafted the abolition decree in his role as under-secretary of the Navy
He was absent from the Assembly for the entire 1848-1850 session
context: Sequencing: Bastiat elected April 23, decree April 27, Assembly opens May 4. He supported the abolition, had a decades-long antislavery record in print, and voted for the implementation and compensation measures the Assembly took up. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The Austrians say only people, each with their own tastes, can decide what one thing is worth to them. So what does that mean about the 'true' price of a candy bar?
answer: There is no single true price -- it is worth different amounts to different kids
choices: There is no single true price -- it is worth different amounts to different kids
A government committee can calculate the true price exactly
The true price is always one dollar
The true price is written on every candy bar's atoms
context: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action: A Treatise on Economics was published by Yale University Press on September 14, 1949. Mises had left Vienna for the Graduate Institute in Geneva in 1934 and emigrated to New York City in 1940 after the Nazi occupation of Europe closed in. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: While living in Geneva, Ludwig von Mises wrote an early German version of what would become 'Human Action.' It came out in 1940. He spent most of the 1940s rewriting it, not just translating it, for readers in America. What was the 1940 German book called?
answer: Nationaloekonomie
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Die Gemeinwirtschaft
Kritik des Interventionismus
Grundprobleme der Nationaloekonomie
context: Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens was published in Geneva in 1940. When Henry Hazlitt urged an English translation, Mises insisted on rewriting for the American audience -- the result was Human Action (1949). The other three titles are real earlier Mises books but not the direct precursor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: In 1920 Ludwig von Mises wrote a famous paper. Under socialism, no one owns the factories or the land or the machines, so there are no real market prices for them. Then planners have no reliable way to tell which projects are worth doing. What is the missing tool that socialism removes?
answer: Real market prices that reveal what things actually cost
choices: Real market prices that reveal what things actually cost
The freedom to buy imported goods
The right to hold elections
The number of workers in each factory
context: The 1920 paper appeared in the Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, volume 47, and was translated by S. Adler as 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth,' reprinted in the 1935 volume Collectivist Economic Planning that Friedrich Hayek edited. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: In September 1945, Friedrich Hayek published a short essay in The American Economic Review. It became one of the most-cited papers in modern economics. Its main claim: no central planner can gather all the small pieces of local knowledge held in millions of heads. What was the title?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
The Pretence of Knowledge
The Constitution of Liberty
context: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the September 1945 American Economic Review as a rebuttal to Oskar Lange's proposal for 'market socialism.' It was reprinted in Hayek's 1948 essay collection Individualism and Economic Order. The other three titles are real Hayek works from different decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society.

question: A group of economists trained in the Austrian tradition argue that big economic downturns are usually not caused by markets themselves. They point to something else instead. What do they say is the main cause of these financial crashes?
answer: Central banks pushing interest rates below where savings and borrowing would naturally meet
choices: Central banks pushing interest rates below where savings and borrowing would naturally meet
Farmers refusing to grow enough food during good years
Consumers being naturally too selfish to keep the economy stable
Small shopkeepers charging prices that are too fair
context: Murray Rothbard (1926-1995) published Man, Economy, and State in 1962 at age 36. The three distractors are all real Mises students from the New York seminar of the 1950s. Rothbard's book was commissioned by the Volker Fund as an accessible companion to Human Action; it grew into a full-scale rival treatise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: In 1980 Basic Books published a book by Thomas Sowell. It took the central argument from Hayek's 1945 essay -- that useful knowledge is spread across many heads and cannot be centralized -- and expanded it with real-world examples for regular readers. Hayek himself endorsed the book. What was Sowell's title?
answer: Knowledge and Decisions
choices: Knowledge and Decisions
Basic Economics
A Conflict of Visions
The Vision of the Anointed
context: Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) is explicitly built on Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.' Hayek endorsed it as expanding admirably on his original concepts. The book won the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. The three distractors are all real later Sowell books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_and_Decisions.

question: In 1946 an American writer published a short book that boiled Bastiat's method down to one lesson about policy. What is that one lesson?
answer: Look at the effect of a policy on every group, not just the group it is meant to help
choices: Look at the effect of a policy on every group, not just the group it is meant to help
Every policy helps every group equally over time
Only the visible effects of a policy ever really matter
Government spending is always free money for the country
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is a chapter-by-chapter extension of Bastiat's seen/unseen method, with Hazlitt explicitly acknowledging the debt in his preface. Hazlitt was also the New York Times economics columnist who first urged Mises to write an English successor to Nationaloekonomie -- the project that became Human Action. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/broken-window.

question: In his 1954 book 'History of Economic Analysis,' published after his death, Joseph Schumpeter dismissed Frederic Bastiat in one famous line. That line shut down mainstream study of Bastiat for a whole generation. Which line did Schumpeter write?
answer: I do not hold that Bastiat was a bad theorist. I hold that he was no theorist.
choices: I do not hold that Bastiat was a bad theorist. I hold that he was no theorist.
Bastiat is the most dangerous socialist ever to have written in French.
Bastiat's Sophisms are the finest work of economics in the 19th century.
Bastiat and Marx must be read as complementary halves of a single vision.
context: Schumpeter's dismissal in History of Economic Analysis (published posthumously in 1954) discouraged academic economists from taking Bastiat seriously for decades. Rothbard's later Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (1995) was in part an explicit answer to Schumpeter, treating Bastiat as a genuine French classical-liberal theorist. Source: https://mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bastiats-legacy-economics.

question: In 1995, Edward Elgar published Murray Rothbard's two-volume history of economics after his death. In it, Rothbard answered Schumpeter's put-down by treating Bastiat as a real theorist, not just a pamphleteer. What was the book's title?
answer: An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought
choices: An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
The Panic of 1819
context: Rothbard's two-volume An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought was published posthumously by Edward Elgar in 1995 (Rothbard died in January 1995). The book devotes serious attention to Bastiat and the wider French classical-liberal tradition -- an implicit rebuke of Schumpeter's 1954 dismissal. The three distractors are all real earlier Rothbard books. Source: https://mises.org/library/book/austrian-perspective-history-economic-thought.

question: The line from Bastiat through Mises's Human Action to Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State is not just a genealogy of names -- each book teaches the same reasoning move applied more formally. Which move is that shared analytic backbone?
answer: That because human action is purposive, economic reasoning must trace the seen and unseen consequences of every choice
choices: That because human action is purposive, economic reasoning must trace the seen and unseen consequences of every choice
That empirical macro-econometrics is the only rigorous form of economic knowledge
That all economic laws must be established through controlled laboratory experiments
That government spending stimulates growth by expanding aggregate demand
context: Mises's praxeology -- reasoning from the axiom that human action is purposive -- is the formal core of Human Action, and it inherits Bastiat's plain-language habit of tracing consequences past the seen effect to the unseen. Rothbard rebuilds the same method in Man, Economy, and State (1962). The reader can accept or reject Austrian conclusions; the reasoning MOVE is the seen/unseen chain of consequences. Source: https://mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bastiats-legacy-economics.

question: In 1840, a young French printer's apprentice named Pierre-Joseph Proudhon wrote a book on money. He asked 'What is property?' His answer became a famous slogan. Which one?
answer: 'Property is theft'
choices: 'Property is theft'
'Property is liberty'
'Property is order'
'Property is labour'
context: Proudhon (1809-1865) meant the phrase strictly of ABSENTEE property that draws rent or interest without labour, not of a workman's tools -- a distinction later socialists frequently blurred. The 1840 book was Qu'est-ce que la propriete? (What is Property?). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Pierre-Joseph Proudhon'.

question: In January 1849, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon started a lending group in Paris. It aimed to lend to workers at zero interest, using notes traded for members' goods. About 3,600 people signed up and put in around 18,000 francs. Then Proudhon was jailed and the group was shut down. What was it called?
answer: The Bank of the People
choices: The Bank of the People
The Society of the Rights of Man
The National Workshops
The Society of the Seasons
context: Proudhon's Banque du peuple was the concrete institutional test of his mutualist idea that competing lenders could organise credit gratuit -- interest-free lending -- outside the state and outside profit. Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux (National Workshops) were a different 1848 scheme; the Society of the Rights of Man and the Society of the Seasons were older republican secret societies. Source: recma.org 'Proudhon et la Banque du Peuple'.

question: From late 1849 into early 1850, Frederic Bastiat and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon traded long public letters. They argued whether it was fair to charge interest on a loan. Almost every letter ran in the same Paris paper, Proudhon's own daily, edited from his prison cell. Name the paper.
answer: La Voix du Peuple
choices: La Voix du Peuple
Le National
La Presse
Le Constitutionnel
context: La Voix du Peuple ran from October 1849 into the summer of 1850 as Proudhon's third and last major daily; he continued editing it from Sainte-Pelagie prison. Publishing the exchange in his OWN paper meant Bastiat argued in front of Proudhon's readership. Source: praxeology.net 'The Bastiat-Proudhon Debate on Interest'.

question: Bastiat's central argument against interest-free lending was not that lenders deserved a reward or that borrowers were ungrateful. It was a claim about what price interest actually is. On his account, interest paid on a loan of 1,000 francs for a year is the price of exactly what?
answer: The lender's foregone use of the money for that year
choices: The lender's foregone use of the money for that year
The paperwork and risk of writing the loan
The borrower's expected profit from the loan
The scarcity of gold coin in the economy
context: A century before the Austrian school named it 'time preference', Bastiat had the argument's core: a lender is a person who does without his capital for a period; the interest compensates him for that period of doing without, not for any labour of lending. Paperwork, risk, and borrower profit are separate items. Source: praxeology.net Letter 2b.

question: Frederic Bastiat pressed on Pierre-Joseph Proudhon a consequence that Proudhon would not accept. If the law forced lenders to give credit at zero, Bastiat argued, borrowers would not get cheap loans at all. Something worse would happen. What?
answer: Savings would stop flowing into loans, and there would be nothing left to borrow
choices: Savings would stop flowing into loans, and there would be nothing left to borrow
Only the wealthy would still be able to borrow, at higher secret rates
The state would have to nationalise every bank at once
Prices of all consumer goods would fall by about the old interest rate
context: The disappearance-of-lenders argument runs: at zero interest, savers cease to LEND -- they hold cash or hoard specie instead -- so the volume of loanable funds collapses toward nothing. This is the same reasoning modern economists use against binding usury caps. Source: praxeology.net Letter 2b.

question: Proudhon insisted, against Bastiat, that ending interest would not need the state to force anyone. In his ideal society, a force inside the economy itself would drive the rate to zero. Which mechanism did he propose?
answer: Free competition among mutually organised lenders
choices: Free competition among mutually organised lenders
A single state monopoly bank issuing paper money
Public shaming of anyone charging any interest at all
A universal tax on capital equal to the interest rate
context: Proudhon insisted his scheme was not coercive: multiply the number of mutual banks, let them compete for borrowers, and the rate would fall organically to zero. Bastiat rejoined that competition could push the rate down only to the value of time-preference itself, and no further. Source: praxeology.net Letter 13.

question: In 1850 Frederic Bastiat gathered the whole exchange with Pierre-Joseph Proudhon into a single book, published in Paris by the Guillaumin house. He gave the volume a title that ironically named Proudhon's own slogan for the scheme -- one French noun and its qualifier. What title?
answer: Gratuite du credit
choices: Gratuite du credit
Interet et principal
Contradictions economiques
Solutions du probleme social
context: Gratuite du credit -- literally 'Free Credit' or 'The Gratuity of Credit' -- was Proudhon's own slogan for the interest-free-lending idea, and Bastiat used it as the book's ironic title. Proudhon in turn published a rival edition of the same letters under his own preferred title Interet et Principal. Source: worldcat.org record 4078594.

question: By convention the Bastiat-Proudhon exchange is described as fourteen letters, the count in Bastiat's Paris edition. In Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's own rival edition of the same debate the letter count is different. How different?
answer: Thirteen letters -- Proudhon dropped Bastiat's closing letter
choices: Thirteen letters -- Proudhon dropped Bastiat's closing letter
Twelve letters -- Proudhon dropped both the opening piece and Bastiat's last
Fifteen letters -- Proudhon added a summary letter of his own
Ten letters -- Proudhon printed only his own contributions
context: The opening letter of the exchange was by C.F. Cheve, a Proudhon disciple; then twelve letters ran between Bastiat and Proudhon in strict alternation. Bastiat added a closing fourteenth letter (Letter 14) which Proudhon refused to answer, and Proudhon's Interet et Principal simply omitted it. Source: praxeology.net 'The Bastiat-Proudhon Debate on Interest'.

question: Bastiat had told Proudhon in plain prose that interest is the price of time preference. That idea got its full formal statement in a multi-volume work called 'Kapital und Kapitalzins' (Capital and Interest). It came out in Innsbruck across the 1880s and 1890s. Which Austrian economist wrote it?
answer: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Carl Menger
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
context: Bohm-Bawerk's Kapital und Kapitalzins appeared in three parts between 1884 and 1889, with a second edition into the 1890s. He credited Bastiat as one of the nineteenth-century predecessors of the theory. Menger founded the Austrian school (1871) but did not write on interest at that length; Wieser worked on opportunity cost; Mises came a generation later. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Eugen Bohm von Bawerk'.

question: In 1949, the mature Austrian argument came back as the core chapter of a thousand-page English book. Its author saw time preference not as a quirk of capitalism, but as a basic feature of any person's choice between now and later. Which book?
answer: Human Action, by Ludwig von Mises
choices: Human Action, by Ludwig von Mises
The Road to Serfdom, by Friedrich Hayek
Man, Economy and State, by Murray Rothbard
The Theory of Money and Credit, by Ludwig von Mises
context: Human Action (Yale University Press, 1949) is Mises's systematic English treatise; its chapters on interest treat originary time-preference as an inescapable category of acting man. The Road to Serfdom (1944) was Hayek's political tract; Rothbard's Man, Economy and State came later (1962); Mises's Theorie des Geldes was much earlier (1912). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Ludwig von Mises'.

question: A big investment company borrows money from other banks every single night to keep running. One week the other banks all get scared and refuse to lend. What is likely to happen to the company by Friday?
answer: It collapses -- it cannot last a few days without the borrowed money
choices: It collapses -- it cannot last a few days without the borrowed money
Nothing -- companies do not really need to borrow
It grows twice as big overnight
It quietly turns into a farm
context: Bear Stearns, founded in 1923, was heavily exposed to subprime mortgages and mortgage-backed securities. Its two internal hedge funds collapsed in July-August 2007, previewing the firm's own collapse eight months later. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: A huge bank is about to collapse. Over one weekend, the government helps a healthier bank buy the whole company quickly. Why does the government step in to arrange the sale?
answer: To keep the collapse from spreading and scaring every other bank
choices: To keep the collapse from spreading and scaring every other bank
To collect all the pens from the bank's desks
Because the government already owns the bank
To lower the price of coffee at the bank
context: JPMorgan Chase, led by Jamie Dimon, was the buyer. The Fed's involvement made the sale possible on a compressed timeline. Source: Grokipedia 'JPMorgan Chase acquisition of Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: Over the March 2008 weekend, JPMorgan Chase agreed to buy the collapsing investment bank Bear Stearns. The first announced price per share was famously low. What was that first price, before shareholder lawsuits forced a bump?
answer: Two dollars
choices: Two dollars
Ten dollars
Fifty cents
Twenty dollars
context: The initial Sunday-night announcement was $2 per share. Bear shareholders threatened lawsuits over the price; JPMorgan raised it to $10 the following week. The stock had traded at $172 fourteen months earlier -- a 99% loss for shareholders in a single weekend. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2008 the US Federal Reserve helped one bank buy a collapsing rival by taking the worst bad loans off the failing bank's books first. Who ended up owning those bad loans in the end?
answer: The Federal Reserve, and through it US taxpayers
choices: The Federal Reserve, and through it US taxpayers
The failing bank's original shareholders
The buyer paid full price for them
Foreign central banks
context: Maiden Lane LLC, named after the New York Fed's address, held $30 billion of Bear's worst mortgage-backed securities. The Fed took the assets off JPMorgan's books via a non-recourse loan. Source: Grokipedia 'Maiden Lane Transactions' (2026-09-05).

question: The March 2008 rescue set an important precedent about how failing investment banks would be handled. Shareholders and executives would suffer losses, but one specific group would be made whole. Who did the Fed rescue protect at 100 cents on the dollar?
answer: Creditors and counterparties whose panic had caused the run
choices: Creditors and counterparties whose panic had caused the run
Junior employees at the collapsing firm
Retail brokerage clients
Municipal pension funds holding the stock
context: The Bear precedent: shareholders got wiped out but creditors and counterparties were paid in full. This was designed to prevent a broader panic but also trained the market to expect similar rescues in future crises. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: When one bailout makes people expect more bailouts later, market discipline weakens and future risk-taking grows. Economists have a name for this. What is it called?
answer: Moral hazard
choices: Moral hazard
Adverse selection
Ricardian equivalence
Regulatory capture
context: Moral hazard is the classic problem where insurance against a loss weakens the incentive to avoid it. Applied to bank rescues: if creditors expect government to make them whole, they discipline banks less carefully. Source: Grokipedia 'Moral hazard' (2026-09-05).

question: The Bear rescue shaped what people expected in September 2008, when another big investment bank, Lehman Brothers, was also collapsing. What did Lehman's creditors and trading partners expect the Fed to do?
answer: Broker a similar rescue so Lehman's creditors would also be paid in full
choices: Broker a similar rescue so Lehman's creditors would also be paid in full
Let Lehman fail immediately to punish executive risk-taking
Nationalize Lehman directly under a special Treasury charter
Merge Lehman with Bank of America without Fed involvement
context: Markets had priced in the Bear precedent. When Lehman was allowed to fail on September 15 2008, the counterparty network priced in exactly the outcome the Bear rescue had trained them not to expect. The moral-hazard trap sprung the other way. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Critics from both left and right warned in real time that the Bear rescue would encourage more risk-taking, not less. Which two figures made this argument publicly in early 2008?
answer: Nouriel Roubini on the left; Peter Schiff on the right
choices: Nouriel Roubini on the left; Peter Schiff on the right
Paul Krugman on the left; Larry Kudlow on the right
Alan Blinder on the left; Milton Friedman on the right
Joseph Stiglitz on the left; John Taylor on the right
context: Roubini (NYU) and Schiff (Euro Pacific Capital) both publicly warned in spring 2008 that the Bear rescue was setting up worse crises. Both were widely dismissed at the time and vindicated within six months. Source: Grokipedia 'Nouriel Roubini' (2026-09-05).

question: The Bear rescue is now a textbook case in the specific reasoning the Austrian tradition makes about repeat central-bank interventions. Which recognition move does the ladder press?
answer: Each rescue changes the expectations for the next crisis; the sudden removal of an expected rescue can cause the panic the earlier rescue was meant to prevent
choices: Each rescue changes the expectations for the next crisis; the sudden removal of an expected rescue can cause the panic the earlier rescue was meant to prevent
Rescues always work as intended and stabilize markets permanently
Rescues fail only when the Fed misprices the collateral for its loan
Rescues encourage moral hazard only when they involve foreign banks
context: The Bear rescue trained markets to expect the Lehman rescue; the September 15 Lehman failure violated that trained expectation. The Fed's discretionary rescue policy is not neutral -- each intervention writes the script for the next crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: When a big investment bank ran into trouble in 2007, its chairman was reportedly playing a card-game tournament instead of managing the crisis. What lesson do critics draw from stories like this about huge failing firms?
answer: Top leaders can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own firm
choices: Top leaders can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own firm
Card games improve executive decision-making under stress
Big banks always have perfect information about their own risk
Employees will always cover for a distracted boss
context: Jimmy Cayne, then Bear's chairman, was playing at a bridge tournament while the July 2007 collapse of Bear's internal hedge funds unfolded. The anecdote became emblematic of Wall Street executive detachment during the run-up to the crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'James Cayne' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1914 the United States started a central bank called the Federal Reserve. Its main power is to change how much money is in the country. If it prints a lot of new money, what usually happens to prices?
answer: Prices go up -- more money chasing the same goods
choices: Prices go up -- more money chasing the same goods
Prices stay exactly the same forever
Prices fall to zero
Prices change to a different color
context: Strong had been at the 1910 Jekyll Island meeting as president of Bankers Trust. He led the New York Fed from 1914 until his death in 1928. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: From 1914 until he died in 1928, Strong pioneered a Fed policy tool. With it, the Fed buys Treasury bonds to add reserves to the banking system. What is this tool called?
answer: Open market operations
choices: Open market operations
Reserve requirements
The discount window
Quantitative easing
context: Open market operations became the Fed's most important standing tool. Strong built the New York Fed's Open Market Committee into the operational center of American monetary policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Open market operation' (2026-09-05).

question: Benjamin Strong ran the New York Fed. He became close friends with the man who ran the Bank of England from 1920 to 1944. Their friendship shaped world money policy in the 1920s. Who was the Bank of England chief?
answer: Montagu Norman
choices: Montagu Norman
John Maynard Keynes
Winston Churchill
Hjalmar Schacht
context: Montagu Norman led the Bank of England for 24 years -- one of the longest tenures at any major central bank. His friendship with Strong shaped 1920s international monetary coordination. Source: Grokipedia 'Montagu Norman' (2026-09-05).

question: Britain returned to the gold standard in 1925 at a specific price for the pound sterling. That price made the currency overvalued and caused painful deflation. At what prewar rate did Britain return?
answer: The 1914 prewar parity of about $4.86 per pound
choices: The 1914 prewar parity of about $4.86 per pound
A 20% devaluation from prewar levels
A 10% appreciation above prewar levels
A floating market rate with no fixed peg
context: Britain's 1925 return to gold at the prewar parity, on Chancellor Churchill's decision, was economically painful. Strong agreed to help by keeping US rates low so gold would not flow from London to New York. Source: Grokipedia 'Return to gold' (2026-09-05).

question: In July 1927 Strong hosted a secret meeting on Long Island with three foreign central bankers. Days later the Fed cut its discount rate from 4% to 3.5%. Which three foreign central bankers attended?
answer: Montagu Norman of Britain, Emile Moreau of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany
choices: Montagu Norman of Britain, Emile Moreau of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany
John Maynard Keynes of Britain, Rene Coty of France, and Konrad Adenauer of Germany
Winston Churchill of Britain, Georges Clemenceau of France, and Otto von Bismarck of Germany
Nicholas Biddle of Britain, Charles de Gaulle of France, and Otto von Habsburg of Germany
context: The July 1927 Long Island meeting brought together the heads of the four leading Western central banks. It produced the rate cut that Austrian economists later blamed for the final phase of the 1920s boom. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: Strong reportedly described his July 1927 interest-rate cut in private using a distinctive alcoholic metaphor. It was about the stock market. Which phrase did he use?
answer: A little coup de whiskey to the stock market
choices: A little coup de whiskey to the stock market
A friendly nudge to the bond market
A helping shot for the London Fund
A quiet toast to European stability
