context: 'Unmasking' (razoblachenie) redefined kulak-status as anyone who resisted collectivization. The label became a catch-all administrative tool for eliminating opposition. Source: Fitzpatrick, Stalin's Peasants (1994).

question: The Soviet Union declared millions of hard-working farmers to be enemies of the state just because they owned a little land, some tools, or a cow. Whole families were shipped to distant camps. What was the government really trying to do?
answer: Force farmers off their land so the state could seize and run all farms
choices: Force farmers off their land so the state could seize and run all farms
Reward the most successful farmers with better land
Make sure every family had exactly the same size of farm
Move farmers closer to cities so they could work in factories
context: Lynne Viola's The Unknown Gulag (Oxford, 2007) uses newly opened OGPU archives to reconstruct the settlement system for deported peasants. Fitzpatrick, Conquest, and Applebaum work on adjacent Soviet-terror topics. Source: global.oup.com.

question: Dekulakization pulled the best farmers out of the villages first. That set up a huge 1932-33 disaster. What was the disaster?
answer: The Holodomor famine in Ukraine
choices: The Holodomor famine in Ukraine
The Great Terror purges
The 1937 nationalities operations
The Siege of Leningrad
context: With the most productive farmers gone, forced grain requisitions in 1932-33 stripped Ukrainian villages of their remaining food. The resulting famine killed several million Ukrainians. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: The Bastiat-style seen-versus-unseen reading of dekulakization: the visible move was 'expropriating rich peasants for social justice'. What was the unseen cost the villages bore in the following years?
answer: The permanent loss of agricultural competence and the famine that followed
choices: The permanent loss of agricultural competence and the famine that followed
A shortage of Party recruitment
An inflation in the price of textiles
A drop in industrial productivity in Moscow
context: The Bastiat move: the SEEN was 'redistributing kulak property'; the UNSEEN was the collapse of village agricultural knowledge (which farmer knew which fields, which seed variety, which threshing techniques) and the famine that used the resulting vulnerability. Source: mises.org/library/theft-of-a-nation-holodomor.

question: One economist wrote a small book with this idea. The government should not be the only one allowed to make money. Private banks and firms could issue their own money and compete for customers. What is this idea called?
answer: Currency competition
choices: Currency competition
Total price control
One-world central bank
Bartering only
context: Hayek (1899-1992) had won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics two years earlier, in 1974, sharing it with Gunnar Myrdal. The 1976 pamphlet was the most radical monetary proposal of his career. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: In 1976 Friedrich Hayek put out a short book on money in London. It came from a think tank Antony Fisher started on Hayek's own advice. Which think tank was it?
answer: The Institute of Economic Affairs
choices: The Institute of Economic Affairs
The Cato Institute
The Adam Smith Institute
The Mont Pelerin Society
context: The IEA, founded 1955, is Britain's oldest classical-liberal think tank; Hayek personally counselled Antony Fisher to start it after Fisher read The Road to Serfdom. The Cato Institute (1977) and Adam Smith Institute (1977) did not yet exist. The Mont Pelerin Society is a scholarly society, not a publisher. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet made a single bold monetary proposal. What did he propose that governments do?
answer: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
choices: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
Return to a fixed exchange rate anchored on a single ounce of gold
Adopt a common global reserve currency issued by the International Monetary Fund
Delegate all monetary policy to an independent panel of academic economists
context: Hayek argued money is no different from any other good: competition between private issuers, checked by consumer choice, would supply it better than a state monopoly. The proposal was radical enough that even fellow Austrian economists mostly rejected it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet carried a full title naming the historical practice it studied. Which full title did it carry?
answer: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies
choices: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies
The Constitution of Liberty: A Restatement of the Principles of a Free Society
The Fatal Conceit: A Study of the Errors of Socialism from Marx to the Present
Prices and Production: Four Lectures Delivered at the University of London
context: 'Concurrent currencies' referred to the historical episodes, such as pre-Civil-War American free banking or private banknote issuance in nineteenth-century Scotland, in which several currencies circulated together. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet rested on a claim about the historical record of every paper currency ever issued by a government monopoly. He said the record showed a clear pattern. What was it?
answer: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
choices: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
Every such currency has appreciated against gold across the twentieth century
Every such currency has stabilized once its central bank became independent
Every such currency has held value so long as its government retained a fiscal surplus
context: Hayek's examples ran from the Roman denarius under Diocletian to the Weimar mark of 1923 to modern post-war fiat currencies. His conclusion was that debasement is not a scandal but the predictable equilibrium of a monopoly issuer facing short-run political incentives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet answered the natural objection 'but how would competing private currencies stay honest?' with a specific mechanism. Which discipline did he say would keep them honest?
answer: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
choices: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
Government auditors inspecting each issuer's reserve ratios annually
International treaty obligations enforced through the World Bank
A gold-parity peg required by domestic constitutional law
context: Hayek's mechanism was identical to the market discipline any producer faces. Issuers whose currency lost purchasing power would see it refused in commerce, lose deposits, and fail; issuers who kept it stable would win business. No government auditor, treaty, or peg was needed. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/hayeks-plan-private-money.

question: An Austrian-tradition economist wrote a book saying governments should not be the only ones allowed to print money. Instead, private banks and companies could each issue their own currencies, and people could freely choose the best one. What outcome did he predict from that competition?
answer: Only currencies that held their value would survive, and inflation would fall
choices: Only currencies that held their value would survive, and inflation would fall
Prices would swing wildly and no trade could happen
One company would seize control and print even more money than governments
Every currency would collapse within a year
context: In the second edition Hayek added the speculation that a free monetary market would not sustain an unmanageable number of currencies but would converge on a limited number of stable standards. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: In 1976 Hayek said private paper money should be allowed to compete. Even his fellow Austrian Murray Rothbard said no to that. Rothbard wanted one more rule for any free-market money. What did he require?
answer: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
choices: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
That the currency circulate only within a single sovereign jurisdiction
That the currency be issued exclusively by chartered depository institutions
That the currency be redeemable at par into government-issued specie
context: Rothbard remained a strict commodity-money advocate: free banking, yes, but the notes had to be redeemable claims on a real commodity such as gold. On this account Hayek's proposal for competing PAPER currencies with no commodity backing was more radical than Rothbard would go. Source: cameronharwick.com/writing/hayek-vs-rothbard-on-money.

question: A student asks: why should we let different companies compete to supply money, when the government does it now? An Austrian economist answers: for the same reason we let companies compete to supply bread and phones. Why?
answer: Competition gives customers choice and pushes suppliers to serve them better
choices: Competition gives customers choice and pushes suppliers to serve them better
Money is a natural monopoly that only one issuer can supply well
Only a central authority can measure the right amount of money
Bread and phones follow completely different economic laws
context: The Austrian methodological move: reject the special-pleading claim that money is uniquely unsuited to markets. Hayek argued the same competitive discipline that improves other goods would improve currency; the burden falls on defenders of the state monopoly to say why money is the exception. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Bitcoin backers like Saifedean Ammous point to Hayek's 1976 book as the grandfather of their project. Which engineering trick did Bitcoin use that Hayek could not have used in 1976?
answer: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
choices: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
A gold-parity peg administered by an international clearinghouse
A one-to-one deposit-insurance guarantee from a sovereign issuer
A statutory reserve requirement enforced by domestic banking regulators
context: Hayek imagined competing private BANKS disciplined by consumer refusal to hold debased notes; Bitcoin, launched thirty-three years later by Satoshi Nakamoto, hard-codes the discipline into the protocol itself with a 21-million-coin cap and a halving schedule no operator can override. Ammous's 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard makes the intellectual-descent argument explicit; the European Central Bank has publicly noted the same theoretical lineage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: In December 1978 China's Communist Party turned away from Mao's strict command system and toward markets with real prices. The program has a two-word English name. What is it usually called?
answer: Reform and Opening
choices: Reform and Opening
The Great Leap
The Four Modernizations
The Cultural Revolution
context: Gaige kaifang -- Reform and Opening -- was launched at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee, December 18-22, 1978, under Deng Xiaoping. It ended pure central planning first in agriculture, then in industry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform.

question: After 1978, a new Chinese leader made big changes. Farmers could keep part of their crop. Some private shops could open. Foreign companies could build factories. Compared to Mao's old rules, was this more central-planning or more market?
answer: More market
choices: More market
More central-planning
Exactly the same
Neither -- it banned all trade
context: Deng Xiaoping had been purged in 1966 and again in 1976. He returned to power in 1977 and by December 1978 had consolidated his faction's control. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: In the late 1970s, China changed a big rule. Before, the village took all the crops. Now each family could keep and sell anything extra they grew. What happened to how hard the farmers worked?
answer: They worked much harder because they now got to keep the extra
choices: They worked much harder because they now got to keep the extra
They worked less because the pressure was off
It made no difference to their work
They stopped growing food and moved to cities
context: The Household Responsibility System (baochan daohu) tested in Anhui in late 1978 (informally in Xiaogang village) then rolled out nationally by 1982-83. Households farmed their own plots and sold surplus at market. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household-responsibility_system.

question: In 1978 a group of Chinese peasants secretly signed a contract dividing their village's collective farmland into private family plots. They knew they could be arrested. Why did they take the risk?
answer: So each family would be rewarded for the food it grew, not just the village as a whole
choices: So each family would be rewarded for the food it grew, not just the village as a whole
To donate more grain to the state warehouse
To please the Communist Party leaders in Beijing
To attract tourists to their village
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang village, Fengyang County, Anhui signed a secret agreement in December 1978 to divide land plots, pledging to raise each other's children if any were arrested. Local officials tolerated the pact after harvest yields rose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: The return of market prices to Chinese agriculture in the late 1970s brought a startling result. Roughly what happened to grain output between 1978 and 1984?
answer: It rose about 34 percent
choices: It rose about 34 percent
It fell by about half
It stayed roughly flat
It quadrupled
context: Chinese grain output rose about 34% from 1978 to 1984 on essentially the same land and labor -- once farmers again had market price signals to guide planting and keep the surplus. The famine memory of 1959-61 (36 million dead) was over within five years. Source: World Bank data.

question: The industrial reforms of the 1980s created zones for foreign investment with market pricing rules. The first four opened at coastal locations in 1980. What are these zones called?
answer: Special Economic Zones
choices: Special Economic Zones
Free Trade Territories
Foreign Investment Bureaus
Coastal Enterprise Parks
context: The first four SEZs were Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, and Xiamen (1980); Hainan Island became a fifth SEZ in 1988. Shenzhen grew from a fishing village of 30,000 to a metropolis of over 17 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China.

question: During the 1980s Chinese reforms operated a hybrid arrangement. State-planned quotas kept old prices for required output, while any output above the plan could be sold at market rates. What is this scheme called?
answer: Dual-track pricing
choices: Dual-track pricing
Ratchet planning
Convertible planning
Ratcheted quotas
context: Dual-track pricing (shuang gui zhi) let firms sell state quotas at planned prices and any additional output at market prices. This let market signals reach production margins without a shock discontinuation of the plan. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual-track_pricing.

question: Deng defended his reforms with a famous animal saying. The point was that the method did not matter as long as the method worked. What was the heart of his 'cat' saying?
answer: It does not matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
choices: It does not matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
The best cat sleeps by day and hunts by night
One cat is not enough for a granary of rats
Feed the cat with rice and it will forget the mice
context: Deng's black-cat-white-cat saying, from a 1961 speech he revived in the reform era, meant that empirical results should outweigh ideological purity. It became the shorthand slogan of Reform and Opening. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: Deng also gave the reform a caution about incremental method, using a river metaphor. It meant that policy should proceed by testing what actually works rather than by following a grand theoretical design. What is the phrase?
answer: Crossing the river by feeling the stones
choices: Crossing the river by feeling the stones
Climbing a mountain step by step
Planting a forest one seed at a time
Building a wall from small bricks
context: 'Mo zhe shi tou guo he' -- crossing the river by feeling the stones -- became a rule for the whole reform: experiment locally, adopt what works, avoid theoretical grand plans. Xiaogang, then Anhui, then nationally. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform.

question: For a Mises-Hayek reading, Reform and Opening was the largest natural experiment the socialist calculation debate ever received. The World Bank measured how many Chinese were lifted out of extreme poverty between 1981 and 2015. What is that standard number?
answer: About 800 million
choices: About 800 million
About 80 million
About 8 billion
About 250 million
context: World Bank data show roughly 800 million Chinese moved above the extreme-poverty line between 1981 and 2015 as market pricing extended sector by sector. This is the largest sustained poverty reduction ever measured. Source: worldbank.org China country data.

question: After 1978, China let families farm their own plots again and set up special zones where private businesses could operate. Those zones grew fastest. Which parts of the Chinese economy grew slowest during the same years?
answer: The state-owned banks and factories that planners kept controlling
choices: The state-owned banks and factories that planners kept controlling
The private township workshops
The rural family farms
The coastal export factories
context: Chinese state-owned banks and SOEs continued to underperform the private and township-enterprise sectors through the 1990s and 2000s. The Austrian reading of Chinese growth attributes it to the market-priced sectors, not to state industrial policy. Source: mises.org/library/china-and-austrian-school.

question: Bitcoin adds a new block about every ten minutes. Some blocks come in a minute, some take thirty, but the long-run average stays fixed. What keeps that average steady when more miners join or leave?
answer: The difficulty adjustment
choices: The difficulty adjustment
The halving schedule
The proof-of-stake vote
The Federal Reserve's discount rate
context: Every node in the Bitcoin network computes the difficulty target identically from the timestamps of recent blocks. It is Bitcoin's homeostatic clock. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment runs on a fixed schedule: every N blocks, every node checks how long those N blocks took and turns the difficulty up or down. What is N?
answer: 2,016 blocks
choices: 2,016 blocks
1,000 blocks
10,080 blocks
210,000 blocks
context: 2,016 blocks equals two weeks at exactly ten minutes per block. The 210,000-block figure is the halving interval (roughly four years), a separate protocol constant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: If the last 2,016 Bitcoin blocks arrived faster than the target two weeks, the network automatically responds at the next retarget. What does it do?
answer: Increases difficulty so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros
choices: Increases difficulty so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros
Rewards existing miners with a one-time bonus in newly minted coin
Reduces the block-reward payout for the next 2,016 blocks
Sends a policy signal to the Federal Reserve to raise rates
context: The target hash gets a smaller numerical value, making valid hashes rarer. Miners then take longer per block on average, restoring the ten-minute cadence. If blocks had been slow, the adjustment goes the other way. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: In May and June 2021 China's central government banned Bitcoin mining, and roughly half of the world's mining power went offline within weeks. Blocks began arriving noticeably slower than every ten minutes. What did Bitcoin do next, without any human decision-maker?
answer: At the July 3 2021 retarget, difficulty dropped by roughly 28 percent -- the largest downward adjustment in Bitcoin's history
choices: At the July 3 2021 retarget, difficulty dropped by roughly 28 percent -- the largest downward adjustment in Bitcoin's history
The remaining miners voted to switch the algorithm to proof-of-stake
The Bitcoin Core developers issued an emergency patch changing the block interval
Coinbase paused all Bitcoin trading until the network recovered
context: Every node computed the adjustment independently and identically. Blocks returned to a ten-minute cadence immediately after the retarget. Chinese miners then physically relocated to Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland, and Paraguay. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_China.

question: A high-school student asks how the Bitcoin network kept its ten-minute cadence in July 2021 when half the world's miners had just been forced offline. A Hayekian economist points to a specific systems property that no central bank possesses. Which property?
answer: The homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that requires no human decision-maker
choices: The homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that requires no human decision-maker
The discretionary override of a benevolent central authority
The one-off emergency bailout mechanism triggered by a supervisory committee
The centrally-planned reallocation of hashing capacity by a global regulator
context: Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem argument is exactly this: no central agency could set the correct difficulty target in real time across a global mining industry it did not know intimately. A rule-based system aggregates the dispersed information automatically. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: After China's mining ban in mid-2021, Bitcoin's mining difficulty dropped sharply. By March 2022, about nine months later, what had the network's total mining power done?
answer: Recovered to a new all-time high
choices: Recovered to a new all-time high
Remained roughly half of pre-ban levels
Fallen further as miners quit permanently
Migrated entirely to a single US state
context: Displaced Chinese miners physically shipped their hardware to Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland, and Paraguay. The rule-based difficulty adjustment absorbed a 50-percent supply shock in weeks and then handled the recovery just as automatically. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: In 301 AD a Roman emperor made a rule capping the price of over 1,000 goods, with the DEATH PENALTY for sellers who charged more. Sellers hid their goods or stopped making them. What did shoppers find in the markets?
answer: Empty shelves and shortages
choices: Empty shelves and shortages
Cheaper goods for everyone
More goods than ever before
Nothing changed at all
context: Diocletian's Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium (Edict on Maximum Prices) is the earliest documented major price-control experiment. Fragments survive on stone in over 100 places across the eastern empire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: Diocletian issued a price edict in 301 AD that set a ceiling on what goods could cost. The penalty for selling above the ceiling was the harshest imaginable. What was it?
answer: Death
choices: Death
Exile
Slavery
A fine of ten denarii
context: The edict's own text prescribed death for sellers exceeding the fixed prices. Enforcement was uneven but the threat was real; the historian Lactantius records that 'much blood was shed for the sake of small and cheap things'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: For years, Rome had put less and less silver in its coins to pay the army. Prices kept rising. In his 301 edict, whom did Diocletian blame for the rising prices?
answer: The merchants for their 'unbridled fury' and 'greed'
choices: The merchants for their 'unbridled fury' and 'greed'
The Sassanid Persians for currency counterfeiting
The African provinces for hoarding grain
The Christian communities for boycotting Roman markets
context: The edict's preamble cursed sellers rather than acknowledging that the emperor's own mint had cheapened the coin. This is the emblematic 'blame the messenger' move in the history of price controls. Source: primary text of the Edict of Diocletian.

question: Within weeks of Diocletian's edict, one thing happened all over the empire. What was the quick effect on shop shelves?
answer: Goods disappeared from the open market
choices: Goods disappeared from the open market
Prices dropped further than mandated
Merchants opened new shops
Public revenue rose sharply
context: Sellers withdrew goods rather than sell at a loss. Merchants preferred to hoard, sell only to family, or move goods to black markets in other cities. The visible-shelf empty is the seen-versus-unseen result. Source: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors.

question: A Christian writer named Lactantius wrote about the edict's failure in his book 'On the Deaths of the Persecutors.' Roughly how long after Diocletian's edict was it quietly dropped?
answer: About a decade
choices: About a decade
About a century
About a year
About a millennium
context: The edict was allowed to fall into disuse within roughly a decade. Diocletian himself abdicated in 305 AD -- the only Roman emperor to voluntarily step down. Source: Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum c. 315 AD.

question: The Bastiat-style seen-versus-unseen reading of Diocletian's edict: SEEN was the low legal price stamped on the tablet. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The seller who would rather hoard than sell at a loss, and the buyer who now goes hungry
choices: The seller who would rather hoard than sell at a loss, and the buyer who now goes hungry
The tax revenue that continued to flow
The Roman legions that continued to be paid
The Byzantine trade that continued to flow
context: Bastiat's method applied 15 centuries earlier: the visible ceiling gives the illusion of low prices; the invisible cost is the goods that disappear because their sale at the ceiling would be at a loss. Source: bastiat.org.

question: Fragments of Diocletian's price edict still survive today. They are found on stone inscriptions scattered across the eastern Mediterranean. Where is the most complete surviving copy located?
answer: Aphrodisias in Turkey
choices: Aphrodisias in Turkey
Delphi in Greece
Palmyra in Syria
Ravenna in Italy
context: Aphrodisias, in southwestern Turkey, has the fullest surviving copy of the edict inscribed on stone. Archaeologists reconstructed hundreds of specific price lines from the fragments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisias.

question: Modern Austrian economists like Rothbard and Sowell treat Diocletian's edict as the founding case of one recurring reasoning error. What is that error?
answer: Blame merchants for the price rises the government's own currency debasement caused
choices: Blame merchants for the price rises the government's own currency debasement caused
Assume that lowering prices raises supply
Believe that inflation is always transitory
Ignore secondary market effects entirely
context: The archetypal pattern: currency debasement raises prices; the state blames sellers; a ceiling is imposed; goods disappear; the ceiling is eventually withdrawn. This pattern recurs from 301 AD through modern hyperinflations. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: A Roman emperor around 300 AD tried to stop rising prices by ordering that no merchant could sell above a set price, with the death penalty for those who did. What was the actual result?
answer: Goods vanished from the markets and shortages spread
choices: Goods vanished from the markets and shortages spread
Prices fell and stayed stable for centuries
Merchants happily obeyed and made steady profits
Wages rose but food prices stayed low
context: Diocletian's Palace at Split (modern Croatia) has been continuously inhabited since 305 AD -- housing today's Old Town within its walls. UNESCO World Heritage site. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian%27s_Palace.

question: After the 2008 crash, Congress passed a huge new law with lots of new rules for banks. What is the word for rules a government sets to tell banks and companies what they can and cannot do?
answer: Regulation
choices: Regulation
Deregulation
Privatization
Deflation
context: Formally the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Pub. L. 111-203), named for Senate Banking chair Chris Dodd and House Financial Services chair Barney Frank. It ran over 800 pages and delegated hundreds of rulemakings to regulators. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Dodd-Frank_Wall_Street_Reform_and_Consumer_Protection_Act.

question: The 2010 Dodd-Frank Act made a new agency. Its job was to watch over the loans families use most: home loans, credit cards, and payday loans. What kind of agency is it best called?
answer: A consumer financial protection agency
choices: A consumer financial protection agency
A bank-charter licensing agency
A housing-finance regulator
A public-company accounting overseer
context: The CFPB was the signature institutional creation of Dodd-Frank, championed by then-Harvard-professor Elizabeth Warren. It absorbed consumer-protection authority previously spread across the Fed, OCC, FDIC and other agencies. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Consumer_Financial_Protection_Bureau.

question: After the 2008 crisis, a new rule was passed, named after a former Federal Reserve chairman. It stopped federally insured banks from making risky bets with the bank's own money. What is the point of a rule like that?
answer: Banks with government-insured deposits should not gamble with those deposits
choices: Banks with government-insured deposits should not gamble with those deposits
Banks should hire more government inspectors
Banks should pay their executives less
Banks should offer higher interest rates on savings accounts
context: Named for Paul Volcker (Fed chairman 1979-87), who argued that banks with federal deposit insurance should not be running hedge-fund-style trading books. The rule took years to finalize and became a byword for the compliance-cost burden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Volcker_Rule.

question: A big US banking law passed in 2010 added many pages of new rules on small and mid-sized banks. In 2010 there were about seven thousand US commercial banks. By 2023, how many were left?
answer: About 4,700 -- down by roughly a third
choices: About 4,700 -- down by roughly a third
About 6,200 -- barely changed
About 3,000 -- down by more than half
About 5,900 -- down by only a small amount
context: A decline of roughly one third in thirteen years. Consolidation into regional and money-center banks accelerated after 2010; most community banks were acquired rather than closed. Source: congress.gov/crs-product/R47014.

question: Before a big 2010 US banking law, regulators approved about 130 brand-new banks every year. In the six years right after that law passed, the yearly average collapsed. Roughly how many brand-new banks were being approved per year?
answer: Fewer than six per year
choices: Fewer than six per year
About thirty per year
About eighty per year
About a hundred per year
context: The 2022 Congressional Research Service report (R47014) documents the collapse. In 2009 regulators had also raised the de novo review period from three years to seven years and stiffened capital requirements for new-bank applicants. Source: congress.gov/crs-product/R47014.

question: A new law says every US bank must hire five extra lawyers to check paperwork. A giant national bank splits this cost across millions of customers. A small-town bank with 500 customers cannot. Which bank feels the rule more?
answer: The small bank -- fixed rule costs hurt small players most
choices: The small bank -- fixed rule costs hurt small players most
The giant bank, because it has more paperwork to check
Both banks feel it the same, since the rule is the same
Neither bank -- lawyers can be hired cheaply anywhere
context: Charles Calomiris of Columbia Business School and Stephen Haber made this the standard critique in Fragile by Design (Princeton 2014). Compliance-officer and legal staffing is largely a fixed cost per institution, so it consumes a much larger share of a small bank's revenue. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Charles_Calomiris.

question: A US state bans selling alcohol on Sundays. Two very different groups quietly want the rule kept: churches who want a quiet Sunday, and illegal liquor sellers who profit when legal stores must close. What name did economist Bruce Yandle give this pattern?
answer: Bootleggers and Baptists
choices: Bootleggers and Baptists
The Iron Triangle
Concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
Regulatory capture
context: The pattern is named for Prohibition, where evangelical preachers publicly urged alcohol bans while bootleggers quietly welcomed the elimination of legal competition. Yandle argues the same coalition structure recurs whenever a rule concentrates benefits on a well-organized incumbent. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bootleggers_and_Baptists.

question: After the 2008 mega-bank crisis, Congress wrote strict rules for the giants but applied them to every bank the same way. Small hometown banks struggled with paperwork built for firms a hundred times their size. What lesson does this pattern usually teach?
answer: Rules meant for the biggest players usually crush the small ones hardest
choices: Rules meant for the biggest players usually crush the small ones hardest
Small banks are always more dangerous than large ones
Strict paperwork always makes finance safer, whatever the cost
A rule that fits every bank equally is the fairest rule
context: Signed May 24, 2018 by President Trump, sponsored by Senator Mike Crapo (R-Idaho). The law was a bipartisan concession that fixed compliance costs on small banks had shrunk community banking without protecting the system from another 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Growth,_Regulatory_Relief,_and_Consumer_Protection_Act.

question: From 1995 to March 2000, the prices of internet-company stocks shot up wildly -- many companies with no profit at all were worth billions of dollars. Then the prices CRASHED. What is this kind of run-up-then-crash usually called?
answer: A bubble
choices: A bubble
A steady climb
A depression
A boom that lasts forever
context: The NASDAQ peaked at 5,048 on March 10 2000 -- a five-fold gain in five years. Many internet companies had no profits at all. Source: Grokipedia 'Dot-com bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: On December 5, 1996, Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan warned about high asset prices in a speech. He used a specific two-word phrase. But he did not act to restrain the market. What phrase did Greenspan use?
answer: Irrational exuberance
choices: Irrational exuberance
Speculative excess
Bubble psychology
Investor overconfidence
context: Greenspan's December 5 1996 speech to the American Enterprise Institute used 'irrational exuberance' to describe asset markets. The warning was widely quoted; the policy response was minimal. Source: Grokipedia 'Irrational exuberance' (2026-09-05).

question: From March 2000 through October 2002, the main index of big American tech stocks crashed spectacularly. How large was the drop from its peak to its bottom?
answer: About three-quarters of its value
choices: About three-quarters of its value
About one-third of its value
About one-tenth of its value
About half of its value
context: The NASDAQ fell from 5,048 to 1,114 -- a 78% decline over 31 months. Trillions of dollars of paper wealth vanished and hundreds of dot-com companies failed. Source: Grokipedia 'Dot-com bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed responded to the 2000-02 crash with an aggressive rate-cutting cycle. Between January 2001 and June 2003 it cut the federal funds rate from 6.5% down to a specific low, then held it there for over a year. What was the low?
answer: 1.0 percent
choices: 1.0 percent
3.0 percent
0.25 percent
2.5 percent
context: The Fed cut 13 times between January 2001 and June 2003, reaching 1.0% on June 25 2003 -- the lowest US policy rate in 46 years. It held the 1.0% rate through June 2004. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2001-03 rate-cutting cycle had one massive unintended effect that the Fed did not anticipate: fueling a bubble in another asset class. Which asset class did the cheap-money response inflate?
answer: US housing
choices: US housing
US commercial real estate
European sovereign debt
Emerging-market equities
context: The Case-Shiller 20-City Home Price Index rose over 100% from January 2000 to April 2006. Cheap mortgages (subprime adjustable-rate loans at low teaser rates) drove the boom. Source: Grokipedia 'United States housing bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: From 2005 to 2007, one financial analyst went on cable news shows again and again, warning that very low interest rates were fueling a huge housing bubble that would soon burst. Other guests laughed at him on camera. What happened next?
answer: The housing market collapsed in 2007-2008 and he was proven right
choices: The housing market collapsed in 2007-2008 and he was proven right
Housing prices kept climbing steadily for another twenty years
The government banned him from speaking on financial shows
Interest rates immediately rose and the bubble never grew
context: Schiff's CNBC and Fox Business appearances 2005-07 were compiled into the viral 'Peter Schiff was right' YouTube video (over 3 million views). His warnings were vindicated by the 2008 crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Peter Schiff' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian business-cycle-theory reading of the 2001-2008 sequence identifies a specific causal chain the Fed's actions produced. Which chain does the theory describe?
answer: The 2001-03 rate cuts (a response to the 2000-02 crash caused by 1990s easy money) were the direct origin of the 2008 crisis; the Fed solved one bubble by inflating a bigger one
choices: The 2001-03 rate cuts (a response to the 2000-02 crash caused by 1990s easy money) were the direct origin of the 2008 crisis; the Fed solved one bubble by inflating a bigger one
The 2001-03 rate cuts had no relationship to the housing bubble that followed
The 2001-03 rate cuts prevented all subsequent financial crises
The 2001-03 rate cuts caused a sustained fall in commodity prices
context: The Austrian reading: each bubble is caused by the monetary response to the previous bubble. The 1990s cheap money produced the dot-com bubble; the 2001-03 cheap money produced the housing bubble; the 2008-14 QE produced the 2020-24 everything bubble. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Federal Reserve researchers later documented the link between the 2001-04 low rates and the subprime lending boom. Two Boston Fed economists produced the internal paper. Which two wrote it?
answer: Paul Willen and Kristopher Gerardi
choices: Paul Willen and Kristopher Gerardi
Ben Bernanke and Alan Blinder
Charles Plosser and Jeffrey Lacker
Janet Yellen and Stanley Fischer
context: Willen and Gerardi, at the Boston Fed, produced research linking the 2001-04 rate cuts directly to subprime mortgage origination. Their finding was implicit acknowledgment from inside the Fed system that the Austrian critique had a real basis. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2000-2008 sequence teaches a specific recognition move about Fed reaction functions and future crises. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The Fed's monetary response to a bust plants the seeds of the next bust; there is no exit from the cycle without accepting the liquidation the theory requires
choices: The Fed's monetary response to a bust plants the seeds of the next bust; there is no exit from the cycle without accepting the liquidation the theory requires
The Fed can smooth out business cycles indefinitely by lowering rates aggressively
Each Fed response fully resolves the underlying imbalances of the prior cycle
Fed rate cuts have no effect on asset prices in later cycles
context: The Austrian point: the boom-bust cycle is not an exogenous shock to a stable economy; it is generated by discretionary monetary policy. Attempting to prevent each bust by easing produces the next bust larger. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In 1996 the Federal Reserve chair warned about 'irrational exuberance' in stock prices, but never raised rates to slow the growing bubble. Which recognition move does the ladder press about this failure?
answer: A central-bank chair who publicly warns about a bubble without acting to restrain it has effectively endorsed continued speculation
choices: A central-bank chair who publicly warns about a bubble without acting to restrain it has effectively endorsed continued speculation
Public warnings by central-bank chairs always successfully deflate asset bubbles
Central banks lack the tools to affect asset prices during a bubble
Verbal intervention is always more effective than actual rate changes
context: Greenspan's 'irrational exuberance' warning was famous precisely because the Fed did nothing to follow through. Markets read the non-action as a green light. The speech is now studied as an example of failed verbal intervention. Source: Grokipedia 'Irrational exuberance' (2026-09-05).

question: In communist East Germany, one government-run factory made ONE tiny two-stroke car. Buyers waited 10+ years to get one. It was smoky, slow, and low quality. What does this show about central-planned economies?
answer: Without competition, quality gets stuck
choices: Without competition, quality gets stuck
Central planning makes the best products
Waiting lists mean everyone is happy
Governments always make better cars than companies
context: The Trabant ('little satellite') was manufactured at the Zwickau plant from 1957 to 1991 -- about 3 million total. Its body was made of Duraplast (resin mixed with cotton fibers) because the DDR lacked steel supply chains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: In East Germany the government ran every factory. The car plant could not get enough steel, so cars were built from plastic and cotton. What does this teach?
answer: One small group cannot plan every material for a whole country
choices: One small group cannot plan every material for a whole country
Plastic is stronger than steel
Cotton cars are safer in crashes
East Germans just did not like metal
context: Duraplast was a fiberglass-like resin reinforced with waste cotton fibers -- cheap, lightweight, and produced from materials the DDR could source without hard currency. The material also famously would not rust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: In East Germany the government set the price of the Trabant car well below what people would have paid for it. The state then handed out cars from a long waiting list. Families sometimes signed up for one when a baby was born. Roughly how long was the wait?
answer: Ten to fifteen years
choices: Ten to fifteen years
One to two years
Six months
Fifty years
context: Delivery queues stretched to 10-15 years. Used Trabants sold at higher prices than new ones (because you could have it today), inverting the usual depreciation curve. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: The Bastiat seen-versus-unseen reading of the Trabant supply system: SEEN was the affordable sticker price. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The 10-15-year queue and the used market that priced above new
choices: The 10-15-year queue and the used market that priced above new
The plant's steady employment record
The DDR's export earnings
The environmental cost of two-cycle engines
context: The visible low price hid the invisible time-cost (years in queue) and the black secondary market above the state sticker. The waiting list was the real 'price'. Source: mises.org/library/east-germany.

question: In East Germany, one state company produced every car, and no competitor could enter the market. The same basic engine remained in production for 34 years. Why did the maker never improve the design?
answer: No competitive pressure to redesign since no rival could enter the market
choices: No competitive pressure to redesign since no rival could enter the market
State engineers were forbidden to sketch alternatives
The Zwickau plant lacked qualified engineers
The Politburo mandated periodic conservative redesigns
context: The last Trabants rolled off the line in 1991 with essentially the same 1957 two-cycle engine. No competitor could enter the DDR market to force redesign. This is the incentive side of the calculation debate applied to industrial design. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: On the night of November 9, 1989 and in the weeks after, thousands of small blue East German cars puffing two-cycle exhaust drove through the checkpoints into West Berlin. Which event triggered this iconic sight?
answer: The fall of the Berlin Wall
choices: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The Warsaw Pact dissolution
The Chernobyl disaster
The 1980 Moscow Olympics
context: November 9, 1989 photographs of Trabants at the checkpoints became one of the visual symbols of the DDR's collapse. Within months of reunification, West-German used cars flooded the market and the Trabant disappeared almost overnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall.

question: The Trabant is called 'the calculation debate on wheels' because its 34-year design freeze shows a classic Austrian argument at physical scale. Whose 1920 essay predicted this exact pattern?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth'
choices: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth'
Friedrich Hayek's 'The Road to Serfdom'
Milton Friedman's 'Free to Choose'
Murray Rothbard's 'Man, Economy, and State'
context: Mises's 1920 argument: without market prices reflecting real scarcities and consumer preferences, planners cannot know when a design needs updating -- so they build the same one for decades while the world moves on. The Trabant is the argument made physical. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: In East Germany, buying a car meant putting your name on a list and waiting ten years, sometimes more. The car itself barely changed in design for decades. What causes this pattern in a state-run economy?
answer: No competing makers, so no reason to build more or improve
choices: No competing makers, so no reason to build more or improve
People in East Germany did not really want cars
The government secretly hid better cars for later years
The cars were too advanced for regular customers to use
context: The Wartburg (Eisenach plant) was the DDR's larger sedan, with 10-year queues of its own. Like the Trabant, production ended shortly after reunification. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wartburg_(car).

question: The Trabant case study collapses three Austrian reasoning-moves at once. Which pair of moves does the design-freeze most sharply illustrate (alongside the seen-vs-unseen queue)?
answer: The knowledge problem plus the incentive-to-improve problem
choices: The knowledge problem plus the incentive-to-improve problem
The Cantillon effect plus the Fisher effect
The Kondratiev cycle plus the Kuznets curve
The Phillips curve plus Okun's law
context: The knowledge problem: planners cannot know when a design needs updating. The incentive problem: with no competition, no reason to bear the cost of redesign. Together they produce the 34-year design freeze. Source: mises.org/library/east-germany.

question: In 1920, a Vienna economist wrote an essay in German. In English, the title is 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' The essay started a forty-year debate. Who wrote it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Joseph Schumpeter
context: Mises (born 1881) was 39 in 1920, working as chief economist for the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Hayek was still a 21-year-old student who would later attend Mises's private seminar. Boehm-Bawerk had died in 1914. Schumpeter was a contemporary Austrian but held Keynesian-adjacent views on money. Source: Wikipedia, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In his 1920 essay on socialist planning, Mises made a narrow claim. He did not argue that socialism was immoral, or that its workers were lazy, or that its officials were corrupt. What did he actually argue?
answer: That rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible
choices: That rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible
That socialist regimes will always turn to political violence
That socialism destroys the incentive to work hard
That planners will inevitably use their power to enrich themselves
context: Mises deliberately set aside every other objection to isolate a technical one: without market prices for capital goods, a planner has no way to compare the cost of alternatives. It is not that planning is unwise -- it is that no rational plan can be drawn up at all. Source: Wikipedia, Economic calculation problem.

question: Mises's 1920 essay first came out in a German journal from Heidelberg. Max Weber had helped edit it before the war. Which journal printed the essay in its volume 47?
answer: Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik
choices: Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik
Zeitschrift fuer die gesamte Staatswissenschaft
Weltwirtschaftliches Archiv
Jahrbuecher fuer Nationaloekonomie und Statistik
context: The essay appeared as 'Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen' in Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, volume 47 (1920), pages 86 to 121. The other three were also real German-language economics journals of the era but did not publish this essay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: In 1922, an Austrian economist named Ludwig von Mises published a long book with a one-word title: the very system he wanted to critique. The book argued that a fully planned economy has no way to know the true value of anything. What was its main claim?
answer: Without free-market prices, planners cannot calculate what things really cost
choices: Without free-market prices, planners cannot calculate what things really cost
Planning always produces more consumer goods than markets do
Poor countries always beat rich ones under central planning
A committee can always outperform millions of buyers and sellers
context: 'Die Gemeinwirtschaft: Untersuchungen ueber den Sozialismus' (1922) was translated by J. Kahane in 1936 as simply 'Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis.' The Road to Serfdom (1944) was Hayek's; Human Action (1949) came later, from Mises himself; Bureaucracy (1944) was another shorter Mises book. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: A Soviet planner in 1925 is deciding whether to build a new rail line using rolled steel or aluminum. Both are available; both would work; each pulls labor and raw material from other uses. Mises's 1920 essay says the planner cannot rationally choose between them. What specifically is missing that would allow a rational choice?
answer: Exchange-generated prices for the capital goods involved
choices: Exchange-generated prices for the capital goods involved
A larger central-planning bureau with more statisticians
Better labor-hour accounting for each metal
A more accurate five-year forecast of demand
context: Prices arise only when privately-owned goods change hands. Abolish private ownership of the means of production, and iron ore and aluminum ore are no longer exchanged -- they are merely moved from one state enterprise to another. Without money prices, there is nothing to compare. More statisticians, better labor-hour books, and better forecasts all presuppose a common unit of value the planner does not have. Source: mises.org/online-book/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth/3.

question: Engels claimed that socialist bookkeeping would be simple. Society could just calculate the labor hours in a steam engine or a bushel of wheat. In 1920, Mises quoted this passage and rejected the argument. Which reasoning move did Mises press against Engels?
answer: That labor hours cannot capture how scarce the different material inputs are
choices: That labor hours cannot capture how scarce the different material inputs are
That workers will always misreport how many hours they worked
That machines age at different rates, so hours-per-output changes
That some labor is skilled and some unskilled
context: Two goods can each embody ten hours of labor, yet the first may swallow scarce iron ore while the second uses abundant clay -- the labor count is identical, the real cost is not. Only exchange-set prices reflect scarcity across all inputs at once. The skilled/unskilled point was actually granted by Marx himself and does not touch the calculation problem. Source: mises.org/online-book/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth/3.

question: A group of economists argued in the 1930s that no committee, no matter how smart, can plan a whole country's production. The core reason: without free-market prices, planners cannot tell what people actually want. What is that argument called?
answer: The socialist calculation problem
choices: The socialist calculation problem
The tragedy of the commons
The paradox of thrift
The lump of labor fallacy
context: 'Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism' (George Routledge and Sons, London, 1935), edited by Hayek at the LSE, put Mises's argument in front of the English-speaking economics profession for the first time. Robbins was Hayek's LSE colleague; Keynes was Hayek's Cambridge opponent; Schumpeter was writing at Bonn and later Harvard. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: After Mises's essay reached English readers in 1935, two economists offered a reply. Their idea was to let the state own the factories, but have plant managers copy market prices by tweaking output until shortages and surpluses went away. This late-1930s answer was named for its two authors. What is that reply called?
answer: The Lange-Lerner theorem of market socialism
choices: The Lange-Lerner theorem of market socialism
The Keynes-Hansen doctrine of secular stagnation
The Samuelson-Solow doctrine of the neoclassical synthesis
The Sraffa-Robinson critique of capital theory
context: Oskar Lange and Abba Lerner argued central planners could simulate market prices by trial and error. Mises and Hayek replied that simulation without genuine private ownership still lacks the profit-and-loss discipline that generates real price information. The other three were real 20th-century economic controversies but on different questions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: In 1945 Hayek recast Mises's argument in a famous American Economic Review paper. He argued that prices are not just numbers, but compress the private knowledge of millions of people into signals no planner could gather. What did Hayek title the paper?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretence of Knowledge
Economics and Knowledge
The Meaning of Competition
context: Published September 1945 in the American Economic Review, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' is now the most-cited paper in the whole Austrian tradition. 'Economics and Knowledge' was Hayek's 1937 warm-up; 'The Meaning of Competition' was his 1946 follow-up; 'The Pretence of Knowledge' was his 1974 Nobel lecture. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: At its peak, Soviet planners set about 22 million prices, 460,000 wage rates, and over 90 million work quotas. Even so, stores ran out of basic goods while warehouses filled with things nobody wanted. When the planned economies fell in 1989-1991, some Western economists like Robert Heilbroner said a Vienna economist had been right all along. What did they admit?
answer: That Mises's 1920 calculation argument had been vindicated
choices: That Mises's 1920 calculation argument had been vindicated
That Keynesian demand management would have saved the East
That the Soviet failure was due chiefly to a shortage of computers
That the fault lay only with Stalin's personal cruelty, not with planning
context: Heilbroner wrote in 1990: 'Mises was right.' The other three explanations were all offered during the Cold War and all set aside once the archives opened: computing power was irrelevant if the prices being computed did not track real scarcity; the same shortages appeared in every planned economy, not just Stalin's. Source: econlib.org/the-collapse-of-the-soviet-union-and-the-continued-relevance-of-ludwig-von-mises; fee.org/articles/the-soviets-tried-to-run-an-economy-without-market-prices.

question: Most of Bastiat's writing tears bad ideas apart. But he wrote one book to lay out his own theory of a free economy. It came out in Paris in 1850. What is its short title?
answer: Economic Harmonies
choices: Economic Harmonies
Economic Sophisms
The Law
Cobden and the League
context: Harmonies economiques (Guillaumin, 1850) was Bastiat's positive treatise, cut short by his December 1850 death. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat had one big idea about people in a free society. Marx said the classes must fight. Bastiat said the opposite. What was his idea?
answer: Interests in a free society are naturally harmonious rather than antagonistic
choices: Interests in a free society are naturally harmonious rather than antagonistic
Interests in any society always trend toward violent revolution
Interests are always aligned only under state central planning
Interests are unknowable and unpredictable in every case
context: Bastiat argued that when exchange is voluntary, one party's gain does not require another's loss, so class interests are not fundamentally opposed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In one famous passage Bastiat compares two equally-useful diamonds, one found by chance in a stream and one dug from a mine at great labor. What does he say the two share equally to their buyers?
answer: Value
choices: Value
Weight
Origin
Reservation price
context: The diamond example: value depends on the service rendered to the user, not on labor spent producing the good. This move anticipated Menger's 1871 subjective-value revolution. Source: bastiat.org/en/harmonies.html.

question: A famous 1945 essay said that market prices act like a message system. They let millions of strangers work together without any central planner. Why does this coordination through prices work so well?
answer: Each price silently tells buyers and sellers something no single planner could know
choices: Each price silently tells buyers and sellers something no single planner could know
Prices are set by a small expert committee in each country
Prices are randomly generated by market computers
Prices are always exactly the true cost of production
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' made the same point about price signals aggregating dispersed information -- ninety-five years after Bastiat. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: For centuries, economists believed the price of a thing came from the labor invested in making it. In 1871, two economists working alone proposed a different answer. Value depends on how much a person wants the next unit. What is this idea usually called?
answer: Subjective value -- value depends on the person, not on the labor spent
choices: Subjective value -- value depends on the person, not on the labor spent
The labor theory of value
The cost-plus theory of pricing
The gold-backed theory of money
context: Jevons's Theory of Political Economy (1871) and Menger's Principles of Economics (1871) launched the marginal-utility revolution independently and near-simultaneously. Bastiat's 1850 hint predated both. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_utility.

question: Bastiat finished only part of his book Economic Harmonies before his death, leaving the rest as drafts and fragments. Roughly how many chapters did he complete?
answer: Ten
choices: Ten
Two
Twenty
Fifty
context: Bastiat completed ten chapters and drafted portions of ten more; Prosper Paillottet edited the drafts into an expanded 1851 second edition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: A farmer's barn burns down. A neighbor says: at least this creates work for carpenters! Bastiat answered: yes, but the farmer's money now goes to a new barn instead of a new plow -- and the plow was never built. What idea did Bastiat name?
answer: The seen and the unseen
choices: The seen and the unseen
The invisible hand
Comparative advantage
Marginal utility
context: Schumpeter's History of Economic Analysis (Oxford, 1954) is famously dismissive of Bastiat's positive theory; modern Austrian scholarship has reappraised the diamond passage upward. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_Schumpeter.

question: Bastiat wrote a set of funny essays. The first group came out in Paris in 1845, and the second in January 1848. What is the short title of the collection?
answer: Economic Sophisms
choices: Economic Sophisms
Economic Harmonies
The Law
Cobden and the League
context: Sophismes economiques (Guillaumin, 1845 and 1848) is Bastiat's satirical corpus, comprising 39 short essays across two series. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: A country puts big taxes on shoes made in other countries so its own shoemakers can charge more at home. Who is HURT by this rule that helps the shoemakers?
answer: Every family who now pays more for shoes
choices: Every family who now pays more for shoes
The shoemakers who now sell more
Only foreign countries
Nobody -- it helps everyone
context: Jacques Bonhomme is Bastiat's literary device; he lets the arguments play out through dialogue rather than lecture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: In one famous essay in Economic Sophisms, Bastiat imagines a mayor banning a specific carpentry tool. He says using it would put unskilled workers out of a job. Which tool does the mayor ban?
answer: The sharp axe
choices: The sharp axe
The mechanical loom
The steam-powered saw
The plow
context: Bastiat's 'Two Axes' essay has the mayor forbidding a woodcutter's sharp axe to protect the jobs of dull-axe men -- a reductio of make-work arguments. Source: bastiat.org/en/two_axes.html.

question: The First Series of Economic Sophisms opens with a short essay pairing two words. Bastiat argues the goal of economic activity is more goods at lower prices, not fewer at higher. What is the two-word title?
answer: Abundance and Scarcity
choices: Abundance and Scarcity
Cause and Effect
Effort and Result
Obstacle and Cause
context: 'Abundance and Scarcity' is the opening essay of the First Series (1845); it clarifies the direction of economic reasoning. Source: bastiat.org/en/es1.html.

question: The most famous essay in Economic Sophisms is a fake petition. In it, one home industry begs the government to shield it from unfair foreign rivals. Which industry files the petition?
answer: The candlemakers
choices: The candlemakers
The blacksmiths
The vintners
The weavers
context: The Petition of the Candlemakers demands a law against the sun to protect domestic makers of candles and lamps -- a reductio of protectionism that appears in the First Series (1845). Source: bastiat.org/en/petition.html.

question: Economic Sophisms goes after both political sides. Which pair of policies does the book attack most often?
answer: Make-work schemes and tariffs for domestic producers
choices: Make-work schemes and tariffs for domestic producers
Central banking and gold-standard restoration
Personal income tax and corporate income tax
Antitrust regulation and price controls
context: Bastiat's seen/unseen method is applied to left-flavored make-work schemes and right-flavored protective tariffs alike; that even-handedness makes the collection a METHOD text. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: A country blocks cheap foreign shoes so its own shoemakers can charge more. Shoemakers cheer. But everyone else pays more for shoes, and the country's tailors, who traded shoes for jackets, lose sales too. Which type of cost did Bastiat teach us to look for?
answer: The hidden cost paid by many, spread thin enough to overlook
choices: The hidden cost paid by many, spread thin enough to overlook
The cost the shoemakers pay for advertising
The cost of shipping shoes across borders
The cost of teaching new shoemakers
context: Stirling's 1873 English edition, retitled Economic Sophisms, was the standard English text until the FEE editions of the mid-20th century and the Liberty Fund Collected Works of the 2010s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: A shopkeeper's window is smashed. A crowd says, "Cheer up! Now the glazier gets paid, and he'll spend that money too — the town is richer!" Frederic Bastiat's answer was that the crowd only counts one side. What did they forget?
answer: The money the shopkeeper would have spent on something else is gone forever
choices: The money the shopkeeper would have spent on something else is gone forever
The glazier will overcharge because he knows the shopkeeper is desperate
Windows are cheaper to fix than to install new
Insurance will pay for it, so no one really loses anything
context: Jane Willems's Liberty Fund translation restored many chapters and cleaned up 19th-century Britishisms; it is the current best English-language edition. Source: libertyfund.org/collected-works-bastiat-vol-3.

question: In 2021 El Salvador made Bitcoin real money alongside the US dollar. What is odd about Bitcoin compared with normal cash?
answer: No government or bank issues it -- it is made by computers around the world
choices: No government or bank issues it -- it is made by computers around the world
Only rich people are allowed to own it
A single company in the US prints all of it
It is made of gold coins
context: The Bitcoin Law passed the Salvadoran Legislative Assembly on June 9 2021 and took effect September 7 2021, making Bitcoin legal tender alongside the US dollar, which had been El Salvador's official currency since 2001. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: In 2001, El Salvador dropped its old money and picked a foreign one. That was 20 years before it added Bitcoin. Which money did it pick in 2001?
answer: The US dollar
choices: The US dollar
The euro
The Mexican peso
The Central American peso
context: El Salvador dollarized in 2001, abandoning its colon; the dollar remained the official currency after the 2021 Bitcoin adoption -- Bitcoin was added ALONGSIDE the dollar, not as a replacement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_El_Salvador.

question: In 2021, El Salvador became the first country ever to make Bitcoin legal tender. Any business had to accept it. What was the government hoping this would do for Salvadorans who work abroad and send money home?
answer: Let them send money home faster and with lower fees than banks charge
choices: Let them send money home faster and with lower fees than banks charge
Force them to move back to El Salvador
Increase the taxes they pay to the government
Prevent them from ever spending their earnings
context: Nayib Bukele, elected 2019, announced the Bitcoin plan at the Bitcoin 2021 conference in Miami in June 2021 and pushed the Bitcoin Law through the assembly within days. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nayib_Bukele.

question: Bukele announced El Salvador's Bitcoin plan at a June 2021 conference held in Miami. What was the conference called?
answer: Bitcoin 2021
choices: Bitcoin 2021
Consensus 2021
Coindesk Live 2021
Miami Crypto Week
context: Bitcoin 2021 (Wynwood, Miami, June 4-5 2021) was a live-streamed Bitcoin conference; Bukele's video announcement of the coming legal-tender law hit thousands of attendees in real time. Source: b.tc/conference.

question: El Salvador also built a national mobile wallet running on the Lightning Network, so small merchants could take Bitcoin without paying heavy on-chain fees. What is the wallet called?
answer: Chivo
choices: Chivo
Colibri
Cabal
Cortez
context: Chivo (Salvadoran slang for 'cool') was distributed to every adult who signed up, with a $30 Bitcoin signing bonus. It had significant early bugs but did drive initial mass adoption. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivo_(wallet).

question: Every adult Salvadoran who set up the Chivo wallet was offered a sign-up bonus paid in Bitcoin. What was the amount?
answer: $30 in Bitcoin
choices: $30 in Bitcoin
$300 in Bitcoin
$3 in Bitcoin
$100 in Bitcoin
context: The $30 signing bonus (paid at Bitcoin's market rate at the moment of registration) was intended to hard-launch wallet adoption; it drove millions of downloads in the first weeks. Source: reuters.com (September 2021 rollout coverage).

question: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) told a small country to stop using Bitcoin as an official currency. It gave a reason based on the risk of price swings. What was the fund's stated concern?
answer: That Bitcoin's price jumps up and down too much to safely back a nation's economy
choices: That Bitcoin's price jumps up and down too much to safely back a nation's economy
That Bitcoin was harder to trace than paper cash
That Bitcoin transfers are too slow for daily use
That Bitcoin cannot be broken into small units
context: The IMF's stated reasoning was Bitcoin's price volatility and its consequences for macroeconomic stability, fiscal reporting, and financial-sector supervision. El Salvador refused; Bukele mocked the IMF on Twitter and pressed on. Source: imf.org (Article IV consultations with El Salvador, 2021-2024).

question: From 2021 to 2024, the El Salvador government bought Bitcoin on a fixed schedule, no matter the price. What was the pace?
answer: One Bitcoin per day
choices: One Bitcoin per day
Ten Bitcoin per week
One Bitcoin per hour
One Bitcoin per week
context: Bukele announced in November 2022 that El Salvador would buy one BTC per day into national reserves; treasury holdings grew accordingly over 2022-2024. Source: bloomberg.com (El Salvador BTC treasury coverage, 2022-24).

question: El Salvador became the first modern country to legalize as money an asset whose supply no state or central bank could control. The move directly defied one group of international financial institutions. Which group did it defy?
answer: The consensus of international financial institutions like the IMF
choices: The consensus of international financial institutions like the IMF
The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision recommendations
The World Trade Organization Financial Services Annex
The Bank for International Settlements clearing protocols
context: The Bastiat/Austrian sound-money reading of the move: any successful sovereign adoption of a non-state monetary asset weakens the influence of the international financial institutions built around fiat currency. The IMF's opposition was rational from that perspective. Source: mises.org/library/el-salvador-bitcoin.

question: A small country wants to mine Bitcoin without burning fossil fuels or straining its power grid. It happens to sit on top of an active volcano. What is the clever idea?
answer: Use the volcano's heat to make steam, run generators, and mine Bitcoin with that electricity
choices: Use the volcano's heat to make steam, run generators, and mine Bitcoin with that electricity
Set fire to old car tires near the crater to double the available power
Import diesel and burn it faster than the neighboring countries do
Print more of the country's paper money and use it to buy Bitcoin abroad
context: 'Bitcoin City' near the Conchagua volcano in La Union department was announced November 2021, to be powered by geothermal energy from the volcano and funded by Bitcoin-denominated bonds. Development has been slow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_City.

question: In 2009, an Indiana University professor won the Nobel Prize in Economics. She was the first woman ever to win it. She studied how everyday users can share a resource with no state or private owner in charge. Who was she?
answer: Elinor Ostrom
choices: Elinor Ostrom
Anna Schwartz
Joan Robinson
Deirdre McCloskey
context: Elinor Ostrom (1933-2012) won the 2009 economics Nobel with Oliver Williamson 'for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.' She was the first woman to win in the field. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom.

question: Elinor Ostrom's most famous book came out in 1990. It shocked many economists. It said user groups could manage a shared resource for hundreds of years with no state in charge. What was the book's main title?
answer: Governing the Commons
choices: Governing the Commons
Understanding Institutional Diversity
Rules, Games, and Common-Pool Resources
Bloomington and the Public Choice
context: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (Cambridge University Press, 1990). Its case studies became the empirical spine of her Nobel citation. Source: cambridge.org/core/books/governing-the-commons.

question: A famous 1968 article said that when no one owns a resource, like a fish pond or a common pasture, each user has a reason to take a lot before others do. What is the usual result?
answer: The shared resource gets overused and eventually ruined
choices: The shared resource gets overused and eventually ruined
The shared resource grows steadily forever
People self-organize and always share equally
The government automatically appears and manages it
context: Garrett Hardin's 'The Tragedy of the Commons' (Science, December 13, 1968) became the standard citation for the pessimistic view. Ostrom argued that Hardin's tragedy was conditional, not inevitable. Source: science.org (Hardin, Science 1968).

question: Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel Prize in Economics. She showed that people can share things like a village well or a fishery with no state or private owner. What did she find they use to make it work?
answer: Local rules and social pressure that the users themselves invent and enforce
choices: Local rules and social pressure that the users themselves invent and enforce
A random-lottery system decided each year
Full turn-taking supervised by outsiders
Complete equal shares handed out by a bank
context: The 2009 Nobel citation honored Ostrom for commons governance and Williamson for the economics of the firm and hierarchies. Both work on how real-world institutions solve coordination problems. Source: nobelprize.org (2009 Economic Sciences).

question: One famous researcher on shared land studied a mountain pasture in the Alps where cows from a dozen villages have grazed the same slopes for centuries under village-made rules. The pasture is not fenced or owned by one person, but it has not been ruined. What is the main lesson?
answer: A community can share a resource well if it makes and enforces its own rules
choices: A community can share a resource well if it makes and enforces its own rules
Only private ownership can protect land from overuse
Only government control can protect land from overuse
Shared land always ends up destroyed within a generation
context: Swiss alpine grazing commons (Toerbel and other villages in Valais) have been governed by user-written rules on stocking rates since the 1200s. The rules survived centuries of state changes and remain in force. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (Cambridge 1990), Chapter 3.

question: In one of Ostrom's American case studies, local lobstermen guard their own patches of sea. They punish outsiders who drop traps in claimed water. This user-run fishery has worked for generations. In which state did she study it?
answer: Maine
choices: Maine
Massachusetts
Louisiana
Alaska
context: The Maine lobster fishery's informal harbor gangs enforce territorial boundaries with cut buoy lines and social pressure. Ostrom's coauthor James Acheson wrote The Lobster Gangs of Maine (1988) alongside her project. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), Chapter 5.

question: A key chapter of Ostrom's book lists traits shared by long-lasting user-run commons. Traits like clear borders, local rules, and cheap ways to settle fights. How many such design principles did she pull from her case studies?
answer: Eight
choices: Eight
Four
Twelve
Twenty
context: Governing the Commons Chapter 3 lists exactly eight design principles for successful long-lived commons. She derived them from case comparison, not from theory. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), Chapter 3.

question: Elinor and Vincent Ostrom built a research home at Indiana University in Bloomington. It grew into a world-famous school of political economy. What did they name the institute they started there in 1973?
answer: The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
choices: The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
The Center for the Study of Public Choice
The Bureau of Applied Political Economy
The Institute for Constitutional Governance
context: The Ostroms founded the Workshop at IU Bloomington in 1973. Its research program became known as the 'Bloomington School' of institutional analysis. Source: ostromworkshop.indiana.edu.

question: A group of fishing villages shares one lake. Instead of one big rule made in the capital, each village keeps its own rules for its own dock, and they meet up to handle shared problems. Ostrom's name for this many-centers, many-levels arrangement is what?
answer: Polycentricity
choices: Polycentricity
Federalism
Subsidiarity
Devolution
context: Vincent Ostrom introduced the term 'polycentricity' in his 1961 paper on metropolitan governance; Elinor made it central to her nested-enterprise principle for large commons. Source: Ostrom + Tiebout + Warren, American Political Science Review (1961).

question: A senator says every unmanaged shared resource must collapse, so only state ownership or full privatization can save it. Ostrom's decades of case studies add a third option to that either/or. Which option does her work document?
answer: User groups can self-govern the resource with the right institutional design
choices: User groups can self-govern the resource with the right institutional design
The resource inevitably collapses regardless of governance form
Only religious authorities can enforce sustainable use
The resource must be split into individual homesteads
context: Ostrom's central contribution: SEEN is the state-vs-market binary; UNSEEN is the polycentric self-organized alternative that empirically works when the eight design principles are present. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), preface and conclusion.
