Might makes right
context: Rothbard secularizes Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689): self-ownership, the labor theory of homesteading, and the strict limits on legitimate coercion. Rothbard drops Locke's theological grounding but keeps the natural-rights framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: In 1973 Murray Rothbard put out For a New Liberty. That same year another American wrote a similar book, The Machinery of Freedom. It argued for the same setup, but on results rather than natural rights. Who wrote it?
answer: David Friedman, Milton Friedman's son
choices: David Friedman, Milton Friedman's son
Robert Nozick, Harvard philosopher
Hans-Hermann Hoppe, Rothbard's own student
Israel Kirzner, Austrian entrepreneurship theorist
context: David D. Friedman's The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism (Harper and Row, 1973) argued anarcho-capitalism on results-oriented grounds. The two 1973 manifestos, published within months of each other, defined the two branches of the modern anarcho-capitalist tradition, deontological (Rothbard) and consequentialist (Friedman). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: One libertarian thinker says a government should exist but only do three things: protect people from force, from theft, and from broken contracts. Nothing else. What nickname is given to such a very small government?
answer: A night-watchman state
choices: A night-watchman state
A total-planning state
A welfare state
A no-state anarchy
context: Nozick argued that a minimal state limited to protecting rights against force and fraud would arise from an anarchic starting point without violating anyone's rights, but that anything more would. Rothbard rejected the derivation and insisted the state itself is a rights-violation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy,_State,_and_Utopia.

question: A student reads that The Ethics of Liberty devotes an entire Part IV to critical review of rival theories. Which four theorists does Murray Rothbard critique in that Part IV?
answer: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
choices: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
Milton Friedman, James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Ronald Coase
John Rawls, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, and Michael Sandel
Ayn Rand, Nathaniel Branden, Leonard Peikoff, and Tibor Machan
context: Rothbard reviews Mises's utilitarianism, Hayek's rule-of-law liberalism, Berlin's two-concepts-of-liberty essay, and Nozick's minimal-state derivation, and argues each falls short of a fully consistent libertarian position. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: A French writer told a story about a boy who broke a shop window. Some people said 'Good -- it gives the glass-maker work!' What did the writer say they were forgetting?
answer: The shopkeeper cannot now buy shoes -- the shoemaker loses that sale
choices: The shopkeeper cannot now buy shoes -- the shoemaker loses that sale
The glass-maker gets richer for free
Broken things always help the economy
The boy's parents get a small tax refund
context: Bastiat was born in Bayonne on 30 June 1801 to a merchant family, orphaned by tuberculosis at nine, and raised by his grandfather on the family estate near Mugron. Bordeaux, Nantes and La Rochelle are the other three major French Atlantic ports of the period. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frederic Bastiat lived on his family farm and read about money for twenty years. In 1844 a Paris journal printed his first paper. He was famous overnight. Which journal was it?
answer: Journal des Economistes
choices: Journal des Economistes
Revue des Deux Mondes
Le Constitutionnel
La Gazette de France
context: The Journal des Economistes was founded in 1841 by the Guillaumin house as the flagship of the French free-trade school. Bastiat's article 'The Influence of English and French Tariffs on the Future of the Two Peoples' appeared in the October 1844 issue. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frederic Bastiat wrote his essays in short, plain French that a shopkeeper or farmer could follow. He did this on purpose, against the style of other economists then. Which style did he refuse to use?
answer: Mathematical formalism
choices: Mathematical formalism
Historical narration
Satirical dialogue
First-person voice
context: Bastiat wanted his readers to be able to check the argument at each step without algebra. He used satirical dialogue (the Candlemakers' Petition), historical narration (the Sophisms), and first-person voice (Ce qu'on voit) freely; the one continental fashion he refused was the equation. Source: fee.org 'The Life of Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In the 1840s a British group organized rallies, pamphlets, and speeches to convince Parliament to end the tax on imported grain. The tax made bread expensive and hurt poor families the most. What kind of movement was this?
answer: A free-trade movement
choices: A free-trade movement
A workers-only union
A movement to make bread illegal
A tax-raising campaign
context: Cobden's Anti-Corn Law League was founded in Manchester in 1838 and secured repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846. Bastiat visited England, met Cobden, and returned to Paris to build a French version of the League structure -- provincial chapters, a weekly paper, and public lectures. The Cobden Club came later (1866). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: After the 1848 revolution Bastiat was elected to the French assembly and re-elected the next year. He sat on the finance committee. Most of his speeches there attacked one group. Which one?
answer: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
choices: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
The legitimists of Henri de Chambord and Berryer
The Bonapartists of Louis-Napoleon and Persigny
The Orleanists of Thiers and the Duke de Broglie
context: Bastiat's parliamentary speeches, published in the Assembly journals of 1848-49, mostly opposed Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux and Proudhon's Bank of the People. He was not primarily engaged with the royalist, Bonapartist or Orleanist blocs. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In June and July 1850, dying of tuberculosis in Paris, Frederic Bastiat sent two short pamphlets to the printer in the space of a few weeks. Together they became the most-quoted pages he ever wrote and remain his two best-known short works. Name the pair.
answer: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
choices: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
Sophismes economiques and Petition des fabricants de chandelles
Harmonies economiques and Cobden et la Ligue
Propriete et loi and Capital et rente
context: La Loi (The Law) appeared in June 1850 and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen) in July 1850. The Sophismes had appeared as two earlier collections (1845, 1848); Harmonies was his unfinished positive treatise; Propriete et loi and Capital et rente were earlier short pieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In the autumn of 1850 Frederic Bastiat's doctors sent him south, hoping the warm winter climate would ease his failing lungs. He travelled first to Pisa in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Which second Italian city did he then move to, and where he died on Christmas Eve?
answer: Rome
choices: Rome
Naples
Florence
Venice
context: Bastiat left Pisa for Rome in the late autumn of 1850 and lodged near the Piazza di Spagna. He died there on 24 December 1850 and is buried in the French national church of San Luigi dei Francesi. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Bastiat set out to answer the socialists on their own ground by showing that free exchange produces spontaneous cooperation rather than class conflict. He died before finishing the book, and only the first part appeared in his lifetime; editors later assembled the rest from his notebooks. What is the book called?
answer: Harmonies economiques
choices: Harmonies economiques
Cours d'economie politique
Traite d'economie politique
Principes d'economie politique
context: Harmonies economiques was Bastiat's attempt at a systematic positive doctrine, and he considered it the work he would be remembered for; only about half was in print at his death. Traite d'economie politique was Jean-Baptiste Say's 1803 textbook; Cours and Principes are common French treatise titles used by others. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: According to the friends who kept vigil at his bedside, Frederic Bastiat spent his last hour on 24 December 1850 murmuring the same two-word French phrase over and over, as if to remind them what he had spent his life defending. The phrase was:
answer: 'La verite, la verite'
choices: 'La verite, la verite'
'La liberte, la liberte'
'La justice, la justice'
'La patrie, la patrie'
context: The account of the deathbed scene comes from Prosper Paillottet, one of the editors of the posthumous Oeuvres completes, who was in the room. Bastiat had built his method around the discipline of not lying about consequences; the reported dying words -- 'the truth, the truth' -- were taken by his friends as the summary of that vocation. Legend, but well-attested. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Two economic concepts still standard in every modern textbook were introduced by Frederic Bastiat in the essays of 1848-1850. One is the parable of the broken window, which teaches the student to count what a policy destroys as well as what it creates. What is the OTHER concept?
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Comparative advantage
Diminishing marginal utility
The velocity of money
context: Bastiat argued that every choice must be judged against the foregone alternative -- what the broken-window essay calls 'that which is not seen' -- and modern textbooks credit him with the first clear statement of opportunity cost. Comparative advantage is Ricardo (1817); marginal utility is Menger, Jevons and Walras (1871-74); the velocity of money goes back to the classical quantity theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In 1970 a magazine ran a short essay by Milton Friedman about how a company should act. It became one of the most famous business essays ever. What title did they give it?
answer: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
choices: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
The Corporation as a Moral Agent
Ethics in the Marketplace
The Purpose of the Firm
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits' (New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970). Often called the Friedman Doctrine. Source: nytimes.com/1970/09/13/archives.

question: Friedman's 1970 essay says a company executive works for one group. That group's interests set his duties. Which group is it?
answer: The shareholders
choices: The shareholders
The customers
The federal government
The neighborhood community
context: Friedman: the executive is an employee of the shareholders and should generally maximize corporate profits within the rules of law and ethical custom. Any expenditure of shareholder money on the executive's own social projects is other people's money on his priorities. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (September 13, 1970).

question: An economist wrote that a company's boss can give his own paycheck to any cause he wants -- that is his money. But if he spends the company's money on a cause the owners never approved, that is a different matter. What is the boss free to do only with his own salary?
answer: Donate to whatever cause he chooses
choices: Donate to whatever cause he chooses
Deposit it in a personal bank account
Pay his personal income taxes
Buy shares in his own company
context: Friedman's careful distinction: private-individual charity is voluntary and comes from one's own money; corporate-resource philanthropy uses shareholders' money for the executive's own priorities without their consent. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Friedman's 1970 essay says an executive can chase profit, but must follow two kinds of rules. Which pair does he name?
answer: Both law and ethical custom
choices: Both law and ethical custom
Only the letter of federal statutes
Only the moral code of the CEO's church
Only quarterly earnings targets
context: Friedman's precise phrasing: the executive should run the business to make as much money as possible 'while conforming to the basic rules of the society, both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom.' He is not defending fraud or predation. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: In 1970 Milton Friedman said that if a company's leaders must serve workers, the town, nature, and shareholders all at once, a serious problem shows up. What is the problem?
answer: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
choices: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
They must consult a national advisory panel
They automatically qualify for federal subsidies
They lose access to corporate liability protection
context: Friedman's institutional-design point: multi-stakeholder mandates leave the executive without a specific principal to answer to. Any decision can be justified by naming which stakeholder it served. The shareholder-only mandate is disciplining precisely because it names one clear principal. Source: Friedman (1970); Jensen + Meckling, 'Theory of the Firm' (JFE 1976).

question: The Friedman doctrine was expanded from a chapter in an earlier Friedman book that had been published eight years before the New York Times essay. Which book was that?
answer: Capitalism and Freedom
choices: Capitalism and Freedom
A Monetary History of the United States
A Theory of the Consumption Function
Free to Choose
context: Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 8, made the shareholder-primacy argument that the 1970 NYT essay condensed and popularized. Friedman had been making the argument for at least a decade before the magazine version. Source: Friedman (1962), Chapter 8.

question: Environmental, Social, and Governance investing (called ESG) is a modern approach followed by many corporations. Friedman's argument is the main intellectual pushback against the ESG approach. In one phrase, what was his critique of ESG?
answer: Other people's money charity by executives with no shareholder mandate
choices: Other people's money charity by executives with no shareholder mandate
A regressive tax on middle-class households
A violation of federal antitrust law
An invitation to hostile foreign takeover
context: Classical-liberal critics of ESG apply the Friedman 1970 frame directly: fund managers directing corporate votes toward ESG goals are spending beneficiaries' assets to pursue the managers' own values without explicit consent. Source: Friedman (1970) as applied in Fink CEO-letter debates 2018-24.

question: In August 2019 the Business Roundtable, a group of nearly 200 top CEOs, put out a Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation. It broke with Friedman's view. How many CEOs signed the statement?
choices: About 50
context: The Business Roundtable's Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation (August 19, 2019) was signed by 181 CEOs and formally endorsed stakeholder capitalism over pure shareholder primacy. It was widely read as a direct response to renewed attention to the Friedman doctrine. Source: businessroundtable.org (August 2019).

question: Friedman's 1970 essay is often boiled down to one memorable phrase. It captures the problem when an executive spends company money on his own causes without asking shareholders. Which phrase is it?
answer: Spending other people's money on his own priorities
choices: Spending other people's money on his own priorities
Serving all masters at once
Building the corporate community
Protecting long-term brand value
context: The Friedman phrase focuses attention on WHOSE money is being spent and WHOSE priorities are being served. Even a well-meaning executive-imposed cause is a use of shareholder assets without shareholder mandate. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Modern critics of Friedman include Porter with 'shared value,' Mayer on the purpose of firms, and Henderson on reimagining capitalism. What do they all say Friedman gets wrong about companies?
answer: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
choices: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
That the shareholder-only mandate should be criminalized federally
That the shareholder-only mandate applies only to European firms
That the shareholder-only mandate is unconstitutional under state law
context: The pro-stakeholder rebuttal, in various forms: attending to environmental, social, and community outcomes builds long-term corporate value that shareholder-narrow maximization misses. Friedman's response is that such considerations can be voluntarily adopted by shareholders themselves; executive imposition still lacks mandate. Source: Porter + Kramer, HBR (2011); Mayer, Prosperity (Oxford 2018); Henderson, Reimagining Capitalism (Public Affairs 2020).

question: In 1963 two economists put out a huge 860-page book on a hundred years of US money history. Ben Bernanke later called it the best account of the worst US economic disaster. Who wrote it together?
answer: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
choices: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow
John Maynard Keynes and Roy Harrod
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
context: Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research through Princeton University Press. It became one of the most influential economics books of the 20th century. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: Chapter 7 of the 1963 book, The Great Contraction 1929-1933, said the Great Depression was mainly a money failure. The M2 money supply shrank sharply in those four years. The Fed had tools to stop it. By about what percent did it shrink?
answer: About 33 percent
choices: About 33 percent
About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 5 percent
context: The M2 money supply contracted roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933. Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed could have prevented this by acting as lender of last resort during bank failures. It did not. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: The United States had about 25,000 banks operating in 1929. Then between 1930 and 1933 a catastrophic number of them collapsed. How many banks failed during the Great Contraction?
answer: About 9,000
choices: About 9,000
About 500
About 25,000
About 1,200
context: Roughly 9,000 US banks failed 1930-33 -- about a third of all banks. Each failure destroyed the deposits held there (no FDIC until 1933), further contracting the money supply. The Fed, chartered specifically to be lender of last resort, mostly stood aside. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Depression' (2026-09-05).

question: Two economists argued the Federal Reserve made the Great Depression much worse. One reason: in 1928 the strong leader who had guided the Fed for over a decade died. Without him the Fed had no clear plan. What did this leadership gap show?
answer: A single institution can be shaped heavily by one person
choices: A single institution can be shaped heavily by one person
Central banks always make the same choices no matter who leads
Only elected officials matter in economic policy
Committees always outperform any single leader
context: Strong died in October 1928, less than a year before the crash. His absence left the Fed without a dominant voice able to force the system into aggressive lender-of-last-resort action during the 1930-33 bank failures. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: Friedman and Schwartz identified an internal Federal Reserve doctrine that helped destroy the banking system. The doctrine said the Fed should not rescue banks it judged unsound. What is this rescue-averse doctrine usually called?
answer: The real-bills doctrine (in its liquidationist form)
choices: The real-bills doctrine (in its liquidationist form)
The gold-standard doctrine
The Bagehot doctrine
The monetarist doctrine
context: The real-bills doctrine's liquidationist descendant held that the Fed should not lend to banks whose portfolios contained questionable loans -- exactly the banks needing rescue in 1930-33. The doctrine ensured the Fed refused to provide the liquidity that could have stopped the cascade. Source: Grokipedia 'Real bills doctrine' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002 a Fed governor who had studied the Great Depression as a historian gave a speech in Chicago. He ended by speaking to the old authors of the 1963 book. What did he admit at the close?
answer: You're right, we did it, we're very sorry, but thanks to you we won't do it again
choices: You're right, we did it, we're very sorry, but thanks to you we won't do it again
You were partly right, we admit some errors were made
You were largely wrong, but your work provoked useful thinking
You were right about the mechanics but wrong about the ultimate cause
context: Bernanke's November 8 2002 speech at Friedman's 90th-birthday conference conceded institutional Fed responsibility for the Great Depression -- an extraordinary public admission that made the Friedman-Schwartz thesis officially accepted. Source: federalreserve.gov (Bernanke 2002 speech text).

question: The Austrian school looks at the roaring 1920s and says the loose credit and easy money of the boom years were themselves the cause of the 1929 crash. In their view, the crash and the Great Depression that followed were what?
answer: The unavoidable hangover after an artificial boom
choices: The unavoidable hangover after an artificial boom
A random bad-luck event with no economic cause
A result only of tariffs, not money or credit
A normal year, no worse than any other
context: The Austrian addition: the 1929 bust was not just an accident that the Fed mishandled; it was the necessary correction of the malinvestment the Fed's own 1921-29 easing had produced. The two 1963 books agree that the Fed erred; they disagree about which decade's error was primary. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Milton Friedman won the Nobel Prize in Economics. His coauthor Anna Schwartz never won one, though the pair wrote the definitive American monetary history. In which year did Friedman get his Nobel?
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on monetary theory and consumption analysis. Schwartz's absence from the prize list is often cited as an example of the discipline's gender-biased recognition practices. Source: Grokipedia 'Anna Schwartz' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1963 book said the Fed's tight money in 1929-33 caused the Depression. That view is now standard even inside the Fed. What point about political economy does Bernanke's 2002 admission press?
answer: Institutional acceptance of a critical thesis by the very institution being criticized changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses -- for better or worse
choices: Institutional acceptance of a critical thesis by the very institution being criticized changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses -- for better or worse
Institutional acceptance of criticism has no effect on future policy
The Fed rarely acknowledges past errors publicly
Fed doctrine is entirely determined by whoever chairs the FOMC
context: The 2002 concession shaped Bernanke's own 2008 response (aggressive lender-of-last-resort action, massive QE). Austrian critics argue that by avoiding the 1930s error Bernanke created a different error -- long-lasting cheap money that seeded the 2020-24 inflation. Institutional learning has costs as well as benefits. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In a 2008 Wall Street Journal interview at age 92, Anna Schwartz delivered a striking verdict on Ben Bernanke's crisis response. It effectively reversed the endorsement Bernanke had claimed six years earlier at Friedman's birthday party. What did she say about him?
answer: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
choices: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
That he was implementing exactly the policy she and Friedman had recommended
That his response would restore price stability within one year
That she remained firmly in agreement with his approach
context: Schwartz's October 2008 Wall Street Journal interview sharply criticized Bernanke's crisis response. Six years after Bernanke had claimed the Friedman-Schwartz mantle at the birthday party, the surviving coauthor publicly withdrew the endorsement. Source: Wall Street Journal (October 18 2008).

question: In March 1975 Milton Friedman took a six-day trip to a South American country. A private group had asked him. He met the ruler for about 45 minutes. He gave talks in the capital on inflation. Which country was it?
answer: Chile
choices: Chile
Argentina
Peru
Brazil
context: Friedman visited Chile March 1975 at the invitation of a private Chilean foundation. He met Augusto Pinochet briefly and wrote one follow-up letter with monetary and economic recommendations. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: In the late 1970s Chile moved from a tightly controlled economy to a free-market one. It cut price controls, opened up trade, and let private firms grow. What happened over the next 20 years?
answer: The country grew much richer over the next 20 years
choices: The country grew much richer over the next 20 years
The country immediately got much poorer
Nothing changed at all
Everyone left the country
context: 'The Chicago Boys' were about 25 Chilean economists trained at Chicago under a 1955-founded exchange with the Catholic University of Chile. Their leaders included Sergio de Castro (Finance Minister 1976-82) and Hernan Buchi. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Boys.

question: Friedman's 1975 Chile trip stirred up a lot of anger. Chile was under a military government at the time. It had taken power in September 1973. Who ruled the country when Friedman visited?
answer: Augusto Pinochet
choices: Augusto Pinochet
Salvador Allende
Eduardo Frei
Juan Peron
context: Augusto Pinochet came to power in the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew the elected socialist president Salvador Allende. He ruled until 1990. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet.

question: Some people accused Friedman of endorsing the dictator Pinochet after his visit to Chile. In a 1976 letter to Newsweek he replied with one specific phrase about the government. Which line matches what he said?
answer: A regime that I have nothing but dislike for
choices: A regime that I have nothing but dislike for
A shining example of Latin American governance
The best hope for South American development
A necessary transitional phase toward liberty
context: In his 1976 Newsweek letter Friedman described the Pinochet regime as 'one that I have nothing but dislike for.' He compared his visit to a doctor treating a patient in a country whose government he disapproved of. Source: Friedman, Newsweek (1976); Two Lucky People (1998).

question: In 1980 Friedman also visited a large communist state and gave its leaders similar advice. Almost no one protested that trip. Which country was it?
answer: Communist China
choices: Communist China
The Soviet Union
Vietnam
Cuba
context: Friedman visited China in 1980, meeting Chinese leaders including Zhao Ziyang. He argued the selective outrage over his Chile visit reflected a political double standard, since the China visit went uncontested. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Starting in 1975, a group called the Chicago Boys reformed Chile's economy. They sold off state industries, cut tariffs, and opened up trade. In 1973 about 45% of Chileans were poor. What was the poverty rate by 2010?
answer: About 10 percent
choices: About 10 percent
About 60 percent
About 40 percent
Essentially unchanged
context: Chilean poverty fell from ~45% (1973) to ~10% (2010) as measured by the Chilean national statistics agency and the World Bank. Chile went from poorest to richest per-capita economy in South America. Source: worldbank.org (Chile poverty and inequality data).

question: On October 5, 1988, Chileans voted in a special election on whether General Augusto Pinochet should remain in power. What was the outcome of the vote?
answer: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
choices: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
Pinochet won and remained in power for another decade
The plebiscite was cancelled by the military
Pinochet abdicated before the vote was counted
context: The October 5, 1988 plebiscite voted Pinochet out. Free elections in December 1989 chose Patricio Aylwin as president; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Chilean_national_plebiscite.

question: Chile went back to democracy in 1990, and center-left governments took over. First the Christian Democrats came in, then Socialist-led coalitions. What did those elected governments do about the Chicago Boys' free-market reforms?
answer: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
choices: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
They reversed nearly every reform within the first two years
They nationalized every privatized industry immediately
They abolished the central bank
context: Successor democratic governments in Chile substantially retained the market-economy framework across three decades of alternating center-left and center-right rule. Chile continued as the wealthiest South American economy per capita through the 2010s. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run macro data).

question: Friedman's 1975 Chile visit generated protests at his 1976 Nobel Prize ceremony in Stockholm. Which specific prize did Friedman win that year?
answer: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
choices: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
The Nobel Peace Prize
The Nobel Prize in Literature
The Franklin Institute Bower Award
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel in Economic Sciences 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' Protests at the Stockholm ceremony centered on the Chile visit. Source: nobelprize.org (Friedman 1976).

question: The Chile case is often used to argue that free-market economics could not be separated from military rule. Friedman rejected that by pointing to a pattern in his other trips to authoritarian countries. What was that pattern?
answer: He also visited China, the USSR, and Yugoslavia without comparable protest
choices: He also visited China, the USSR, and Yugoslavia without comparable protest
He refused ever to enter any country ruled by a dictator
He only visited democracies aligned with the US
He limited his travel exclusively to Western Europe
context: Friedman visited Communist China (1980), the Soviet Union, and Yugoslavia in earlier years, giving similar advice without generating comparable protests. He argued the selective outrage over Chile reflected political, not analytical, judgment. Source: Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: The full Chile story from 1973 to the 2010s is often cited as a real-world natural experiment in economic-reform outcomes. Which one-sentence summary is most accurate to the record?
answer: Chile went from poorest to richest South American economy while eventually returning to peaceful democracy
choices: Chile went from poorest to richest South American economy while eventually returning to peaceful democracy
Chile remained the poorest South American economy throughout the entire period
Chile experienced total economic collapse and mass emigration
Chile abandoned all market reforms within five years of democratization
context: The record: Chile in 1973 was the poorest large South American economy; by the 2000s it was the richest per capita; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful and free-market reforms were substantially retained by successor democratic governments. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run data).

question: In 1968 a famous economist said that when a central bank prints money to cut unemployment, it works for a bit. Then prices just keep rising and jobs don't stay. What is that steady price rise called?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
Deflation
Full employment
Barter
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (American Economic Review, March 1968), from his December 29, 1967 AEA presidential address. Source: jstor.org (Friedman AER 1968).

question: In a 1968 speech, Milton Friedman said the long-run US jobless rate is set by real things. Think job-search time, worker choices, and minimum-wage laws. What did he call this long-run floor?
answer: The natural rate of unemployment
choices: The natural rate of unemployment
The equilibrium wage floor
The frictional threshold
The employment ceiling
context: Friedman's natural-rate hypothesis: there is a rate of unemployment determined by real, non-monetary factors. Monetary policy cannot push unemployment permanently below it; it can only produce temporary reductions at the cost of accelerating inflation. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: For years many economists believed a government could always trade a little more inflation for a little less unemployment. One skeptic in 1968 warned that in the long run this trade-off would break down. What did he say would happen to the trade-off over time?
answer: Collapse
choices: Collapse
Steepen sharply
Move upward for a decade
Remain constant forever
context: Friedman argued that once workers expected 4% inflation, they would demand 4% higher nominal wages, and unemployment would return to the natural rate -- with 4% inflation now baked in. The trade-off vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: In the late 1960s, two economists working apart agreed on one thing. No matter how much money a government prints to cut unemployment, the jobless rate always drifts back to the same level. What is that level called?
answer: The natural rate of unemployment
choices: The natural rate of unemployment
The full-employment ceiling
The minimum-wage floor
The consumer price line
context: Edmund Phelps published 'Phillips Curves, Expectations of Inflation and Optimal Unemployment over Time' (Economica, August 1967) shortly before Friedman's AER paper. Phelps won the Nobel in 2006 specifically for this work. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Phelps 1967).

question: Two economists updated an old chart about jobs and prices. They added one big missing piece: what workers and shoppers think prices will do next year. What is this missing piece called?
answer: Inflation expectations
choices: Inflation expectations
Federal deficit levels
International trade balances
Corporate tax rates
context: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve: workers demand nominal wages that account for expected inflation. Once expectations adjust, the trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman (1968); Phelps (1967).

question: In 1968 an economist warned that pushing unemployment too low would cause runaway inflation. By 1980, how high had the yearly jump in American prices reached?

About 1 percent
Over 30 percent
About half a percent
context: US CPI inflation ran ~2% in 1965, rising to ~13% by 1980. Unemployment did not fall permanently; both inflation and unemployment were high (stagflation) -- exactly what Friedman's 1968 address had predicted twelve years earlier. Source: bls.gov (CPI historical).

question: In the 1970s an American economy had high inflation (prices rising fast) and high unemployment (many out of work) at the same time. Older theory said one problem was supposed to push down the other. What one-word name did economists give this new mix?

choices: Stagflation
Depression
Deflation
Recession
context: Stagflation (stagnation + inflation) is the name for the 1970s combination of high unemployment and high inflation. The word was coined by British politician Iain Macleod in 1965. It marked the failure of the stable-Phillips-curve consensus. Source: Grokipedia 'Stagflation.'

question: Friedman said that if the government tries to lower unemployment with surprise inflation, the trick stops working once people start to expect the higher prices. What happens to unemployment once people expect it?

It stays permanently low forever
It falls all the way to zero
It becomes disconnected from prices entirely

question: The natural-rate idea carries a warning for central banks. Say a bank tries to hold unemployment below the natural rate. What does the theory say must happen?

Doing so requires only a one-time inflation shock

Doing so imposes no long-run inflation cost at all
context: The accelerationist implication: if the Fed keeps trying to push unemployment below natural, it must keep raising expected inflation to keep workers surprised. 4% then 8% then 16% -- eventually the monetary system breaks down. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: Friedman's 1968 address is the foundation for a specific modern central-bank practice adopted in most developed economies since the early 1990s. What practice?

Complete abandonment of any monetary rule
context: Modern inflation targeting (New Zealand 1990, then dozens of countries) rests on the Friedman-Phelps insight: keep inflation expectations stable and the economy tends toward the natural rate. question: An Austrian-born economist won the 1974 Nobel Prize for one idea. No small group of planners can ever know all the local facts in a whole economy. What is this idea called?

question: When Hayek accepted the 1974 Nobel, he gave a lecture warning that economists had copied the look of the natural sciences without the real knowledge those methods require. What title did Hayek give the Stockholm lecture that mocked his own field?

question: An old thinker argued that morals, family, property, and the market grew slowly over thousands of years, and no small group of clever planners could redesign them from scratch without breaking them. What did he name the mistake of thinking otherwise?

question: A veteran economist rejects both "conservative" and "libertarian" as labels. He wants a name for defenders of old freedoms — free speech, jury trial, honest money — against planners on every side. Which broad economic idea does his tradition most defend?

question: If you spend your Saturday morning playing video games, you cannot ALSO spend it mowing lawns for money. The lost lawn money is a cost of playing video games. What is this kind of cost called?

context: Friedrich von Wieser (1851 Vienna - 1926 St. Gilgen) succeeded Menger at the University of Vienna in 1903 and held the chair until 1922. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: One trader will pay $50 for a baseball card because he loves the team. Another trader will pay only $2 for the same card because he does not care about baseball. What does this show about the 'value' of a card?

choices: Value is not a fixed number -- it depends on what each person wants

context: Paula Wieser's marriage to Eugen Boehm-Bawerk made Boehm-Bawerk Friedrich Wieser's brother-in-law. The two studied together as students and worked in parallel for the rest of their careers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser came back to Vienna in 1903. Before that he spent nearly twenty years teaching in another Habsburg capital. He taught at a German-language school there. In which city was it?

question: In 1917 the emperor of Austria-Hungary picked a famous economist for his cabinet. The economist was put in charge of trade and business. What is that branch usually called?
answer: Commerce

question: A hungry man eats one apple, then a second, then a third. The pleasure the third apple gives him is less than the pleasure the first one did. Nineteenth-century economists needed a word for the extra usefulness of that LAST unit added. Which term is the English translation of Wieser's 1884 coinage?
answer: marginal utility
choices: marginal utility
consumer surplus
producer surplus
elasticity of demand
context: Grenznutzen = MARGINAL UTILITY -- the value of the last (marginal) unit consumed, and the reason a thirsty man in the desert pays a fortune for the first canteen and nothing for the tenth. Alfred Marshall coined 'consumer surplus' and 'producer surplus'; 'elasticity of demand' is also Marshall. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A farmer stares at his field in early spring. He can plant it with wheat or with barley -- not both. If he plants wheat, the real cost he bears is not the money for the seed; it is the barley crop he could have grown on that same field and now will not. Friedrich Wieser coined a German word for exactly this idea (Alternativkosten), and the English translation is now standard in every economics textbook. answer: opportunity cost
choices: opportunity cost
sunk cost
marginal cost
fixed cost
context: Wieser's Alternativkosten translates as OPPORTUNITY COST -- the value of the next-best alternative use foregone. Sunk cost is spent-and-unrecoverable; marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; fixed cost does not vary with output. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: In 1889 an Austrian economist wrote a much easier book teaching a new idea called subjective value. What does subjective value say decides what a thing is worth?

For many 1890s German readers, Wieser -- not Menger -- was HOW they first met the theory. Karl Menger the mathematician was Carl Menger's son. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A steel mill makes train wheels using iron ore, coal, and skilled workers. The classical economists said the wheels' value came from adding up the labor in each part. With the age of the machinery used

Arbitrage is exploiting price gaps; aggregation adds micro-quantities; depreciation reduces capital value over time. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued that no small group of central planners can ever gather all the little local details — who wants what, where, when — that regular people and market prices already carry through the whole economy. What did Hayek call this?

question: An economist watched horse-and-buggy makers lose out to cars, silent-film stars lose out to talkies, and typewriters lose out to home computers. He said the market's most important trait is exactly this sweeping-away of the old by the new. What two-word phrase did he coin?

question: Friedrich Wieser was born a commoner (plain 'Friedrich Wieser') but died a nobleman ('Friedrich von Wieser'). question: The rule 'bad money drives out good' was first written down by a medieval bishop. Later a Polish astronomer wrote it, and later still an Englishman. Why do you think three people in three places all found the same rule?
answer: The rule describes a real pattern that repeats whenever coins are debased
choices: The rule describes a real pattern that repeats whenever coins are debased
They all read the same secret book from ancient Greece
Their kings paid each of them to say it
The rule was made up and passed on as a joke
context: Macleod's 1858 book The Elements of Political Economy attached Gresham's name to the maxim. Naming honors are downstream of who happens to publish the compilation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Dunning_Macleod.

question: In 1965 the United States passed a Coinage Act. It removed one metal from newly minted dimes and quarters. A copper-nickel mix took its place. Which metal did the 1965 act remove?
answer: Silver
choices: Silver
Gold
Zinc
Bronze
context: The Coinage Act 1965 removed silver from dimes and quarters and clad them in copper-nickel; Americans quickly pulled the pre-1965 silver coins out of pocket circulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Coinage_Act_of_1965.

question: Within a few years of the 1965 US Coinage Act, pre-1965 US silver dimes and quarters largely vanished from pocket change. Gresham's Law names the specific mechanism that made them disappear. What did Americans do with the silver coins?
answer: They pulled them from circulation and hoarded or melted them
choices: They pulled them from circulation and hoarded or melted them
They deposited them at the Federal Reserve to be re-issued
They mailed them to the US Treasury for silver certificates
They exchanged them at banks for the new clad coins
context: The classic modern instance of Gresham's Law: as soon as the copper-nickel dime and quarter appeared, ordinary savers pulled pre-1965 silver coins from change and kept them for their metal value. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: Gresham's Law depends on one very specific legal condition being in force. Without that condition, the mechanism does not fire. Which condition must be present?
answer: Both coins are declared legal tender at the same face value
choices: Both coins are declared legal tender at the same face value
One coin is manufactured by a foreign mint
The economy is under a fixed gold standard
The central bank is targeting a specific inflation rate
context: The law's engine is legal-tender equality: only when the state forces the two coins to trade at the same face value will spenders unload the worth-less coin and hoard the worth-more one. Without that fiat equality, they would simply trade at their true weights. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: Bitcoin is money that lives only on computers. No government prints it. Instead of a bank, hard math puzzles protect it. What is the general name for money like Bitcoin that runs on computers and math?
answer: Cryptocurrency
choices: Cryptocurrency
A stablecoin
A stock
A treasury bond
context: Hal Finney (1956-2014) was a cryptographer at PGP Corporation who had spent the 1990s and 2000s writing PGP's encryption code. His January 11 2009 tweet: 'Running bitcoin.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Hal Finney's famous January 11 2009 tweet was exactly two words describing what his computer was doing. What did the tweet say?
answer: Running bitcoin
choices: Running bitcoin
Mining bitcoin
Testing bitcoin
Downloading bitcoin
context: 'Running bitcoin.' Finney was the second-ever Bitcoin node operator, running the software days after Satoshi's own machine started the network. Source: twitter.com/halfin (January 11 2009).

question: In January 2009 the maker of Bitcoin sent 10 coins to another programmer. It was the first time Bitcoin ever moved between two people. Why was that small transfer so important?
answer: It proved the new digital money actually worked as designed
choices: It proved the new digital money actually worked as designed
It made both programmers instantly rich forever
It was declared legal currency by the United States
It replaced credit cards worldwide within a month

question: Before working on Bitcoin, a programmer helped build tools that scramble emails so only the person with the right key can read them. What is this scrambling of messages called?
answer: Encryption
choices: Encryption
Advertising
Downloading
Copying
context: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), designed by Phil Zimmermann and developed at PGP Corporation, was Finney's day job through the 1990s and 2000s. He wrote much of the code behind PGP as journalists and dissidents relied on it worldwide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy.

question: Later in 2009, Hal Finney was diagnosed with a nerve disease. It slowly took away his ability to move. By 2013 he could only type by tracking his eyes. Which disease did he have?
answer: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
choices: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Parkinson's disease
Multiple sclerosis
Huntington's disease
context: ALS -- Lou Gehrig's disease -- progressively paralyzed Finney. His 2013 bitcointalk.org essay 'Bitcoin and Me' was typed with eye-tracking software when almost all voluntary movement was gone. Source: bitcointalk.org (Bitcoin and Me, 2013).

question: Hal Finney's 2013 bitcointalk.org essay recounts running the second Bitcoin node, receiving the first person-to-person transaction, and watching Bitcoin grow while his body failed. What is the essay's title?
answer: Bitcoin and Me
choices: Bitcoin and Me
Running Bitcoin
The First Node
Notes from a Cryptographer
context: 'Bitcoin and Me' (bitcointalk.org, March 19 2013) is Finney's own account of everything from the first mailing-list post to his ALS diagnosis. It reads as a plain first-person history from inside the earliest Bitcoin community. Source: bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=155054.

question: An early cypherpunk programmer worked on a digital cash idea long before Bitcoin existed. The unsolved problem in his design was that his system still needed one central trusted server. Why is a single trusted server a big weakness for a would-be currency?
answer: If that server is taken down or corrupted, the whole currency breaks
choices: If that server is taken down or corrupted, the whole currency breaks
It always makes the currency more valuable
It has never caused any real system to fail
It is exactly what Bitcoin uses today
context: Alcor (Scottsdale, Arizona) performed Finney's cryopreservation; Finney had been a long-term life-extension advocate. Bitcoin was one of many long-view bets in his life. Source: alcor.org (case report A-2643).

question: Hal Finney's 2004 paper was one of the direct sources Satoshi Nakamoto cited in the Bitcoin white paper. It was called 'Reusable Proofs of Work.' What short name did Finney give his system?
answer: RPOW
choices: RPOW
HashCash
b-money
bit gold
context: RPOW (Reusable Proofs of Work), 2004, built on Adam Back's earlier hashcash and pushed the idea toward a spendable digital token. Satoshi cited RPOW as prior art in the Bitcoin white paper. Source: rpow.net.

question: For years Hal Finney was one of the small handful of people accused of being Satoshi Nakamoto. Two lines of evidence rule out that theory. Which pair?
answer: His own explicit denial, plus timeline evidence that he was training for a marathon while Satoshi was posting
choices: His own explicit denial, plus timeline evidence that he was training for a marathon while Satoshi was posting
His documented US citizenship, plus the fact that Satoshi's writing style was clearly non-American
His public retirement announcement, plus his stated preference for gold-backed money over digital cash
His employer's NDA obligations, plus his lack of interest in cryptographic proofs
context: Finney explicitly denied being Satoshi. Timing evidence: he was training for a marathon and posting run-times during periods Satoshi was posting emails elsewhere; forensic-text analysis has not matched. Source: newyorker.com (Andy Greenberg profile, 2014).

question: In the Bitcoin community Hal Finney is remembered as the first person besides Satoshi to see clearly what Bitcoin was going to be. What specific role did he play in the first weeks of the network?
answer: He ran the second-ever Bitcoin node, one day after the network went live
choices: He ran the second-ever Bitcoin node, one day after the network went live
He wrote the first Bitcoin exchange to trade coins for dollars
He mined the very first block, the genesis block, before Satoshi did
He edited the final draft of the Bitcoin white paper for Satoshi
context: Satoshi's own machine was Bitcoin node 1; Finney's was node 2, running January 11 2009. He received the first person-to-person transaction on Block 170 the following day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Adam Back made a system in 1997 called Hashcash. It asked every email to carry a small proof-of-work stamp to slow spam. But each stamp had a strict limit compared to money. What was that limit?
answer: Each stamp was single-use and could not be transferred like a coin
choices: Each stamp was single-use and could not be transferred like a coin
Each stamp had a fixed expiration date measured in seconds
Each stamp required a live connection to a central bank server
Each stamp was only redeemable on Microsoft-issued hardware
context: Hashcash proved you had done real computational work, but the stamp was spent after one use. Making stamps transferable required solving double-spending -- the same problem Bitcoin later solved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hashcash.

question: In 2004 a coder took Hashcash proof-of-work stamps and made them into tokens you could pass to a friend, who could pass them again. What did he name the system?
answer: Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW)
choices: Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW)
The Lightning Network
The Merkle Chain
The Cypherpunk Ledger
context: The cryptographer was Hal Finney. The RPOW acronym stands for Reusable Proofs of Work (plural of 'proof'). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Hal Finney's 2004 Reusable Proofs of Work system needed some way to prevent a token holder from spending the same token twice. What architectural choice did Finney make to solve that problem?
answer: A trusted server that tracked which stamps had been spent and issued replacements
choices: A trusted server that tracked which stamps had been spent and issued replacements
A blockchain distributed across thousands of independent nodes
A cryptographic zero-knowledge proof stored on every user's device
A quorum vote among the top 21 stamp holders
context: Finney ran the server himself on an IBM 4758 secure coprocessor, whose signed open-source code could be audited. But the trusted server was still a single point of failure. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Before Bitcoin, one early digital-cash design used special tamper-proof server hardware so users could trust the server was running honest code. Bitcoin took a totally different route to trust. What does Bitcoin trust instead of a special piece of hardware?
answer: A public network of computers all checking each other
choices: A public network of computers all checking each other
One giant government-run server in Washington
A single billionaire's private data center
The honor system between anonymous strangers
context: The 4758 was a tamper-resistant special-purpose chip designed for cryptographic key storage. Finney used it to prove the RPOW server code was the audited version -- but the trusted-server architecture itself remained a weakness. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: An early digital-cash design used a trusted server. Its designer knew the setup had one weakness that no amount of tamper-proof hardware could fix — the same weakness Bitcoin was later built to remove. What was that weakness?
answer: A single server that could be shut down or corrupted
choices: A single server that could be shut down or corrupted
The cost of buying computers
The size of individual payments
The language of the software code
context: This is the weakness Satoshi's proof-of-work + longest-chain rule solved four years later -- consensus without a trusted third party. Finney's own public writings had named the problem he could not solve. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Before 2008, digital-cash inventors could not solve one problem: how to make sure the same digital coin isn't spent twice, without trusting a central server that could freeze your money or shut down. What did the 2008 Bitcoin white paper invent to solve this?
answer: A public ledger that many strangers keep in sync using proof-of-work
choices: A public ledger that many strangers keep in sync using proof-of-work
A single trusted bank server run by a well-known company
A rule that every user must physically hand coins to each other
A promise from world governments to never seize digital money
context: One of the earliest public traces of anyone besides Satoshi running the Bitcoin software. Finney had downloaded the software the day after Christmas 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: On January 12, 2009, Satoshi Nakamoto sent Hal Finney the first person-to-person Bitcoin transfer, recorded in block 170. How much Bitcoin did that first transfer move?
answer: 10 BTC
choices: 10 BTC
50 BTC
100 BTC
context: Block 170 was the first Bitcoin transaction between two people (rather than a miner's block reward paying itself). Finney had answered Satoshi's forum post volunteering to test the network. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: About every four years, Bitcoin's rules cut the reward miners get for each new block in half. What is this event called?
answer: The halving
choices: The halving
The retarget
The airdrop
The fork
context: The halvings occurred in November 2012 (50 to 25 BTC per block), July 2016 (25 to 12.5), May 2020 (12.5 to 6.25), and April 2024 (6.25 to 3.125). The schedule caps the total supply at 21 million. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_halving.

question: Bitcoin's price history shows a rough four-year pattern of bull peaks. Which sequence gives the approximate peaks in order?
context: Each peak followed a halving by roughly 12-18 months, until the 2024-25 cycle, which peaked faster (about 8 months after the April 2024 halving) partly due to spot ETF flows. Source: grokipedia.com/page/History_of_Bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin's four-year cycle has four parts. First a crash after the peak. Then quiet buying at the low. Then a slow rise as people notice again. Then a wild spike before the next crash. Which classic Austrian pattern does this match?
answer: The boom-bust cycle Mises and Hayek attributed to monetary supply shocks
choices: The boom-bust cycle Mises and Hayek attributed to monetary supply shocks
The permanent-income consumption smoothing hypothesis of Milton Friedman
The animal-spirits investment theory of John Maynard Keynes
The productivity-growth model of Robert Solow
context: Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT) treats booms and busts as monetary phenomena rather than psychological ones. Bitcoin's cycles have been interpreted as this shape applied to a monetary asset in an early-adoption phase. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: A Palestinian-American economist wrote a 2018 book making the Austrian case for Bitcoin as sound money. He argued the halving schedule forces hard money discipline. Who wrote it, and what is the book?

choices: Saifedean Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard
Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan
Peter Thiel, Zero to One
Michael Lewis, The Big Short
context: Ammous made the argument that Bitcoin's programmatic supply schedule and its historical price cycles fit an Austrian monetary framework. Vijay Boyapati (The Bullish Case for Bitcoin) and Lyn Alden made related arguments. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: An analyst using the name 'PlanB' published a 2019 Medium post proposing a model to predict Bitcoin prices from the halving schedule alone. What is the model called, and how has it held up since?
answer: The stock-to-flow model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
choices: The stock-to-flow model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
The stock-to-flow model; it has tracked actual prices exactly through 2024
The Elliott wave model; it has tracked actual prices exactly through 2024

context: PlanB's model became famous during the 2020-21 bull market but has failed as a forecast since. The Austrian recognition move survives -- past cycles are real -- but the specific PlanB quantitative claim did not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: The 2024-25 Bitcoin cycle broke $100,000 in December 2024, only about eight months after the April 2024 halving. Prior cycles had taken 12-18 months to peak. A specific new source of demand introduced in January 2024 helps explain the compressed timing. What was it?
answer: US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, approved by the SEC on January 10, 2024

A Chinese central-bank purchase program for Bitcoin reserves
A European Central Bank digital-currency swap facility

question: A first-time Bitcoin holder in 2025 wants to know whether the past cycle pattern guarantees a next four-year peak. What is the honest analytical answer?
answer: The past cycles are real observations, but the 2024-25 cycle already broke the pattern -- past patterns do not guarantee future ones

question: Some thinkers say courts, roads, and even police could be run by private firms competing with each other. No government at all. What is this idea called?

Mixed economy
context: Hoppe was born September 2, 1949 in Peine, West Germany; joined Rothbard at UNLV in 1986; taught there until retiring in 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: In 2001, Hans-Hermann Hoppe wrote his best-known book. He argues that a king plans better for the long run than a modern rival system. What is the book's title?

The Ethics of Liberty
Man, Economy, and State
The Road to Serfdom

question: A young European scholar in the 1970s studied under one of the leading left-wing philosophers of his day. Years later he changed his mind about many things and became a well-known defender of free markets. What does this story show?

question: In 2006 Hoppe founded an annual libertarian conference held each summer in a specific Turkish coastal resort town. What is the town?

question: Hoppe uses one clear analogy to show how a king and an elected leader treat a country differently. Which analogy captures his point?

question: Hoppe's argument says an elected leader with a fixed term handles public borrowing one way. A hereditary king handles it another. What does the argument predict about the elected leader?

question: One libertarian argument goes like this: the moment two people start arguing at all, each is already using their own voice, their own body, their own time. So arguing itself assumes each person owns something. What does the argument say each person must own?

A patch of common land
The other person's attention

question: Hoppe's Democracy: The God That Failed splits the Austrian school. Two Austrians accept parts of his incentive analysis but reject his anti-democratic conclusion. Which pair is often cited?

Prices and Production

question: The 1935 book's centerpiece was the first English version of a 1920 German essay. Few English-speaking economists had ever read it. Whose essay was newly translated?

question: In 1908, an Italian economist wrote a math paper on how a fully planned economy might work. Planners would need to solve a huge number of equations to set every price. What turned out to be the practical problem with that idea?

question: Hayek added two essays to the 1935 book. The opening one covered the debate's origins. The closing one reviewed the 1920s German writing on it. What is the closing survey's short title?

question: Hayek collected his own later essays on the calculation and knowledge problem in a 1948 University of Chicago Press book. What is its title?

question: A newspaper columnist spends twelve years writing about one simple point. To judge a rule, don't just look at who it helps right now. Look at everyone it affects, including the people you can't easily see. What is this idea usually called?

question: A magazine keeps its economics writer for twenty years. Editors print what readers want, and readers can quit any time. What system keeps the magazine trying hard to please them?

question: In 1946, the same year Economics in One Lesson came out, Henry Hazlitt and Leonard Read started America's first free-market think tank. It sat in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Which group did they found?

The Reason Foundation
context: FEE (1946) predates Cato (1977), the Mises Institute (1982), and Reason Foundation (1978); Read was president, Hazlitt sat on the founding board. Source: fee.org/about/our-history.

question: In 1959 Henry Hazlitt published a book-length reply to John Maynard Keynes, working chapter by chapter through Keynes's 1936 General Theory and answering each argument in order. Which Hazlitt book was that?
answer: The Failure of the New Economics
choices: The Failure of the New Economics
Man vs. the Welfare State
The Way to Will Power
The Great Idea
context: The 1959 book is the closest thing to a full Austrian-tradition rebuttal of the General Theory, section by section; Hazlitt also edited The Critics of Keynesian Economics (1960), an anthology of every major published critique. Source: mises.org/library/failure-new-economics.

question: Friedrich Hayek publicly praised Economics in One Lesson in one short line printed on later editions of the book. Which two-word verdict did Hayek deliver?
answer: A brilliant performance
choices: A brilliant performance
A useful contribution
A necessary reminder
A worthy attempt
context: John Chamberlain gave it the Wall Street Journal review; F.A. Hayek's 'a brilliant performance' has adorned the back cover of most editions since. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson takes a French pamphleteer's 1850 essay and turns it into a mid-20th-century American book. The essay it restates was written by a dying tuberculosis patient months before his death. Which essay did Hazlitt restate?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
The Wealth of Nations
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Principles of Political Economy
context: Bastiat published the essay in July 1850 and died that December. Hazlitt's book applies its seen/unseen method to public works, tariffs, minimum wage, rent control, and every other 1946 American policy in turn. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Milton Friedman and Ron Paul both told beginners to start with Economics in One Lesson. For generations, American libertarians read it as their first book on how markets work. What single method does the book teach a reader to use on any proposed policy?
answer: Trace the consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups over time
choices: Trace the consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups over time
Sum the private benefits and subtract them from the private costs the sponsors disclose in advance
Compare the proposed policy against a randomly-selected historical policy of the same category
Accept the sponsors' stated aggregate multiplier and evaluate against that benchmark
context: This is Hazlitt's 'one lesson' verbatim from chapter 1: extend the analysis in TIME (past the immediate effect) and in SCOPE (past the visible group). Every remaining chapter applies it. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: Deflation means prices fall over time. Next year, a dollar buys more than today. That sounds nice, but it can hurt jobs, because people wait to buy, hoping prices drop again. What happens to workers when nobody buys anything?
answer: Businesses lay off workers
choices: Businesses lay off workers
Wages rise quickly
Rent goes way up
New factories open
context: Bernanke was a Fed governor from 2002 to 2005, then Council of Economic Advisers chair in 2005-06, then Fed chair from February 2006. The 2002 speech previewed nearly every unconventional tool he later deployed. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In a 2002 speech, Ben Bernanke used a famous idea Milton Friedman had first shared in 1969. It showed one wild way a central bank could create money to fight deflation. What was the teaching image?
answer: Dropping money from a helicopter
choices: Dropping money from a helicopter
Burying coins in bottles for people to dig up
Sending cheques to every household
Buying every unsold house in the country
context: Friedman used the helicopter image in his 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' as a pedagogical device -- not as policy advocacy. Bernanke's citation converted the device into a proposed toolkit. Source: Grokipedia 'Helicopter money' (2026-09-05).

question: The nickname 'Helicopter Ben' stuck to the future Fed chair for the rest of his career. It came from his citation of a specific 1969 essay by Milton Friedman that used the helicopter image. What is that essay called?
answer: The Optimum Quantity of Money
choices: The Optimum Quantity of Money
A Program for Monetary Stability
The Role of Monetary Policy
Free to Choose
context: Friedman's 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' used the helicopter as a thought experiment for a one-time increase in the money stock. Bernanke's 2002 reuse of the image gave him a nickname that outlasted his tenure. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: Bernanke's 2002 speech listed tools a central bank could use once short-term rates hit zero. Which asset purchase headed his list?
answer: Buying long-term Treasuries to lower long-term yields
choices: Buying long-term Treasuries to lower long-term yields
Buying gold bullion at fixed prices
Selling foreign-currency reserves against domestic bonds
Issuing zero-coupon perpetual bonds directly to the public
context: The 2002 speech listed buying long-term Treasuries, buying agency debt, buying foreign government bonds, and (in extreme cases) directly funding tax cuts by printing. All but the last were deployed 2008-14. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: Nearly every tool listed in the 2002 speech was deployed between 2008 and 2014 under three named Fed programs. Which trio corresponds to what Bernanke had previewed?
answer: QE1, QE2, and Operation Twist
choices: QE1, QE2, and Operation Twist
TARP, PDCF, and PPIP
SLR, GSIB, and TLAC
SDR, IMF SDR-A, and SDR-B
context: QE1 (November 2008-March 2010, $1.75T), QE2 (November 2010-June 2011, $600B), Operation Twist (September 2011-December 2012), and QE3 (September 2012-October 2014) implemented in reality what Bernanke had merely sketched in 2002. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 speech's core argument was a claim about what a specific kind of central bank can always do to fight deflation, regardless of how low interest rates already are. What was the claim?
answer: A central bank with a fiat currency can always create money at zero marginal cost
choices: A central bank with a fiat currency can always create money at zero marginal cost
A central bank must always coordinate with the fiscal authority
A central bank cannot inflate without abandoning its inflation target
A central bank must convert to a gold standard to maintain credibility
context: The core Bernanke claim: unlike a gold-backed central bank, a fiat central bank faces no natural limit on money creation. The only constraint is political will. This was reassurance to markets facing deflation risk; it was warning to Austrians. Source: Grokipedia 'Fiat money' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian critics called the 2002 speech a blueprint for eventual currency debasement. Three Austrian-tradition voices attacked it in real time. Which trio is usually cited?
answer: Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, and Jim Rogers
choices: Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, and Jim Rogers
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Larry Summers
Alan Greenspan, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz, and Karl Brunner
context: Murphy at the Mises Institute, Schiff on television, and commodities investor Jim Rogers all publicly warned that a fiat central bank willing to buy anything creates the conditions for eventual currency crisis. Source: mises.org/library/robert-p-murphy (2002-2010 articles).

question: Exactly six years after the 2002 speech, in November 2008, the same figure -- now Fed chair -- launched the first program of asset purchases at unprecedented scale. What was the first program called?
answer: QE1
choices: QE1
TARP
TALF
MMLF
context: QE1, launched November 25 2008, initially bought $600 billion of mortgage-backed securities and $300 billion of Treasuries. It grew from there. The 2002 speech now reads as the most accurate preview of Fed crisis policy ever given -- everything Bernanke said the Fed could do, he did. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 2002 speech, Bernanke admitted one power central banks always have. Critics called it 'monetary financing of fiscal policy.' What did he say a central bank could always do?
answer: Fund direct tax cuts by printing money if necessary
choices: Fund direct tax cuts by printing money if necessary
Freeze all commercial bank deposits by decree
Impose negative interest rates on retail savings
Suspend all foreign-exchange transactions overnight
context: The speech acknowledged that a fiat central bank could in extremis monetize a tax cut. Critics said this was the door to 'helicopter money' in the literal sense: government spending funded directly by the printing press, bypassing bond markets. Source: federalreserve.gov (Bernanke 2002 speech text).

question: The 2002 Bernanke speech teaches a specific recognition move about how central-bank crisis rhetoric relates to future policy. Which move?
answer: Public speeches by central bankers about what they could do in a hypothetical crisis often preview exactly what they will do in a real one
choices: Public speeches by central bankers about what they could do in a hypothetical crisis often preview exactly what they will do in a real one
Central bank speeches are cheap talk and rarely predict actual future policy
Central banks always follow through on rate cuts announced in advance
Central bank crisis toolkits are never used because they exist to reassure
context: Read carefully, the 2002 speech told a listener exactly what would happen if a large financial crisis struck. Six years later it did, and the toolkit was deployed. Austrians took the speech seriously; most others did not. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: One book argues a bottle of water is worth more to a thirsty hiker in the desert than to someone standing by a river. So a thing's value depends on who wants it and when. What is this idea about value called?
answer: Subjective value
choices: Subjective value
Labor theory of value
Fixed pricing
A price ceiling
context: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics (Yale University Press, 1949), roughly 881 pages. Socialism (1922, English 1936), The Theory of Money and Credit (1912), and Bureaucracy (1944) were the earlier Mises books it drew together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Mises opened his 1949 book Human Action with one seven-word line. He said the whole book rested on it. Which sentence begins Human Action?
answer: Human action is purposeful behavior.
choices: Human action is purposeful behavior.
In the long run we are all dead.
The proper study of mankind is man.
There is no such thing as society.
context: The line is the opening of Chapter I, Section 1 -- and the axiom from which the entire treatise is deduced. The Keynes line, Pope line, and Thatcher line were all real but from other authors. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/human-action-purposeful-action.

question: One economist said economics is like geometry: start from an obvious truth about people, then reason step by step. No lab tests needed. He rejected the opposing view that economics should copy physics and test ideas with real-world data. What is that opposing view called?
answer: Positivism, which models economics on natural-science hypothesis testing
choices: Positivism, which models economics on natural-science hypothesis testing
Scholasticism, which grounds economics in medieval theology
Historicism, which denies any general economic laws at all
Mercantilism, which measures national wealth by the trade balance
context: Mises's target was the mid-20th-century positivist program (later associated with Milton Friedman's 1953 essay 'The Methodology of Positive Economics') that wanted economics to work like physics -- form hypotheses, test them statistically, discard the failed ones. Praxeology instead deduces laws from the action axiom and uses history only to illustrate. Historicism was the OLDER German quarrel with Menger; mercantilism was pre-Smithian; scholasticism belonged to an earlier era. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: In Human Action, Mises says only one kind of thing actually chooses. Markets, societies, and economies are just the result of many such choices, planned by nobody. What does he call this rule?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Methodological holism
Methodological pluralism
Methodological monism
context: 'The market' does not act; only Alice at the fruit stall and Bob at the cash register act. A price, a boom, a shortage are the aggregate outcome no individual planned. Methodological holism (the whole society acts as a unit) was the position Mises rejected; the other two are unrelated terms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Human Action wasn't written first in America. Mises had already published a long German book while in exile in Geneva in 1940. What was the title of that earlier German book?
answer: Nationaloekonomie
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Gemeinwirtschaft
Kapital und Kapitalzins
Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre
context: Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens (Union, Geneva, 1940) was completed in the spring of 1940, weeks before the fall of France. Mises rewrote and expanded it into English as Human Action. Gemeinwirtschaft (1922) was his book on socialism; Kapital und Kapitalzins was Boehm-Bawerk; Grundsaetze was Menger's 1871 founding text. Source: mises.org/library/book/nationalokonomie-theorie-des-handelns-und-wirtschaftens.

question: Chapter 26 of Human Action folded in a much older Mises argument. He had first made the case in a 1920 German journal essay. Which argument does Chapter 26 grow into?
answer: That rational calculation under socialism is impossible without market prices
choices: That rational calculation under socialism is impossible without market prices
That business cycles are caused by central-bank credit expansion
That the value of money regresses back to a prior barter demand
That interest rates reflect the community's time preference
context: Mises's 1920 essay 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' became Chapter 26 of Human Action ('The Impossibility of Economic Calculation Under Socialism'). The credit-expansion theory of the cycle became Chapter 20; the regression theorem for money is Chapter 17; the time-preference theory of interest is Chapter 19. Each has its own chapter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.
