question: A major Austrian-school economist taught for twenty-four years at a big New York university that paid him nothing. His salary came instead from a private foundation set up by a rich donor. What is this way of funding out-of-favor scholars called?
answer: Private philanthropy
choices: Private philanthropy
Government grant funding
Student tuition
Corporate advertising
context: The Kansas City-based William Volker Fund quietly financed several classical-liberal appointments (Hayek at Chicago's Committee on Social Thought, Mises at NYU) that the mainstream foundations would not touch. The Rockefeller, Ford, and Carnegie foundations were the era's dominant funders but tilted toward the postwar Keynesian and behavioral-science consensus. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/anonymous-funding-academic-right-william-volker-and-henry-earhart.

question: An Austrian economist argues that a single company is only a lasting monopoly if the government blocks rivals from entering. Say there is no legal block, and the big company keeps prices very high. What tends to happen next?
answer: New competitors enter and undercut the price
choices: New competitors enter and undercut the price
The company holds high prices forever
The government must always break it up first
Prices only rise even faster
context: Murray Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (1962) was the direct fruit of the NYU seminar and the Volker commission. The Constitution of Liberty (1960) was Hayek's; Prices and Production (1931) was Hayek's LSE lectures; Capital and Interest (1884-1889) was Boehm-Bawerk's earlier three-volume work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: A 1949 book argues that economics starts from a single fact: people choose. Every choice ranks options against each other and takes one. From this starting point, the book claims, the whole shape of markets can be worked out. Which broad approach does this describe?
answer: Reasoning outward from the fact that people act with purpose
choices: Reasoning outward from the fact that people act with purpose
Measuring past prices and predicting the next number
Running large surveys to find average behavior
Copying the methods of physics to find fixed economic laws
context: The 1963 second edition (still Yale) was marred by typographical errors, which the 1966 Regnery edition corrected. Regnery had been publishing conservative and classical-liberal titles from Chicago since 1947. The Mises Institute's current scholar's edition (1998, Auburn) is set from the Regnery text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Inside the Austrian tradition, Mises's students and later Austrian economists refer to Human Action by a nickname so short it needs no adjective. Which one-word label do Austrians use when they say 'go read the ___' and mean Human Action?
answer: the treatise
choices: the treatise
the primer
the compendium
the manifesto
context: The book's subtitle already announced it ('A Treatise on Economics'); inside the tradition the definite article is enough. Ayn Rand's Atlas Shrugged is 'the novel'; Marx's Capital is 'Kapital'; Mises's Human Action is 'the treatise.' Source: fee.org/articles/ludwig-von-misess-human-action-a-50th-anniversary-appreciation.

question: A big country tells a trading partner: we could put a huge tax on your cars, but instead, could you just agree to ship us fewer cars each year? The partner agrees, so US carmakers can keep selling more of their own. What kind of trade limit is this?
answer: A voluntary export restraint
choices: A voluntary export restraint
A blockade
A currency swap
A patent
context: Called 'voluntary' because Japan self-imposed the cap under diplomatic pressure, avoiding a formal US tariff. The cap was renegotiated upward through the 1980s and formally ended in 1994. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Voluntary_export_restraint.

question: In 1981, the US and Japan agreed on a cap for Japanese cars sold in America each year. About how many cars per year did the deal allow?
answer: About 1.68 million
choices: About 1.68 million
About 500,000
About 3.2 million
About 800,000
context: Below the roughly 1.9 million Japanese cars sold in the US in 1980. The cap was raised to 1.85 million in 1984 and to 2.3 million in 1985 as Detroit stabilized. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Voluntary_export_restraint.

question: The 1981 auto deal was made to protect a set of American carmakers losing sales to Japan. Which carmakers?
answer: General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler
choices: General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler
Boeing, Lockheed, and Northrop
US Steel, Bethlehem, and Republic
Kodak, Polaroid, and Xerox
context: Detroit's Big Three. United Auto Workers jobs in Michigan, Ohio, and Indiana were the politically visible beneficiaries; the Reagan administration framed the deal as breathing space for domestic industry. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trade_policy_of_the_Reagan_administration.

question: Robert Crandall studied the 1981 Japan car deal for the Brookings Institution. His 1987 paper worked out how much the deal raised the average US car price. In 1983 dollars, about how much per car?
answer: About $1,000 per car
choices: About $1,000 per car
About $50 per car
About $200 per car
About $8,000 per car
context: Later Feenstra work and the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1999 AER paper put the total consumer cost at $5-8 billion per year. Domestic makers raised prices under the umbrella of reduced import competition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Crandall.

question: During the 1980s Japan car quota, models like the Honda Accord, Toyota Camry, and Nissan Maxima grew bigger, fancier, and more expensive. The cheap little hatchback almost vanished. Which feature of the quota caused that shift?
answer: The cap was set in vehicles rather than in dollars, so each unit had to earn more profit
choices: The cap was set in vehicles rather than in dollars, so each unit had to earn more profit
A separate side-agreement banned imports below a set retail price
American dealers refused to stock any small Japanese cars
The Reagan administration imposed emissions rules only on smaller vehicles
context: This is the quality-upgrading response Robert Feenstra documented in his 1988 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper 'Quality Change Under Trade Restraints.' A per-unit cap rewards higher-margin models; a value-cap or tariff would not have. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Feenstra.

question: A country tells foreign carmakers: you may sell us only so many cars per year, no more. With fewer cars available, each car's price goes up. That extra money on each car does not go to the buying country's government. Where does it go?
answer: To the foreign carmakers as extra profit per car
choices: To the foreign carmakers as extra profit per car
To the buying country's treasury as import tax
To car dealerships as sales commissions
To the buying country's autoworker union
context: This is called quota rent. Feenstra estimated roughly $2,000 of quota rent per car flowed to the Japanese producers. An equivalent tariff would have collected the same revenue for the US Treasury; the VER simply transferred it to the foreign producers the policy claimed to punish. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Voluntary_export_restraint.

question: In 1985, a senator defends the auto Voluntary Export Restraint. He points to UAW jobs it saved in Michigan and Ohio. A Brookings economist answers that the seen worker in Michigan cost an unseen American buyer priced out of a $4,500 Japanese car. Which classical reasoning move is he using?
answer: Frederic Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen: name the invisible victim
choices: Frederic Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen: name the invisible victim
Ronald Coase's transaction-cost analysis of externalities
Milton Friedman's monetary theory of nominal-price inflation
John Maynard Keynes's argument for aggregate-demand stimulus
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' set the pattern: any policy has a visible beneficiary and an invisible one who bears the cost. The auto VER had three unseens (buyer, low-income buyer priced out of the small-car segment, quota rent to Japan). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: In one country, a business needs a permit to open. Another to hire workers. Another to buy foreign parts. Another to change its prices. Every step needs a stamp from an official. What is this system called?
answer: Central planning
choices: Central planning
Free markets
A stock exchange
A tax refund
context: 'License Raj' -- 'rule by permits' -- described the system in which Indian firms needed government approval to open a factory, expand capacity, import a machine, hire above a certain scale, produce a new product, or set prices. Often 80 or more separate approvals were required. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licence_Raj.

question: During the License Raj, India's output per person grew about 1 percent a year. Economists made up a wry nickname for this slow rate. What did they call it?
answer: The Hindu rate of growth
choices: The Hindu rate of growth
The Delhi consensus
The Nehru pace
The Bharat lag
context: 'Hindu rate of growth' was coined by economist Raj Krishna as a self-critical analytic term (not a slur) for the roughly 1% per-capita growth rate India averaged 1950-80 while its Asian neighbors grew 5-8x faster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_rate_of_growth.

question: For decades India kept heavy rules on business. Factories needed government permits for almost every choice, and growth was slow. Meanwhile South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, and Hong Kong opened up trade and boomed. What nickname did those four fast-growing economies earn?
answer: The Four Asian Tigers
choices: The Four Asian Tigers
The Pacific Rim Bears
The Little Kingdoms
The Golden Islands
context: The 'Four Asian Tigers' -- South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong -- averaged 5-8x India's per-capita growth rate over 1950-80. Their more open trade regimes are the standard counterfactual for the License Raj's opportunity cost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Asian_Tigers.

question: Some firms spend money lobbying for favors like tariffs or permits. They chase these instead of making better products. What is this called?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Fair competition
Honest advertising
Product improvement
context: Anne Krueger's 1974 AER paper 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' introduced the term based on Indian and Turkish empirical work. Krueger later served as World Bank Chief Economist 1982-86 and IMF Deputy Managing Director 2001-06. Source: aeaweb.org (AER June 1974).

question: A country requires a special government permit to import cars, and the permit itself becomes worth more than the cars. Businesses spend most of their time and money chasing permits instead of making better products. What is this waste of effort called?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Regulatory arbitrage
Adverse selection
Moral hazard
context: Rent-seeking: dissipation of real resources in pursuit of state-created privileges rather than value-creation. Krueger estimated License-Raj rent-seeking dissipation at up to 7% of Indian GDP. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: In 1991 India was running out of money and could barely pay for its imports. The finance minister cut a giant system of permits. Before, companies had to get government approval for almost every business choice. What happened once the permits were gone?
answer: New businesses could start much more easily and the economy grew faster
choices: New businesses could start much more easily and the economy grew faster
All existing businesses were forced to close
The government took over every farm
India stopped trading with every other country
context: Manmohan Singh (Finance Minister 1991-96, later Prime Minister 2004-14) worked with Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to enact the reforms. The July 24, 1991 budget speech is the landmark. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manmohan_Singh.

question: After 1991, India's real per-capita income grew fast. The growth ran three decades. By 2020, roughly what multiple of the 1991 level did it reach?
answer: More than four times its 1991 level
choices: More than four times its 1991 level
About double its 1991 level
About 15 percent higher than 1991
About the same as 1991
context: India's real per-capita income more than quadrupled 1991-2020. Growth rates approximately doubled after 1991 and accelerated further in the 2000s. Hundreds of millions rose out of extreme poverty. Source: World Bank India data.

question: A 2008 scholarly synthesis of India's post-1991 reform-to-growth chain was written by an Indian-American economist based at Columbia. What is the book's title?
answer: India: The Emerging Giant
choices: India: The Emerging Giant
India Unbound
The Elephant Awakes
The Argumentative Indian
context: Arvind Panagariya's India: The Emerging Giant (Oxford UP, 2008) documents the reform-to-growth chain in detail. Panagariya later served as vice-chairman of NITI Aayog under PM Modi. Source: global.oup.com.

question: The 1991 reforms did not remove all of India's red tape at once. Which description better fits the reform's real effect?
answer: Growth accelerated dramatically without overnight transformation
choices: Growth accelerated dramatically without overnight transformation
The economy became fully deregulated within a year
All state industry was privatized within eighteen months
Tariffs went to zero within a decade
context: The reforms opened investment, cut tariffs, ended most industrial licensing -- but many state enterprises, banking regulations, and labor rules remained. The pattern is reform-and-growth-acceleration, not overnight transformation. Source: Panagariya, India: The Emerging Giant.

question: The License Raj shows how permits, licenses, and forced approvals act like a hidden tax on making things. What is the standard name for this hidden burden?
answer: Rent-seeking dissipation
choices: Rent-seeking dissipation
Consumer surplus loss
Deadweight monetary loss
Fiscal drag
context: Krueger's founding measurement: the real resources spent chasing state-created privileges are pure dissipation, adding nothing to output. This is why License-Raj-style regimes underperform: production is not just taxed but partially redirected into unproductive lobbying. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: In the 1840s, Frederic Bastiat wrote a famous line about how a good cause can lose. He said the worst thing for a good cause is not being cleverly attacked, but rather being what?
answer: Ineptly defended
choices: Ineptly defended
Loudly denounced
Silently ignored
Legally suppressed
context: The full line: 'The worst thing that can happen to a good cause is not to be skillfully attacked but to be ineptly defended.' Bastiat had watched French classical liberals lose public arguments through bad advocacy. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: Bastiat took a simple writing rule from his 'ineptly defended' idea. What rule did his own essays follow?
answer: First state the opposing case in its strongest form, then answer it
choices: First state the opposing case in its strongest form, then answer it
First denounce the opposition, then argue your own case
First appeal to authority, then invoke tradition
First mock the opponent, then move on quickly
context: Nearly every essay in Economic Sophisms first states the protectionist argument fairly, even sympathetically, then dismantles it. Anything less discredits the defender's cause. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: In a debate, before you argue against someone's idea, you first say their idea out loud in the strongest way you can. Why is this a good habit?
answer: It stops you from beating up a weaker version of their argument
choices: It stops you from beating up a weaker version of their argument
It gives you time to think of a joke about them
It makes the other person agree with you faster
It hides your own weakest points
context: Thomas Sowell (born June 30, 1930 in Gastonia, North Carolina) has repeatedly cited Bastiat as a formative influence on his method. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Thomas Sowell wrote a 2000 intro to the field. It's now in its 5th edition. He lays out the best case for each policy before he answers it. What is the book's title?
answer: Basic Economics
choices: Basic Economics
Knowledge and Decisions
A Conflict of Visions
The Vision of the Anointed
context: Basic Economics: A Citizen's Guide to the Economy (Basic Books, 2000; 5th ed. 2014) is Sowell's most widely-read book. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Sowell's 1987 William Morrow book presents two opposing political worldviews in their strongest form and then traces where each leads. What is the book's short title?
answer: A Conflict of Visions
choices: A Conflict of Visions
The Vision of the Anointed
Cosmic Justice
Intellectuals and Society
context: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles (1987) presents the 'constrained' and 'unconstrained' visions each in the strongest terms before analyzing the resulting policy disagreements. Source: grokipedia.com/page/A_Conflict_of_Visions.

question: A town uses tax money to build a shiny new stadium. People see the stadium and cheer. Frédéric Bastiat would tell you to think about a hidden cost. What is that hidden cost?
answer: All the things the taxpayers would have bought or built with that money instead
choices: All the things the taxpayers would have bought or built with that money instead
The paint used on the outside walls
The wages of the stadium workers
The price of tickets to future games
context: Thomas Sowell's memoir A Personal Odyssey (Free Press, 2000) traces his intellectual formation and lists Bastiat among the formative early influences. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Before arguing against an idea, first restate it in the strongest possible form its supporters would agree with — no cheap distortions, no easy targets. This is the opposite of the "straw man." What one-word verb do writers online use for that move?
answer: Steelman
choices: Steelman
Deconstruct
Debunk
Weaponize
context: 'Steelman' entered the rationalist vocabulary around 2010 (LessWrong, Slate Star Codex) meaning to state the opponent's view in its strongest form before responding -- essentially Bastiat's 1845 rule with a new label. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Steelman_argument.

question: Milton Friedman's most-quoted line says inflation always has one cause. He said it in a 1963 lecture, in Free to Choose, in Money Mischief, and in many columns. Which cause does the line name?
answer: A monetary phenomenon
choices: A monetary phenomenon
A psychological phenomenon
A wage-push phenomenon
A supply-shock phenomenon
context: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' -- Milton Friedman's most-repeated sentence, first delivered in his 1963 LSE lecture 'The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory,' repeated across three decades. Source: Friedman, 'The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory' (IEA 1970 publication of 1963 lecture).

question: A country's government prints twice as much money and hands it out, but the country still makes the same amount of stuff as before. Store owners see more dollars chasing the same goods and raise their prices. What causes prices to rise in this story?
answer: Too much money for too few goods
choices: Too much money for too few goods
Cold weather
Union contracts
A shipping strike
context: Friedman's monetarist move: inflation is caused by the money supply growing faster than real economic output. Every historical inflation tracks the monetary expansion; no lasting inflation has ever occurred without it. Source: Friedman (1963); Friedman + Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States (Princeton 1963).

question: Two economists studied a hundred years of American money history. Their big finding: in the worst part of the Great Depression, the money supply dropped by about a third. What did they say made the Depression so deep?
answer: The sudden shrinking of the money supply
choices: The sudden shrinking of the money supply
A wave of new inventions replacing workers
Farmers growing too much wheat
Foreign countries refusing to trade with America
context: Milton Friedman + Anna Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 (Princeton University Press, 1963). It documented that changes in the money supply preceded and predicted changes in nominal income and inflation across a century of data. Source: press.princeton.edu (Friedman + Schwartz 1963).

question: From 1929 to 1933, the amount of money in America fell by about one-third. Two famous economists argued this drop turned a bad recession into the worst depression in history. What lesson does this teach?
answer: When the money supply shrinks fast, businesses and jobs collapse with it
choices: When the money supply shrinks fast, businesses and jobs collapse with it
Depressions are caused only by too much money being printed
Only bad harvests can cause a real depression
The money supply has nothing to do with jobs
context: Chapter 7 of A Monetary History, titled 'The Great Contraction,' documented that the US money supply fell by roughly one-third between 1929 and 1933 -- a Fed failure Friedman argued caused the depth of the Depression. Source: Friedman + Schwartz (1963), Chapter 7.

question: In 1963, Milton Friedman gave a lecture called 'The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory.' It was a direct challenge to the ruling school of economics at the time. Which school was he trying to push aside?
answer: Keynesian macroeconomics
choices: Keynesian macroeconomics
Classical Ricardian economics
Marxist labor theory of value
Physiocratic agricultural economics
context: Friedman's 1963 LSE lecture called for overturning the Keynesian consensus that had governed US monetary policy since WWII. Keynesians treated the money supply as mostly passive; Friedman argued it was the driver. Source: Friedman, IEA (1970) publication of 1963 lecture.

question: In the 1970s America had both rising prices and rising unemployment at the same time. Older textbooks said that could not happen. In which decade did most economists finally change their textbooks to accept the newer view?
answer: The 1980s
choices: The 1980s
The 1950s
The 1990s
The 2010s
context: By the mid-1980s the economics profession had substantially accepted the monetarist critique of the stable Phillips curve, though not every technical detail. Friedman was the intellectual victor of the 1960s-80s macroeconomic debate. Source: Blinder, 'The Monetarist Counterrevolution' (JEP 2001).

question: Friedman explicitly did NOT claim to invent monetarism. He credited earlier economists for elements of the framework. Which trio of predecessors did he most often name?
answer: Henry Simons, Clark Warburton, and Anna Schwartz
choices: Henry Simons, Clark Warburton, and Anna Schwartz
John Maynard Keynes, Michal Kalecki, and Piero Sraffa
Karl Marx, Rosa Luxemburg, and Louis Althusser
Aristotle, Aquinas, and Adam Smith
context: Friedman credited his Chicago mentor Henry Simons, Clark Warburton (a pre-Friedman quantitative monetarist), and his co-author Anna Schwartz for pieces of the framework. His claim was demonstration with US century-long data, not invention. Source: Friedman, autobiographical Nobel essay (1976); IEA 1970 lecture.

question: Friedman and the Austrian school both say inflation comes from money. But they focus on different things. Which claim best marks the split between Friedman and the Mises-Hayek view?
answer: Friedman focuses on aggregate money supply growth; Austrians focus on credit-driven malinvestment structure
choices: Friedman focuses on aggregate money supply growth; Austrians focus on credit-driven malinvestment structure
Friedman believes inflation is caused by unions; Austrians believe it is caused by monopolies
Friedman rejects the concept of money supply entirely
Friedman advocates commodity money exclusively
context: Both traditions agree on the monetary origin of inflation. They differ on transmission and business-cycle dynamics: Friedman focuses on aggregate M vs Y; Austrian ABCT (Mises-Hayek-Rothbard) focuses on the structure of malinvestment produced by artificially low interest rates. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963); Friedman, IEA (1970).

question: In the 1970s prices climbed month after month across America. Politicians and television reporters kept giving new villains to blame — usually anyone but the government printing extra money. Whom did they blame most often?
answer: Greedy businesses, unions demanding wages, and oil sheikhs
choices: Greedy businesses, unions demanding wages, and oil sheikhs
The Federal Reserve and its money-printing
Consumers who chose too many local products
The old gold standard's tight limits on the money supply
context: Popular explanations in the 1970s recycled corporate greed, union wage demands, and OPEC as inflation causes. Friedman's move: point at the multi-year monetary expansion behind them all. The specific blame targets are effects, not causes. Source: Friedman, IEA (1970).

question: The 'always and everywhere' phrase is a strong empirical claim. Friedman meant it not as a metaphysical truth but as a hypothesis supported by which specific body of evidence?
answer: A century of US money-supply-and-inflation data documented in A Monetary History
choices: A century of US money-supply-and-inflation data documented in A Monetary History
A single laboratory experiment run in Chicago in 1961
A theological argument from natural law
A survey of contemporary US Federal Reserve staff
context: Friedman's empirical basis was the 1867-1960 US data he and Anna Schwartz assembled and analyzed in A Monetary History. That century of correlation is the evidentiary claim behind 'always and everywhere.' Source: Friedman + Schwartz, A Monetary History (Princeton 1963).

question: A kid sees his school never sells hot drinks on cold days. So he brings hot chocolate to sell at lunch and makes a small profit. What do we call someone who spots a need and starts a business to fill it?
answer: An entrepreneur
choices: An entrepreneur
A regulator
A landlord
A tax collector
context: Israel Meir Kirzner, born London 1930, moved to South Africa at age 10, then to the United States for graduate work at NYU. Rothbard took his Ph.D. at Columbia in 1956 (under Arthur Burns, not Mises); Boettke and Hoppe are younger scholars trained in the Kirzner-Rothbard generation's wake. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: In 1957 Kirzner finished his PhD in New York. His teacher was an older Austrian economist who had escaped from Vienna. Who was that teacher?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Joseph Schumpeter
Fritz Machlup
context: Mises had joined NYU as a visiting professor in 1945 and ran a graduate seminar there for two decades; Kirzner was his most consequential doctoral student. Hayek was at Chicago from 1950; Schumpeter had died at Harvard in 1950; Machlup was a Vienna-circle friend but at Johns Hopkins and Princeton. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: In 1973 Israel Kirzner published the book that made his name, laying out the modern Austrian account of the market process. What was the book called?
answer: Competition and Entrepreneurship
choices: Competition and Entrepreneurship
Human Action
Man, Economy, and State
Individualism and Economic Order
context: Competition and Entrepreneurship, University of Chicago Press, 1973. Human Action (1949) was Mises's; Man, Economy, and State (1962) was Rothbard's; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected essays by Hayek. Source: Econlib, 'Competition and Entrepreneurship: The Fountainhead of the Contemporary Austrian School'.

question: Two kids walk past the same empty parking lot every day. One kid suddenly notices that on hot days, families walking to the park could use cold lemonade. He sets up a stand and does great. What single word best names what the successful kid had?
answer: Alertness
choices: Alertness
Invention
Caution
Luck
context: Alertness -- attention to hitherto-unnoticed opportunities -- is the load-bearing concept in Competition and Entrepreneurship. Innovation is Schumpeter's key term; prudence is Aristotelian; foresight belongs to Frank Knight's risk-bearing entrepreneur. Source: Econlib biography, Israel Kirzner.

question: One economist said business owners quietly find small chances the market missed, while another said they storm in with new ideas that wipe out whole industries. What is that stormy process called?
answer: Creative destruction
choices: Creative destruction
Perfect competition
Rent-seeking
Moral hazard
context: Schumpeter's Theory of Economic Development (1911) and Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942) present the entrepreneur as disruptive innovator; Kirzner's 1973 book is the deliberate Austrian counter-account. Knight (1921) emphasized uncertainty-bearing; Drucker was a management theorist; Coase worked on transaction costs. Source: mises.org, 'Schumpeter vs. Kirzner on Entrepreneurs'.

question: In one view, entrepreneurs invent brand-new opportunities out of thin air. In the other view, opportunities already sit in the market waiting for a sharp person to spot them. In that second view, what best describes what the entrepreneur does?
answer: Discovers opportunities that were already there
choices: Discovers opportunities that were already there
Invents opportunities from nothing
Manufactures opportunities in a factory
Passes laws to make opportunities exist
context: Kirzner's language of DISCOVERY versus Schumpeter's CREATION is the standard shorthand for the two accounts in the entrepreneurship literature. Source: mises.org, 'Schumpeter vs. Kirzner on Entrepreneurs'.

question: In 2006 Israel Kirzner won the top world prize for studying entrepreneurs. It is the highest honor in that field. Which prize did he receive?
answer: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
choices: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
The John Bates Clark Medal
The Adam Smith Prize
The Bank of Sweden Prize
context: Awarded in Stockholm 2006 by the Global Award Foundation -- the entrepreneurship field's senior prize, sometimes called 'the Nobel of entrepreneurship.' The John Bates Clark Medal is for American economists under 40; the Adam Smith Prize is a Cambridge undergraduate award; the Bank of Sweden Prize is the Nobel in Economics itself. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: An Austrian-school economist named Israel Kirzner spent his career studying entrepreneurs. He said their most important skill is not risk-taking or hard bargaining. What did Kirzner say the entrepreneur's real skill is?
answer: Noticing a profit opportunity that everyone else has missed
choices: Noticing a profit opportunity that everyone else has missed
Being willing to take huge financial risks with borrowed money
Managing large teams of workers efficiently
Predicting exactly what the government will do next
context: Kirzner joined NYU on completing his Ph.D. in 1957 and remained until his 2002 retirement, based in the business school (later Stern). Chicago was the mainstream free-market department; Columbia was Rothbard's Ph.D. institution; George Mason became the leading Austrian department AFTER Kirzner's generation, largely staffed by his students. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: A group of Austrian economists taught that the entrepreneur is not a "capitalist" or a "manager" but the person who spots a chance — a gap between prices in two places, or a good nobody has made yet. What is the entrepreneur's key skill?
answer: Alertness — noticing profit chances that others have missed
choices: Alertness — noticing profit chances that others have missed
Predicting the exact price of every good next year
Convincing regulators to shut out competitors
Copying whatever last year's most successful firm did
context: Kirzner's NYU Austrian Economics Colloquium ran for decades and produced Peter Boettke (now at George Mason), Sanford Ikeda, and many others. The Mises Circle was the Vienna Privatseminar of the 1920s; the Bastiat Society and FEE are separate American educational organizations. Source: Econlib, 'Competition and Entrepreneurship: The Fountainhead of the Contemporary Austrian School'.

question: In 1960 Kirzner published his first book, a revised version of his 1957 doctoral thesis under Mises about the history of economic thought. What title did Kirzner give this first book?
answer: The Economic Point of View
choices: The Economic Point of View
The Theory of Money and Credit
The Ultimate Foundation of Economic Science
The Constitution of Liberty
context: The Economic Point of View (1960) was Kirzner's revised dissertation, a history of how economists have defined their own field. The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was Mises's; The Ultimate Foundation of Economic Science (1962) was Mises's late methodological book; The Constitution of Liberty (1960) was Hayek's. Source: EconJournalWatch author page, Israel M. Kirzner.

question: An Austrian economist argues that a real profit is not a payment for paperwork or for supplying money — those are already priced. Real profit shows up when someone spots that oranges cost one dollar in one town and three in the next, and moves some. What does the profit signal to everyone else?
answer: That resources were being wasted in the low-value place
choices: That resources were being wasted in the low-value place
That the mover has broken a fair-price law and should be fined
That the price gap was the government's plan all along
That prices between towns can never be equal in a free market
context: Kirzner is an Orthodox rabbi; his father was a well-known rabbi and Talmudist, and Kirzner has written on ethics and enterprise from within that tradition. The other three are distinct American Jewish movements. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Kirzner, Israel M(ayer) 1930-'.

question: A senator has to decide how to vote on a new law. What does the public-choice branch of economics say she will most often care about first?
answer: Getting re-elected
choices: Getting re-elected
Reading every page of the law
What her grandma thinks
World peace
context: James McGill Buchanan (October 3, 1919 - January 9, 2013) was born on a Tennessee farm, the grandson of a Reconstruction-era governor. Middle Tennessee State Teachers College was his undergraduate school. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_M._Buchanan.

question: You can put a number on some risks, such as a coin flip that is always 50-50, but for future events like a new war, no clear odds can be given. Which word describes future events like that?
answer: Uncertainty
choices: Uncertainty
Risk
Interest
Depreciation
context: Buchanan later insisted that six weeks in Frank Knight's price-theory course flipped his intellectual orientation. He took his 1948 Chicago PhD under Knight's supervision. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: In 1957 Buchanan and Warren Nutter opened a research center at the University of Virginia. What did they name it?
answer: The Thomas Jefferson Center for Political Economy
choices: The Thomas Jefferson Center for Political Economy
The Mercatus Center
The Center for Study of Public Choice
The Cato Institute
context: Buchanan and Nutter founded the Thomas Jefferson Center at UVa in 1957. It was Buchanan's first institutional home before Tullock arrived and the two founded the Public Choice Society together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_Center_for_Political_Economy.

question: A mayor promises new sidewalks in one part of town right before an election, and he delivers them the next month. Public-choice economists say this shows what?
answer: Politicians respond to incentives just like anyone else responds to incentives
choices: Politicians respond to incentives just like anyone else responds to incentives
Politicians never think about being re-elected after they win once
Sidewalks are always a bad public investment for any neighborhood
Voters always know exactly what they need from a mayor
context: The Center for Study of Public Choice was founded at Virginia Tech in Blacksburg in 1969. It moved with Buchanan and Tullock to George Mason University in 1983. Source: mercatus.org (Center biographical history).

question: In October 1986 James Buchanan won the Nobel in economics. It was the first Nobel for his field. The prize honored his work on the rules and contracts behind what?
answer: The theory of economic and political decision-making
choices: The theory of economic and political decision-making
General-equilibrium price theory
Growth accounting
Consumer-choice utility theory
context: The 1986 Nobel citation, October 16, 1986: 'for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' The committee generalized rather than saying 'public choice.' Source: nobelprize.org (Buchanan 1986).

question: Two economists opened a research center to study one big question about politicians and government workers. What did they actually want when they made choices? What did the research find?
answer: They respond to incentives, just like people in business do
choices: They respond to incentives, just like people in business do
They always act only for the public good
They follow whatever economists tell them
They ignore money and power completely
context: The Center moved to George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, in 1983. GMU has hosted public-choice research ever since, alongside the Mercatus Center. Source: gmu.edu (public choice program history).

question: A young American went to Italy in the 1950s. He studied with a scholar who wanted a country's constitution to cap government spending. Why put those limits in the constitution instead of trusting politicians?
answer: Politicians face short-term pressure to spend and print money, and firm rules bind them
choices: Politicians face short-term pressure to spend and print money, and firm rules bind them
Constitutions must be written in gold letters
Only a constitution is allowed to raise taxes
Politicians never read a constitution
context: Buchanan spent 1955-56 in Italy on a Fulbright, working with Luigi Einaudi (former President of Italy 1948-55) and the Italian public-finance tradition. He credited that year with shaping his constitutional-fiscal focus. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: At his 1986 Nobel ceremony in Stockholm, Buchanan wanted a tribute to his Chicago teacher shown with his own work. He was thanking the man who had changed his thinking. What did Buchanan display next to himself?
answer: A portrait of Frank Knight
choices: A portrait of Frank Knight
A page from Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations
A Tennessee state flag
A copy of the Constitution of the United States
context: Buchanan brought Frank Knight's portrait to the Stockholm ceremonies and referred to Knight as his intellectual father. The gesture was widely reported. Source: Buchanan Nobel-week press coverage; Boettke + Marciano biography.

question: Buchanan's grandfather was a Tennessee politician during Reconstruction, and young James was named for him. What top state office had John Price Buchanan held?
answer: Governor of Tennessee
choices: Governor of Tennessee
US Senator from Tennessee
Chief Justice of the Tennessee Supreme Court
Mayor of Nashville
context: John Price Buchanan served as Governor of Tennessee from 1891 to 1893, elected on a Farmers' Alliance platform. James Buchanan often noted the family political inheritance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_P._Buchanan.

question: Buchanan often described his change at Chicago as going from a 'libertarian socialist' to a market-order view. What does that phrase tell us about where he really started, before Frank Knight's course?
answer: He was a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to redistribution
choices: He was a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to redistribution
He was a Chicago-machine urban liberal
He was already a doctrinaire Austrian
He was a Trotskyist committed to permanent revolution
context: Buchanan was the son of Tennessee farming Democrats, sympathetic to New Deal redistribution when he arrived at Chicago. The 'libertarian socialist' label was his own description of that starting point. Do not overstate an early conservatism -- he had none. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: Buchanan's biographical arc runs from a Tennessee dairy farm to the Royal Swedish Academy. In shaping the whole field of public choice from that unlikely path, what did the man do in a single sentence?
answer: He taught the world that politicians are self-interested actors, not benevolent planners
choices: He taught the world that politicians are self-interested actors, not benevolent planners
He proved mathematically that market prices reflect all available information
He founded the doctrine of comparative advantage in international trade
He reformed monetary policy by inventing the money-supply target rule
context: Public choice is politics without romance. Buchanan's contribution: strip the assumption that politicians act from pure public spirit; treat them as ordinary humans responding to ordinary incentives. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: In 2020, during COVID lockdowns, a Canadian tech founder wrote a book. It says falling prices from tech are a good thing, but central banks hide it. The book is a top modern Bitcoin book. What is its title?
answer: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future
choices: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future
The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
The Sovereign Individual: Mastering the Transition to the Information Age
The Ascent of Money: A Financial History of the World
context: Written by Jeff Booth, formerly the founder of BuildDirect, an online building-materials company. He had spent 30 years building and selling companies before turning to monetary writing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth's 2020 book says one fact about tech is called bad news but is really a gift to normal people. Which trait of tech does he mean?
answer: Technology naturally cheapens things over time (computing power, solar energy, storage all fall in cost)
choices: Technology naturally cheapens things over time (computing power, solar energy, storage all fall in cost)
Technology always requires a government subsidy to develop
Technology inherently favors older workers over younger ones
Technology can only be produced by monopolies
context: Moore's Law (Gordon Moore, 1965) captures the classical case: the number of transistors on a chip doubles every two years for the same cost. Solar photovoltaics, LEDs, memory, and storage follow parallel curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Moore%27s_law.

question: In Booth's account, central banks respond to technology's natural cheapening effect in a specific way that hides the gift from savers and workers. What does he say central banks do?
answer: Expand the money supply, letting asset prices rise instead of consumer prices falling
choices: Expand the money supply, letting asset prices rise instead of consumer prices falling
Buy technology stocks directly on the open market to raise their share prices
Print physical dollar bills at a fixed rate matching Moore's Law
Ban the sale of foreign-made technology to protect national producers
context: The technology-deflation benefit gets absorbed into rising stock, real-estate, and bond prices. Owners of assets gain; workers and savers whose wages and cash holdings should have bought more each year do not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: A saver in 2025 asks why her wages have risen only modestly since 2010 while the S&P 500 has more than tripled. A Booth-influenced analyst points to a specific Bastiat-style unseen. Which is it?
answer: The technology-cheapening she should have seen in her cost of living was absorbed into asset prices instead
choices: The technology-cheapening she should have seen in her cost of living was absorbed into asset prices instead
The Federal Reserve directly transferred wages from workers to investors by executive order
Chinese manufacturing subsidies alone explain the entire stock-market rise
European Central Bank interest-rate cuts caused the entire US wage stagnation
context: The seen: relatively stable consumer prices, a 'successful' Fed inflation target. The unseen: the prices should have fallen substantially given the underlying productivity gains. The gap accrues to asset holders. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Booth says one kind of money lets you keep the gains from cheaper tech. Central banks usually wipe those gains away. Which kind of money does he pick?
answer: Bitcoin, whose 21 million cap prevents any authority from expanding the supply to hide falling prices
choices: Bitcoin, whose 21 million cap prevents any authority from expanding the supply to hide falling prices
The US dollar, backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government
The euro, coordinated by the European Central Bank across 20 nations
Gold-backed central-bank digital currencies
context: Booth's argument connects Bitcoin to technology-optimism in a way that reaches audiences who resist harder Austrian or goldbug framings. The point is monetary design, not price prediction. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth is often interviewed as one of a three-voice synthesis of modern Bitcoin monetary theory, alongside two other prominent figures. Who are the other two?
answer: Michael Saylor and Saifedean Ammous
choices: Michael Saylor and Saifedean Ammous
Vitalik Buterin and Sam Bankman-Fried
Peter Thiel and Elon Musk
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger
context: Saylor (MicroStrategy chairman, corporate-treasury Bitcoin advocate) and Ammous ('The Bitcoin Standard') provide the corporate and Austrian frames; Booth provides the technology-optimist frame. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: In 1910 a small group of bankers and politicians met secretly at a hunting retreat to draft the plan for a new central bank in America. That plan later became the Federal Reserve. What is a central bank's main job?
answer: Managing a country's money supply
choices: Managing a country's money supply
Running the army
Building highways
Writing school textbooks
context: The Jekyll Island Club, off the Georgia coast, was owned by a small group of America's richest families. The November 1910 meeting produced the blueprint for what became the Federal Reserve. Source: Grokipedia 'Jekyll Island Club' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1910 a group of senators and bankers met in secret to plan a new central bank, and the plan later became a federal law. Which branch of the US government can pass a law like that?
answer: Congress
choices: Congress
The Supreme Court
The Army
The state governors
context: Nelson Aldrich (R-Rhode Island) chaired the National Monetary Commission and was the political sponsor of the plan that emerged from the meeting. His daughter Abby married John D. Rockefeller Jr. in 1901. Source: Grokipedia 'Nelson Aldrich' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1910 a small group of powerful bankers met in secret on a private island off Georgia. Their goal was to design a new central bank for the United States. What is the main worry critics later raised about this meeting?
answer: A powerful money system was designed by insiders, not by the public
choices: A powerful money system was designed by insiders, not by the public
The bankers picked the wrong island for the weather
They forgot to invite any economists at all
The plan was published in every newspaper the next day
context: Warburg (1868-1932) brought the expertise on European central-banking design that shaped the American plan. He later became one of the first members of the Federal Reserve Board. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Warburg' (2026-09-05).

question: Another man at the Jekyll Island meeting ran a big New York bank tied to the Rockefellers. Which bank did Frank Vanderlip lead?
answer: National City Bank of New York
choices: National City Bank of New York
Chase National Bank
First National Bank of New York
Bankers Trust
context: Frank Vanderlip led National City Bank of New York -- the Rockefeller bank, later Citibank and eventually Citigroup. His Jekyll Island participation was carefully hidden until his 1935 confession. Source: Grokipedia 'Frank Vanderlip' (2026-09-05).

question: At the Jekyll Island meeting one banker was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company, and another was Benjamin Strong, the president of Bankers Trust. Where did Henry Davison work?
answer: Senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company
choices: Senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company
President of Chase National Bank
Chairman of Kuhn Loeb and Company
President of First National Bank of New York
context: Henry Davison was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company. The Jekyll Island meeting essentially assembled the leadership of the New York financial establishment plus one German-American central-banking specialist. Source: Grokipedia 'Henry Pomeroy Davison' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1910 a few bankers and one Treasury official met in secret on a private island, and they drew up the plan that became America's central bank. Why does it matter that the plan was written in private?
answer: The people being regulated helped write the rules that would govern them
choices: The people being regulated helped write the rules that would govern them
Private islands are legally not part of the country
The meeting was too short for the plan to work
Bankers do not understand how banks actually work
context: A. Piatt Andrew was serving as Assistant Treasury Secretary under Franklin MacVeagh. His presence gave the meeting official Treasury representation without formal Treasury endorsement. Source: Grokipedia 'A. Piatt Andrew' (2026-09-05).

question: For roughly ten days the six men worked in secret at Jekyll Island to draft what became known as the Aldrich Plan. When did Frank Vanderlip publicly acknowledge the meeting for the first time?
answer: 1935, in a Saturday Evening Post article
choices: 1935, in a Saturday Evening Post article
1913, at the passage of the Federal Reserve Act
1920, in his memoir
1928, in a Senate hearing
context: Vanderlip's 1935 Saturday Evening Post article 'From Farm Boy to Financier' was the first public acknowledgment of the meeting -- 25 years after it happened. The other participants had died or maintained the sworn secrecy. Source: Grokipedia 'Jekyll Island (Federal Reserve)' (2026-09-05).

question: In December 1913 the US Congress passed a law that created America's central bank — the bank that now controls the dollar supply and sets interest rates. What is that 1913 law called?
answer: The Federal Reserve Act
choices: The Federal Reserve Act
The Glass-Steagall Act
The National Banking Act
The Bland-Allison Act
context: The Federal Reserve Act was signed by Wilson on December 23 1913. It preserved the Aldrich Plan's essential structure (regional banks, note-issue power, private-bank ownership of regional-bank stock) with cosmetic changes for political viability. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In his 1935 confession, Vanderlip picked one specific word to describe how the Jekyll Island group actually behaved during the secret meeting. What word did he use?
answer: Furtive, as any conspirator
choices: Furtive, as any conspirator
Formal, as a governmental commission
Cheerful, as a social gathering
Studious, as an academic seminar
context: Vanderlip's 1935 article: 'I was as secretive -- indeed as furtive -- as any conspirator... our secret expedition to Jekyll Island as the occasion of the actual conception of what eventually became the Federal Reserve System.' Source: Grokipedia 'Jekyll Island (Federal Reserve)' (2026-09-05).

question: The Jekyll Island meeting teaches a specific recognition move about the political economy of central-bank design. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The specific individuals who design a central bank tend to be the very people whose institutions and dynasties will benefit from its structure
choices: The specific individuals who design a central bank tend to be the very people whose institutions and dynasties will benefit from its structure
Central banks are always designed by disinterested academic economists
Central-bank design is a purely technical question with no distributional implications
Public participation in central-bank design has been the norm throughout American history
context: The men at Jekyll Island were the leaders of the very New York financial establishment whose banks would become primary dealers to the new central bank. G. Edward Griffin's 1994 book The Creature from Jekyll Island popularized this line of critique for a mass audience. Source: Grokipedia 'The Creature from Jekyll Island' (2026-09-05).

question: Long ago in China, merchants had to haul heavy iron coins to buy things, and some loads needed a whole cart. One clever fix was to leave the coins with a trusted holder and use a paper slip to trade. That paper slip later turned into what?
answer: Paper money
choices: Paper money
A checkbook
A credit card
A gold coin
context: Iron-coin-backed paper receipts (later called jiaozi) first circulated in Sichuan province during the Song dynasty. Guangdong, Yunnan, and Zhejiang are other Chinese provinces without the same paper-money origin story. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: Around 1023 AD, the Song dynasty took over paper notes first used by merchants in Sichuan. This became the world's first paper money from a government. What was it called?
answer: jiaozi
choices: jiaozi
chao
yuan
cash
context: Jiaozi was the Song dynasty government paper (from ~1023 AD). Chao was the later Mongol Yuan dynasty paper; yuan is the modern name for the Chinese currency unit; 'cash' is the English name for old Chinese round coins with a square hole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: The Song dynasty's paper-money system worked well for about 40 years and then started breaking down. Which pressure forced the government to print paper faster than its metal backing could support?
answer: military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols
choices: military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols
the construction of the Great Wall extensions
irrigation projects in the Yangtze delta
silk trade with the Roman Empire
context: Late-Song military spending against the Jin (northern rival) and later the Mongols drove the fatal jiaozi over-issuance; by the early 13th century the currency had lost most of its value. Great Wall extension (Ming era), Yangtze irrigation, and Roman silk trade are the wrong causes or wrong eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: A powerful ruler of old China printed paper money that was not backed by any gold or silver. He ordered by law that everyone had to accept it. What tends to happen to money like that over time?
answer: The ruler prints more to pay his bills and each note buys less than before
choices: The ruler prints more to pay his bills and each note buys less than before
The ruler stops printing and the money holds its value for centuries
The money becomes stronger than gold within a few years
Everyone burns the notes and returns to trading only in cattle
context: Kublai Khan (reigned 1260-94) issued the chao. Genghis Khan (1162-1227) founded the Mongol empire but did not issue Chinese paper money; Timur was the later Turco-Mongol ruler (1370-1405); Möngke Khan was Kublai's brother. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kublai_Khan.

question: Marco Polo wrote that Kublai Khan forced people to take the chao paper money. Polo said the Khan used one harsh punishment to keep the notes in use. What was it?
answer: death for refusing to accept the notes
choices: death for refusing to accept the notes
banishment for two years
a fine of one hundred silver taels
public flogging
context: Marco Polo reported that refusing the chao was punishable by death under Kublai. Banishment, fines, and flogging were common Mongol punishments for other offenses but Polo specifies death for chao refusal. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels of Marco Polo (c. 1298), Book II ch 24.

question: Marco Polo devoted a whole chapter of his 1298 Travels to describing Kublai Khan's paper currency. He described the notes as being made from the bark of a specific tree stamped with imperial vermilion. Which tree's bark did Polo describe the chao being made from?
answer: the mulberry tree
choices: the mulberry tree
the English oak
the white willow
the silver birch
context: Polo described the chao as being made from mulberry bark. Oak, willow, and birch bark have been used for other papers in other places but Polo specifies mulberry for the chao. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels (Book II ch 24).

question: Marco Polo came from a Europe where money meant gold and silver, and he described Kublai Khan's paper-money system in words that captured his surprise. Which comparison did Polo use in the Travels to describe how the paper worked?
answer: a kind of alchemy -- the Khan's magic that turns bark into wealth
choices: a kind of alchemy -- the Khan's magic that turns bark into wealth
a form of taxation the citizens paid willingly
a religious offering the citizens made to the Khan
a military tribute the conquered peoples paid
context: Polo compared the chao system to alchemy: bark being transmuted into wealth by the Khan's stamp. He did not frame it as tax, offering, or tribute in the passage. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels (Book II ch 24).

question: The chao paper currency held its value only while Kublai lived and his empire could project force. What happened to the chao within a generation of Kublai's death in 1294?
answer: successor emperors printed at will to fund crises, and by the 1350s the chao was worthless
choices: successor emperors printed at will to fund crises, and by the 1350s the chao was worthless
the chao was formally backed by silver and stabilized for another two centuries
the Ming dynasty adopted it as their own currency in 1368
Marco Polo returned to enforce its acceptance
context: After Kublai, later Yuan emperors printed chao at will; by the 1350s it was worthless and the Yuan dynasty was collapsing. The Ming (founded 1368) inherited the ruin, not the currency; silver backing did not stabilize it; Polo had died in 1324. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty.

question: The jiaozi in the 1000s and the chao in the 1200s were the world's first two paper-money crashes. Both hit China only a few centuries apart. Which reasoning move do modern Austrian economists make about this early record?
answer: That the very first two government paper currencies in world history hyperinflated, suggesting the failure pattern is structural rather than a modern accident
choices: That the very first two government paper currencies in world history hyperinflated, suggesting the failure pattern is structural rather than a modern accident
That Chinese culture was uniquely unsuited to paper money, so the Song and Yuan collapses tell us nothing about later fiat currencies elsewhere in the world
That the paper-money failure in both dynasties was caused primarily by insufficient literacy among the population handling the notes rather than by over-issuance
That the Song and Yuan governments simply lacked modern accounting tools, so a modern central bank with proper spreadsheets would not repeat the same mistake
context: The Austrian move: paper money is nine hundred years old and hyperinflated the first two times anyone tried it; the failure pattern is structural, not modern-specific. Cultural, literacy, and accounting explanations are the alternative arguments the Austrian analysis specifically rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021); Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?.

question: A Bastiat-style retelling of the Kublai Khan paper story asks one clear question about what Marco Polo really saw when he called the paper alchemy. Which claim does the story make about the mechanism?
answer: That the SEEN was the Khan turning bark into wealth, and the UNSEEN was the future price collapse absorbing the wealth of every current chao holder within a generation
choices: That the SEEN was the Khan turning bark into wealth, and the UNSEEN was the future price collapse absorbing the wealth of every current chao holder within a generation
That Marco Polo simply misunderstood Chinese economics and misreported what Kublai's paper system actually did in daily commerce inside the Mongol empire
That paper money worked reliably in Kublai's China as long as the Khan personally guaranteed it, and no monetary lesson generalizes to any later fiat system elsewhere
That the chao would have lasted indefinitely if the Mongol empire had lasted longer, and the collapse says nothing about paper money's structural incentive to over-issue
context: The Bastiat move: SEEN (the wealth Kublai's paper appeared to create); UNSEEN (the future currency collapse quietly transferring that wealth away from every holder). Personal guarantee, imperial duration, and mistaken observer are the standard alternative theories the argument rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: In 1715 France was nearly broke from too many wars. A visitor promised the king's government he could fix everything by printing lots of new paper money and using it to buy up land and shares. His plan later crashed. What do we call it when too much printed money loses value fast?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
A tariff
A dividend
A tax cut
context: John Law (1671-1729), a Scot who had fled London after killing a man in a duel, arrived in France in 1715 and won the ear of Philippe, Duke of Orleans, regent for the child-king Louis XV. Source: Antoin Murphy, John Law: Economic Theorist and Policy-Maker (1997).

question: In France in 1717 a Scottish planner started a huge trading company and printed piles of new money to fund it. Shares in the company were sold to the public, and their price shot up, then crashed in 1720, ruining thousands. What is it called when share prices rise wildly and then crash?
answer: A bubble
choices: A bubble
A subsidy
A rebate
A dividend
context: Founded in 1717 as the Compagnie d'Occident and quickly known as the Compagnie du Mississippi, it held the exclusive right to develop the vast French Louisiana territory. Source: Grokipedia 'Mississippi Company' (2026-09-05).

question: In old France, a bank was allowed to print paper money and was fully backed by the king's government. With no real limit on how much paper it could print, what happened next?
answer: It crashed, and people lost their savings in a giant bubble
choices: It crashed, and people lost their savings in a giant bubble
It stayed steady for hundreds of years without any trouble
It became the strongest currency in the world
It was quietly replaced by silver coins with no bubble
context: Law founded the Banque Generale in 1716. In 1718 the crown nationalized it and renamed it the Banque Royale, guaranteeing its notes as legal tender. Banque de France (a different institution) was founded by Napoleon in 1800. Source: Grokipedia 'Banque Royale' (2026-09-05).

question: In the Paris Mississippi Company boom of 1719 to 1720, many shareholders got rich on paper. A new French word was coined for people worth a million livres. Which word came out of this bubble?
answer: Millionaire
choices: Millionaire
Bourgeois
Rentier
Speculateur
context: The word 'millionaire' first appears in French in about 1719 to describe the newly rich shareholders in Law's Mississippi Company. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Oxford English Dictionary etymology entry.

question: Between 1719 and early 1720 shares in the Scottish theorist's Louisiana trading company rose from about 500 livres each to a peak that made the whole scheme famous. Roughly what peak did the share price reach?
answer: About 10,000 livres per share
choices: About 10,000 livres per share
About 1,000 livres per share
About 100,000 livres per share
About 3,000 livres per share
context: Mississippi Company shares climbed roughly twenty-fold from about 500 livres in mid-1719 to around 10,000 livres by early 1720 -- one of the sharpest speculative rises in monetary history. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Grokipedia 'Mississippi Bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: The Scottish projector's scheme in France rested on a self-reinforcing loop tying his state-backed bank to his Louisiana trading company. Which loop did he construct?
answer: The bank printed notes that were used to buy shares, whose rising price fed demand for more notes, which the bank printed
choices: The bank printed notes that were used to buy shares, whose rising price fed demand for more notes, which the bank printed
The bank taxed foreign trade and used the revenue to buy shares back from the public at a fixed price
The company shipped Louisiana silver to France, and the bank issued notes backed 100 percent by that silver
The bank borrowed from Dutch and English merchants and lent the proceeds to the company at low interest
context: The circular mechanism was the core of Law's scheme: paper money financed share purchases, rising share prices created demand for more paper, and the bank obliged. This is the shape every asset-inflation bubble since has followed. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997).

question: In February 1720, big shareholders started cashing in Mississippi Company stock and asking for gold coin instead of paper. The Scottish controller-general tried a desperate legal weapon. What did he try to do to gold?
answer: He banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion
choices: He banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion
He fixed the price of gold at half its market rate
He required all gold to be deposited with the Mississippi Company
He nationalized every French goldsmith's shop
context: Law's February 1720 edict forbade private holdings of gold and silver bullion above small amounts, hoping to force the public back into paper. It failed within weeks. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Grokipedia 'Mississippi Bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1710s a Scottish gambler convinced France to print heaps of paper money backed by shares in a Louisiana trading company. Prices soared, then everything crashed. What is the deeper cause the Austrian school blames for these boom-and-bust cycles?
answer: Cheap money and easy credit flooding the economy
choices: Cheap money and easy credit flooding the economy
A sudden shortage of factory workers
A war with a neighboring country
Bad harvests that raised food prices
context: Law fled France in December 1720, drifted through European cities, and died in Venice in March 1729, largely forgotten and in poverty. Source: Grokipedia 'John Law (economist)' (2026-09-05).

question: A revolutionary government seizes church land, then issues paper notes "backed by" that land. To pay its bills it prints more notes, then more, then more. Within five years the paper is worth almost nothing. What is the general term for what happened to the value of those notes?
answer: Hyperinflation — prices exploding as money loses value
choices: Hyperinflation — prices exploding as money loses value
Deflation — prices falling because money is scarce
Deleveraging — households and firms paying off debts
Devaluation — a government cutting a fixed exchange rate
context: The 1789-1796 Assignat was the second modern paper-money experiment in France, backed by seized Church lands. It hyperinflated just as Law's system had, confirming the pattern. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian economists point to the 1719-1720 French episode as the first modern case of the boom-bust pattern their theory describes. Which specific Austrian move fits Law's scheme most exactly?
answer: Credit expansion produces malinvestment concentrated in one sector, then collapses when redemption is demanded
choices: Credit expansion produces malinvestment concentrated in one sector, then collapses when redemption is demanded
Government spending stimulates aggregate demand and drives permanent growth
A fixed money supply causes deflation and long-run unemployment
Free banking causes an excess of small denominations to circulate
context: The Austrian business-cycle pattern: newly created money distorts capital toward a favored project (Louisiana), the boom looks like prosperity, and when holders of the new money try to convert it back to real goods or hard money, the whole edifice collapses. Ludwig von Mises named the mechanism in 1912. Source: Mises, Theory of Money and Credit (1912).

question: A Brooklyn-born economist at Pace University is the top modern scholar of the 1920 Mises calculation debate. He argues for a strict reading, not the Hayek view. Who is he?
answer: Joseph Salerno
