Peter Boettke
Israel Kirzner
Don Lavoie
context: Joseph T. Salerno (born 1950 in Brooklyn, New York) is professor emeritus at Pace University and academic vice president of the Ludwig von Mises Institute. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_Salerno.

question: Salerno edits the main modern Austrian journal. The Mises Institute has printed it since 1998. What is its title?
answer: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
choices: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
Review of Austrian Economics
Journal of Political Economy
American Economic Review
context: Salerno has edited the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics since its founding in 1998; the older Review of Austrian Economics (edited by Boettke) is a separate journal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_Salerno.

question: In a system with no private ownership of factories, tools, or land, no one can bid to buy them. Without those bids there are no real market prices for those things. What problem does this create for a planner trying to run the whole economy?
answer: The planner has no way to know which uses of resources are worth it
choices: The planner has no way to know which uses of resources are worth it
The planner will always pay workers too much money
The planner will run out of workers to hire
The planner will make too many small mistakes to count
context: Salerno's strict-Misesian reading: without real market prices for producer goods, no cost comparison is possible; the calculation problem is a monetary problem, not primarily a knowledge problem. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Socialist_calculation_debate.

question: A farmer knows his own soil, a shopkeeper knows what shoppers are buying today, and a truck driver knows which roads are closed. A central planner in the capital could never gather all this knowledge in time. What name is often given to this obstacle to central planning?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The wage problem
The tax problem
The interest-rate problem
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' framed the calculation debate in knowledge-problem terms; Israel Kirzner and Don Lavoie extended this reading. Salerno argues it displaces Mises's original monetary-calculation point. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Socialist_calculation_debate.

question: Salerno's big move in the Austrian debate was a 1990 article in the Review of Austrian Economics. It argued for his strict Mises reading. What was the article's short title?
answer: Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist
choices: Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist
The Use of Knowledge in Society
Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
The Meaning of Market Process
context: 'Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist' (Review of Austrian Economics, 1990) is the paper that shifted majority Austrian opinion within the Mises Institute tradition toward Salerno's reading. Source: mises.org/library/ludwig-von-mises-social-rationalist.

question: Salerno's 2010 book from the Mises Institute collects his essays that apply strict Misesian money theory to the Federal Reserve and the 2008 crisis. What is the book's title?
answer: Money: Sound and Unsound
choices: Money: Sound and Unsound
The Theory of Money and Credit
Human Action
America's Great Depression
context: Money: Sound and Unsound (Mises Institute, 2010) is Salerno's applied-Misesian essay collection on monetary policy. Source: mises.org/library/money-sound-and-unsound.

question: In 2004 Salerno edited the modern scholar's edition of a Rothbard book, printed by the Mises Institute with both volumes reunited. Which Rothbard book did he edit?
answer: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market
choices: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market
America's Great Depression
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
context: Salerno's 2004 scholar's edition finally reunited Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (1962) with its originally-excised political-economy volume Power and Market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: Mises's 1920 founding essay of the socialist calculation debate ran under a specific title in the journal Archiv fur Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik. In English translation, what is the essay's title?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretense of Knowledge
The Nature and Significance of Economic Science
context: 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' (1920) is Mises's founding contribution; the entire subsequent Austrian tradition, including the intra-tradition dispute Salerno intervened in, argues about how to read it. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: One famous Milton Friedman rule warns not to judge a policy by its nice-sounding goals. Judge it by what it does to people over time. Which sentence best fits this rule?
answer: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
choices: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
Judge policies by the party that sponsors them
Judge policies by their popularity in the polls
Judge policies by their moral rhetoric
context: 'One of the great mistakes is to judge policies and programs by their intentions rather than their results' -- Milton Friedman, spoken repeatedly in interviews including the 1975 Richard Heffner Open Mind interview, and written in Free to Choose (1980). Source: pbs.org (Free to Choose archive).

question: Friedman used his results-not-intentions rule to attack one job-market law. He said this law forces bosses to shut out workers with low skills. Which law was he talking about?
answer: The minimum wage
choices: The minimum wage
The forty-hour workweek
Union-shop right-to-work rules
The Fair Labor Standards Act as a whole
context: Friedman: 'The minimum wage law is most properly described as a law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills.' It appears repeatedly in his columns and in Free to Choose Chapter 8. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (Harcourt 1980), Chapter 8.

question: Friedman's minimum-wage argument looks at two workers affected by a legal wage floor. Which worker is the seen benefit and which is the unseen cost?
answer: SEEN: the worker who keeps the job. UNSEEN: the worker whose job is priced out of existence
choices: SEEN: the worker who keeps the job. UNSEEN: the worker whose job is priced out of existence
SEEN: the employer who pays the wage. UNSEEN: the government that collects payroll tax
SEEN: the union that negotiated the wage. UNSEEN: the pension fund that received the dues
SEEN: the retailer's customers. UNSEEN: the retailer's shareholders
context: The Bastiat SEEN vs UNSEEN move applied to the minimum wage: the worker who keeps the job at the higher wage is visible; the marginal worker whose job is automated away or moved offshore is invisible. Friedman presses attention to the invisible category. Source: Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), Chapter 8.

question: A city passes a law saying landlords can never charge more than a set low rent for apartments. Over the years that follow, what does this kind of price cap usually cause?
answer: Fewer new apartments and worse upkeep of old ones
choices: Fewer new apartments and worse upkeep of old ones
A big boom in fancy new apartment buildings
Landlords always doing extra repairs for free
More apartments than people who need them
context: Milton Friedman + George Stigler, 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem' (Foundation for Economic Education, 1946). It was Friedman and Stigler's first major joint work, before both became Chicago-school leaders. Source: fee.org (Roofs or Ceilings 1946 reprint).

question: Rent control has kind goals but real results. When we use the results-not-intentions rule, what does research show happens to buildings under rent control?
answer: Landlords let them decay and new construction stops
choices: Landlords let them decay and new construction stops
Landlords invest heavily in luxury upgrades
The buildings receive federal subsidies for maintenance
Occupancy drops sharply as tenants vacate
context: Rent-controlled buildings suffer deferred maintenance and the housing stock stops growing because new construction is unprofitable at the controlled rate. Existing tenants stay for decades because leaving means losing the rate. Source: Friedman + Stigler (1946); Diamond + McQuade + Qian, AER (2019) on San Francisco.

question: The results-not-intentions rule pairs with another Thomas Sowell test. He asks a short two-word question when he checks a policy. What is it?
answer: Compared to what?
choices: Compared to what?
Who benefits?
How much?
What next?
context: Sowell's 'compared to what?' presses the alternative any proposed reform is being measured against. Combined with Friedman's 'judge by results,' the pair produces a mature policy-analysis toolkit: what does the policy actually do, and compared to what alternative? Source: Sowell, Knowledge and Decisions (Basic 1980).

question: Friedman said we should judge a policy by results, not by good intentions. Apply that rule to state licenses for hairdressers and interior designers. Whose income do the licenses mostly protect?
answer: The incumbent licensed professionals
choices: The incumbent licensed professionals
The state licensing-board staff
The consumers of the services
The federal Department of Labor
context: Friedman + Kleiner: occupational licensing raises incumbent incomes by restricting entry, with little measurable consumer-safety benefit. The stated intent is consumer protection; the result is incumbent rent extraction. Source: Friedman (1962) Chapter 9; Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006).

question: Friedman used his results-not-intentions rule on the old US welfare system and its effect on family structure. What specific problem did the old welfare rules create?
answer: A marriage penalty embedded in household-income aggregation rules
choices: A marriage penalty embedded in household-income aggregation rules
A required 40-hour work week for all beneficiaries
A ban on any bank account with a balance over one dollar
A prohibition on private tutoring for beneficiaries' children
context: The pre-reform welfare system counted household income for eligibility; a two-parent household could lose more benefits from marrying than the added income was worth. Friedman documented this in Capitalism and Freedom and Free to Choose. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), Chapter 4.

question: The results-not-intentions rule gives the analyst a habit. Instead of trusting a policy's own reasons for itself, what should the analyst do?
answer: Look at what actually happened when the policy was applied
choices: Look at what actually happened when the policy was applied
Look at the political party that sponsored the policy
Look at whether the policy was passed unanimously
Look at whether the policy has a memorable acronym
context: The Friedman move is a form of empiricism: policies come with their own theories about how they work; the honest analyst compares the theory to the observed outcome. This is what unites the minimum-wage, rent-control, and welfare cases. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (1980).

question: The Friedman results-not-intentions move fuses with Sowell's two questions ('compared to what?' and 'at what cost?') into a three-part diagnostic. Which sentence best captures what a responsible policy analysis asks?
answer: What does the policy INTEND, what does it actually DO, and at what COST compared to what alternative
choices: What does the policy INTEND, what does it actually DO, and at what COST compared to what alternative
Which political party sponsors it, which lobbyists supported it, and which president signed it
How long is the statute, who wrote it, and when was it introduced
How much does it cost, how much does it raise in revenue, and how much does the CBO score it
context: The Friedman-Sowell three-part diagnostic: (a) intended outcome; (b) actual result; (c) cost, compared to the honest alternative. Skipping any of the three is standard practice in unserious policy debate. Source: Sowell + Friedman across their popular books.

question: Under a gold standard, each paper dollar can be traded in for a set bit of real gold. That rule stops the government from printing too many dollars. What problem does a gold standard try to prevent?
answer: Endless money printing
choices: Endless money printing
Cold winters
Population growth
Empty gas stations
context: Judy Shelton (born 1954) had served in the US delegation to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Her nomination was formally submitted January 16 2020. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: When Judy Shelton was up for a Fed seat, people said she came from one school of money thinking. That school doubts central-bank power and likes tying money to a metal. Which school?

New Keynesian mainstream
Post-Keynesian MMT-adjacent
Chicago-school monetarist

question: Shelton's Fed pick faced strong pushback. Over 100 former Fed officials signed a letter against her, and some had led the Fed. About how many former Fed chairs and vice chairs signed?
answer: Seven

Two
Fifteen
None

question: The president picks a new central bank board member. Some senators fear the pick will just do what the president wants on money. Why should central bankers stay somewhat free from the president?
answer: So money decisions are not bent to help one politician win the next election

question: An economist wrote a 1994 book called Money Meltdown, warning that the world's money system was in danger from too much printing. In her argument, what does 'sound money' mean?
answer: Money that keeps its value because it cannot be printed at will

Money issued by a single private company

question: In the 1980s one economist correctly said the Soviet economy would collapse. Her school argued that no small planning board can gather enough facts to run a whole economy. What is this missing-facts problem called?
answer: The knowledge problem

The tariff problem
The population problem
The gold problem
context: Shelton's 1998 The Coming Soviet Crash predicted USSR economic collapse from the calculation-debate perspective -- the same Mises 1920 argument that Venezuela later illustrated in real time. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2020 the US central bank announced it would buy unlimited amounts of government bonds, pushing huge amounts of new money into the economy. Austrian-school critics call this policy a hidden tax. Why do they call it a tax?
answer: The new money makes existing dollars worth less, so savers quietly lose buying power
choices: The new money makes existing dollars worth less, so savers quietly lose buying power
The government adds a special new line to every income tax return
Banks are forced to charge higher fees on every checking account
The government takes a share of every bank deposit each year

Her published writings had specifically warned about central-bank-driven asset inflation and currency debasement -- the very phenomena that then materialized. Whether one dissenting vote would have changed policy is unknowable. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Democrats pushed back on Shelton for her writings. She had doubted one old rule that has shielded the Fed from politics since a 1951 deal with the Treasury. Which rule did she question?
answer: Federal Reserve independence from the executive branch

The dual mandate for employment and price stability
The rotation of regional Fed presidents on the FOMC
The publication of FOMC minutes with a lag
context: Shelton had questioned whether the Fed should be as insulated from elected oversight as the current norm makes it. Democrats framed this as a threat to the Fed's political neutrality; Republicans on the fence were nervous about her gold-standard sympathies. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian-tradition analysts say Shelton got closer than any hard-money voice in a generation to a Fed seat. What lesson does this ladder press about how central bank picks work in real politics?
answer: A candidate who explicitly proposes to constrain the institution she would join tends to be blocked by that institution's alumni network
choices: A candidate who explicitly proposes to constrain the institution she would join tends to be blocked by that institution's alumni network
Senate cloture votes are always decided on strictly ideological grounds
Fed nominees are always approved regardless of controversy
Central bank independence is unrelated to appointment politics
context: The seven-former-chair opposition letter is the visible mechanism. An institution defends itself against reform-minded appointees by mobilizing its retired officials. The Fed alumni network functions as an implicit veto. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: The Shelton nomination was the first modern Fed fight to turn on one monetary-policy question, not the usual vetting. Which question drove it?
answer: Whether a gold-linked international monetary system is a legitimate policy option
choices: Whether a gold-linked international monetary system is a legitimate policy option
Whether the Federal Reserve should hire economists over lawyers
Whether regional Fed banks should be reorganized
Whether the FOMC should meet monthly instead of every six weeks
context: Shelton's gold-curious writings put a live monetary-doctrine question at the center of a modern Fed nomination for the first time in decades. The rejection settled the political question; the intellectual question survives in the growing Austrian-tradition public sphere. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Some programmers want to build online tools that no government can shut off, even a powerful one. For a tool to be un-shutoffable, what MUST be true of it?
answer: No single person or place controls it
choices: No single person or place controls it
It has a very strong password
It costs a lot of money to run
It uses a rare programming language
context: Assange had already been convicted of hacking in Australia in 1996. His decade on the cypherpunk list predated WikiLeaks by roughly ten years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Julian_Assange.

question: You lock a diary with a code so strong that no computer could ever crack it. A bully grabs you and threatens to hurt you until you unlock it yourself. What does this show about the limits of even a perfect code?
answer: A code can still be broken by force applied to the person who knows it
choices: A code can still be broken by force applied to the person who knows it
Strong codes cannot ever be defeated by any means at all
Bullies can never guess a good password by trying letters
A code always fails on its own after a few weeks
context: Rubberhose was written in Melbourne. TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013) later adopted similar deniable-encryption designs. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rubberhose_(file_system).

question: Rubberhose was a specific kind of encryption designed to protect users who might be tortured for their passwords. What was the key idea behind it?
answer: Multiple hidden encrypted volumes on one disk, so revealing one password does not prove other volumes do not exist
choices: Multiple hidden encrypted volumes on one disk, so revealing one password does not prove other volumes do not exist
A single very long password that took decades to memorize but was impossible to guess
A one-time-pad shared physically with a trusted friend
Automatic deletion of all data after a wrong password attempt
context: The attacker cannot tell how many volumes exist -- only how many the victim has chosen to reveal. This is called plausibly-deniable encryption. Assange said the target user was a human-rights worker whose sources could die if the wrong files were found. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rubberhose_(file_system).

question: Rubberhose let you deny even having hidden files. This idea was big enough to spread to two later disk-encryption tools that many people use. Which two?
answer: TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013)
choices: TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013)
PGP (1991) and GnuPG (1999)
Kerberos (1988) and SSL (1995)
Signal (2014) and Wire (2014)
context: TrueCrypt became the standard cross-platform disk-encryption tool of the 2000s; VeraCrypt is its actively-maintained successor. Both borrowed Rubberhose's hidden-volume idea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/TrueCrypt.

question: Julian Assange started WikiLeaks in 2006. He used cypherpunk mailing-list ideas to publish leaked papers. What tech design let WikiLeaks survive when governments tried to shut it down?
answer: Documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many jurisdictions
choices: Documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many jurisdictions
Documents were stored only on physical media in Assange's home
Documents required an in-person appointment with WikiLeaks staff to access
Documents were held in escrow by the United Nations
context: A direct scale-up of 1990s cypherpunk censorship-resistance principles. No single government could shut all the mirrors down without cross-border legal cooperation that was often unavailable. Source: grokipedia.com/page/WikiLeaks.

question: Julian Assange spent seven years (2012-2019) inside a London embassy after taking asylum there. Later he spent years in a British high-security prison. Which embassy hosted him?
answer: The Ecuadorian embassy
choices: The Ecuadorian embassy
The Russian embassy
The Cuban embassy
The Swedish embassy
context: Ecuador granted him asylum in 2012; the asylum was revoked in April 2019 and British police arrested him inside the embassy the same day. He was then held in Belmarsh prison until his 2024 plea deal and release. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Julian_Assange.

question: A student asks how the 1990s cypherpunks led to today's world politics. A cryptographer points to one idea that links the two eras: the same tool that hides one worker's files can also mirror thousands of files across many countries. Which idea?
answer: Distributed censorship-resistance: no single actor can seize what many independent copies preserve
choices: Distributed censorship-resistance: no single actor can seize what many independent copies preserve
Central authorization: a single trusted third party must approve every access
Physical secrecy: sensitive information must be stored on paper only
Legal compliance: encryption must obey all national import-export restrictions
context: The principle traces from the cypherpunk mailing list through Rubberhose to WikiLeaks to Bitcoin. The same design property -- deniability of destruction -- is what makes both a private encrypted disk and a public censorship-resistant ledger work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cypherpunk.

question: In 1981 a Maryland economist wrote a book. It said the real limit on human progress is not any raw material. It is human creativity. What phrase names the book's main idea?
answer: The ultimate resource
choices: The ultimate resource
The infinite frontier
The perpetual bounty
The eternal spring
context: Julian L. Simon (1932-1998), The Ultimate Resource (Princeton University Press, 1981; reissued as The Ultimate Resource 2 in 1996). Source: press.princeton.edu (Simon 1981/1996).

question: Julian Simon made a bold claim about the prices of things like metal, oil, and grain. He said that even as the world's population kept growing, the real prices of most of these goods moved in one clear direction over the long run. Which way did they move?
answer: They have fallen
choices: They have fallen
They have risen
They have remained essentially flat
They have oscillated randomly
context: Simon documented that real prices of copper, tin, wheat, aluminum, and iron were cheaper in 2000 than in 1800 even as world population sextupled. If resources were becoming scarcer, prices would rise; they did not. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: In 1968 a famous scientist wrote a bestselling book saying hundreds of millions of people would starve to death in the 1970s because the world had too many people. The 1970s came and went and this did not happen. What does this teach us about big scary predictions?
answer: Confident doomsday predictions often turn out to be very wrong
choices: Confident doomsday predictions often turn out to be very wrong
Every prediction a scientist makes always comes true
There are hardly any people left in the world today
Famines only happen in countries that ignore science
context: Paul Ehrlich, The Population Bomb (Ballantine, 1968), predicted global famines in the 1970s. The predicted famines did not occur; food supply per capita rose. Simon spent much of his career debating Ehrlich. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Population_Bomb.

question: In 1980 Julian Simon offered a bet to anyone who thought the world was running out of stuff. Pick any five metals and any span of 1 to 100 years, and Simon would bet the real prices would fall. Paul Ehrlich took the bet with two friends, John Harte and John Holdren. Which five metals did they pick?
answer: Chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten
choices: Chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten
Gold, silver, platinum, palladium, and rhodium
Iron, aluminum, lead, zinc, and magnesium
Uranium, plutonium, thorium, cesium, and radium
context: Ehrlich, Harte, and Holdren chose chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten for a 10-year wager ending September 1990, totaling $1,000 ($200 per metal). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: The Simon-Ehrlich wager ran from September 1980 to September 1990. On October 10, 1990, John Holdren mailed Simon a check for a specific amount. Who won each metal?
answer: Simon won all five metals
choices: Simon won all five metals
Ehrlich won all five metals
Simon won three; Ehrlich won two
The bet ended in an exact draw across the five
context: All five metals had fallen in real (inflation-adjusted) price over the wager decade. Some had also fallen in nominal terms. Simon won every commodity -- a total refutation of the Malthusian pricing prediction over the wager decade. Source: nyt.com (Simon-Ehrlich wager coverage 1990).

question: Ehrlich's Malthusian view said population growth would use up resources. Simon's counter-view has been carried forward by writers like Matt Ridley and Hans Rosling. Which of the following is not part of the Simon counter-argument?
answer: That governments should impose one-child policies
choices: That governments should impose one-child policies
That people are producers as well as consumers
That human ingenuity finds substitutes as scarcity rises
That real prices are the honest measure of scarcity
context: Simon's argument is anti-Malthusian, not pro-population-control. He argued people are producers of ideas as well as consumers, that ingenuity finds substitutes, and that real prices are the honest scarcity measure. One-child policies belong to the opposing Ehrlich tradition. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: An economist named Julian Simon once bet a doomsayer that the prices of key raw materials would fall, not rise, over ten years. Simon won. What did Simon say was the true 'ultimate resource' that keeps making shortages disappear?
answer: Human ingenuity and problem-solving
choices: Human ingenuity and problem-solving
Government stockpiles of raw materials
International trade agreements
Nationwide recycling programs
context: John Holdren served as Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and science advisor to President Obama from 2009 to 2017. He had signed onto the losing Ehrlich side of the 1980 Simon wager. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Holdren.

question: A British writer's book The Rational Optimist says human progress comes from trade and mixing ideas -- not central planners in charge. Where does the book say most new ideas come from?
answer: Ideas meeting and combining, like people, through free exchange
choices: Ideas meeting and combining, like people, through free exchange
Government research grants aimed at big national problems
A single lone genius working alone in a lab
Careful national plans set by expert committees
context: Matt Ridley, The Rational Optimist (Harper 2010) and How Innovation Works (Harper 2020), popularizes the Simon case for continued improvement in human welfare through ingenuity. Hans Rosling's Factfulness (2018) also fits the tradition. Source: mattridley.co.uk.

question: The Simon-Ehrlich bet is often called the closest thing we have to a real-world test of late-20th-century worries that people were running out of resources. What point about scarcity does the bet show?
answer: Falling real prices are the honest empirical marker of decreasing scarcity
choices: Falling real prices are the honest empirical marker of decreasing scarcity
Rising real prices always indicate that resources are getting rarer
Government subsidies always distort scarcity signals beyond usefulness
Commodity markets are irrelevant to any long-run resource question
context: The Simon move: real prices, not headlines, are the honest scarcity measure. Falling real prices for a commodity mean it is becoming LESS scarce, not more. This is the empirical test that decides the population-resource debate. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: Paul Ehrlich has continued into the 2010s and 2020s to argue that the 1980-90 wager decade was atypical and his broader Malthusian predictions remain correct. What does the honest record of the 1980-90 wager actually show?
answer: All five metals fell in real price; Ehrlich lost every commodity
choices: All five metals fell in real price; Ehrlich lost every commodity
The metals rose in real price; Simon lost every commodity
The outcome was too close to call between the two
The metals were not actually tracked over the decade
context: The record on the specific wager: all five metals fell in real price over 1980-90; Holdren wrote the check. Ehrlich's continuing broader argument is separable from that specific outcome; the specific outcome is unambiguous. Source: Simon 1990 correspondence; Sabin, The Bet (Yale 2013).

question: Karl Marx wrote a famous book, Das Kapital. He argued that private factories and farms should not exist. Who did Marx say SHOULD own them instead?
answer: The government, on behalf of the workers
choices: The government, on behalf of the workers
Rich merchant families
Individual small owners
Local churches
context: Engels published Volume 2 in 1885 and Volume 3 in 1894 (eleven years after Marx's death) from the scattered manuscripts Marx left behind. The manuscript pages Engels used for Volume 3 were themselves drafted 1863-1883. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Kapital.

question: In 1867 Karl Marx put out the first book of Das Kapital. It laid down one sharp rule: when two goods trade in a market, the ratio of their prices comes from the ratio of one thing each of them holds. What was that one thing?
answer: labor-hours
choices: labor-hours
raw materials
capital equipment
land area used
context: This is the LABOR THEORY OF VALUE: a coat that took twice as many socially necessary labor-hours to make as a pair of shoes should exchange for two pairs of shoes. Marx inherited the theory from Ricardo and made it the foundation of Volume 1. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Kapital.

question: Every careful reader of Volume 1 (1867) noticed the same gap. Real market prices do not match the labor-hours in goods. A capital-heavy factory sold its products for more than labor-hours would predict. A labor-heavy workshop sold for less. Marx promised to solve this in a later volume. What did the Marxist tradition come to call this puzzle?
answer: the transformation problem
choices: the transformation problem
the calculation problem
the socialization problem
the accumulation problem
context: The transformation problem = converting Volume 1's labor-values into Volume 3's actual prices of production. Mises's later calculation problem is a DIFFERENT critique (no market prices at all under socialism); the socialization and accumulation problems are further-downstream Marxist debates. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: Eugen Boehm-Bawerk waited almost 30 years for Marx to fix the gap between labor-hours and market prices. In 1894 Friedrich Engels finally put out the missing volume of Das Kapital. Which volume was it?
answer: Volume 3
choices: Volume 3
Volume 1
Volume 2
Volume 4
context: Volume 3 (1894) was expected to contain Marx's promised transformation of labor-values into market prices. Volume 1 (1867) posed the problem; Volume 2 (Engels 1885) covered the circulation of capital; there is no completed Volume 4 (Kautsky later assembled Theories of Surplus Value from Marx's notes and gave it that number). Source: marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1894-c3/editorial/heinrich.htm.

question: In 1896 an Austrian economist wrote a sharp reply to Karl Marx's economics. His main objection was against Marx's claim that a thing's value comes from the hours of labor put into it. What did he say actually decides what a thing is worth?
answer: How much any one person values it at that moment
choices: How much any one person values it at that moment
The number of labor hours it took to make
The rules set by the government that year
The weight of the raw materials inside it
context: Karl Knies (1821-1898) was one of the founding generation of the German Historical School. Boehm-Bawerk's essay first appeared in the 1896 festschrift for Knies before being reissued as a standalone book the same year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay pushed one main charge at Marx. The labor-hours rule in Volume 1 (1867) and the price-of-production rule in Volume 3 (1894) could not both be true in the same economy. What flaw did Boehm-Bawerk say the two volumes had?
answer: internal contradiction
choices: internal contradiction
empirical falsification
mathematical over-simplification
definitional circularity
context: Boehm-Bawerk's charge was NOT that Marx failed a data test; it was that Marx's own two volumes CONTRADICT each other. Volume 3 quietly drops what Volume 1 confidently asserted -- and no data are needed to see the internal inconsistency. This is why his essay is called the CLASSICAL critique of Kapital: the flaw is logical, not empirical. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: A Marxist economist tried to defend Karl Marx's labor theory of value against an Austrian critic named Boehm-Bawerk. What was Boehm-Bawerk's main point against the labor theory of value?
answer: Prices come from what buyers actually want, not from hours of work put in
choices: Prices come from what buyers actually want, not from hours of work put in
Labor is worth exactly whatever workers say it is worth
Only gold and silver can measure any real value
Value equals the average of every past price
context: Rudolf Hilferding (1877-1941) served as Weimar Germany's Finance Minister in 1923 and again in 1928-29. He fled the Nazis in 1933, was captured in Vichy France in 1941, and was murdered by the Gestapo the same year. Source: hetwebsite.net/het/profiles/hilferding.htm.

question: Karl Marx said an item's value equals the labor hours put into it. His Austrian critic said Marx quietly abandoned that idea in Volume 3 of Capital and sneaked in an older theory: that price simply equals what it cost to make the item. What is the name for that older theory?
answer: A cost-of-production theory of price
choices: A cost-of-production theory of price
A supply-and-demand theory of price
A subjective marginal utility theory of price
A quantity theory of money
context: Boehm-Bawerk showed that Marx's Volume 3 prices are effectively determined by the sum of costs (wages plus capital-input costs plus average profit) -- the classical COST-OF-PRODUCTION theory of price associated with Adam Smith. That is not a transformation of the labor theory; it is a quiet substitution for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: An old idea claims that a jacket's price should equal the hours of work that went into it. A critic asked: then why do handmade horseshoes now sell for less than the labor time it takes to make them? Which one-word idea from Austrian economists answers this puzzle?
answer: Subjective value — worth depends on what each buyer wants
choices: Subjective value — worth depends on what each buyer wants
Central pricing — a bureau sets fair prices from above
Labor equivalence — hours of work should equal price
Fixed exchange — one product must trade for a set amount
context: Paul Sweezy's 1949 combined volume (Karl Marx and the Close of His System, by Boehm-Bawerk, plus Boehm-Bawerk's Criticism of Marx, by Hilferding) is the standard English-language source for the whole debate. Baran was Sweezy's later Monopoly Capital co-author; Dobb the leading British Marxist economist; Mandel the Belgian trotskyist economist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: A famous 19th-century book gets a serious math refutation. Over the next century its defenders quietly abandon the original math. They try to rebuild the same conclusion on different assumptions. What does that pattern most honestly amount to?
answer: Conceding the original refutation and starting over from other passages
choices: Conceding the original refutation and starting over from other passages
Reproducing the original solution with slightly cleaner algebra
Proving the original critic was completely mistaken
Showing the book's conclusions do not need any argument at all
context: The New Interpretation does not defend Volume 3's original transformation equation (that would be reproducing Marx's math); it builds a substitute from a different reading of scattered Marx passages -- which is a concession that Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 diagnostic held for the printed text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: By the 1920s Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay had produced a striking result in one specific arena. Which arena did the essay effectively close for a generation?
answer: academic defense of Marxian value theory in German universities
choices: academic defense of Marxian value theory in German universities
political influence of the European socialist parties
public sales of Das Kapital across the continent
translation of Marx into non-German European languages
context: Boehm-Bawerk's essay did not damage socialist party politics (which grew rapidly after 1900) or public sales of Marx (which continued). What it ended for a generation was serious ACADEMIC defense of the Volume 1 labor-value equation inside German-language universities; that defense only resumed with the Anglo-American revival in the 1940s-70s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: The founder of the Austrian School had a son born in Vienna in 1902. The son became a top mathematician, not an economist. What was his first name?
answer: Karl
choices: Karl
Hans
Otto
Josef
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985) was born when his father Carl Menger was 62. Father became the economist; son became the mathematician. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: One famous fractal is a solid cube with smaller cubes drilled out at every scale. What is it called?
answer: The Menger sponge
choices: The Menger sponge
The Cantor set
The Sierpinski triangle
The Mandelbrot set
context: Karl Menger the younger described the sponge in 1926. It is a 3-dimensional analogue of the 1D Cantor set. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Menger_sponge.

question: Karl Menger the younger earned his doctorate at the University of Vienna under Hans Hahn. He worked in a branch of math that asks how many numbers you need to name each point in a space. What was his field?
answer: Dimension theory
choices: Dimension theory
Number theory
Group theory
Probability theory
context: Menger's 1924 doctorate under Hans Hahn produced original work on the topological definition of what it means for a space to be n-dimensional. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: In the 1920s and early 1930s the city of Vienna was one of the world's centers of new ideas in economics and mathematics. Many of those thinkers had to flee later in the 1930s. What forced them to leave?
answer: The rise of Nazi Germany and its takeover of Austria
choices: The rise of Nazi Germany and its takeover of Austria
The Austrian government banned all economic study
A giant fire destroyed the University of Vienna
The city ran out of money to pay professors
context: Menger's Mathematical Colloquium was one of the most important mathematics seminars of the interwar era. Kurt Godel presented parts of his incompleteness work through it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: The Menger fractal has a dimension between 2 and 3, not a whole number, because it has holes at every scale. About what is that dimension?
context: The Menger sponge's Hausdorff dimension is log(20)/log(3), approximately 2.727 -- a solid cube that is dimensionally between a 2D surface and a full 3D volume. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Menger_sponge.

question: A group of friends meets once a week to talk about how prices, jobs, and trade work in their small town. Over years they build a shared way of thinking about the economy. What do we usually call a shared set of ideas that grows from a group like this?
answer: A school of thought
choices: A school of thought
A trading company
A stock exchange
A budget office
context: The Vienna Circle of logical positivists was the philosophy scene through which Menger's mathematics work interacted with Godel, Carnap, and Wittgenstein-as-influence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Karl Menger the younger saw where Central European politics was heading. In 1937 he left Austria for a Catholic research university in Indiana. Which American school gave him a chair?
answer: The University of Notre Dame
choices: The University of Notre Dame
Georgetown University
Boston College
Fordham University
context: Menger accepted a Notre Dame chair in 1937, moving permanently to America a year before the March 1938 Anschluss. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: Karl Menger the younger wrote a memoir about the math seminar he ran and the philosophy circle he sat in on in Vienna between the wars. It came out in 1994, after he died. What is the memoir's title?
answer: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle and the Mathematical Colloquium
choices: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle and the Mathematical Colloquium
Human Action
The Open Society and Its Enemies
Notes on Godel's Theorems
context: Menger's 1994 memoir is one of the best insider accounts of Vienna's twin scientific-philosophical circles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: On August 23, 1939, two foreign ministers signed a treaty in Moscow. In public it promised no war between them. In secret it split Eastern Europe between them. Which two countries signed?
answer: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union
choices: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union
Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy
The Soviet Union and Republican Spain
The Soviet Union and the United Kingdom
context: The signers were Nazi Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov; the treaty is universally known as the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: In September 1939 Nazi Germany invaded Poland from the west. Sixteen days later a second huge country invaded Poland from the east, and the two split the country between them under a secret agreement. Which country came from the east?
answer: The Soviet Union
choices: The Soviet Union
Fascist Italy
Imperial Japan
Francoist Spain
context: The USSR annexed eastern Poland immediately, and in June 1940 annexed the three Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), all consistent with the pact's secret territorial protocol. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: In 1940 Soviet police killed about 22,000 Polish officers, cops, and teachers. Killing a country's leaders is a common early step for a communist regime. Why do these rulers go after the educated first?
answer: Educated people can organize resistance to the new rulers
choices: Educated people can organize resistance to the new rulers
Educated people eat much more food than others
Educated people cannot do farm work
Educated people spread disease
context: Katyn was one of three main execution sites; the other two were the NKVD facilities at Kalinin and Kharkiv. The category of victim was deliberately chosen to decapitate Polish national leadership. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: In 1940 Soviet police killed Polish officers, police, and educated workers. This became known as the Katyn massacre. About how many people were killed?
answer: About 22,000
choices: About 22,000
About 500
About 200,000
About 1.5 million
context: The victims were specifically the categories most likely to lead a Polish national resistance or postwar state. The class-decapitation intent is what NKVD execution lists document. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: From 1943 to 1990 the Soviet Union publicly blamed Nazi Germany for Katyn. On April 13, 1990 the Soviet government finally admitted the truth. Which Soviet leader was in office at the acknowledgment?
answer: Mikhail Gorbachev
choices: Mikhail Gorbachev
Leonid Brezhnev
Yuri Andropov
Nikita Khrushchev

question: On October 14, 1992, Russian President Boris Yeltsin gave Polish leaders the original Politburo files on Katyn. One paper was dated March 5, 1940, and it named who had ordered the killings. What did the paper carry?

Molotov's diplomatic notes on the Ribbentrop pact
Ribbentrop's telegrams to Berlin
Beria's private diary from 1940

question: In 2007 the Polish director Andrzej Wajda released a film about Katyn. It is told from the viewpoint of Polish families searching for missing officers. What personal history gave the director a direct claim to the story?
answer: Wajda's own father, an officer, had been killed at Kharkiv

Wajda had personally filmed the German 1943 exhumations
Wajda had led the March 1990 protests demanding acknowledgment

question: The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact plus Katyn together illustrate a specific historical fact about the two-year period from August 1939 to June 1941, when Hitler broke the pact by invading the USSR. Which fact does the pair establish?
answer: The Soviet Union was a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany from August 1939 to June 1941

The Soviet Union was neutral throughout World War II
The Soviet Union was allied with the United Kingdom throughout 1939-41
The Soviet Union invaded no other country between 1939 and 1945
context: The pact and its secret territorial protocol, the September 1939 Soviet invasion of Poland, the June 1940 annexation of the Baltics, and the 1940 Katyn massacre are one continuous historical arc. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: A woman in Connecticut owned a small pink house. The city wanted to knock it down so a big company could build offices there. What is the power a government uses to take private land like this?
answer: Eminent domain
choices: Eminent domain
A property tax
Zoning
A tariff
context: Kelo's pink house was in the Fort Trumbull neighborhood of New London, Connecticut. The city and New London Development Corporation adopted a plan to build offices, retail, and residential development around the Pfizer campus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelo_v._City_of_New_London.

question: Susette Kelo would not sell her New London home. So the city moved to take it using a Fifth Amendment power. That power lets the government take private land for 'public use' if it pays a fair price. What is that power called?
answer: Eminent domain
choices: Eminent domain
Sovereign immunity
Regulatory taking
Manifest necessity
context: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause authorizes eminent domain -- government seizure of private property for public use, with just compensation. Historically 'public use' meant roads, schools, or military bases. Source: constitution.congress.gov (Fifth Amendment).

question: A city government forces a family to sell their home so a private company can build offices on the land. The city argues that new jobs and taxes count as 'public use.' Why do critics say this stretches the meaning of public use too far?
answer: The property is going to another private owner, not to a park or a road
choices: The property is going to another private owner, not to a park or a road
Building offices takes a very long time and delays other work
Companies never pay any taxes on land they take over
Cities are not allowed to buy or sell land under any law
context: Justice John Paul Stevens wrote for the majority in Kelo v. City of New London, 545 US 469 (2005), joined by Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Source: supremecourt.gov (Kelo 545 US 469).

question: The main dissent in Kelo had a famous warning. It said the state could replace any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton, any home with a shopping mall, or any farm with a factory. Which justice wrote that dissent?
answer: Sandra Day O'Connor
choices: Sandra Day O'Connor
Antonin Scalia
Clarence Thomas
William Rehnquist
context: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor's principal dissent was joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia and Thomas. The Motel-6-to-Ritz-Carlton passage became the most-quoted line of the case. Source: Kelo, 545 US 469 (2005), dissent.

question: Susette Kelo lost her home. But what happened to the Pfizer research campus that was the whole point of the plan?
answer: Pfizer closed the facility within about five years
choices: Pfizer closed the facility within about five years
Pfizer doubled the campus size
Pfizer moved its global headquarters there
Pfizer converted it to an art museum
context: Pfizer closed the New London research facility in 2009-10. The cleared land where Kelo's house and her neighbors' homes had stood then remained vacant for more than a decade. Source: nytimes.com and courant.com (Pfizer New London closure coverage).

question: In the 10 years after the Kelo ruling, most states passed new laws to limit taking one owner's land to give to another. About how many states did so?
answer: About 45
choices: About 45
About 15
About 5
Essentially none
context: Roughly 45 states enacted post-Kelo constitutional amendments or statutes restricting economic-development takings, largely driven by campaigns from the Institute for Justice, Kelo's counsel. Source: ij.org (post-Kelo state legislation tracker).

question: Kelo's legal team came from a public-interest law firm started in 1991 by Chip Mellor and Clint Bolick. It has become the leading American property-rights litigation firm. What is its name?
answer: The Institute for Justice
choices: The Institute for Justice
The Pacific Legal Foundation
The Federalist Society
The Cato Institute
context: The Institute for Justice, founded in 1991, represented Susette Kelo and has litigated dozens of eminent-domain cases since. Source: ij.org.

question: The Kelo case shows a common public-choice pattern for why private-to-private takings keep happening even though they clash with the Constitution. Which story best captures the pattern?
answer: A politically connected developer captures takings power over dispersed homeowners
choices: A politically connected developer captures takings power over dispersed homeowners
A benevolent city planner balances competing public interests
A federal environmental review paralyzes local government
A random judicial error assigns rights inefficiently
context: The public-choice reading combines Tullock 1967 rent-seeking (real resources burned on the political process) with Olson 1965 concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost (one organized developer versus many un-organized neighbors). Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: A supporter of the Kelo ruling would defend the outcome by pointing to a specific public purpose named in the redevelopment plan. What was that stated purpose?
answer: Increased jobs and expanded tax base for the city
choices: Increased jobs and expanded tax base for the city
Federal defense readiness in New England
Access to a natural harbor for shipping
Preservation of a historic Colonial neighborhood
context: The New London plan's stated purpose was economic development -- jobs and tax base -- which the Kelo majority accepted as satisfying 'public use' under the Fifth Amendment. The public-choice reading focuses on WHO actually benefited concentrated-ly, and how organized they were. Source: Kelo, 545 US 469 (2005), majority opinion.

question: Kelo teaches a move public-choice thinkers use when the government forces one private party to give up things to another. What should the analyst look for behind the stated reason?
answer: Who is the concentrated beneficiary and who bears the concentrated cost
choices: Who is the concentrated beneficiary and who bears the concentrated cost
Which political party holds the mayor's office
How large the total municipal budget is
Whether the seized property is above or below the median value
context: The stated public purpose is often sincere but incomplete. The public-choice reading identifies the concentrated beneficiary (developer) and concentrated cost-bearers (individual homeowners) whose organizational asymmetry drives the outcome. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965); Kelo (2005) as case study.

question: The wave of state reforms after Kelo is unusual in public-choice work. It is a rare case where a spread-out victim group actually organized well enough to reverse a concentrated-benefit outcome. What made that reversal possible?
answer: Sustained litigation and advocacy by the Institute for Justice organized the dispersed interest
choices: Sustained litigation and advocacy by the Institute for Justice organized the dispersed interest
The federal government abolished eminent domain entirely
Insurance companies refused to insure any seized property
The Supreme Court reversed itself in a follow-up case
context: IJ served as the selective-incentive engine (documentation, model legislation, media) that turned diffuse public concern into effective 45-state legislative action. This is Olson's own solution to the collective-action problem in action. Source: ij.org (post-Kelo advocacy history).

question: A mathematician proved something odd. There is no perfect way to combine many people's votes into one group ranking. Some fairness rule always breaks. What did he prove could not be done?
answer: A perfectly fair way to combine everyone's votes
choices: A perfectly fair way to combine everyone's votes
A perfectly efficient factory
A perfectly free market
A perfectly balanced budget
context: Kenneth Arrow (1921-2017) won the 1972 Nobel jointly with John Hicks. He was 51 -- then the youngest economics Nobel. His doctoral book Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951) contained the impossibility result. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Arrow.

question: Kenneth Arrow's 1951 book grew out of his doctoral paper at Columbia. Its title named two things at once: how to combine what each person wants into what a group picks. What is the book called?
answer: Social Choice and Individual Values
choices: Social Choice and Individual Values
General Equilibrium and Welfare
The Theory of Voting Systems
Preferences and Aggregation
context: Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951; second edition 1963). The book launched the modern field of social-choice theory. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (2012 reprint of the second edition).

question: Arrow's theorem sets a short list of fairness rules on any voting method and asks whether all can be met at once. One rule says: if every voter prefers A to B, the group must too. What is this basic requirement called?
answer: Pareto efficiency (or unanimity)
choices: Pareto efficiency (or unanimity)
Independence of irrelevant alternatives
Non-dictatorship
Universal domain
context: Arrow's five criteria include unanimity (if all voters rank A above B, so does the group), independence of irrelevant alternatives, universal domain, transitivity, and non-dictatorship. The theorem proves no method satisfies all simultaneously. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963).

question: One of Arrow's fairness rules says that no single voter should be able to set the group outcome no matter what everyone else picks. What is that rule called?
answer: Non-dictatorship
choices: Non-dictatorship
Anonymity
Neutrality
Monotonicity
context: The non-dictatorship condition rules out any voting method that always follows one specified voter. Arrow proved that dropping this condition is the only way to make the other criteria consistent -- which is why the theorem is so provocative. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Three friends vote on pizza toppings: pepperoni, cheese, or mushrooms. Even simple voting rules can end up giving strange results where no clear winner appears. What does math actually say about a perfect voting rule that is always fair for every group?
answer: No such perfect voting rule exists
choices: No such perfect voting rule exists
One exists only when there are exactly three voters
Ranked-choice voting solves every possible case
It works only if every voter is completely honest
context: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem: for any group of three or more voters facing three or more alternatives, no method can satisfy the five fairness criteria simultaneously. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Arrow's result kicks in only above a certain number of options. Below that, majority rule works fine. What is the smallest number of choices where the problem starts?
answer: Three
choices: Three
Two
Five
Seven
context: With only two alternatives, majority rule satisfies every Arrow criterion. The impossibility applies for any group of three or more voters facing three or more alternatives. The classic Condorcet paradox is a three-voter, three-option case. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Two candidates run for class president. Most kids want moderate rules. Both candidates want to win the most votes. Where do the two candidates usually end up standing on the issues?
answer: Right in the middle, to appeal to the average voter
choices: Right in the middle, to appeal to the average voter
At the far left, to stand out from the crowd
At the far right, to stand out from the crowd
Refusing to state their views at all
context: Duncan Black, 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making' (Journal of Political Economy, 1948), showed that if preferences are single-peaked on one dimension, majority rule picks the median voter's preferred option. It is the narrow exception to Arrow's impossibility. Source: jstor.org (Black 1948).

question: American economist Kenneth Arrow proved a famous math result. No voting system can turn each person's picks into a fair group choice while meeting a few basic rules of fairness at the same time. What is this idea called?
answer: Arrow's impossibility theorem
choices: Arrow's impossibility theorem
The median voter theorem
The invisible hand principle
The efficient markets hypothesis
context: John Hicks and Kenneth Arrow shared the 1972 Nobel 'for their pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory and welfare theory.' Source: nobelprize.org (1972 Economic Sciences).

question: The most sweeping lesson of Arrow's theorem for democratic theory is that a phrase used every election night names no coherent object at all. Which phrase does his mathematics dissolve?
answer: The will of the people
choices: The will of the people
The consent of the governed
The public interest
The rule of law
context: If different voting methods produce different winners from the same voter preferences, there is no method-independent 'will of the people' waiting to be discovered. The winner is jointly produced by voters AND the aggregation rule. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (Freeman 1982).

question: Arrow's theorem strengthens a specific move public choice already wanted to make about political institutions. If no method-free group preference exists, which set of choices does the theorem give added weight to?
answer: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
choices: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
The particular slate of candidates matters more than the rules
Party discipline can substitute for any voting-method choice
Judicial review can always correct impossibility results
context: James Buchanan built on this insight: rules that determine HOW votes are aggregated do not merely process a preexisting will; they partly DEFINE what the aggregate looks like. Constitutional political economy takes the rules-choice question with new seriousness. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (1982).

question: An Austrian-school economist said the entrepreneur is someone who spots a chance to make money that others have missed. It could be a shop no one has opened or a product no one has made yet. What is the key skill he said they have?
answer: Alertness to opportunities others miss
choices: Alertness to opportunities others miss
Having the most money to invest
Being the best at math
Knowing the government well
context: Israel Kirzner (b. February 13, 1930), Competition and Entrepreneurship (University of Chicago Press, 1973). Kirzner was a student of Ludwig von Mises at NYU. Source: press.uchicago.edu (Kirzner 1973).

question: Kirzner's 1973 theory splits from two rival views. Frank Knight said the entrepreneur is mostly a risk-taker. Joseph Schumpeter said he is mostly an inventor. What did Kirzner say?
answer: Someone alert to profit opportunities others missed
choices: Someone alert to profit opportunities others missed
Someone who assembles the largest possible capital
Someone who lobbies government for protective regulation
Someone who monopolizes an existing market
context: Kirzner separates alertness from Knight's risk-bearing and Schumpeter's creative-destruction innovation. The entrepreneur perceives an opportunity in the flow of prices and technology that competitors with the same information failed to see. Source: Kirzner, Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago 1973).

question: Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997 and led the launch of the iPhone in June 2007. In Kirznerian terms, what did Jobs see that his rivals at BlackBerry, Nokia, and Motorola did not act on?
answer: That touchscreens, music players, and phones could be integrated into one mass-market product
choices: That touchscreens, music players, and phones could be integrated into one mass-market product
That mobile phones should be limited to voice calls only
That physical keyboards would dominate for the next thirty years
That personal computers should replace all mobile devices
context: Jobs saw the integration opportunity. Touchscreens (LG Prada 2006), music players (Apple's iPod since 2001), and phones (Nokia, BlackBerry, Motorola) all existed. The Kirznerian alertness was seeing they could combine. BlackBerry's Jim Balsillie publicly derided the iPhone in 2007. Source: Isaacson, Steve Jobs (Simon & Schuster 2011).

question: In 2002 Elon Musk started SpaceX to chase a chance that NASA, Boeing, and Lockheed Martin had missed for 40 years. What was that chance?
answer: Reusable orbital rockets that land and fly again
choices: Reusable orbital rockets that land and fly again
Traditional expendable rockets built cheaper offshore
Government-funded space colonies on Mars
Suborbital tourism using balloons
context: The launch industry had assumed rockets were disposable for decades. Musk's insight was that per-launch cost drops dramatically if the first stage lands and is reused. Falcon 9's first successful landing was December 21, 2015. Source: spacex.com (Falcon 9 mission archive).

question: By the mid-2020s SpaceX had landed and flown its first-stage boosters many times. That proved Musk's bet right: the space industry was wrong to treat rockets as one-use. About how many first-stage landings and reuses had SpaceX done?
answer: Over 300
choices: Over 300
About 10
About 30
About 3,000
context: By 2024 SpaceX had landed and reused Falcon 9 first stages over 300 times, some individual boosters twenty times or more. It has driven launch prices down substantially and captured most of the commercial launch market. Source: spacex.com (launch archive).

question: On July 5, 1994 Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in Seattle with a single product category. In Kirzner's view, what made this category the perfect start for a large online store?
answer: Books are standardized, durable, easily shipped, with a long-tail catalog
choices: Books are standardized, durable, easily shipped, with a long-tail catalog
Books have the highest per-unit profit margins in all of retail
Books face no competition from physical bookstores
Books are exempt from state sales tax on federal statute
context: Bezos's Kirznerian alertness: books were the perfect starting product for internet-scale retail. No physical bookstore could stock the long-tail catalog. Chain bookstores had the same information but did not move decisively online. Source: Stone, The Everything Store (Little Brown 2013).

question: Kirzner studied under a famous teacher at New York University. That teacher wrote a book on human action that shaped Kirzner's whole approach. Who was the teacher?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Carl Menger
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
context: Ludwig von Mises taught at NYU from 1945 to his death in 1973. Kirzner was among his most prominent students and inherited the Austrian entrepreneurship-and-market-process tradition. Source: mises.org (Mises + Kirzner biographical materials).

question: Kirzner never won a Nobel Prize. But in 2006 he won a big international prize for his work on entrepreneurs. Which prize was it?
answer: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
choices: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
The Presidential Medal of Freedom
The Templeton Prize
context: Israel Kirzner received the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research (Swedish Entrepreneurship Forum) in 2006 for his lifetime work. He is widely regarded as the leading Austrian theorist of the entrepreneurial function. Source: e-award.org (Kirzner 2006 laureate).

question: Kirzner's framework asks one key question about a company founder. Think of Amazon, SpaceX, or the iPhone. What does the framework tell you to ask?
answer: What did the founder see that competitors with the same technology and capital did not act on
choices: What did the founder see that competitors with the same technology and capital did not act on
How much capital did the founder inherit from family
Which lobbying firm secured the founder's early contracts
How many patents did the founder personally hold
context: Kirznerian analysis: technology and capital are usually accessible to many; alertness is not. The reason a new firm succeeds where competitors failed is usually a specific perception of an integration or application others considered impossible. Source: Kirzner (1973), Chapter 2.

question: Real founders often mix all three Austrian views of the entrepreneur: Kirzner's alertness, Knight's risk-taking, and Schumpeter's invention. What is the teaching value of pulling the three apart when we study one founder?
answer: It clarifies which theory fits which specific move being analyzed
choices: It clarifies which theory fits which specific move being analyzed
It proves one of the three theories is always correct
It refutes the other two theories permanently
It replaces the need to look at any actual data
context: The point is not that a founder is 'a Kirznerian' or 'a Schumpeterian' in every action. The point is that different moves within a founder's career fit different theories: Bezos's book-choice was Kirznerian alertness; Musk's Mars ambition is Schumpeterian innovation; both took Knightian risks. Source: Kirzner (1973); Schumpeter (1911); Knight (1921).

question: The knowledge to run an economy is spread across millions of people. No one place holds it all. What follows from that?
answer: No small group of planners can know enough to run the whole economy
choices: No small group of planners can know enough to run the whole economy
The government should hire more economists
Only computers can plan an economy
People should stop specializing at all
context: Thomas Sowell published Knowledge and Decisions with Basic Books in 1980; it ran 422 pages in hardcover and won that year's Law and Economics Center Prize. Stigler, Becker and Friedman were all Chicago colleagues of his, which is why they make honest distractors. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Knowledge_and_Decisions); Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: Thomas Sowell built his book Knowledge and Decisions on a single article by F.A. Hayek from September 1945. Hayek argued that prices carry information no central office could ever gather on its own. Which Hayek article was it?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretence of Knowledge
Economics and Knowledge
The Road to Serfdom
context: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review 35(4), September 1945. 'Economics and Knowledge' is his 1937 lecture, 'The Pretence of Knowledge' his 1974 Nobel lecture, and The Road to Serfdom the 1944 book. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions' and 'Hayek'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Tin grows scarce -- maybe a mine floods, maybe a new use for it is found -- and the price rises. Manufacturers in a dozen industries economize on tin; none ever learns which cause it was. F.A. Hayek built his 1945 argument on this example, and Sowell built Knowledge and Decisions on Hayek's. What does Hayek say no central planning board could manage here?
answer: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
choices: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
Proving in advance that the scarcity was real and not a speculator's rumour
Keeping its own officials honest once tin was valuable enough to bribe over
Matching the speed with which foreign factories would switch to substitutes
context: Hayek's point is not that planners are stupid but that the knowledge is not theirs to have: it exists only as millions of particular circumstances of time and place. The price is not a summary of that knowledge -- it is the only form in which it can travel. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Hayek' and 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: In a 2018 interview, Thomas Sowell was asked which of his books he was proudest of. He named a shorter, easier-to-read book as his personal favorite. Which book?
answer: A Conflict of Visions
choices: A Conflict of Visions
The Vision of the Anointed
Intellectuals and Society
Basic Economics
context: Sowell to Reason, November 26 2018: Knowledge and Decisions 'certainly was at the time, and it's certainly among the books that I'm proudest of now,' but his 'own personal favorite is Conflict of Visions, which is perhaps a third of the size and more readable.' Source: Reason, 'Thomas Sowell Returns' (https://reason.com/2018/11/26/thomas-sowell-returns/).

question: Knowledge and Decisions had rested its entire case on one 1945 essay by F.A. Hayek. In December 1981 Hayek, then 82 and seven years past his Nobel, took up Sowell's book himself in the pages of Reason magazine. What did he do there?
answer: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
choices: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
Objected in a letter to the editor that his 1945 essay had been flattened into slogans
Listed it among ten books he wished that he had written himself before the war
Warned readers that Sowell had confused his 1945 essay with Mises's 1920 one
context: Hayek's review ran in Reason, December 1981, under exactly that title. He wrote that Sowell had expanded admirably on his original concepts and made them clear to lay readers, with examples of economic activity drawn from the real world. Sources: Reason, December 1981 (https://reason.com/1981/12/01/the-best-book-on-general-econo/); Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: In the autumn of 1973 the pump price of American gasoline was held down by federal ceilings while queues at filling stations ran for hours. Oregon's Governor Tom McCall had no power to move the price, so he changed the rule about who could fill up -- the first state scheme of its kind, and other states soon copied it. What was Oregon's rule?
answer: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
choices: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
Every registered household received a coupon book good for a fixed number of gallons
The first two hours of every morning were reserved for commercial and farm vehicles
Each station auctioned off its remaining supply to the highest bidders at opening time
context: Oregon adopted odd-even rationing in the autumn of 1973, Governor Tom McCall urging stations to sell by the last digit of the plate. It is the clean illustration of Sowell's point: stop the price from rationing scarce gasoline and something else must ration it -- a queue, a coupon, a calendar. Source: Grokipedia, 'Odd-even rationing' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Odd-even_rationing) and '1970s energy crisis'.

question: The Law and Economics Center gave its 1980 prize to Knowledge and Decisions, calling the book a landmark work. The citation did not praise it in general terms; it named one specific thing the book had helped its readers understand. What did the committee name?
answer: The differences between the market process and the process of government
choices: The differences between the market process and the process of government
The reasons wage and price controls had failed in every decade since 1940
The drift of American courts away from the intentions of the Constitution's framers
The gap between what academic economists publish and what voters actually believe
context: The Law and Economics Center called Knowledge and Decisions a landmark work, chosen 'because of its cogent contribution to our understanding of the differences between the market process and the process of government.' Sources: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions); ContemporaryThinkers.org, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Through the winter of 1973-74 American drivers queued for hours at filling stations, and much of the coverage treated those queues as proof that the oil had simply run out. National inventories in fact remained adequate. Washington had capped the price of domestic oil and refined products. On Sowell's account, what did that cap do?
answer: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
choices: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
Moved the shortage from the pump back to the refinery, where it could be managed out of public sight
Raised the cost of hoarding so sharply that drivers ran their tanks down to fumes before refilling
Concentrated the loss on the oil companies while spreading the gain thinly across every single driver
context: The 1973 Arab embargo was a real supply shock -- crude went from about $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. Sowell's argument is not that the controls caused the shortage but that they made it far worse: with the price frozen, refiners had little reason to produce more, drivers little reason to buy less, and hoarding paid. Source: Grokipedia, '1970s energy crisis' (https://grokipedia.com/page/1970s_energy_crisis) and 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: In Knowledge and Decisions, Sowell warns that modern societies face a growing split. Real hands-on knowledge, he says, gets pushed aside by abstract theory about how society ought to work. What gap does he describe?
answer: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
choices: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
Between what a government promises at election time and what it can actually afford to pay for later
Between the wealth held by a country's oldest households and the wealth held by its youngest ones
Between the speed at which a society's technology changes and the speed at which its laws get rewritten
context: Sowell's framing worry is a widening gap between firsthand knowledge and decision-making authority: the further a decision travels from the person who knows the particulars, the more it must run on somebody's general theory instead. Source: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: A student sums up Knowledge and Decisions as 'markets good, government bad.' Sowell's actual structure is different: he takes markets with their prices and profits, elected legislatures with their votes and lobbying, and courts with their rules of evidence, and runs every one of them through the same single test. What is that test?
answer: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
choices: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
Whether the people who designed the process meant well by those it would govern
How thinly the process spreads its costs and how narrowly it piles up its benefits
Which rival process would otherwise do the same job, and how badly it would do it
context: This is why the book is not a market-versus-state pamphlet: Sowell asks the identical question of every institution, markets included, and the answers come out different by institution rather than by team. The other three choices are real analytic moves too -- Sowell's own 'compared to what?', Mancur Olson's dispersed costs and concentrated benefits, and Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: A college admits a student through a racial preference into a program where most classmates arrived far better prepared. Sowell argued this hurts the very students it was meant to help.
