question: Some states let nurse practitioners run a clinic on their own, with no doctor supervising. About half the states allow this by 2024. Studies of those states keep finding one clear pattern. What pattern?
answer: Lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference from physician-only states
choices: Lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference from physician-only states
Sharply worse patient outcomes and higher malpractice rates
Sharply higher primary-care prices and lower quality
Identical prices and quality but shorter waits
context: Multiple studies, including RAND Corporation work and AANP meta-analyses, find lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference. State medical societies routinely oppose scope expansion; state nursing associations support it. Source: rand.org (NP scope-of-practice studies).

question: A group of licensed dentists tried to stop cheaper non-dentist teeth-whitening kits by using their state's dental board to ban competitors. Free-market economists say this shows a common pattern. What is the term for using government rules to shut out your competition?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Free trade
Comparative advantage
Creative destruction
context: North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, 574 US 494 (2015). The board had been trying to stop non-dentists from offering teeth-whitening services. The Court held that industry-majority boards without active state supervision lose Parker antitrust immunity. Source: supremecourt.gov (NC Dental 574 US 494).

question: Friedman wanted to keep quality signals for patients without giving doctors a state-backed monopoly. What did he suggest in place of licensing?
answer: Certification rather than licensing
choices: Certification rather than licensing
Free-for-all with no state role at all
Federal licensing replacing state licensing
Direct government provision of the service
context: Friedman's certification / licensing distinction: the state may certify credentials, but should not forbid uncertified practitioners from offering services to informed adults who accept the trade-off. Quality signaling without monopoly. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962), Chapter 9.

question: The heart of the medical-licensing critique is a default suspicion. When a state licensing board is filled with members of the same profession it licenses, what should you suspect first?
answer: That entry restrictions serve incumbent incomes more than public safety
choices: That entry restrictions serve incumbent incomes more than public safety
That the board will always adopt the safest possible rules
That state legislatures will oversee it closely
That patients enjoy full transparency into board decisions
context: The Stigler-Olson combined move: incumbents are the concentrated beneficiary organized to write the entry rules; patients are the dispersed party unable to organize. The default should be suspicion; specific safety justifications must be shown, not assumed. Source: Friedman (1962); Stigler (1971); Kleiner (2006).

question: The Austrian school says only people can really act, choose, or decide. Every social outcome has to trace back to those people. What is this rule called?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Methodological holism
Structural functionalism
Historical materialism
context: Methodological individualism, made central to praxeology in Mises's Human Action (Yale, 1949), holds that groups, classes, and markets are useful shorthand but never literally act. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_individualism.

question: The rival view says groups, classes, or whole societies act as units in their own right. Marxist class analysis leans on this move. What is it called?
answer: Methodological holism
choices: Methodological holism
Methodological individualism
Praxeology
Utilitarianism
context: Methodological holism (sometimes 'organicism') is the position Mises argued against. Marxist statements like 'the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat' are the paradigm case. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_holism.

question: One school of economics argues that a whole country's economy is really millions of people acting on purpose. Each is trying to make life better. Every price and every trade is one of those choices. Where does this school say the study of economics has to begin?
answer: With the choices of individual people acting on purpose
choices: With the choices of individual people acting on purpose
With the total amount of money in the country
With the government's official five-year plan
With the average behavior of a whole social class
context: Human Action (Yale, 1949) makes methodological individualism the foundation of praxeology in chapter 1 section 2, 'The Fundamental Task of Praxeology'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: Some thinkers argue that "society" cannot make choices — only the individual people in it can. A plan that treats a whole nation like one big person will miss what real people actually want. What is this idea called?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Collective rationalism
Central planning theory
Social holism
context: Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies (Routledge, 1945) uses the same phrase and endorses the same doctrine from outside the Austrian tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Open_Society_and_Its_Enemies.

question: A Marxist says the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat. A follower of Mises rewrites that sentence to make the real incentives easy to see. What move does the Misesian make?
answer: Replace class terms with specific persons acting in specific transactions
choices: Replace class terms with specific persons acting in specific transactions
Replace class terms with abstract aggregate demand curves
Replace class terms with statistical correlations across populations
Replace class terms with equilibrium price vectors
context: The analytical payoff of methodological individualism: 'the government intervened' hides everything; 'this senator, facing this lobby, cast this vote for this reason' opens up the incentive picture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_individualism.

question: Some people think this idea means every social outcome was planned on purpose. That is a misread. What qualifier does the idea actually make room for?
answer: Outcomes can be the result of human action but not of any human design
choices: Outcomes can be the result of human action but not of any human design
Outcomes are always the intended plan of a central authority
Outcomes can be reduced to statistical population means
Outcomes emerge from unconscious biological instincts
context: The doctrine coexists with spontaneous order: a market price is not chosen by anyone yet emerges from individuals choosing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: An 18th-century Scottish writer coined a famous phrase: important human institutions like language and markets are 'the result of human action, but not of human design.' What kind of order does this phrase describe?
answer: A spontaneous order that grows without any single planner in charge
choices: A spontaneous order that grows without any single planner in charge
A carefully engineered order designed by government experts
A random order with no useful patterns at all
A dictatorship where one leader controls everything
context: Adam Ferguson's An Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767) contains the phrase that Hayek would use to describe spontaneous orders like markets, law, and language. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Adam_Ferguson.

question: Rothbard's own great treatise, published in 1962, opens with the same methodological-individualist premise as Human Action. What is Rothbard's book's title?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
The Ethics of Liberty
What Has Government Done to Our Money?
context: Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) is the postwar American restatement of the Misesian system on the same foundational premise. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: In 2020 the US Federal Reserve was printing many new dollars. Some firms feared their savings would lose value. So they moved company cash into Bitcoin instead. Why would a firm do that?
answer: Bitcoin has a fixed supply and can't be printed
choices: Bitcoin has a fixed supply and can't be printed
Bitcoin pays interest every month
Bitcoin is backed by the US government
Bitcoin is guaranteed by the Federal Reserve
context: MicroStrategy, headquartered in Tysons Corner Virginia and founded in 1989, was the first US public company to make Bitcoin a corporate-treasury reserve asset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MicroStrategy.

question: A tech CEO moved huge amounts of his company's savings into Bitcoin. He said it was to guard against a threat: when governments print more money, each dollar buys less. What is this money-printing problem usually called?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
Deflation
Recession
Tariffs
context: Michael Saylor founded MicroStrategy in 1989 while at MIT. He stepped down as CEO in 2022 to become executive chairman but remained the public face of the Bitcoin strategy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Saylor.

question: MicroStrategy said in August 2020 that holding dollars was a losing bet. They blamed one Fed policy of the pandemic era. Which policy?
answer: Trillion-dollar balance-sheet expansion
choices: Trillion-dollar balance-sheet expansion
Setting the federal-funds rate at 5 percent
Selling off Treasury holdings under quantitative tightening
Raising bank reserve requirements sharply
context: The Fed's balance sheet grew by trillions in 2020-21 as it bought Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities to backstop pandemic markets. Saylor argued this made cash a certain loser and Bitcoin the hedge. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2020-21).

question: MicroStrategy's first Bitcoin buy in August 2020 came from cash the company already had. How much did they spend?
answer: $250 million
choices: $250 million
$25 million
$2.5 billion
$50 million
context: MicroStrategy's August 11 2020 announcement: $250M converted from cash into Bitcoin. Subsequent purchases over 2020-2025 pushed total holdings well above 200,000 BTC. Source: microstrategy.com (August 11 2020 press release).

question: Michael Saylor's public case for holding Bitcoin sounds Austrian in almost every important way. He points to a monetary distortion in which new money benefits the first people who receive it, before market prices adjust. What is the name of that distortion?
answer: The Cantillon effect
choices: The Cantillon effect
The Fisher effect
The Balassa-Samuelson effect
The Baumol cost disease
context: Richard Cantillon's 18th-century observation: newly printed money enters the economy at specific points (banks, government contractors, financial-asset holders) and lifts those first-recipients' purchasing power before the broader price level catches up. Saylor frames Bitcoin as the escape hatch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantillon_effect.

question: MicroStrategy kept buying Bitcoin through the 2022 crash, even when the stash was down billions on paper. They funded many buys with one type of corporate debt. Which one?
answer: Convertible bonds
choices: Convertible bonds
Preferred stock
Bank revolvers
Municipal bonds
context: MicroStrategy issued multiple tranches of convertible senior notes 2020-2024 and used the proceeds to buy Bitcoin, effectively increasing its Bitcoin-per-share leverage. The stock ticker MSTR became a leveraged Bitcoin proxy. Source: microstrategy.com (investor filings 2020-2024).

question: A software company chose to store most of its cash reserves in Bitcoin instead of dollars, hoping to protect those savings from inflation. What is this practice called when a company parks its cash reserves in Bitcoin?
answer: A Bitcoin treasury strategy
choices: A Bitcoin treasury strategy
Bitcoin mining
Bitcoin arbitrage
Bitcoin day-trading
context: As of early 2026 MicroStrategy is the largest CORPORATE Bitcoin holder in the world by a wide margin; other categories (individual wallets, exchange custodians, sovereign holdings) are larger overall but no single company approaches MicroStrategy's public treasury holding. Source: bitcointreasuries.net.

question: A software company changed its whole business identity to focus on holding Bitcoin as its main reserve. It even switched its logo to Bitcoin orange. What kind of asset does the company now treat Bitcoin as?
answer: A long-term store of value
choices: A long-term store of value
A short-term trading chip
A daily payment currency only
A speculative penny stock
context: The rebrand was announced February 5 2025 and the legal name change to Strategy Inc took effect August 11 2025; the MSTR ticker was retained. Source: cnbc.com/2025/02/05/bitcoin-treasury-pioneer-microstrategy-rebrands-with-a-new-name-strategy.html.

question: Michael Saylor's Bitcoin case flips a standard rule of corporate finance. In his view, protecting shareholders from dollar debasement is not an optional choice. What is it instead?
answer: A requirement of fiduciary duty
choices: A requirement of fiduciary duty
A public-relations decision
A regulatory-compliance obligation
A shareholder-vote matter
context: Saylor's move: if directors have a fiduciary duty to preserve shareholder value, and cash certainly loses purchasing power at a debasing central bank, then holding a scarce non-state asset is the fiduciary-consistent trade. It shifts the corporate-finance default. Source: saylor.org (public speeches 2020-2024).

question: After MicroStrategy started the trend, another US public company added Bitcoin to its treasury in 2021. It famously sold much of the stash within months. Which company made that retreat?
answer: Tesla
choices: Tesla
Block (formerly Square)
Marathon Digital
Coinbase
context: Tesla bought $1.5B in Bitcoin in January 2021 and sold roughly 75% of the holding within 18 months, taking the position mostly off its balance sheet. Block (formerly Square) and Marathon kept theirs. Source: sec.gov (Tesla 10-K filings 2021-22).

question: An American won the 1976 Nobel Prize in economics. His famous line was that inflation is always a money problem. What did he mean by that?
answer: Inflation is caused by printing too much money
choices: Inflation is caused by printing too much money
Inflation is caused by greedy shopkeepers
Inflation is caused by too many jobs
Inflation is caused by weather changes
context: Milton Friedman (1912-2006). His parents, Sara Ethel Landau and Jeno Saul Friedman, came from Beregszasz in Carpathian Ruthenia -- then the Kingdom of Hungary, today Berehove in Ukraine. Samuelson, Arrow and Kuznets were all real Nobel economists of the same era, which is why they make honest distractors. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Milton Friedman' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Milton_Friedman); Wikipedia, 'Milton Friedman'.

question: The economist Milton Friedman wrote a bestselling book called 'Free to Choose' with his wife. Its big claim: letting people freely spend their OWN money beats what?
answer: Letting government experts spend it for them
choices: Letting government experts spend it for them
Letting big companies spend it for them
Nobody spending it at all
Letting neighbors spend it for them
context: Rose Director Friedman was a Chicago-trained economist in her own right; in the mid-1930s she worked on the National Resources Committee's nationwide survey of consumer purchases. Reid and Brady were real consumption economists whose work fed into Milton's; Joan Robinson was the Cambridge economist. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rose Friedman' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Rose_Friedman).

question: A factory worker gets a one-time bonus of a thousand dollars. The Keynesian consumption rule of the 1940s predicted he spends a set fraction of it, just as he does of his wages. Milton Friedman's A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957) said that rule had missed something. What had it missed?
answer: That he plans his spending around the income he expects over years, and reads the bonus as a one-off
choices: That he plans his spending around the income he expects over years, and reads the bonus as a one-off
That he spends the bonus faster than his wages, because unearned money feels less real to him
That he cannot know whether the bonus is taxable until the spring, so he holds off spending it
That his employer set the size of the bonus knowing roughly how he was likely to spend it
context: This is the permanent income hypothesis. Friedman's charge against Keynes was precise: Keynes had related consumption to measured income without separating transitory income from permanent income. Published by Princeton University Press, 1957. Sources: Princeton University Press, 'Theory of the Consumption Function'; NBER, 'The Permanent Income Hypothesis'; Britannica.

question: By 1980, Milton Friedman had left Chicago for Hoover and was famous well beyond economics. That year he and Rose made the case for free markets to a huge audience. It came out as both a best-selling book and a public TV series. What was it called?
answer: Free to Choose
choices: Free to Choose
Capitalism and Freedom
The Road to Serfdom
A Monetary History
context: Free to Choose (1980) was a book and a PBS series, with Rose Friedman as associate producer. Capitalism and Freedom (1962) is Milton's earlier book, The Road to Serfdom (1944) is Hayek's, and A Monetary History (1963) is the Friedman-Schwartz volume. Source: Grokipedia, 'Free to Choose' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose).

question: In 1969 President Nixon appointed a commission under Thomas Gates to study ending the draft, and Milton Friedman sat on it. General William Westmoreland, then Army Chief of Staff, testified that he did not want to command an army of mercenaries. Friedman stopped him with a single question. What did he ask?
answer: General, would you rather command an army of slaves?
choices: General, would you rather command an army of slaves?
General, what would you pay to keep the men you now command?
General, what price does your own patriotism carry today?
General, who is paying for the army you command right now?
context: Westmoreland objected that he did not like hearing patriotic volunteers called slaves; Friedman answered that he did not like hearing them called mercenaries -- 'If they are mercenaries, then I, sir, am a mercenary professor, and you, sir, are a mercenary general.' The commission's February 21 1970 report unanimously recommended ending conscription. Sources: Friedman and Friedman, Two Lucky People; Duke HOPE working paper, 'Slaves or Mercenaries'; Cato Institute centennial appreciation.

question: A famous 1963 book traced the amount of money in circulation in America year by year from just after the Civil War to 1960. It argued that the Great Depression was made much worse by the central bank letting the money supply shrink. What is the main lesson the book urged central bankers to learn?
answer: Do not let the money supply collapse during a banking panic
choices: Do not let the money supply collapse during a banking panic
Print unlimited money whenever growth slows down
Fix the exchange rate to gold once every ten years
Ignore money entirely and focus only on interest rates
context: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 (Princeton, 1963) is by Milton Friedman AND Anna Jacobson Schwartz. She was a full co-author, not an assistant, spent seven decades at the NBER, and lived until 2012. Source: Grokipedia, 'Anna Schwartz' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Anna_Schwartz).

question: In 1976, the Royal Swedish Academy gave Milton Friedman the Nobel Prize in economics. The award named three of his works. Its closing line was almost a warning: it noted how hard it is for a government to steady an economy. Which three did the award name?
answer: Consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy
choices: Consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy
Price theory, the economics of the family, and the measurement of national income accounts
Monetary history, the theory of public choice, and the analysis of regulatory institutions
Consumption analysis, international trade theory, and the design of central-bank independence
context: The full citation: 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' The three strands map onto A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957), A Monetary History (1963), and the natural-rate argument. Sources: NobelPrize.org, Economic Sciences 1976 press release; NBER.

question: The common account of the Great Depression in 1963 was that markets had collapsed of their own accord and government had arrived to rescue what was left. Friedman and Anna Schwartz answered it with a measurement of the American money stock between August 1929 and March 1933. What had happened to it?
answer: It fell by about a third, from $26.6 billion to $17.3 billion
choices: It fell by about a third, from $26.6 billion to $17.3 billion
It rose by about a fifth, from $26.6 billion to $32.1 billion
It held almost flat, moving from $26.6 billion to $26.1 billion
It fell by about a twentieth, from $26.6 billion to $25.2 billion
context: Friedman and Schwartz's charge was not that the Fed had done too much but that it had done far too little: it let a third of the money supply disappear and turned an ordinary recession into the Great Depression. Friedman was no gold-standard partisan, which is what makes the finding so awkward for defenders of the Fed's record. Source: Grokipedia, 'Great Contraction' and 'A Monetary History of the United States'.

question: In 1967, Milton Friedman gave his big speech as president of the American Economic Association. The popular idea then was that a bit more inflation could buy lasting low unemployment. Friedman said the deal will not hold. Why not?
answer: Because once people come to expect that inflation, unemployment climbs back to where it started
choices: Because once people come to expect that inflation, unemployment climbs back to where it started
Because the extra money reaches exporters first and drives the currency down before wages move
Because no government can measure inflation fast enough to know when it ought to stop printing
Because employers meet rising prices by buying machinery, so unemployment never falls at all
context: Published as 'The Role of Monetary Policy' in 1968. Friedman called the level unemployment returns to the natural rate. The 1970s -- high inflation AND high unemployment together -- were widely read afterwards as the test his argument passed and the older view failed. Sources: American Economic Association, 'Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of Milton Friedman's Presidential Address'; Bruegel.

question: Congress wants to lift consumer spending and mails every household a single rebate cheque of six hundred dollars, announced in advance as a one-time payment. A supporter predicts households will spend most of it within the quarter. An economist holding Milton Friedman's 1957 account of consumption expects much less. What is the reasoning he presses?
answer: The cheque changes this year's cash, not the long-run income a household budgets against
choices: The cheque changes this year's cash, not the long-run income a household budgets against
The cheque lands after the downturn has already turned, so the spending arrives unwanted
The cheque is funded by borrowing that households expect to repay in later taxes anyway
The cheque means far more to a poor household than a rich one, so the average misleads
context: This is the permanent income hypothesis doing policy work. Note what the argument is and is not: it says the rebate will move spending less than its sponsors expect, not that the sponsors are acting in bad faith. The three other choices are also real arguments made about rebates -- the lag problem, Ricardian equivalence, and distributional averaging -- each pressed by real economists. Sources: NBER, 'The Permanent Income Hypothesis'; Britannica, 'A Theory of the Consumption Function'.

question: Ludwig von Mises and Milton Friedman both concluded that central banking had made the twentieth century's worst downturns worse -- and they could barely stand each other's methods. Mises reasoned from principles about how acting people must behave, principles he held no statistic could overturn. Friedman thought that route unusable. What did he insist an economic claim had to do instead?
answer: Stand or fall on measured series -- money stock, prices, output -- that another researcher could check
choices: Stand or fall on measured series -- money stock, prices, output -- that another researcher could check
Rest on a written constitution that binds the central bank before any downturn actually begins
Begin from what a policymaker intends, since intentions determine which levers ever get pulled
Be reducible to a single equation, since anything not written as one cannot be argued about clearly
context: This is why Friedman must not be filed as an Austrian. He was a Chicago-school monetarist and a methodological empiricist: A Monetary History is a hundred years of data, not a chain of deductions. Austrians answer that human action is not laboratory chemistry and that the data themselves only mean anything inside a theory -- a live argument, not a settled one. Choice two is closer to James Buchanan's constitutional political economy. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Monetarism' and 'Chicago school of economics'.

question: A US Senator wants to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour to help low-wage workers. In Friedman's Bastiat-style read, whose job gets priced out by the new floor?
answer: A 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8 per hour
choices: A 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8 per hour
A senior union electrician earning $42 per hour under a long-standing collective bargain
A civil-service accountant on a fixed grade paying $58,000 per year
A hospital physician with a fellowship contract paying $190 per hour
context: Friedman's Bastiat-style worked example: at $15/hr floor, no employer can legally pay $15 for $8 of work; the 16-year-old's job does not exist, it does not appear as a fired employee, and so it is UNSEEN. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-the-minimum-wage.

question: Milton Friedman's 1966 Newsweek column and 1980 book Free to Choose both quote him giving a one-line description of what the minimum wage law actually is. Which line did he use?
answer: A law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills
choices: A law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills
A law saying employers must pay their workers fair market value
A law saying government fixes the price of labor for all industries
A law saying workers cannot bargain individually for wages
context: Friedman's exact 1966 Newsweek line, quoted again in Free to Choose (1980): the minimum wage forbids hiring low-skill workers at a wage that would clear the market. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-the-minimum-wage.

question: Seattle phased in a $15 minimum wage that hit full force in 2017-18. Right after that, three big fast-food chains rolled out a new piece of gear in their stores. Which gear showed up?
answer: Self-order kiosks
choices: Self-order kiosks
Robotic burger flippers
Automated deep fryers
Motion-sensor drink dispensers
context: McDonald's, Panera, and Wendy's led a mass kiosk rollout after Seattle's $15 floor took full effect; touch-screens do not need a wage, and became worth buying only once labor was made expensive by law. Source: seattletimes.com (2017-18 rollout coverage).

question: The Seattle kiosk story is a clean case of one simple idea in microeconomics. When labor gets pricier, employers swap in more machines. What is that swap called?
answer: Capital-for-labor substitution
choices: Capital-for-labor substitution
Labor-supply elasticity
Income-effect dominance
Cross-price complementarity
context: Employers substitute capital equipment (kiosks) for labor (cashiers) once the relative price of labor rises above the price of the capital that can replace it. This is standard price-theory in every textbook including Sowell's Basic Economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_rate_of_technical_substitution.

question: In a famous 1994 paper, David Card and Alan Krueger checked jobs at fast-food chains near a state line. One state raised its wage floor. The other did not. They reported little short-term job loss. Which state pair did the paper make famous?
answer: New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food
choices: New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food
California vs Arizona agriculture
New York vs Connecticut retail
Texas vs Oklahoma construction
context: Card & Krueger 1994 became the standard mainstream citation for 'minimum wage does not cost jobs'; the paper is the reason Card later shared the 2021 Nobel Memorial Prize. Source: American Economic Review 84(4), 1994.

question: David Neumark and William Wascher pushed back on Card and Krueger in their 2008 book Minimum Wages. They said the earlier finding falls apart when you use a better kind of data than phone surveys. Which kind did they push?
answer: Payroll records from state unemployment-insurance filings
choices: Payroll records from state unemployment-insurance filings
Consumer-survey purchasing questionnaires
Store-window help-wanted sign counts
Chamber of Commerce membership rolls
context: Neumark & Wascher's response (2000 AER; Minimum Wages, MIT Press 2008) showed the Card-Krueger effect flips sign in long-run panels and in administrative payroll data rather than short phone surveys. Source: MIT Press catalog.

question: In his book Basic Economics, Thomas Sowell states the case against the minimum wage in one line. It has an unseen victim, a person who never gets that first job. In Sowell's phrasing, who exactly pays the real price of the minimum wage?
answer: The chronically-unemployed teenager
choices: The chronically-unemployed teenager
The rising cost of restaurant meals
The shrinking size of retail chains
The falling profit margin of employers
context: Sowell's summary: there is no employer who 'refuses to pay a decent wage'; there are only employers who value particular workers below the floor and hire NO ONE at that skill. The unemployed teenager is the price. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics, 5th ed., chapter on price floors.

question: Free-market economists say one national minimum wage cannot be right for every worker in every industry in every region. What key knowledge does the local shop owner have that a distant lawmaker does not?
answer: What each specific worker is actually worth at that specific job in that specific town
choices: What each specific worker is actually worth at that specific job in that specific town
The total number of workers across the entire country
The average wage paid across every US industry
The interest rate set by the central bank
context: Hayek's 1945 knowledge-in-society argument applied to labor: the employer's local knowledge of a worker's productivity in a specific job is not available to a legislator setting a single national floor. This is the Hayekian bite of the minimum-wage debate. Source: fee.org/articles/hayek-and-the-minimum-wage.

question: In his 2011 book Race and Economics, Walter Williams anchors the minimum-wage debate on a single number. He points to teen unemployment in an era when the federal wage floor, in real terms, was very low. About what was the US teenage unemployment rate in the 1950s?
answer: About 10 percent
choices: About 10 percent
About 25 percent
About 40 percent
About 55 percent
context: US teenage unemployment averaged around 10% in the 1950s at a low real federal minimum wage; the rate averaged 15-20% after repeated 1970s+ increases, with especially high rates in black-teen cohorts (per Williams, Race and Economics 2011). Source: bls.gov historical LFS data.

question: Milton Friedman, Thomas Sowell, and Walter Williams all made the same Bastiat-style closing move about how to judge a policy like the minimum wage. What did their move say to judge?
answer: The results, not the intentions of its sponsors
choices: The results, not the intentions of its sponsors
The rhetoric, not the arithmetic of its opponents
The optimism, not the pessimism of its forecasters
The popularity, not the theory of its academic critics
context: 'One of the great mistakes is to judge policies by their intentions rather than their results' -- Friedman, restated by Sowell and Williams. The Bastiat move: the intended visible good is the SEEN; the actual outcome for the unseen victim is what matters. Source: fee.org/articles/friedman-intentions-versus-results.

question: In November 2010, a Czech coder using the name 'Slush' set up a new service. It let small Bitcoin miners join up, share their computing power, and split the payouts. Each miner got a small steady trickle instead of a rare lucky hit. What is this kind of service called?
answer: A mining pool
choices: A mining pool
A crypto exchange
A hardware wallet
A stablecoin issuer
context: The service was originally called Slush Pool and is now Braiins Pool. It solved the variance problem: as the network grew, a solo miner might wait years between block wins even with steady hashing effort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Braiins_Pool.

question: In a Bitcoin mining pool, miners get paid for each valid partial hash they turn in, not just for finding the winning hash. What is one of those partial-hash entries called?
answer: A share
choices: A share
A halving
A block reward
A dividend
context: A share is a hash that would have been a valid block at a much lower difficulty than the actual network target. It proves the miner did real work. Payout schemes like PPS, PPLNS, and FPPS all key off share counts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: Bitcoin miners often join 'pools' that combine their computers and share the rewards. Why do individual miners with just one or two machines choose to join a big pool rather than mine on their own?
answer: Alone they may go months or years without ever winning a block reward
choices: Alone they may go months or years without ever winning a block reward
Solo mining is banned by Bitcoin's code
Pools give miners access to secret shortcuts
Solo miners must pay a fee to the government
context: Foundry USA rose to prominence after the 2021 China mining exodus. Other leaders include Antpool (Bitmain-affiliated), F2Pool (originally China, now Singapore), ViaBTC, and Binance Pool. Market shares rotate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: If any single Bitcoin miner or mining pool ever gained more than half of the network's hashing power, that miner could rewrite recent blocks or block chosen transactions. What is this danger called?
answer: A 51-percent attack
choices: A 51-percent attack
A soft fork
A double-signature freeze
A Byzantine handshake
context: The name refers to the threshold at which a single actor's chain becomes longer than the honest network's chain. Bitcoin's security assumes the largest actor stays below 50 percent. Source: grokipedia.com/page/51%25_attack.

question: In July 2014 the GHash.io mining pool briefly exceeded 51 percent of the Bitcoin network's total hash rate. What actually happened next?
answer: Individual miners voluntarily left the pool, and the pool operators publicly asked users to switch away
choices: Individual miners voluntarily left the pool, and the pool operators publicly asked users to switch away
The Bitcoin Foundation banned GHash.io from participating in the network
The US Securities and Exchange Commission ordered GHash.io to close
GHash.io launched a coordinated double-spend attack against Coinbase
context: The incident demonstrated that a mining pool's power depends on user trust. Pool operators knew that keeping >51 percent would undermine the network their own hardware depended on, so they chose to shrink. Source: grokipedia.com/page/51%25_attack.

question: A high-school student worries the 2014 GHash.io near-miss shows Bitcoin is vulnerable because a small number of pools now control most of the network. A public-choice-trained economist points out that the 2014 episode itself illustrates why the vulnerability is bounded. What is his reasoning move?
answer: Pool operators' economic value depends on the network's honesty, so they have private incentive to avoid the attack
choices: Pool operators' economic value depends on the network's honesty, so they have private incentive to avoid the attack
The US Federal Reserve directly regulates pool concentration and would prevent an attack
The 51-percent scenario is mathematically impossible because of Bitcoin's block reward
Miners are legally required by international treaty to leave any pool above 40 percent
context: This is incentive recognition -- the kind of analysis Buchanan and Tullock applied to political actors. Pool operators are not benevolent; they are self-interested actors whose interests align with network security. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: In 1982, a group in Alabama was set up to spread the ideas of Ludwig von Mises. Which school of economics does the group teach?
answer: The Austrian school

The Marxist school

question: A US congressman from Texas ran for president three times mainly to protest the Federal Reserve printing dollars. His slogan was 'End the Fed.' What was his main complaint about the Fed?
answer: Printing money makes the dollar lose value over time

The Fed doesn't have enough employees

The Fed uses old computers

question: The moral warrant for the Institute's use of the Mises name came from a specific person who served on its founding board until 1993. Who authorized the use of the name?
answer: Margit von Mises

Bettina Bien Greaves
Sylvia Nasar
Hazel Kyrk
context: Margit von Mises, Ludwig's widow, gave her personal blessing to the founding and remained on the board until her death in 1993. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: Since 1998, the Mises Institute has run a scholarly journal. It is the flagship outlet for research in the Rothbardian tradition. It prints new research each quarter. What is the journal called?
answer: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
choices: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
Review of Austrian Economics
Journal of Political Economy
Public Choice
context: The Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics, edited by Joseph Salerno, is the flagship modern Mises-Institute journal. Source: mises.org/mises-university.

question: Every summer, a group in Alabama runs a one-week program on Austrian economics for college students from around the world. Why do students fly in for it instead of taking a class at their own college?
answer: Most universities teach little or none of the Austrian tradition
choices: Most universities teach little or none of the Austrian tradition
It is required to graduate from any US college
It is the only program that awards college credit anywhere
Students earn a government salary after completing it
context: Mises University is the Institute's annual weeklong summer program for undergraduates, taught by senior Austrian-school faculty. Source: mises.org/mises-university.

question: After Rothbard died in 1995, the Auburn Institute became the US home of the Rothbardian branch of the tradition. Which money reform is that branch best known for?
answer: 100 percent reserve banking and abolition of the Fed
choices: 100 percent reserve banking and abolition of the Fed
A Milton Friedman k-percent money-supply rule
Explicit nominal-GDP targeting
A permanent zero-interest-rate policy
context: The Rothbardian branch is monetarily hard-line: 100% reserves and immediate abolition of the Federal Reserve. The Hayekian branch at George Mason has a different institutional emphasis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: The main modern life story of Ludwig von Mises came out from the Mises Institute in 2007. Its title refers to Mises as a knight. What is the book's subtitle?
answer: The Last Knight of Liberalism
choices: The Last Knight of Liberalism
The Prophet of Vienna
The Austrian Socrates
The Chancellor's Economist
context: Mises: The Last Knight of Liberalism (2007), by Guido Hulsmann, is the definitive scholarly biography of Ludwig von Mises. Source: mises.org/library/mises-last-knight-liberalism.

question: A think tank that teaches Austrian economics puts its entire founding library online for free. Every book and every essay by its major thinkers is there for anyone with internet. Why does making the primary sources free do more for the school than any advertising ever could?
answer: A student anywhere can read the original arguments and decide for themselves
choices: A student anywhere can read the original arguments and decide for themselves
Free websites are cheaper than magazine ads
It forces every teacher to assign those books in class
Governments have to endorse whichever school offers free texts
context: Mises.org hosts freely readable editions of Menger, Bohm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, Rothbard, and modern Austrian scholars. Source: mises.org.

question: By the late 1920s, Mises had spent ten years arguing that the mixed economy of subsidies, price controls, and targeted taxes was not a stable third path. It was an escalator. In 1929 he put the case in one book. What is its German title?
answer: Kritik des Interventionismus
choices: Kritik des Interventionismus
Die Gemeinwirtschaft
Nationaloekonomie
Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
context: Full title: Kritik des Interventionismus: Untersuchungen zur Wirtschaftspolitik und Wirtschaftsideologie der Gegenwart. Hans F. Sennholz translated the essays into English as A Critique of Interventionism, first published in 1977 by Arlington House. Source: Mises Institute, 'A Critique of Interventionism'.

question: On April 18, 1950, Mises spoke at the University Club in New York. He gave a short, sharp version of his long case against the mixed economy. What was that speech called?
answer: Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism
choices: Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism
Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
Bureaucracy and the Free Market
The Anti-Capitalistic Mentality
context: The Commercial and Financial Chronicle first printed the address on May 4, 1950. The Libertarian Press then made it the opening essay of Planning for Freedom in 1952, and it has been the single most-quoted Mises text on the interventionist ratchet ever since. Source: Mises Institute, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: In a 1950 speech, Ludwig von Mises used an example to show why price caps spread. The government caps the price of one basic food to help poor families. That causes a shortage, so the government caps the price of what goes into it. Then it caps the prices of those inputs too. Which food did Mises start with?
answer: Milk
choices: Milk
Bread
Coal
Rental housing
context: Mises walked from a milk-price ceiling to feed prices, then to cattle prices, then to farm-labor wages, showing that every remedy for the previous shortage required an additional decree until the state was directing every price in the economy. He picked milk because a New York audience in 1950 remembered wartime dairy controls vividly. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: Ludwig von Mises said a mixed economy is not a real middle ground between capitalism and socialism. Either markets run production, or the state does. In a 1950 speech, he stated this either/or in a short three-word rule. What was it?
answer: Control is indivisible
choices: Control is indivisible
Prices reveal knowledge
Property implies liberty
Money is neutral
context: Mises's argument: either consumers direct production through the prices they are willing to pay, or the state does through decree. Any attempt to split the difference leaves neither mechanism doing its job; the resulting malfunction forces an escalation to full state direction. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: Ludwig von Mises ended his 1950 speech with a famous line. He said middle-of-the-road policy is not a lasting system. Instead, it is a way to reach one thing, step by step. What did he say it leads to, and how fast?
answer: Socialism, by installments
choices: Socialism, by installments
Poverty, in a single generation
Central banking, over a business cycle
Fascism, within a decade
context: Full sentence: 'The middle-of-the-road policy is not an economic system that can last. It is a method for the realization of socialism by installments.' The metaphor is deliberate: no single intervention looks like socialism, but the running total does. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: In a 1950 talk, Ludwig von Mises used real history to show the pattern was not just theory. He pointed to one European country. In 1914 it began with ceiling prices on a few consumer goods. By 1917 it ran a near-total war economy under one big named plan. Which case did Mises cite?
answer: Germany's progression to the 1917 Hindenburg Plan
choices: Germany's progression to the 1917 Hindenburg Plan
Britain's slide into the 1918 Defence of the Realm Act
France's move to the 1916 Loucheur decrees
Austria-Hungary's Kriegswirtschaft of 1915
context: The Hindenburg Programme of 1916-17, formally directed by General Erich Ludendorff, subordinated the whole German economy to munitions production. Mises's point was that Germany did not vote for the Hindenburg Plan in 1914; each intervening step looked reasonable given the last one, and the accumulated total was total control. Source: Mises Institute, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: During big wars, depressions, and panics, the size of the US federal government grows a lot. After the crisis ends, government shrinks back -- but only partway, never all the way to where it started. Which everyday tool is often used as a name for this one-way pattern?
answer: Ratchet
choices: Ratchet
Cascade
Spiral
Escalator
context: Higgs's Crisis and Leviathan: Critical Episodes in the Growth of American Government (Oxford, 1987) surveys WWI, the Great Depression, WWII, the Cold War and the post-1960s regulatory expansion, showing that the same governments that grew fastest in the emergency also grew fastest in the calm that followed. The historical documentation is the American case for Mises's 1929 prediction. Source: Wikipedia, 'Crisis and Leviathan'.

question: American farm policy is often called a textbook case of the Mises ratchet. New Deal price supports gave farmers a minimum price for corn and wheat. Harvests then piled up in surplus that Washington could not sell. Which next step did the government take to solve that surplus problem?
answer: Paying farmers to leave land idle under set-aside and payment-in-kind programs
choices: Paying farmers to leave land idle under set-aside and payment-in-kind programs
Nationalizing the grain elevators to store the surplus at cost
Declaring a temporary tariff to force domestic bakeries to buy the surplus
Rationing consumer purchases to draw down accumulated stocks
context: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 first paid farmers to plow crops under; postwar set-aside acreage programs and the 1983 Payment-in-Kind program paid producers in surplus grain not to grow more of it. Ninety years later the policy is still running -- exactly the ratchet Mises described in 1929: the intervention that fixed the last intervention's malfunction generates the next malfunction to fix. Source: Mises Institute, 'Farm Bill Folly'.

question: In 1927 Ludwig von Mises wrote a book on an old political tradition. It said individual freedom, private property, and free markets are the best base for peace and prosperity. What is this tradition called?
answer: Classical liberalism
choices: Classical liberalism
Progressive statism
Democratic socialism
Mercantilism
context: Liberalismus (1927) argued the political and moral case for a market economy; Kritik des Interventionismus (1929) collected the economic essays showing that the halfway house between that market economy and full socialism was inherently unstable. Together they form the pair Mises's students, Hayek and Rothbard among them, later called the interventionist trilogy with Socialism (1922). Source: David M Hart, 'Ludwig von Mises: Interventionismus (1926)'.

question: By the 1930s Ludwig von Mises had argued for a decade that the mixed economy is unstable. It must either move back toward markets or forward to full state control. He used one short label to reject the idea that a real middle path exists at all. Which label?
answer: A third system
choices: A third system
A guided economy
Managed capitalism
The mixed economy
context: Mises used 'a third system' precisely because he thought it did not exist as a stable system. Either consumer sovereignty through prices rules production or the state does; the intermediate cases he documented -- rent-controlled housing, price-supported farming, tariff-protected industry, rate-suppressed banking -- were the disequilibria that generated the ratchet toward the second pole. Source: Mises Institute, 'Why Intervention Persists'.

question: A young Austrian economist joined Mises's office in 1921. He later won the Nobel Prize. His big idea was that prices are messages. They sum up what everyone knows and wants. What did he say no central planner could ever do?
answer: Gather all the knowledge that prices already carry
choices: Gather all the knowledge that prices already carry
Print more money quickly
Set a fair tax rate
Fund a public school
context: Hayek (1899-1992) later called Mises 'my teacher' and won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: An American student of Mises had a simple point. The more taxes a government takes and the more rules it writes, the less people work, save, and invent. What did he say happens when taxes and rules pile up?
answer: People produce less because their reward for effort shrinks

People produce more to catch up on taxes
Nothing changes -- people always work the same
The government starts making better products
context: Rothbard (1926-1995) attended the NYU Mises seminar from 1949 and stayed for two decades, becoming the seminar's most important American product. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: Israel Kirzner was one of Mises's own American students. His 1973 book put one human activity at the center of Austrian economics. It was the source of profit and new ideas. Which activity?
answer: Entrepreneurship as alertness to opportunity
choices: Entrepreneurship as alertness to opportunity
Consumption as revealed preference
Saving as time preference
Central planning as knowledge aggregation
context: Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago, 1973) put alertness to unnoticed opportunities in disequilibrium at the center of Austrian microeconomics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Israel_Kirzner.

question: After World War 2, an Austrian named Ludwig von Mises taught in America. His students spread the Austrian school's ideas through US colleges. What core idea did the Austrian school teach about how prices work in a market?

choices: Prices carry information nobody could gather in one place
Prices are set by government experts using data
Prices only reflect the cost to make each item
Prices always match the true value of a good
context: Hans Sennholz (1922-2007) held a long-tenured post at Grove City College in Pennsylvania and trained a generation of Austrian-friendly American economists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Sennholz.

question: Rothbard restated the Misesian system for a postwar American audience in a specific 1962 treatise from D. Van Nostrand. What is its title?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
For a New Liberty
The Ethics of Liberty
context: Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) was Rothbard's systematic treatise and the anchor of his subsequent trilogy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: In a 1963 book, Rothbard used Austrian Business Cycle Theory on one big American event. He argued the Fed caused the boom, and Hoover's meddling turned the bust into a ten-year slump. Which event was the book about?

question: A famous 1946 book boiled economics down to one lesson: to judge any policy, don't just count how it helps one group right now — trace how it hits everyone else, and how it hits later. What is that one lesson called?
answer: Look at all the effects on all the people, not just the visible ones now

question: A 1996 book of over 1,000 pages tries to combine Austrian economics with Ayn Rand's Objectivism into one giant system. Why do most economists prefer shorter, tightly-argued books to giant treatises?

Only university professors read long books

question: An Austrian economist taught at a New York college, but the college paid him nothing. A wealthy businessman and a private group paid his salary instead. What does this show about how new ideas often get their start?

question: Modern Monetary Theory, or MMT, says a country that prints its own money can never run out. So it does not need to worry about deficits. What real problem do critics say this misses?
