Printing extra money makes exports too cheap for foreign buyers
Printing extra money forces banks to raise interest rates too much
Printing extra money confuses foreign investors who prefer coins
context: Kelton's The Deficit Myth: Modern Monetary Theory and the Birth of the People's Economy (PublicAffairs, 2020) reached the New York Times bestseller list. Its argument was that the traditional view of federal deficits as a constraint is a myth. Source: Grokipedia 'The Deficit Myth' (2026-09-05).

question: Modern Monetary Theory, or MMT, says a government that prints its own money is not really held back by taxes or debt. What does the theory say are the only real limits?
answer: Inflation and real resources
choices: Inflation and real resources
Foreign lender willingness and gold reserves
Tax revenue and treasury solvency
Interest rates and unemployment
context: MMT says deficit financing is fine as long as excess capacity exists; taxes are for controlling inflation and redistributing resources, not for 'paying for' spending. The framing sounds new but is a modern repackaging of an old inflationist position. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020).

question: A famous economist on the Democratic side attacked a modern theory that said a government can safely print all the money it needs. He borrowed a slogan a past US president had used to mock supply-side economics. Which nickname did he reuse?
answer: Voodoo economics
choices: Voodoo economics
Trickle-down economics
Zombie economics
Snake-oil economics
context: Larry Summers's February 4 2019 Washington Post op-ed called MMT 'the new voodoo economics' -- echoing the George H.W. Bush attack on Reagan supply-side economics. Summers was a Democratic economist speaking against a left-favored school. Source: Washington Post (February 4 2019).

question: MMT says a government can safely print money while the economy has 'unused capacity.' What do Austrian economists say is wrong with that idea for the whole economy?
answer: There is no such thing at that scale; prices rise instead of production
choices: There is no such thing at that scale; prices rise instead of production
Unused capacity only exists during wars
Capacity is measured only in barrels of oil
Only communist countries ever have unused capacity
context: The Austrian point (Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, Steve Hanke): the notion of aggregate unused capacity is a Keynesian fiction. In reality, resources are always in some use and monetary expansion always bids competing uses higher. Prices adjust to absorb the excess. Source: Murphy, Contra Krugman (podcast archive 2019-2021).

question: In early 2021 the US government sent out a huge round of new spending, paid mostly with newly created money. A well-known economist warned this would push prices up hard. What actually happened over the next two years?
answer: The worst US price inflation in about forty years
choices: The worst US price inflation in about forty years
Prices dropped as workers spent more freely
Nothing at all — the money vanished into savings
The dollar became the strongest currency in world history
context: The American Rescue Plan Act, signed March 11 2021 at $1.9 trillion, was an MMT-adjacent bet that fiscal stimulus of that size would not overheat prices. Summers had warned publicly against it in February 2021. Source: Grokipedia 'American Rescue Plan Act of 2021' (2026-09-05).

question: After prices shot up in 2021 and 2022, one group of economists blamed shipping backups and stuck ports instead of the trillions of newly printed dollars the government had spent. What was their explanation for the inflation?
answer: Supply-chain problems caused it, not the new money
choices: Supply-chain problems caused it, not the new money
Store owners across the country got greedy at the same moment
Foreign oil producers alone drove up every price
Consumers suddenly switched from spending to saving
context: MMT proponents echoed the Fed's 'transitory' framing, blaming supply chains. But the core MMT claim -- that political will, not math, was the constraint -- was falsified by exactly the mechanism its critics had predicted: prices adjusted to absorb the excess demand. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: A theory called Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) said governments could print lots of money without causing much inflation. Between 2020 and 2022 many countries tried it, and prices rose fast worldwide. What did the real economy teach faster than years of debate could?
answer: A live test in the real economy can disprove a school of thought faster than years of debate
choices: A live test in the real economy can disprove a school of thought faster than years of debate
Schools of thought always survive real-world setbacks
Being popular with politicians makes a theory correct
Academic economists always predict inflation correctly
context: Twelve months of 8-9% inflation did what a decade of Austrian critique could not. The 2021-22 experience settled the empirical question and drained the political oxygen from the movement. Source: Grokipedia 'Modern Monetary Theory' (2026-09-05).

question: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) grew from a 1990s pamphlet by a currency trader who said a government printing its own money can never run out. Why did economists later reject that claim?
answer: A government can always print more money, but each new bill buys less — inflation is the limit
choices: A government can always print more money, but each new bill buys less — inflation is the limit
Governments actually do run out of paper to print money on
Only foreign countries are allowed to print more currency
Currency traders are never allowed to write about money
context: Warren Mosler's 1996 Soft Currency Economics is the founding text. The term 'MMT' itself was popularized by Australian economist Bill Mitchell at the University of Newcastle. Source: Grokipedia 'Warren Mosler' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2014 a big Bitcoin trading website suddenly went bust. About 850,000 Bitcoins that customers had left on the site were gone. What is the main lesson people took from that disaster?
answer: If you don't hold your own coins yourself, someone else can lose them
choices: If you don't hold your own coins yourself, someone else can lose them
Bitcoin itself was broken and had to be rebuilt
Only rich people should be allowed to buy Bitcoin
Trading websites always pay everyone back after a crash
context: Mt Gox at its 2013 peak handled roughly 70-80 percent of global Bitcoin trading volume. The bankruptcy set the world's expectations of what could go wrong with a centralized custodian. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: A person buys Bitcoin and leaves it on the trading website's account instead of moving it to their own wallet. Then the website is hacked and all its money is stolen. What is the well-known Bitcoin saying that warns against this exact mistake?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
Buy the dip, sell the top
A coin saved is a coin earned
Only the miners can lose money
context: The site was launched in 2007 by Jed McCaleb as a card-trading platform for Magic: The Gathering. He repurposed it for Bitcoin in 2010 and sold the domain to Mark Karpeles in 2011. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: At the time of the February 2014 Mt Gox collapse, the exchange was run by a French national living in Tokyo. Who was he?
answer: Mark Karpeles
choices: Mark Karpeles
Craig Wright
Charlie Shrem
Ross Ulbricht
context: Karpeles had bought Mt Gox from Jed McCaleb in 2011. He was later convicted in Japan in 2019 of falsifying data (padding balance records) but acquitted of the theft charges; he received a suspended sentence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mark_Karpel%C3%A8s.

question: In February 2014 Mt Gox halted Bitcoin withdrawals, blaming 'technical issues.' Two weeks later the site went dark. A few days after that, it declared bankruptcy. On which day did the withdrawal freeze begin?
answer: February 7, 2014
choices: February 7, 2014
January 3, 2014
December 24, 2013
March 15, 2014
context: The site went dark February 24 and the Tokyo bankruptcy petition was filed February 28. Karpeles had reassured customers that withdrawal issues were transient, but roughly 850,000 BTC were already missing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: Of the roughly 850,000 Bitcoins Mt Gox reported missing in February 2014, some coins were later recovered from an old wallet. Roughly how many coins were recovered?
answer: About 200,000
choices: About 200,000
About 800,000
About 50
None -- all were permanently lost
context: The trustee retained the recovered coins for a decade of legal proceedings. Distribution to creditors finally began in 2024. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: Jed McCaleb, the original 2007 creator of Mt Gox as a Magic: The Gathering trading site, went on after selling it to build other cryptocurrency projects. Which two did he co-found?
answer: Ripple (XRP) in 2012 and Stellar (XLM) in 2014
choices: Ripple (XRP) in 2012 and Stellar (XLM) in 2014
Ethereum in 2015 and Cardano in 2017
Binance in 2017 and FTX in 2019
Coinbase in 2012 and Kraken in 2013
context: McCaleb had left Mt Gox by 2011. His Ripple and Stellar projects took a very different approach from Bitcoin -- centralized ledgers rather than proof-of-work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jed_McCaleb.

question: By 2024, ten years after Mt Gox collapsed, the trustee finally began giving the 200,000 recovered Bitcoins back to creditors. What specific fact softened the original loss for those who waited?
answer: Bitcoin's price had risen so much that the recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value
choices: Bitcoin's price had risen so much that the recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value
The trustee added a 500-percent bonus in newly minted coin
The Japanese government reimbursed all lost dollar value in yen
The Federal Reserve issued a targeted grant to Mt Gox creditors
context: Creditors who accepted repayment in Bitcoin (an option the trustee offered) received far more purchasing power than they had lost. The lesson survived: not-your-keys-not-your-coins is real, but so is Bitcoin's long-run monetary premium. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: A young man studies under a famous teacher named Ludwig von Mises. He spends his life fighting for free markets, sound money, and smaller government. Which school of economics is he part of?
answer: The Austrian school
choices: The Austrian school
The Marxist school
The Keynesian school
The behavioral school
context: Rothbard entered Columbia at 16 in 1942 and took the doctorate under Joseph Dorfman. Kirzner also attended the Mises NYU seminar but took his PhD under Mises at NYU, not Columbia; Hazlitt was a journalist with no doctorate; Lachmann was an LSE-trained German Austrian. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926, and died January 7, 1995. In which American city was he born, and in which borough of it?
answer: New York City, in the Bronx
choices: New York City, in the Bronx
Chicago, in Hyde Park
Vienna, in Leopoldstadt
Boston, in Back Bay
context: Rothbard's father David was a chemist who had emigrated from Poland; the family were Jewish immigrants to the Bronx. Vienna Leopoldstadt is the classic distractor since so many first-generation Austrians (Mises, Hayek, Machlup) came from there; Chicago and Boston place two rival American economics traditions. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Rothbard's 1956 thesis at Columbia later became a book. It told the money story of the first great American depression. Which depression did it cover?
answer: The Panic of 1819
choices: The Panic of 1819
The Panic of 1837
The Long Depression of 1873
The Panic of 1907
context: Rothbard argued the Panic of 1819 followed the credit expansion of the Second Bank of the United States, a foreshadowing of his later Austrian Business Cycle Theory application to 1929. Dorfman was his adviser. The three distractors are all real 19th- and early-20th-century American financial crises. Source: Mises Institute, 'Toward a Science of Liberty' (Salerno).

question: From the mid-1950s Rothbard joined a private economics seminar in New York City. An Austrian economist who had fled Europe led it, and a pro-market donor fund paid for it. Which seminar was it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at NYU
choices: Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at NYU
Milton Friedman's Chicago money workshop
Kenneth Arrow's Stanford theory workshop
John Kenneth Galbraith's Harvard institutional seminar
context: Mises ran the seminar at NYU from 1948 to 1969, paid for by the William Volker Fund. Rothbard became his most influential American disciple. Friedman's Chicago workshop was the methodological opposite; Arrow at Stanford and Galbraith at Harvard were mainstream mid-century venues. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Rothbard had a Columbia PhD and was a top Austrian thinker. But from 1966 to 1986, no big economics department would hire him because his politics were too radical. Where did he actually teach for those twenty years?
answer: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute -- an engineering school, not an economics department
choices: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute -- an engineering school, not an economics department
Grove City College's small economics program in western Pennsylvania
Auburn University's Department of Economics in Alabama
George Mason University's newly-founded Austrian economics group
context: Rothbard taught part-time at Brooklyn Poly from 1966 to 1986 -- twenty years as an engineering-school instructor while writing the Austrian tradition's flagship American treatise. Grove City housed Hans Sennholz; George Mason built its Austrian program later (1980s onward); Auburn is where the Mises Institute would later be based, but Rothbard never taught for Auburn University itself. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: In 1986 Rothbard finally moved from Brooklyn Polytechnic to a full economics chair, where he stayed until his death in 1995. Which named chair at which university did he take?
answer: S.J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas
choices: S.J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas
Ludwig von Mises Chair in Economics at Grove City College
F.A. Hayek Chair in Political Economy at George Mason University
Adam Smith Chair in Free Enterprise at Auburn University
context: UNLV hired Rothbard in 1986 into the S.J. Hall chair; he taught there until his heart attack in January 1995. The three distractor chairs are plausibly-named posts at institutions that had ties to Austrian or Chicago-adjacent economics but were not where Rothbard actually landed. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: In 1977 Rothbard helped launch a Washington libertarian think tank alongside two other co-founders; four years later a dispute over strategy got him removed from its board. Which think tank did he co-found and then break from?
answer: The Cato Institute, co-founded with Charles Koch and Ed Crane
choices: The Cato Institute, co-founded with Charles Koch and Ed Crane
The Heritage Foundation, co-founded with Paul Weyrich and Edwin Feulner
The Reason Foundation, co-founded with Robert Poole
The Foundation for Economic Education, co-founded with Leonard Read
context: Cato was founded 1977; Rothbard was ousted from the board in 1981 after a dispute with Crane and Koch, largely over political strategy and cultural stance. Heritage (1973), Reason (1978), and FEE (1946) are all real free-market institutions with their own real founders; Rothbard was not a co-founder of any of them. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: In 1982, the year after his break with Cato, Rothbard helped launch a rival Austrian-focused institute where he would serve as academic vice president for the rest of his life. Which institute did he co-found?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute, in Auburn, Alabama, with Llewellyn Rockwell Jr.
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute, in Auburn, Alabama, with Llewellyn Rockwell Jr.
The Independent Institute, in Oakland, California, with David Theroux
The Foundation for Economic Education, in Irvington-on-Hudson, with Leonard Read
The Atlas Economic Research Foundation, in Fairfax, with Antony Fisher
context: Rothbard, Rockwell, and Burton Blumert founded the Mises Institute in 1982 to house Austrian scholarship outside the Beltway-libertarian orbit. The three distractors are all real free-market organizations founded by the named people, but none is where Rothbard landed after Cato. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: One thinker argued there should be no government at all — instead, private property rules and voluntary companies like courts, insurance, and guards would do everything the state does. He coined a special name for this system. What is it called?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism
choices: Anarcho-capitalism
Classical liberalism
Small-government conservatism
Social democracy
context: The term is Rothbard's own, distinguishing his position from Nozickian minarchism (a minimal-state night-watchman position) and from Randian objectivism (which insists on a minimal state). Classical liberalism is the older 19th-century umbrella that all three sit under. Source: Wikipedia, For a New Liberty.

question: Rothbard's popular 1973 book laid out his political system for a general reader. It opens with a history of American liberty. It ends with a plan for a fully private-property society. Which book is it?
answer: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
choices: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
The Ethics of Liberty
Anarchy, State, and Utopia
The Machinery of Freedom
context: For a New Liberty (Macmillan, 1973) is Rothbard's popular manifesto. The Ethics of Liberty (1982) is his systematic philosophical case. Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) is Nozick's minarchist rival. The Machinery of Freedom (1973) is David Friedman's economic-anarchist rival, published the same year. Source: Wikipedia, For a New Liberty.

question: Rothbard's largest American history work ran to four volumes. It covered the colonial period through the American Revolution. It was published between 1975 and 1979. What is it called?
answer: Conceived in Liberty
choices: Conceived in Liberty
The Discovery of Freedom
The American Testament
Empire of Liberty
context: Conceived in Liberty is Rothbard's four-volume libertarian retelling of American colonial history and the Revolution; a fifth volume was assembled posthumously from his notes in 2019. The Discovery of Freedom (1943) is Rose Wilder Lane. The American Testament and Empire of Liberty are titles of unrelated later works. Source: Mises Institute, 'Toward a Science of Liberty' (Salerno).

question: In 1940, France was falling to Nazi Germany. Ludwig von Mises was teaching at a school in Europe. That year he printed a big new economics book. In which city did the book come out?
answer: Geneva, published by Editions Union
choices: Geneva, published by Editions Union
London, published by George Allen & Unwin
New York, published by Yale University Press
Vienna, published by Julius Springer
context: Mises had been at the Geneva Graduate Institute since 1934, having left Vienna. The book, in German, was 'Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens' ('Economics: A Theory of Action and Enterprise'). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1940 German book Nationaloekonomie was one of the great economics works of the century. But what happened after it was printed was very strange. What happened to it?
answer: It attracted almost no readership -- Germany and Austria were closed to it and Switzerland was neutral but small
choices: It attracted almost no readership -- Germany and Austria were closed to it and Switzerland was neutral but small
It sold half a million copies within its first year
It was banned by every European government
It won the Nobel Prize in Literature the year it appeared
context: Mises himself said later that Nationaloekonomie 'attracted no attention.' His works had been on the Nazi blacklist since 1933; Europe was at war; the German-speaking world was under Nazi occupation or blockade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: Ludwig von Mises fled Europe for the United States in the summer of 1940, taking his unread 1940 German book with him. Over the next nine years he rewrote and expanded it in English. In what year did the rewritten version appear, and what was its English title?
answer: 1949; 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics'
choices: 1949; 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics'
1945; 'The Theory of Money and Credit'
1944; 'Bureaucracy'
1957; 'Theory and History'
context: Yale University Press published Human Action in 1949. The English version was longer, more polished, and updated for the postwar American context (Keynesianism, the Cold War, the New Deal experience). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: Human Action (1949) is not just a translation of Nationaloekonomie (1940). Which statement best describes how the two books are related?
answer: The two cover the same terrain (praxeology, calculation, cycle, interventionism) but Human Action is longer, more polished, and updated for postwar American debates
choices: The two cover the same terrain (praxeology, calculation, cycle, interventionism) but Human Action is longer, more polished, and updated for postwar American debates
Human Action's chapters were translated word-for-word from Nationaloekonomie with no additions
Human Action rejects the arguments of Nationaloekonomie and defends the opposite conclusions
Human Action is a condensed abridgment removing more than half the German original
context: Nationaloekonomie is the tighter German-language original; Human Action is the mature English restatement. Scholars now read both to trace how Mises's arguments evolved between Geneva 1940 and New York 1949. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: For four decades the German original of Nationaloekonomie was almost impossible to find. In 1980, one group reprinted it so modern Austrian scholars could read it again. Which group?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Cato Institute
The Foundation for Economic Education
The Hoover Institution
context: The Mises Institute, founded in 1982 by Lew Rockwell and Murray Rothbard, republished (or facilitated republication of) the German original as a scholarly reference in 1980. Jorg Guido Hulsmann's 2007 Mises biography and Joseph Salerno's introductions draw on the text. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: What broader lesson about the history of books does reading both Nationaloekonomie and Human Action teach a student?
answer: A great book's initial reception can be nearly nil and still be preserved by a single author's determination to rewrite it in a new language and context
choices: A great book's initial reception can be nearly nil and still be preserved by a single author's determination to rewrite it in a new language and context
A great book always finds its readership within a year of publication
A great book is best measured by its sales in the first six months
A great book must be translated by an official state translator to have influence
context: Mises's determination -- he was in his sixties, a Jewish refugee starting over in New York -- turned a nearly-unread 1940 German treatise into the 1949 English classic that shaped a whole revival of Austrian economics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: A college sports league runs athletics for over a thousand US schools. Its rule for a hundred years: players cannot be paid ANY money for playing, even though the league makes billions from TV. What is a no-pay rule like that called?
answer: Amateurism
choices: Amateurism
Professionalism
Free agency
Salary cap
context: The National Collegiate Athletic Association, founded 1906, governed approximately 500,000 US college athletes across ~1,100 member institutions. Its amateurism rules held from founding through 2021. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association.

question: A big college sports group takes in around 18 billion dollars a year, mostly from TV deals. Its rule for a hundred years said the players who actually made the games could NOT be paid. About how much of that huge pile of money went to the players in cash?
answer: Basically none of it
choices: Basically none of it
About a tenth of it
About a third of it
About half of it
context: Under amateurism, athletes received scholarships, room and board, and small stipends but no cash compensation. The gap between labor value and cash compensation is the structural feature economists had long identified as cartel behavior. Source: NCAA financial reports 2018-19.

question: A group of colleges all agree that none of them will pay their student athletes any salary. Each school could offer money on its own, but they promise each other they won't. What is this kind of secret group agreement usually called?
answer: Price-fixing among employers who should be competing
choices: Price-fixing among employers who should be competing
Fair-share bargaining between rival workplaces
A friendly market-sharing custom
A legal minimum-wage floor
context: Roughly 1,100 nominally competing 'employers' (universities) collectively agreed to fix the price of athlete labor at zero above standardized in-kind compensation. In any other industry this would be a per-se Sherman Section 1 violation. Source: Zimbalist, Unpaid Professionals (Princeton 1999).

question: A college basketball star finds out his face, name, and jersey number are being used in a video game. The company sells it for millions of dollars, and he was paid nothing. Why is it fair for him to sue for a share of the money?
answer: A person owns their own name and likeness, so a company that sells them owes payment
choices: A person owns their own name and likeness, so a company that sells them owes payment
The company should have used a made-up player instead of a real one
Video game money always belongs half to the athletes
College sports rules ban all video games about players
context: O'Bannon v. NCAA (Ninth Circuit, August 8, 2015, upholding partial 2014 district-court ruling by Judge Claudia Wilken). Wilken held NCAA amateurism rules violated Sherman Section 1 as an unreasonable restraint of trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Bannon_v._NCAA.

question: In 2021 the US Supreme Court ruled against the college-sports governing body in a big antitrust case. All nine justices agreed. Why does a unanimous ruling matter more than a close 5-4 ruling?
answer: It signals that even judges who usually disagree see the issue the same way
choices: It signals that even judges who usually disagree see the issue the same way
It doubles the punishment for the losing side
It automatically overturns all past court rulings
It skips the appeals process forever
context: NCAA v. Alston, 594 US ___ (2021), was decided 9-0 with Justice Gorsuch writing for the Court. The decision affirmed that NCAA restrictions on education-related benefits violated Sherman Section 1. Source: supremecourt.gov (Alston 594 US).

question: In a 2021 college-sports antitrust case, one Supreme Court justice wrote a separate opinion agreeing with the ruling. He warned that the whole 'amateurism' setup was likely an illegal cartel. What is a cartel?
answer: A group of sellers that agree to fix prices or limit competition
choices: A group of sellers that agree to fix prices or limit competition
A single buyer with no other competitors
A government agency that reviews mergers
A tax on imported goods
context: Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence in Alston explicitly extended the reasoning: 'The NCAA is not above the law.' The concurrence signaled that the whole amateurism edifice was legally vulnerable. Source: Alston, 594 US ___ (2021), Kavanaugh concurrence.

question: Since July 2021, US college athletes can finally get paid by outside companies for using their name and image. How does that usually affect the number of top players who stay in college a bit longer?
answer: Some stay longer because they can earn real money without turning pro
choices: Some stay longer because they can earn real money without turning pro
All players immediately drop out to play professionally
Colleges instantly become bankrupt
The number of college teams drops to zero
context: NIL (Name, Image, Likeness) compensation became legal for college athletes on July 1, 2021. Within three years the NIL market was estimated at over $1 billion annually flowing to athletes from endorsement deals. Source: ncaa.org (NIL policy history).

question: For decades US college sports made billions in television money, but the players themselves could not be paid. In 2025 a court settlement finally set up a system to share revenue with the athletes. What basic economic idea did that settlement finally admit?
answer: The people creating the value should be allowed to earn from it
choices: The people creating the value should be allowed to earn from it
Only owners and coaches actually create value in sports
Free labor makes sports leagues fairer for fans
Athletes should pay the schools for the honor of playing
context: The House v. NCAA settlement, approved June 6, 2025 by Judge Wilken, created a revenue-sharing framework of approximately $20-22M per school per year. It effectively converted college athletes into compensated labor. Source: reuters.com (House settlement coverage June 2025).

question: Before the 1980s one big college-sports group controlled which games could appear on television and how many. In 1984 the Supreme Court said each school could sell its own television rights. What happened to the number of games shown after that?
answer: Many more games aired, and television money soared
choices: Many more games aired, and television money soared
Almost no games aired, because schools could not organize alone
The same number aired at the same prices — nothing changed
Fans lost interest and stopped watching college football
context: NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, 468 US 85 (1984), held that NCAA control over member schools' television contracts violated Sherman Section 1. It was an earlier stage of the same antitrust unwinding. Source: supremecourt.gov (468 US 85).

question: For decades US college sports made billions while players got paid zero — the 'amateur' rule kept their price at nothing. Between 2014 and 2025 the rule broke and players got paid. What tends to happen when any industry keeps a key input priced far below its market value?
answer: The legal or cultural rule holding the low price in place will eventually break
choices: The legal or cultural rule holding the low price in place will eventually break
The rule will only get stronger over time
The workers will disappear from the industry
The federal government will formally endorse the low price
context: The amateurism-as-noble-tradition framing was a cultural prop for the price-fixing structure. Once courts began applying standard antitrust analysis, the prop eroded and the cartel collapsed within about a decade. Source: Zimbalist (1999); Alston (2021); House settlement (2025).

question: During World War 2 a big American city froze rents so landlords could not raise the price during the emergency. That 'short' freeze has stayed in place ever since. What is the general name for a rule that caps how much rent can be charged?
answer: Rent control
choices: Rent control
Rent inflation
Free rent
Rent tax
context: November 1943 federal rent freeze on New York City marks the start of continuous US residential rent regulation. The freeze was handed off to New York State, then to NYC itself in successive laws. Source: hcr.ny.gov (rent regulation history).

question: New York City has the oldest rent control program in the country. It began as a 'temporary' wartime freeze in 1943 and never ended. As of 2026, about how long has it been running?
answer: Over 80 years
choices: Over 80 years
About 10 years
About 20 years
About 200 years

The 'temporary' program has been extended through several successor statutes -- the Emergency Housing Rent Control Law 1946, the Rent Stabilization Law 1969, the Emergency Tenant Protection Act 1974, and the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act. Source: hcr.ny.gov.

question: In 1971 a Swedish socialist economist gave a famous warning. He said one housing policy was 'the most efficient way to destroy a city -- except for bombing.' Which policy?
answer: Rent control
choices: Rent control
Public-housing high-rises
Zoning height limits
Property taxes
context: Assar Lindbeck, in The Political Economy of the New Left (1971). Lindbeck was a lifelong democratic-socialist and Nobel-committee-adjacent figure, not a right-winger -- his line is cited across the political spectrum. Source: Lindbeck (1971).

question: The Bastiat seen-versus-unseen reading of New York City rent control: SEEN was the low rent stamped on a lucky tenant's lease. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The apartments never built, landlords deferring maintenance, and vacant units held off market
choices: The apartments never built, landlords deferring maintenance, and vacant units held off market
The government revenue from tenant leases
The reduced traffic congestion in the borough
The higher property taxes on landlords
context: Bastiat's method: the visible benefit was to the specific rent-regulated tenant; the hidden cost was future tenants who could not find apartments, current tenants of deteriorating buildings, and landlords who warehoused units. Source: bastiat.org, mercatus.org.

question: In the 1970s New York City had an epidemic of building fires, mostly in the South Bronx. The economist Assar Lindbeck himself connected the fires to rent regulation. What was the connection he named?
answer: The incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance
choices: The incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance
The lack of fire-code enforcement in regulated buildings
The higher smoker rate in rent-regulated apartments
The greater density of gas heaters in old apartments
context: Rent-controlled buildings that could not cover their mortgage and maintenance costs became liabilities. Insurance payouts on total loss exceeded the market value of an ongoing rent-controlled property. The South Bronx arson wave of the 1970s is the exhibit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx.

question: The first classic rent-control critique, a 1946 pamphlet published by two future Nobel laureates, was called 'Roofs or Ceilings?'. Which pair wrote it?
answer: Milton Friedman and George Stigler
choices: Milton Friedman and George Stigler
John Kenneth Galbraith and Paul Samuelson
Kenneth Arrow and Gerard Debreu
Ronald Coase and James Buchanan
context: 'Roofs or Ceilings?' by Milton Friedman and George Stigler, published by the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946, is the founding classical critique. Both won Nobel Prizes decades later (Friedman 1976, Stigler 1982). Source: fee.org (Roofs or Ceilings 1946).

question: A 2019 study in the American Economic Review by Rebecca Diamond and Chris Palmer of Stanford examined a similar rent-control expansion in San Francisco. The effects matched the New York pattern. What did they find?
answer: Housing-stock destruction and reduced supply
choices: Housing-stock destruction and reduced supply
Increased new construction of luxury units
Widespread lower rent burdens across all tenants
Rising quality of rent-regulated units
context: Diamond and Palmer's study of San Francisco's 1994 rent-control expansion found landlords converted, demolished, or removed roughly 15% of formerly-controlled units from the rental stock over the next two decades. Same mechanism as the New York pattern. Source: aeaweb.org (AER 2019).

question: New York's 2019 rent law, known as HSTPA, made rent rules tighter still. Within two years, what specific measurable effects appeared?
answer: More warehoused units and less new rental construction
choices: More warehoused units and less new rental construction
Rising landlord investment in maintenance
Faster tenant turnover across boroughs
Reduced construction permit backlogs
context: Landlords held rent-regulated units off market ('warehoused') rather than accept new indexed tenancies. New rental construction in NYC dropped. The 2019 tightening's predictable supply effects matched the seen-vs-unseen analysis. Source: Rent Stabilization Association analyses 2020-22.

question: The reasoning-move at the heart of every rent-control critique -- from Friedman-Stigler 1946 through Lindbeck 1971 to Diamond-Palmer 2019 -- is a single incentive story about landlords. What does it say?
answer: Landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add supply
choices: Landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add supply
Landlords with rent below cost invest more heavily in improvements
Landlords with rent below cost lower quality but expand supply
Landlords with rent below cost mostly exit but new entrants rush in
context: The core incentive story: if rent is below what maintenance and construction cost require, the rational landlord defers maintenance, warehouses units, converts to condos, or exits. Future tenants pay the invisible cost. Source: Friedman-Stigler, Roofs or Ceilings? (1946).

question: In 1996 a computer scientist had an idea. Write a contract as code, and it runs itself the moment its rules are met. No lawyer or judge needed. What is this kind of contract called?
answer: A smart contract
choices: A smart contract
A legal loan
A digital receipt
A payment plan
context: Nick Szabo coined 'smart contracts' in a 1996 essay. Vitalik Buterin later built Ethereum around a smart-contract virtual machine (2015); Hal Finney built RPOW; Adam Back built Hashcash. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: In 1998 Nick Szabo shared an essay online. He described a way to make rare digital tokens that would work like real gold but live only in software. What did he call it?
answer: bit gold
choices: bit gold
b-money
Hashcash
DigiCash
context: Szabo drafted bit gold in 1998; a blog post appeared in 2005. b-money is Wei Dai's separate 1998 proposal; Hashcash is Adam Back's 1997 anti-spam PoW; DigiCash is David Chaum's 1989 company. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: Nick Szabo's bit gold made new digital tokens by chaining math puzzles together. Each new token fed the next puzzle. Which crypto tool did he chain to make fresh bit-gold tokens?
answer: proof-of-work
choices: proof-of-work
blind signatures
hash-based message authentication
elliptic-curve key exchange
context: Bit gold works by chaining proof-of-work: solving one puzzle produces a new token whose hash seeds the next. Blind signatures (Chaum's DigiCash), HMACs, and key-exchange are separate cryptographic primitives that bit gold did not use for issuance. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: Nick Szabo's bit gold essay names one money trait that no central bank can be trusted to give. Which trait does he say bit gold can guarantee but fiat money cannot?
answer: a supply whose growth rate is governed by fixed technical difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion
choices: a supply whose growth rate is governed by fixed technical difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion
an instant settlement guarantee with no per-transaction processing delay or waiting period at any point
a reversible-transaction rule for fraud protection that lets any user recall a mistaken transfer within a set window
a printed physical note that an ordinary citizen can hold in the hand and verify by touch and weight
context: Szabo argues bit gold's supply is governed by puzzle difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion; fiat has always been discretionary. Instant settlement, reversibility, and physical notes are properties the essay does not claim as the differentiator. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: Nick Szabo's bit gold system was never fully built. Szabo himself named one technical piece he could not solve, the piece that would keep a distributed record consistent when many people were solving puzzles at once. Which unsolved problem did bit gold leave open?
answer: how to reach consensus on the ordering of new bit-gold entries across a distributed network
choices: how to reach consensus on the ordering of new bit-gold entries across a distributed network
how to make the puzzles asymmetric between solving and verifying
how to encode the tokens in a portable digital format
how to sign transactions to prove ownership
context: Bit gold assumed distributed timestamping but did not specify how the network would agree on the ordering when solutions arrived from many nodes. Puzzle asymmetry, digital-format portability, and signing were already established primitives. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html; Nakamoto 2008 sec 4.

question: The one piece bit gold could not solve in 1998 is the piece Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 Bitcoin paper is best known for solving. Which mechanism did Satoshi introduce to close bit gold's open problem?
answer: the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories
choices: the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories
the blind-signature bank issuance model that Chaum's DigiCash had introduced in 1989
the reusable-proof-of-work token exchange model that Hal Finney had built in 2004
the ring-signature transaction hider that later cryptocurrencies would adopt for privacy
context: Satoshi's longest-chain rule with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker specifically resolves the consensus problem bit gold left open. Blind signatures (Chaum) required a bank; RPOW (Finney) required a central server; ring signatures came later and hide senders, not resolve ordering. Source: Nakamoto 2008 sec 4.

question: Nick Szabo holds a law degree from an American university. He has combined legal analysis with monetary history throughout his career. Which law school did Szabo attend?
answer: George Washington University
choices: George Washington University
Harvard University
Yale University
Stanford University
context: Szabo earned his JD from George Washington University Law School. Harvard, Yale, and Stanford Law are frequently guessed as elite law schools but none is Szabo's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: Because of his writing style, where he lives, his crypto focus, and his 1998 bit-gold plan, Nick Szabo has often been suspected of being Satoshi Nakamoto. What has Szabo always said in public about this?
answer: he has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto
choices: he has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto
he has quietly confirmed the identification in later interviews
he has told journalists he cannot remember
he has been legally prohibited from discussing it
context: Szabo has denied the Satoshi identification publicly on multiple occasions. There has been no confirmation, memory-loss claim, or legal gag reported. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: The Bitcoin white paper lists earlier works in its notes. One cypherpunk project is widely seen as the closest ancestor to Bitcoin's design. Yet Satoshi's 2008 paper does not cite it. Which project?
answer: Nick Szabo's bit gold
choices: Nick Szabo's bit gold
Wei Dai's b-money
Adam Back's Hashcash
Haber and Stornetta's timestamping
context: Satoshi's white paper cites Wei Dai's b-money (Ref 1), Adam Back's Hashcash (Ref 6), and Haber and Stornetta's timestamping papers, but does not cite bit gold directly, even though the design similarity is widely acknowledged. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: A Bitcoin historian sums up the technical distance from bit gold in 1998 to Bitcoin in 2008. He presses one reasoning move about what Satoshi actually contributed on top of Szabo's blueprint. Which move does the argument press?
answer: That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the consensus mechanism -- and consensus was the single hard piece the field had left open until Satoshi
choices: That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the consensus mechanism -- and consensus was the single hard piece the field had left open until Satoshi
That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the proof-of-work mechanism -- Szabo left the puzzle chain unspecified and Satoshi added it
That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the digital signatures -- Szabo did not use signed transactions and Satoshi added them
That bit gold and Bitcoin are cryptographically unrelated designs that arrived at similar shapes by coincidence rather than lineage
context: The bit-gold-vs-Bitcoin move (Song, Antonopoulos, Ammous): Szabo had PoW, chained puzzles, digital signatures and a plan for issuance; the piece he could not close was distributed consensus, which is exactly what Satoshi's longest-chain rule solved. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html; Nakamoto white paper.

question: In one small California town, the neighbors keep voting to block new houses and apartments from being built. There are lots of jobs there and lots of people who want to move in. What is probably happening to the price of the houses that already exist?
answer: It keeps going way up -- some homes cost millions
choices: It keeps going way up -- some homes cost millions
It stays flat forever no matter what
It drops until houses are almost free
It changes only if the mayor announces a new price
context: Palo Alto's median home price approached $3M in 2024 (Zillow/CoreLogic). About 94% of its residential land is zoned for single-family detached homes; apartment construction has been effectively frozen for decades. Source: paloaltoonline.com; zillow.com.

question: In a growing town, neighbors show up at every meeting to block new apartments from being built near their houses -- they say new buildings will change the neighborhood. People joke this attitude fits the shorthand NIMBY. What three words does NIMBY stand for?
answer: Not In My Backyard
choices: Not In My Backyard
New In My Backyard
No Money Big Yield
Never In My Building Year
context: NIMBY (Not In My Backyard) describes the political pattern in which existing local homeowners organize to block new housing in their neighborhoods, even when a region's overall housing shortage produces high rents and long commutes. Source: Grokipedia 'NIMBY.'

question: In Palo Alto, most land is zoned only for single-family homes. That makes new apartments almost illegal across the whole city. About what share of the land is zoned this way?
answer: About 94 percent
choices: About 94 percent
About 25 percent
About 50 percent
Essentially none
context: About 94% of Palo Alto's residential land is single-family only. This is the structural feature that makes multi-family projects require special approvals and lengthy hearings each time. Source: Palo Alto General Plan; ABAG regional data.

question: Two economists, Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko, made up a term. It names the gap between what housing costs in cities where building is hard and what it would cost to just build. What term did they use?
answer: The zoning tax
choices: The zoning tax
The rent premium
The permitting spread
The metro markup
context: Glaeser + Gyourko, 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' (NBER Working Paper 8835, 2002) and follow-up work estimate the zoning tax at 30-60% in Bay Area cities. The wedge is a pure transfer from would-be residents to existing homeowners. Source: nber.org (Glaeser-Gyourko 2002).

question: In Palo Alto, homeowners gain from strict zoning that blocks new housing. The gain is big for them, but the harm spreads across many other people. Who are those hidden losers?
answer: Workers priced out to Modesto, Sacramento, or out of California entirely
choices: Workers priced out to Modesto, Sacramento, or out of California entirely
Palo Alto public-school administrators
Stanford University trustees
Nearby city police departments
context: The dispersed victims cannot vote in Palo Alto, cannot attend Palo Alto hearings, and often do not know that a specific project would have housed them. That is exactly the collective-action failure Olson diagnosed. Source: Olson (1965) applied via Furman et al. (Housing Reform brief).

question: Around 2015, a new group formed in American housing fights. They pushed for more homes to be built. What short name do people call this movement?
answer: YIMBY
choices: YIMBY
SANE
PATH
HOA
context: YIMBY (Yes In My Backyard) organizations like YIMBY Action emerged around 2015-16. They served as the selective-incentive mechanism (organization, model bills, hearings turnout) that begins to solve the collective-action problem on the dispersed side. Source: yimbyaction.org.

question: In 2021 California passed a law letting homeowners build a duplex on land that used to be single-family only. It was a rare win against local zoning rules. What was the bill's short name?
answer: SB 9
choices: SB 9
SB 35
AB 5
AB 32
context: SB 9 (2021) allowed by-right duplex construction on many single-family lots across California, over the strenuous objections of many local governments. It attacked the rule-selection game at state level. Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (SB 9, 2021).

question: For most of the last century one US city near the Great Lakes only allowed single-family houses on most of its land. In 2018 the city changed the rules so any lot could hold up to three units. What did that change do to the supply of homes?
answer: More units per lot became legal, so more homes could be built
choices: More units per lot became legal, so more homes could be built
Every existing home was torn down overnight
People were banned from moving into the city
Everyone was forced into apartments the government owns
context: The Minneapolis 2040 Comprehensive Plan (2018) eliminated single-family-only residential zoning citywide. It was the first US big-city plan to do so, and later became a model for other cities. Source: minneapolismn.gov (2040 Plan).

question: One fast-growing US city let builders put up huge amounts of new apartments over about five years. To the surprise of people who claimed new supply always raises rents, what actually happened to rents there?
answer: Rents fell as more apartments were built
choices: Rents fell as more apartments were built
Rents doubled as more apartments were built
Rents stayed exactly the same
Older apartments were torn down instead
context: Austin's building boom from about 2019 through 2024 produced actual measured declines in market-rate rents. It is the most-cited domestic case that supply matters. Source: apartmentlist.com; Austin American-Statesman coverage 2023-24.

question: The Palo Alto zoning story teaches a general rule. When a bad policy hurts a region's economy but sticks around anyway, look for one thing to explain why. What should you look for?
answer: Existing incumbent asset-holders whose wealth was created by the policy's restriction
choices: Existing incumbent asset-holders whose wealth was created by the policy's restriction
A single hidden corrupt payment to a legislator
A federal preemption blocking local action
A recent Supreme Court decision requiring the policy
context: The zoning wedge is a multi-trillion-dollar wealth transfer to existing homeowners in constrained cities. That concentrated wealth is what organizes to defend the restrictive rule against reform. Source: Glaeser + Gyourko (2002); Olson (1965) as applied.

question: Japan sets housing rules at the national level, and cities have little say. That works very differently from cities like Palo Alto. What has happened to Tokyo's real housing prices over the long run, even as the city keeps growing?
answer: They have been comparatively stable
choices: They have been comparatively stable
They have tripled over the past decade
They exceed Palo Alto's per-square-foot prices
They have collapsed to near zero
context: Japan's national zoning system permits substantial by-right housing construction, and Tokyo's real housing prices have been comparatively stable despite continued metropolitan-area growth. It is the international contrast that Bay Area reformers frequently cite. Source: Grokipedia 'Housing in Japan.'

question: North Korea has been ruled by three generations of one family since 1948. What is that family's last name?
answer: Kim
choices: Kim
Park
Lee
Choe
context: Kim Il-sung (1948-94), Kim Jong-il (1994-2011), and Kim Jong-un (2011- ) form the three-generation dynasty ruling the DPRK. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea.

question: North Korea's official idea says the country must stand alone. It must not lean on outsiders. What Korean word names this idea?
answer: Juche
choices: Juche
Songun
Chuche-hop
Bogus
context: Juche was formally systematized by Kim Il-sung in speeches from 1955 onward. It emphasizes political independence, economic self-reliance, and military self-defense. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juche.

question: In the 1990s, North Korea suffered a famine that killed hundreds of thousands of people. The government owned all the farms and set all the food prices. Why does the Austrian school say a fully planned economy so often ends in shortage?
answer: No planner can gather all the information that free prices carry
choices: No planner can gather all the information that free prices carry
Planned economies always have too much rain and not enough sun
Farmers in planned countries choose to grow only flowers, not food
Free countries always send extra food to planned countries
context: 'Gonan-ui Haenggun' (Arduous March) is North Korea's official term for the mid-1990s famine. The state has never acknowledged a death toll. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korean_famine.

question: Scholars can only estimate how many died in the mid-1990s North Korean famine because the state has never opened its records. What is the standard range for excess deaths?
answer: About 600,000 to 2.5 million
choices: About 600,000 to 2.5 million
About 6 million to 25 million
context: Andrew Natsios's The Great North Korean Famine (2001) argued for the upper end (2-3 million); Marcus Noland's demographic reconstruction argues for the lower end (600K-1M). Out of a population of about 22 million. Source: uspicedu (KEI) reports.

question: North Korea runs a set of political prison camps called kwanliso. We know about them from escapees and satellite photos. Which US non-profit puts out yearly satellite-image reports on the camps?

Reporters Without Borders

question: The North Korean prison camp system punishes not only the person accused of a crime, but also their parents, children, and grandchildren. What is this policy called?
answer: Three generations of punishment
choices: Three generations of punishment
Collective correction
Family rectification
Bloodline restoration

question: One of the most cited pictures in the calculation debate is a nighttime satellite image of the Korean peninsula. What does the image show?
answer: North Korea nearly dark and South Korea blazing with light
choices: North Korea nearly dark and South Korea blazing with light
North Korea heavily forested and South Korea deforested
North Korea covered in snow and South Korea clear
North Korea flooded and South Korea dry
context: NASA and NOAA nighttime imagery show South Korea covered in urban lighting and North Korea (excluding Pyongyang) essentially dark. Same peninsula, same language, split in 1948 into planned and market economies. Source: earthobservatory.nasa.gov.

question: Korea was split into North and South after a war. The South picked markets and trade; the North picked a fully planned communist economy. About 75 years later, how much richer is the average South Korean than the average North Korean?
answer: About 40 times richer
choices: About 40 times richer
About 4 times richer
About 400 times richer
About the same
context: South Korea's per-capita GDP is roughly 40 times North Korea's on standard estimates (both PPP and nominal). This is one of the largest cross-border prosperity gaps ever recorded between countries with the same starting culture and geography. Source: Bank of Korea and World Bank estimates.

question: North Korea has run a near-total command economy — no free markets, prices set by planners — since the 1950s, and has suffered chronic food shortages ever since. What is the Austrian-school explanation for why the planners cannot fix the problem?
answer: Without market prices the state cannot allocate food or resources rationally at large scale
choices: Without market prices the state cannot allocate food or resources rationally at large scale
Without oil imports the state cannot power its industry
Without foreign investment the state cannot modernize
Without democracy the state cannot legitimize taxation
context: The Mises 1920 calculation argument applied: no central planner can determine relative prices across millions of goods and inputs. The DPRK's chronic scarcity is that argument playing out in a country of 22 million for over 70 years. Source: mises.org/library/mises-planned-chaos.

question: North Korea has been running a strict command economy — every price set by planners, no free markets — since 1948. That's the longest single experiment with pure central planning still running. What broad economic result has that experiment produced?
answer: Chronic food shortages and famine, decade after decade
choices: Chronic food shortages and famine, decade after decade
Rapid economic growth that outpaces its neighbors
A booming private trading sector
A famous stock market with worldwide investors
context: The DPRK was founded September 9, 1948, one month after the Republic of Korea in the South (August 15, 1948). Kim Il-sung had returned from Soviet-army training in 1945. The Korean War (1950-53) hardened the division. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_North_Korea.

question: China and Vietnam still call themselves Communist, but both allow real markets and private businesses. Cuba has cautiously started market reforms too. Which statement best describes the modern picture of command versus market-with-Party economies?
answer: Only North Korea stays pure command; China, Vietnam, and Cuba allow markets under Party rule
choices: Only North Korea stays pure command; China, Vietnam, and Cuba allow markets under Party rule
Cuba is still a pure command economy alongside North Korea
Vietnam has ended Communist Party rule entirely
China now has fully private ownership of all industry
context: China (1978), Vietnam (1986 Doi Moi), and Cuba (partial reforms from 1993) all adopted some market pricing. The DPRK remains the outlier -- the calculation-debate case that never took Mises's advice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_North_Korea.

question: In a very controlled country there are no regular stores selling food. The government runs shops that hand out grain, oil, and other food to each family, but the amount depends on your job and how loyal you seem. What is that setup called?
answer: A government rationing system
choices: A government rationing system
A free market
A farmer's market
A private grocery chain
context: The Public Distribution System (PDS) was the DPRK's principal food-allocation mechanism. Private markets were essentially banned outside a narrow set of state-approved farmers' markets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Distribution_System_(North_Korea).

question: In the 1990s, food aid from other countries stopped and a huge famine hit North Korea -- hundreds of thousands of people starved. Instead of calling it a famine, the government gave it a heroic name meaning 'a hard march we all took together.' Why do governments do that?
answer: To hide who is to blame and make the disaster sound noble
choices: To hide who is to blame and make the disaster sound noble

question: In 2007, two economists wrote a book called 'Famine in North Korea.' They guessed 600,000 to 2.5 million people died in the famine, out of about 22 million. Who wrote it?
answer: Marcus Noland and Stephan Haggard

Robert Barro and Ronald McKinnon
context: Noland (Peterson Institute) and Haggard (UC San Diego) published Famine in North Korea in 2007. Their central finding: the famine was PRODUCED by the failure of the PDS itself; regions cut off from Pyongyang's distribution suffered worst. Source: piie.com Noland-Haggard.

question: During the Arduous March famine, private trade was banned in North Korea. But something popped up anyway. It moved food between regions and saved millions of lives. What was it?

The rural collectives

The Kim Foundation shops

By 2019 defector-survey estimates suggested ~70-80% of North Korean private consumption flowed through jangmadang markets. Source: Andrei Lankov, North of the DMZ.

question: Two North Korean escapees wrote famous memoirs about the Arduous March. They told of mothers and grandmothers walking hours to buy rice at illegal markets. Which pair wrote them?
answer: Yeonmi Park and Hyeonseo Lee
choices: Yeonmi Park and Hyeonseo Lee
Kang Chol-hwan and Shin Dong-hyuk
Lee Soon-ok and Kim Yong
Choi Jinyi and Park Sang-hak
context: Yeonmi Park's In Order to Live (2015) and Hyeonseo Lee's The Girl with Seven Names (2015) both document the jangmadang market experience. Both defected via China. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeonmi_Park, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyeonseo_Lee.

question: The 1990s North Korean famine was sharpest in regions cut off from Pyongyang's central distribution. Which pattern does this establish about the mechanism of the collapse?
answer: Central-distribution failure is itself a famine mechanism

Weather variability was the primary cause
International sanctions caused most deaths
Chinese aid cuts were the sole trigger
context: Noland and Haggard's finding: regions closest to Pyongyang's central distribution suffered less; regions farthest and most PDS-dependent suffered worst. The mechanism is Mises 1920 in its most literal form -- central distribution cannot substitute for market allocation. Source: Noland-Haggard (2007).

question: A Russian historian in Seoul has written the most about North Korea's jangmadang street markets. He is the top scholar on the topic. What is his last name?
answer: Lankov

Cumings
Oberdorfer
Myers

question: In North Korea private trade is illegal, but the government stores rarely have enough food. Over time, people set up unofficial street markets in every town. A survey of people who escaped found what share of everyday goods actually flows through those illegal markets?
answer: About 70 to 80 percent

About 7 to 8 percent
Less than 1 percent
About 30 to 40 percent
context: Defector-survey estimates from Kookmin University and Seoul-based think tanks suggest 70-80% of private consumption flows through informal markets. The state tolerates them because the alternative is renewed famine. Source: kookmin university surveys 2018-19.

question: The 1990s North Korean famine and the emergence of jangmadang markets illustrate two Austrian reasoning-moves at once. Which pair does the case teach most sharply?

choices: The calculation problem in acute form plus Hayek's spontaneous order
The Cantillon effect plus moral hazard

The world's most totalitarian environment produced the sharpest confirmation of both moves. Source: mises.org/library/north-korea.

question: A woman in Mississippi wants to open a shop where she braids hair for pay. Before the state will let her, it makes her sit through 300 hours of an expensive class -- and the class does not cover braiding at all. What is this kind of 'you need a permit before you can work' rule called?

Lunsford); in April 2005 the governor signed a reform letting braiders register with the Board of Health for $25 and post sanitation guidelines. More than 6,700 braiders have registered since. Sources: Institute for Justice, 'Mississippi Hair Braiding' (https://ij.org/case/armstrong-v-lunsford/); Armstrong's written testimony to the U.S. House Small Business Committee, March 26, 2014.

question: In the 1950s, only about one American in twenty needed a license to work. By 2013, that had changed. How many workers said they needed one?

About three in ten
About one in two

The roughly 5% baseline for the early 1950s comes from Morris Kleiner, Licensing Occupations: Ensuring Quality or Restricting Competition? (2006). Sources: Kleiner and Krueger, 'Analyzing the Extent and Influence of Occupational Licensing on the Labor Market,' Journal of Labor Economics 31(S1), 2013 (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/669060); NBER working paper 14979 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w14979).

question: Isis Brantley braided hair in Dallas since 1979. In 1997 police arrested her, because Texas made braiders take 1,500 hours of classes that never taught braiding. She fought for eighteen years and won in court in early 2015. What did Texas lawmakers do that June?
answer: Removed natural hair braiding from state licensing altogether

Granted Brantley a personal exemption from the training rule
context: In Brantley v. Kuntz a federal court struck down the rule requiring Brantley to outfit her braiding school like a barber college. House Bill 2717 then passed the Texas House and Senate unanimously and was signed on June 10, 2015, fully deregulating natural hair braiding in Texas. Sources: Institute for Justice, 'Texas Hair Braiding Instruction' (https://ij.org/case/txbraiding/); American University Business Law Review on Brantley v. Kuntz (https://aublr.org/2015/01/brantley-v-kuntz/).

question: For years, Louisiana was the only state that made you pass an exam to sell flower arrangements. In 2003 a legal group sued the state for Sandy Meadows and two other women. The lawsuit focused on how the test was run. What was wrong with the test?
answer: Licensed florists competing with the applicants graded the practical test
choices: Licensed florists competing with the applicants graded the practical test
The wholesale flower distributors' trade group wrote all the test questions
Applicants could sit the test only in Baton Rouge, once every second year
A year of unpaid apprenticeship under a licensed florist came first
context: Meadows v. Odom, 356 F. Supp. 2d 639 (M.D. La. 2005). The exam's subjective practical section was scored by state-licensed florists -- the incumbents an applicant would compete against. Sandy Meadows had been fired from a Baton Rouge grocery store after inspectors found her arranging flowers without a license; she died unemployed and in poverty before the case was decided. Louisiana finally repealed the florist exam in 2024. Sources: Institute for Justice (https://ij.org/case/meadows-v-odom/); Justia (https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp2/356/639/2573021/).

question: A state legislature takes up a bill to let hair braiders work without a cosmetology license. Consumers would pay less and more people could open shops, yet the bill dies in committee for the fourth session running, as it did the three sessions before. Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action explains why bills of this shape keep dying. Which asymmetry did Olson identify?
answer: A few who each gain a lot organize; the many who each lose a little do not
choices: A few who each gain a lot organize; the many who each lose a little do not
Voters skip the details because one vote will never change the outcome
Regulators must lean on the industry for the facts only the industry holds
Rivals burn real resources competing for a privilege, and that spending is waste
context: Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (Harvard University Press, 1965). The three distractors are also real reasoning moves, borrowed from other analysts: rational ignorance (Anthony Downs), informational capture (a strand of the capture literature), and rent-seeking waste (Gordon Tullock, 1967). Source: Olson, The Logic of Collective Action.

question: Shopping-mall kiosks in North Carolina began offering teeth whitening at a fraction of a dentist's price. The state Board of Dental Examiners -- six of its eight members practicing dentists -- mailed the kiosks cease-and-desist letters until they closed. The Federal Trade Commission sued, and the board claimed the immunity from antitrust law that states enjoy. On February 25, 2015 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 against the board. What did the Court hold?
answer: A board run by active competitors keeps that immunity only under real state supervision
choices: A board run by active competitors keeps that immunity only under real state supervision
A licensing board is a private association and has never held any such immunity
Teeth whitening is not dentistry, so the board acted outside its granted authority
A board may bar competitors only after public notice-and-comment rulemaking
context: North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, 574 U.S. 494 (2015). Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote for the majority, joined by Roberts, Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan; Alito dissented with Scalia and Thomas. Where a controlling number of a state agency's decisionmakers are active market participants in the occupation it regulates, Parker state-action immunity applies only if the state actively supervises the agency. Sources: Justia (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/574/494/); Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_Board_of_Dental_Examiners_v._FTC).

question: In 1971, George Stigler wrote a paper that flipped the textbook view of rules. A trade group is not the target of rules. It is the customer. Stigler asked: if a trade could pick one favor from the state, which would it want most?
answer: A rule blocking newcomers from entering the trade
choices: A rule blocking newcomers from entering the trade
A cash subsidy paid out of the state's general revenue
A guaranteed rate of return set and policed by the state
A tax on the imported goods that substitute for its own
context: George J. Stigler, 'The Theory of Economic Regulation,' Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2(1), Spring 1971, 3-21. Stigler catalogued the favors an industry can seek -- direct subsidy, control over entry, rules governing substitutes and complements, and price fixing -- and argued control over entry is worth most, because a cash subsidy draws in new entrants who compete it away while an entry barrier keeps them out for good. Stigler won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1982. Source: https://www.jstor.org/stable/3003160.

question: In his 1962 book, Milton Friedman opened his chapter on job licenses with doctors. He called the American Medical Association 'perhaps the strongest trade union in the country.' Friedman agreed a bad doctor can hurt a patient. Even so, he was against a license rule. He named a different plan. It would warn worried patients but still let them choose. What was it?
answer: State certification that a practitioner has met a published standard
choices: State certification that a practitioner has met a published standard
State registration of each practitioner's name and address before working
Compulsory malpractice insurance priced against each practitioner's record
A national entry examination written by patients rather than by physicians
context: Capitalism and Freedom, chapter 9, 'Occupational Licensure.' Friedman separated three levels of state involvement in a trade -- registration, certification and licensure -- and argued the justification weakens as you climb. Certification publishes who has met a standard while leaving the uncertified free to practice and the patient free to choose; licensure instead restricts the supply of practitioners and raises their incomes. The AMA has shaped entry into American medicine since its founding in 1847. Sources: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962), ch. 9; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism_and_Freedom.

question: Imagine a village with no money. A shoemaker wants bread. He carries his best pair of shoes to the baker and offers them for a loaf. Every trade in the village works this way: goods for goods, no coins. Which name do economists give to this system?
answer: barter
choices: barter
banking
usury
arbitrage
context: BARTER is direct goods-for-goods exchange with no medium of exchange. The obvious problem it faces is called the DOUBLE COINCIDENCE OF WANTS: the shoemaker needs a baker who happens to want shoes AT THAT MOMENT. Solving that problem is what money is for. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11138-022-00600-0.

question: How did money first get started? One old idea says: long ago people traded goods. Over time, they all began using one thing like gold or silver. It was easy to carry. It did not rot. Everyone would take it. Where does this idea say money came from?
answer: Regular people trading with each other, not a king or government
choices: Regular people trading with each other, not a king or government
A king who invented coins one day
A single scientist who wrote a plan for it
A big meeting of bank owners in Europe
context: Menger's essay appeared in The Economic Journal, Volume 2, June 1892, pages 239-255 -- then a very young journal, founded three years earlier by the British Economic Association (later the Royal Economic Society). The American Economic Review dates from 1911; the JPE from 1892 but published in Chicago; the QJE from 1886. Source: scispace.com/papers/on-the-origin-of-money-4ddier28ke.

question: Menger's 1892 essay set out to knock down an old rival theory of money. That theory went back to Aristotle. It said money is whatever the ruler stamps on metal and calls money. So the theory said money must come from whom?
answer: the state
choices: the state
the temple
the merchant guild
the extended family
context: Menger targeted the STATE theory of money (later formalized as Georg Knapp's 1905 Staatliche Theorie des Geldes, 'The State Theory of Money'), which said sovereign authority creates money. Menger's counter: no state stamp could get people to accept a coin unless they already thought others would too. Source: mars.gmu.edu/bitstreams/9013e402-22d7-4cb9-b937-a651fd4d1802/download.

question: A wheat farmer in a barter economy needs a plow. He finds a plow-maker -- but the plow-maker does not need wheat this month; he needs leather. The direct trade cannot happen, so the wheat farmer has to go find a wheat-hungry tanner FIRST, hoping the tanner will have leather to spare. Nineteenth-century economists gave this specific obstacle to direct trade a formal name. What is the obstacle called?
answer: the double coincidence of wants
choices: the double coincidence of wants
the tragedy of the commons
the free-rider problem
the winner's curse
context: The DOUBLE COINCIDENCE OF WANTS -- both traders must simultaneously desire what the other offers -- is the obstacle barter cannot solve, and why every historical trading society has evolved SOME most-saleable good as an indirect medium. Menger's 1892 essay is the classic account of how that emergence happens. Source: moneyness.ca/2012/01/menger-and-origins-of-money.html.

question: Menger's main idea in 1892 was that some goods are easier to trade on than others. A cow trades more easily than a clay pot. Silver trades more easily than a cow. A small silver coin trades more easily than a silver bar. What English word did Menger use for this trait?
answer: saleability
choices: saleability
durability
convertibility
solvency
context: SALEABILITY (also spelled 'salability' in American English) is Menger's translation of Absatzfaehigkeit -- how easily a good can be traded away again for what the holder actually wants, at little loss of price. It is the master concept of the whole essay. Source: moneyness.ca/2012/01/menger-and-origins-of-money.html.

question: In Menger's 1892 story, nobody in the ancient world sat down and planned money. No committee met. No one wrote a plan. Yet money still showed up, from many traders each solving a local need. Hayek later named this pattern for things nobody designed but everyone uses. His three examples were money, language, and common law. What did Hayek call the pattern?
answer: spontaneous order
choices: spontaneous order
central planning
public choice
moral hazard
context: SPONTANEOUS ORDER -- Hayek's name for Menger's pattern -- captures institutions that emerge from countless individual choices without a designer. Money, language, and the common law are the three classic Austrian examples; markets themselves are a fourth. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11138-022-00600-0.

question: Menger's 1892 essay lists six traits that make a good the best fit for money. Five are: durability, portability, divisibility, sameness, and easy recognition. Gold beat copper as money because gold has more of the sixth trait. Bitcoin fans say Bitcoin has more of that trait than any physical good could. Which sixth trait is it?
answer: scarcity
choices: scarcity
beauty
warmth
colour
context: SCARCITY -- a low and predictable supply that cannot be casually expanded -- is what keeps a monetary good's purchasing power stable over time. Copper is too abundant; gold has held ~1.5%/year new-supply growth for centuries; Bitcoin's hard 21-million cap makes it (per Saifedean Ammous's Bitcoin Standard) the modern digital reinvention. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2512.07840.

question: In 1905 a German economist named Georg Friedrich Knapp wrote a book called 'The State Theory of Money.' Its famous line was 'money is a creature of law.' The book is now the founding text of a school of monetary thought. Modern Monetary Theory grew out of it. What school did Knapp start?
answer: chartalism
choices: chartalism
monetarism
bullionism
mercantilism
context: CHARTALISM (from Latin charta = token) is the doctrine that money's value comes from state issuance and tax-acceptance, not from spontaneous market emergence. Knapp founded it in 1905; today's MMT (Kelton, Wray, Mosler) is its direct descendant. Monetarism is Friedman's quantity-theory tradition; bullionism and mercantilism are early-modern doctrines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Friedrich_Knapp.

question: Ludwig von Mises built on Menger's 1892 essay in his 1912 book 'The Theory of Money and Credit.' His key move: today's buying power of a money traces back, step by step, to yesterday's buying power. You can trace it all the way back to the day before the good was money at all. On that day it had value only as a normal good. What is the name of this Mises theorem?
answer: the regression theorem
choices: the regression theorem
the impossibility theorem
the equivalence theorem
the invariance theorem
context: Mises's REGRESSION THEOREM (1912) chains money's exchange value back in time to a first day of non-monetary commodity value -- solving the circularity of 'money is valuable because it buys things and it buys things because it is valuable.' Bitcoiners argue Bitcoin's initial commodity-value was its cypherpunk demand for a censorship-resistant messaging token, which the theorem then permits.
