context: The quantity theory (money supply times velocity equals prices times output) was formalized by Irving Fisher in 1911, but its European roots go back to Azpilcueta and the Salamanca scholastics in the 1550s. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantity theory of money' (2026-09-05).

question: The standard textbook says economics started with Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations in 1776. Some historians of thought point to a group of Catholic scholars in 16th-century Spain who already wrote carefully about prices, money, and value. What does this show about the textbook story?
answer: It skips real economic thinking that came centuries earlier
choices: It skips real economic thinking that came centuries earlier
It is exactly right — nothing came before Adam Smith
Adam Smith did not really exist
Economics only began in the 20th century
context: Rothbard's 1995 An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought traced pre-classical economics back to the Salamancans and the medieval scholastics, undoing the Smith-as-founder story. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-perspective-history-economic-thought.

question: The Salamanca argument, applied to a modern central bank, teaches the reader to see past one misleading look in money policy. Which look does the argument tell you to distrust?
answer: That creating more money makes a nation richer in real terms
choices: That creating more money makes a nation richer in real terms
That international trade always benefits the exporting country
That taxation is always preferable to borrowing
That war spending stimulates long-run growth
context: The Salamanca-to-Austrian line: nominal money and real wealth are different things. Printing more units of currency raises prices, redistributes purchasing power to the first receivers, and leaves the underlying productive capacity unchanged. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective (1995).

question: Bastiat would frame the 1600 Spanish paradox as a contrast between what is visible in Seville and what is invisible across the whole economy. Which pairing best captures that contrast?
answer: Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish industry hollowed out and savers debased
choices: Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish industry hollowed out and savers debased
Seen: high consumer spending; Unseen: rising farmer productivity
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: rising imports
Seen: growing armies; Unseen: shrinking population
context: Bastiat's 'seen and unseen' fits the Spanish silver flood exactly: what looks like national wealth (bullion arriving) hides the destruction of domestic industry and the debasement of every existing peseta of savings. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: During the 2020 lockdowns the US government sent hundreds of billions of dollars to small businesses. The rule was simple: keep paying your workers. In the end, where did all that money come from?
answer: From taxes and borrowing that future citizens will pay back
choices: From taxes and borrowing that future citizens will pay back
From profits the government earned selling goods
From a private charity fund
From a tax on foreign shoppers
context: PPP was administered by the Small Business Administration through private banks. Loans were forgiven if the borrower spent them mostly on payroll within a set window. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: In March 2020, at the start of the pandemic, the US Congress passed an emergency spending package worth about 2.2 trillion dollars, mostly funded by newly created money. Over the next two years, what predictable side effect did the country see?
answer: Sharp inflation, meaning everyday prices rose fast
choices: Sharp inflation, meaning everyday prices rose fast
Long-term deflation, meaning prices kept falling
A sudden strengthening of the dollar against every currency
Interest rates were locked at zero forever by law
context: The Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act was signed March 27, 2020, and was the largest single US relief bill at that time. The American Rescue Plan came later in March 2021 under President Biden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/CARES_Act.

question: During the pandemic the US government's Paycheck Protection Program handed out huge forgivable loans to keep workers on payroll. Economists later crunched the numbers. Roughly how much did each job the program saved end up costing taxpayers?
answer: About $170,000 to $257,000 per job
choices: About $170,000 to $257,000 per job
About $5,000 per job
About $20,000 per job
About $2 million per job
context: Autor et al, 'An Evaluation of the Paycheck Protection Program Using Administrative Payroll Microdata,' NBER Working Paper 29669. The figure came out far higher than the pre-COVID annual wage of the workers whose jobs were preserved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_Autor.

question: Economist David Autor's team asked one question about the PPP program. How much of the money actually reached workers, and how much went to business owners and shareholders? What figure did they report?
answer: About 72 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
choices: About 72 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
About 30 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
About 5 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
About 95 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
context: The bulk of the money flowed to firms that would not have laid off workers even without PPP. Autor and coauthors published the finding in the Journal of Economic Perspectives Spring 2022 and NBER 29669. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: In April 2020 the Small Business Administration sent PPP loans out through banks. Minority-owned and rural firms missed the first round. Big banks' old clients got funded in days. Which Austrian idea does this show?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: no central agency knew which firms actually needed relief
choices: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: no central agency knew which firms actually needed relief
Milton Friedman's monetary theory that inflation is a purely monetary phenomenon
John Kenneth Galbraith's conventional-wisdom theory of institutional inertia
John Maynard Keynes's animal-spirits theory of investment
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' argued that the specific knowledge of who needs help, at what price, and in what shape is dispersed across millions of local actors and irreducible to any central authority. PPP defaulted to whoever had a bank relationship because the agency had no other way to allocate the money at speed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: In 2020 the US ran two big pandemic programs. One sent money to nearly every small business, whether or not the business had lost customers. The other paid extra unemployment only to workers who had actually lost their jobs. Which program was much cheaper per job saved?
answer: The one that paid only workers who actually lost jobs
choices: The one that paid only workers who actually lost jobs
The one that paid nearly every business no matter what
Both cost about the same per job saved
Neither program cost anything at all
context: The CARES Act had raised UI benefits by $600 per week. Because UI pays only workers actually displaced, it avoids paying firms whose employees would have kept their jobs anyway -- addressing the 72 percent leakage documented by Autor and coauthors. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: A congressman in 2021 defends the Paycheck Protection Program by pointing to the millions of small-business owners who received forgivable loans during the lockdowns. A Bastiatian critic responds that the seen beneficiaries were real, but so was an invisible cost future taxpayers now carry. Which specific unseen does that critic press?
answer: Roughly $600 billion in debt for firms whose employees would have kept their jobs without PPP
choices: Roughly $600 billion in debt for firms whose employees would have kept their jobs without PPP
The immediate loss of federal tax revenue from small-business income during lockdowns
The direct destruction of small-business inventories during the closure period
A permanent shortage of qualified accountants to administer future federal relief
context: Applied Bastiat: the seen preserved payroll is real; the unseen is the taxpayer liability for the inframarginal share (Autor's 72 percent leakage) that funded no additional employment. Cato and Mercatus economists made the argument most forcefully. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: Ludwig von Mises used one Greek word as the name of his whole method: the study of human action. Economics is one branch of it. Which Greek word did he pick?
answer: Praxis, meaning action or deed
choices: Praxis, meaning action or deed
Nomos, meaning law or custom
Logos, meaning word or reason
Sophia, meaning wisdom
context: Praxeology (praxis + -logia) was coined in its modern sense by the French sociologist Alfred Espinas in an 1890 essay in the Revue Philosophique. Mises adopted it in the 1940s for the science that starts from human action as its single axiom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Praxeology'.

question: Why do people trade with each other? A shopper hands over money for bread, and the baker hands over bread for money. Both walk away happy. What does this tell you about the two people?
answer: Each one values what they got MORE than what they gave up
choices: Each one values what they got MORE than what they gave up
One of them made a mistake
Prices are always fair
Trading always makes everyone equally rich
context: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics was published by Yale University Press in September 1949. It rebuilt Mises's German-language Nationaloekonomie (1940) for an American audience and defined praxeology as the general theory of action, with economics as its most developed branch. Source: Grokipedia, 'Human Action'.

question: An Austrian economist argued that the entire science of economics begins from one simple truth. Any attempt to deny that truth would itself be a purposeful choice, which proves it. What is that starting truth?
answer: Human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends
choices: Human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends
Every good has a market price equal to its cost of production
The general price level moves in proportion to the money supply
Individuals choose the option that maximizes measurable utility
context: This is the action axiom. Mises treated it as apodictic: the very effort to argue against it is a means-and-ends act, so the axiom cannot be coherently rejected. From it he deduced the whole cascade of Austrian economics. Source: Grokipedia, 'action axiom'.

question: In 1953 Milton Friedman wrote a famous essay. He said we should judge economic theories by how well they predict, not by how real their starting assumptions are. What was the essay called?
answer: The Methodology of Positive Economics
choices: The Methodology of Positive Economics
A Monetary History of the United States
Capitalism and Freedom
Free to Choose
context: Friedman's 1953 essay is often called the most influential piece of methodological writing in twentieth-century economics. It set out the positivist alternative to praxeology: economics as an empirical predictive science whose theorems stand or fall by out-of-sample data, not deduction. Source: Western Sydney University, 'Friedman 1953: The Methodology of Positive Economics'.

question: A mainstream critic says Austrian claims cannot be tested the way physics is tested. Ludwig von Mises has a stock reply, repeated throughout his books. Which analogy does he press?
answer: Human action is not laboratory chemistry -- you cannot re-run 1929 with the money supply held constant
choices: Human action is not laboratory chemistry -- you cannot re-run 1929 with the money supply held constant
Economics is not astronomy -- there are no cycles regular enough to fit an equation
Human action is not biology -- there are no species-level laws below the individual
Economics is not engineering -- there is no fixed material to be shaped
context: The point is not that historical evidence is worthless but that no economic episode is ever a controlled experiment: every other variable moves at the same time as the one under study. Mises concluded that economic laws have to be established by deduction from the action axiom, with history supplying cases the laws help interpret. Source: Wikipedia, 'Praxeology'.

question: One economist argued that logic and math alone can never fully explain history. You also need to understand why real people, at a specific time and place, wanted the specific things they wanted. What is this second kind of understanding mostly about?
answer: Reading the motives and choices of real people in their own time
choices: Reading the motives and choices of real people in their own time
Solving equations that predict every choice a person will make
Building larger and faster computers to model human behavior
Copying the same policies used in ancient Rome
context: Thymology (from Greek 'thymos', the seat of feeling) is for Mises a historical branch of the sciences of human action. Praxeology tells you WHAT it means to act; thymology tells you WHY this actor, in these circumstances, chose those ends and reached for those means. Source: Wikipedia, 'Thymology'.

question: In 1962 a young American student of Mises published the biggest systematic book in the Austrian tradition. He started it as a textbook version of Human Action. It grew into a huge work of its own. Which book?
answer: Murray Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State
choices: Murray Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State
Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson
Israel Kirzner's Competition and Entrepreneurship
Ludwig Lachmann's Capital and Its Structure
context: The William Volker Fund commissioned Rothbard in 1952 to condense Human Action for classroom use. Ten years later he handed in Man, Economy, and State: A Treatise on Economic Principles instead, running to over a thousand pages and covering the whole of praxeological economics from consumer theory through money and banking. Source: Wikipedia, 'Man, Economy, and State'.

question: One school of economics claims its core laws are proven by logic from one simple fact — that people act on purpose to reach goals they care about — instead of being tested by data the way physics is. What does this school claim about its main laws?
answer: They are true by logic once you grant that people act on purpose
choices: They are true by logic once you grant that people act on purpose
They are only true if a lab experiment confirms them
They are true only if a majority of voters agree
They are true only in countries ruled by monarchs
context: Hoppe's lectures at the Mises University argued that the action axiom is a synthetic a priori proposition in Kant's sense -- informative about the world but true by the structure of thought, not by empirical test. The book has been the standard defense of praxeological method for a generation of Austrian graduate students. Source: Mises Institute, 'Economic Science and the Austrian Method'.

question: In 1920 one economist argued by pure logic that a fully planned communist economy could not figure out what to produce, because it had no real market prices to guide it. In 1989 the Soviet planned economy collapsed. How did his school describe that collapse?
answer: As real-world confirmation of a point already proven back in 1920
choices: As real-world confirmation of a point already proven back in 1920
As the very first honest test their argument had ever received
As a total surprise their theory could not explain
As proof that the 1920 argument had been wrong all along
context: The distinction is methodological, not rhetorical. If the calculation problem is a deduced law of action under conditions of no market prices, then the USSR could no more disprove it than a falling apple could disprove gravity; the Soviet experience showed the law working, it did not test whether the law is true. Source: Mises Institute, 'Economic Science and the Austrian Method'.

question: Ludwig von Mises insisted that only one kind of entity ever actually chooses, values, and acts. Every claim about 'the state,' 'society,' or 'the class' must be traced back to that entity, or the claim is meaningless. What is the one-phrase name for this rule?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Reflexive equilibrium
Rational expectations
Positive-sum aggregation
context: The doctrine goes back through Mises's teacher Carl Menger and forward to Hayek and Buchanan. Methodological individualism does not deny that groups exist; it insists only that groups do not act -- individuals within them do -- so an economic law that skips the individual is a category error. Source: Grokipedia, 'Human Action'.

question: A king announces: 'From now on, no shop may sell a loaf of bread for more than one coin.' But bakers say it costs them TWO coins to make a loaf. What will most likely happen on the town's shelves?
answer: Bread will disappear from the shelves
choices: Bread will disappear from the shelves
Bakers will happily bake more bread
Wheat will get cheaper
Everyone will eat more bread than before
context: Emperor Diocletian's Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium (Edict on Maximum Prices) covered over 1,200 goods and services and hundreds of occupations, with death for overcharging. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: A writer named Lactantius wrote soon after Diocletian's price law. He said the law made goods vanish from markets and 'many died on small accounts.' What kind of writer was he?
answer: An early Christian historian
choices: An early Christian historian
A Roman consul
A Byzantine emperor
A medieval monk
context: Lactantius (c. 240-320 AD) was an early Christian rhetorician; his De Mortibus Persecutorum (c. 315 AD) covers Diocletian's reign. He describes the edict as counter-productive from the outset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactantius.

question: In August 1971 a US president froze almost all wages and prices for 90 days. It was the first peacetime price control in US history. What usually happens when a government forces prices below what a market would set?
answer: Shortages, because sellers won't sell as much at the fixed low price
choices: Shortages, because sellers won't sell as much at the fixed low price
Sudden gluts, because buyers refuse to buy at the fixed low price
Higher wages for everyone in the affected jobs
A permanent end to inflation with no side effects
context: Nixon's August 15, 1971 broadcast (which also closed the gold window) imposed a 90-day freeze extended in later Phases through April 1974. Once controls lapsed, the 1973-75 inflation acceleration followed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: In October 1973 several Arab oil states cut off exports to the United States. At the same time, US law capped American gas prices, so stations could not raise them. What everyday image famously captured the crisis?
answer: Fuel lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing
choices: Fuel lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing
Empty grocery-store meat cases
Vacant furniture showrooms
Locked bank vaults
context: Winter 1973-74 gas lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing became the visual argument for a generation that price caps produce shortages. The controls were partially lifted in 1974 but full oil-price decontrol did not come until 1981 under Reagan. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: In 1971 a Swedish left-leaning economist said one housing policy was 'the best way to destroy a city, other than bombing.' Which policy was he attacking?
answer: Rent control
choices: Rent control
Public-housing demolition
Zoning restrictions
Property taxes
context: Assar Lindbeck (1930-2020), a leading Swedish social-democrat economist, made the observation in 1971 and repeated it in many later publications. He was not a libertarian; the line is widely cited across the political spectrum. Source: Lindbeck, The Political Economy of the New Left (1971).

question: In 2020 Berlin passed a strict cap on how much rent landlords could charge. Within a year and a half a German high court struck it down. Setting aside the ruling, what does basic economics usually predict such a cap will do to the housing supply?
answer: Landlords list fewer apartments and let some go into disrepair
choices: Landlords list fewer apartments and let some go into disrepair
New apartment buildings pop up everywhere to meet demand
Rents fall to zero within a year with no side effects
The city gains a huge amount of tax income overnight
context: Berlin's Mietendeckel froze most residential rents from February 2020. The federal Constitutional Court struck it down as beyond state competence in April 2021, requiring landlords to be repaid the difference. Source: bundesverfassungsgericht.de (BVerfG 2 BvF 1/20).

question: New York City has kept some form of rent control without a single break since the middle of the second world war, the longest continuous rent-control program in the country. In roughly what decade did it start?
answer: The 1940s
choices: The 1940s
The 1970s
The 1960s
The 1990s
context: NYC rent control began in 1943 under wartime federal price controls and continued in state and city form after the war. Rent stabilization (a distinct, larger program) began 1969. Source: hcr.ny.gov (rent regulation history).

question: Every price-control failure -- from Diocletian to Nixon to Berlin -- turns on the same move. A ceiling set below the market clearing price produces one particular set of outcomes. Which outcome pattern?
answer: Queuing, black markets, and reduced supply
choices: Queuing, black markets, and reduced supply
Higher taxes, lower wages, and unemployment
Currency devaluation, inflation, and default
Trade barriers, tariffs, and retaliation
context: When the state sets a price below what buyers would pay, demand exceeds supply. The gap is filled by non-price rationing (queues), by illegal secondary markets, or by suppliers exiting entirely (landlords convert to condos, sellers hoard, farmers plant less). Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: The Austrian reading of price controls connects them directly to Mises's 1920 argument: the state does not need to abolish exchange to suppress the price signal. What is that connection?
answer: A ceiling below market suffices to break the local signal, the way full central planning breaks it economy-wide
choices: A ceiling below market suffices to break the local signal, the way full central planning breaks it economy-wide
Price controls create genuinely new information the market lacks
Ceilings work perfectly if enforcement is strict enough
Ceilings raise supply by lowering prices
context: Mises's 1920 argument applied at smaller scale: whether by abolishing exchange or by capping the price, if the market-clearing signal is suppressed the allocation goes wrong. Same mechanism, different scale. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: One popular intro textbook by an American economist walks through Diocletian, Nixon, and rent control to make the same point: price controls cause shortages. Which book?
answer: Basic Economics by Thomas Sowell
choices: Basic Economics by Thomas Sowell
Freakonomics by Steven Levitt
The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith
The Undercover Economist by Tim Harford
context: Sowell's Basic Economics (first edition 2000; multiple later editions) is the standard introductory exposition that runs the price-control-produces-shortage argument across centuries of cases. Source: tsowell.com.

question: Hurricane Fran cut power to a million people around Raleigh in September 1996. Four men trucked in bagged ice from another town and sold it for many times the pre-storm price. Police arrested them and took the truck. What did the customers waiting in the line do?
answer: Clapped and cheered as the sellers were cuffed
choices: Clapped and cheered as the sellers were cuffed
Blocked the police cars until the ice was freed
Emptied the truck while the officers wrote tickets
Chipped in for the sellers' bail
context: Michael Munger, who teaches political science and economics at Duke University, wrote the night up for the Library of Economics and Liberty on January 8, 2007 under the title 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' His line: 'They clapped. I can't for the life of me understand why the people would clap.' The four men had rented two freezer trucks, paid $1.70 a bag for 500 bags per truck, and chain-sawed fallen logs off the road to get in. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: Most US states punish sellers who raise water, fuel, or generator prices after a disaster. Florida's law is not always on. It switches on at one moment, then checks prices against the 30 days before. What switches Florida's law on?
answer: The governor declaring a state of emergency
choices: The governor declaring a state of emergency
A hurricane making landfall inside the state
A county sheriff reporting a supply shortage
The attorney general opening an investigation
context: Florida Statute 501.160 forbids an 'unconscionable' price during a declared state of emergency, defining it as a 'gross disparity' with the average price charged in the usual course of business during the 30 days immediately before the declaration. Penalties run to $1,000 per violation and up to $25,000 for violations inside a single 24-hour period. Sources: https://m.flsenate.gov/statutes/501.160 ; https://www.myfloridalegal.com/price-gouging-hotline/price-gouging-statute.

question: In 2005 John Shepperson of Kentucky watched news of Hurricane Katrina. He bought 19 generators, rented a truck, and drove about 600 miles to Mississippi. Buyers there would pay about double what he had paid. What happened to Shepperson and his generators?
answer: Police jailed him for four days and kept the generators
choices: Police jailed him for four days and kept the generators
The state bought his whole load at the price he had paid
A judge cleared the sale once he agreed to halve his price
FEMA hired him to haul relief supplies for the next month
context: Shepperson was arrested for price gouging, held four days, and the nineteen generators remained in police custody rather than in the hands of anyone in Mississippi. John Stossel used the case on ABC's 20/20; Mark Perry has cited it repeatedly. Sources: https://abcnews.com/2020/Stossel/story?id=1954352 ; https://www.aei.org/carpe-diem/dear-la-times-reporter-your-lack-of-understanding-of-economics-doesnt-mean-that-price-gouging-is-a-bad-thing/.

question: F. A. Hayek published 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' in the American Economic Review in September 1945. He asked readers to suppose that tin has suddenly grown scarce, and that tens of thousands of people who use tin must now use less of it. Hayek's whole argument turns on what those users have to be told first. What did Hayek say they need to know?
answer: Nothing beyond the new price they now face
choices: Nothing beyond the new price they now face
Which mine closed or which war caused it
How long the shortage is expected to last
Which uses of tin the state ranks highest
context: Hayek's marvel was that 'without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' He added that it does not matter which cause made tin scarcer, and called the price system 'a system of telecommunications' whose users watch a few pointers as an engineer watches dials. Sources: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html ; https://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/hayek-the-use-of-knowledge-in-society-1945.

question: Michael Munger gave his account of the Raleigh ice night a two-word title taken from what the crowd did. The subtitle that followed it was a question, and that question is the argument of the whole essay in six words. What did Munger's subtitle ask?
answer: Can price-gouging laws prohibit scarcity?
choices: Can price-gouging laws prohibit scarcity?
Can a state legislate a fair price?
Does the law owe disaster victims a queue?
Should a state ration what a storm spared?
context: 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?', Library of Economics and Liberty, January 8, 2007. Munger's answer is no: a statute can forbid a price, but the ice, generators and chain saws are no less scarce for the ban. As he put it, 'all a state accomplishes by passing an anti-gouging law is to ensure that there is no ice.' Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: A state attorney general announces that any merchant who sells a generator above its pre-storm price after the hurricane will be prosecuted. The stated aim is to keep generators in reach of families who just lost everything, and the first cases are still weeks away. A critic working in Bastiat's tradition does not dispute the aim. Which cost does the critic say the announcement has already imposed?
answer: Every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays there
choices: Every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays there
The state's own emergency stockpile is drawn down faster than planned
Retailers raise prices on unrelated goods to make up the lost margin
Insurance premiums across the state rise for the following season
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' asks, after any law, what does not happen because of it. The prosecuted merchant is seen; the trucker who never loads, never drives and never arrives is not. John Shepperson's nineteen generators reached Mississippi and ended up in an impound lot; the ones that stayed in Georgia never made the news at all. Sources: Bastiat, Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (1850) (https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss.html); https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: Florida's law says a post-disaster price is illegal if it is much higher than the seller's average in the 30 days before the emergency. A Hayekian critic says the law quietly assumes something false. What does it assume?
answer: That the pre-storm price is still the correct price after the storm
choices: That the pre-storm price is still the correct price after the storm
That merchants can compute their own thirty-day averages precisely
That every merchant in the state buys from the same wholesale supplier
That governors declare emergencies at the same point in every storm
context: The benchmark in Florida Statute 501.160 is the average price in the usual course of business during the 30 days immediately preceding the emergency declaration. On Hayek's account a price is a piece of information about present conditions, so freezing the benchmark at the pre-storm figure instructs the market to behave as though the storm carried no information at all. Sources: https://m.flsenate.gov/statutes/501.160 ; https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html.

question: Michael Munger has argued against anti-gouging statutes for two decades, and on EconTalk he boiled the whole position down to one sentence about what a state has to permit if it wants a well-supplied city after a disaster. How did Munger put it?
answer: The only way to guarantee low prices is to allow sellers to charge high prices
choices: The only way to guarantee low prices is to allow sellers to charge high prices
The only way to protect the poor is to ration essentials by household size
The only way to stop hoarding is to cap what any single buyer may carry away
The only way to speed relief is to suspend the state's transport licensing rules
context: Munger's point is that the high price is the thing that pulls supply toward the disaster: it tells a trucker eight hundred miles away that this city is where his load is worth most, it moves the scarce stock toward the buyers who need it most, and it makes the people already holding ice or fuel stretch it. A cap removes all three at once, and the shortage the cap was meant to soften simply lasts longer. The distractors here are real positions people hold in this debate, not straw men. Source: https://www.econtalk.org/munger-on-price-gouging/.

question: A small group of officials in the capital tries to plan how much of every single thing -- bread, shoes, nails, hats -- a country of 50 million people needs. Why is this almost impossible to do well?
answer: No small group can know what all those millions of people want
choices: No small group can know what all those millions of people want
The officials are too lazy to try
The country doesn't have enough paper
There's no way to count that high
context: Robbins had read Hayek's article 'The Paradox of Saving' and brought him to LSE. Mises never took an English professorship; Schumpeter was at Bonn (and later Harvard); Machlup was another Vienna-Circle Austrian but was not the invited lecturer that January. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: When copper suddenly becomes rare, its price shoots up. Factory owners who use copper see the higher price and start looking for other metals or ways to use less. What are prices really doing for these factory owners?
answer: Telling them information about what is scarce
choices: Telling them information about what is scarce
Punishing them for buying copper
Making the government richer
Randomly changing for no reason
context: Prices and Production is Hayek's monetary-theory book; Road to Serfdom (1944) is his popular political tract; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) is an essay collection; The Constitution of Liberty (1960) is his mature political philosophy. Source: LSE History blog.

question: In 1931 an Austrian economist named Friedrich Hayek gave four talks in London. He argued that boom and bust comes from banks handing out cheap credit, not from odd mood swings in the market. What is the general name for that Austrian view?
answer: Austrian business-cycle theory
choices: Austrian business-cycle theory
Keynesian aggregate-demand theory
Marxist crisis theory
Monetarist stability theory
context: The Tooke Chair, endowed in memory of the 19th-century monetary economist Thomas Tooke, was Hayek's home at LSE for nearly two decades. The three distractors are real named chairs at rival departments Hayek never held. Source: LSE History blog.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in the 1930s that a modern economy's boom-and-bust cycle is not just a mood swing or "animal spirits." He said the cause is far more specific. In his view, what kind of thing sets off the boom that must end in a bust?
answer: A flood of cheap credit created by the banking system
choices: A flood of cheap credit created by the banking system
A sudden collapse in shopper confidence and spending mood
A shortage of new inventions and technology breakthroughs
A built-in unfairness in every private-property economy
context: Hayek's answer is monetary and Austrian. The three distractors are the three main rival theories that would dominate the 20th century: Keynes's aggregate-demand-plus-animal-spirits view, the real-business-cycle school of Kydland and Prescott, and Hyman Minsky's financial-instability hypothesis. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: In Hayek's Prices and Production, the harm from fake credit growth is not that prices rise across the board. The harm is that the shape of capital gets twisted. What does Hayek say really happens to the pattern of production?
answer: Long, roundabout capital projects are started that the underlying pool of savings cannot finish
choices: Long, roundabout capital projects are started that the underlying pool of savings cannot finish
Consumer-goods factories are shuttered as households divert spending toward government bonds
Money velocity collapses and idle cash balances swell across every stage of production
Nominal wages become sticky downward and unemployment jumps immediately in every sector
context: Artificially low interest rates falsify the natural rate of interest -- the rate at which voluntary saving would match investment demand. Firms respond as if saving were plentiful and start long-horizon capital projects that must later be abandoned. The other three describe rival theories (crowding out, Keynesian liquidity trap, Keynesian sticky-wage unemployment). Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: To show his theory that production runs in stages -- from raw capital goods down to final consumer goods -- Hayek drew a simple shape in Prices and Production. Austrians have named it after him ever since. What is the shape called?
answer: The Hayekian triangle
choices: The Hayekian triangle
The Phillips curve
The Laffer curve
The Kondratiev wave
context: The Hayekian triangle organizes all spending in the economy as a triangle whose base measures time-to-consumer-good; artificial credit tilts the triangle to a longer, capital-heavy shape it cannot sustain. Phillips (1958), Laffer (1974), and Kondratiev (1920s) are all real diagrams from unrelated traditions. Source: Mises Wiki, 'Hayekian triangle'.

question: For Hayek in Prices and Production the crash at the end of a credit-driven boom is not the underlying illness -- something else was. Which is his view of where the disease actually sat?
answer: The BOOM was the disease and the bust is the painful correction
choices: The BOOM was the disease and the bust is the painful correction
The bust was the disease and the boom had been a healthy real expansion
Both boom and bust are neutral psychological fluctuations around a stable trend
The whole cycle is a statistical artefact with no underlying economic cause
context: This is Hayek's core diagnostic move against Keynes: the mistakes were made during the artificial boom (wrong capital projects, wrong worker locations); the bust is the market discovering the errors and reallocating resources. Stimulus that prolongs the boom prolongs the disease. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: A famous Austrian idea says this: when a central bank pushes rates far below their natural level, firms get fooled into starting projects that only look good while credit is cheap. What is the predictable ending of that boom?
answer: A bust in which many of those projects fail once the cheap credit stops
choices: A bust in which many of those projects fail once the cheap credit stops
Steady growth forever, as long as the central bank keeps rates low
Higher wages for everyone, since more businesses are hiring
A permanent drop in prices as new goods flood the market
context: Mises's 1912 book applied Menger's marginalism to money and introduced the credit-expansion account of the cycle; Hayek's 1931 lectures are the mature LSE presentation. Bohm-Bawerk supplied the capital-theory backdrop; Menger the value theory; Wicksell the natural-rate-of-interest concept Mises then used -- all real, all upstream, but not the direct doctrinal source of ABCT. Source: Mises Institute, Prices and Production and Other Works.

question: In the 1930s Hayek and another famous economist had a long fight in the journals. Hayek wrote a two-part review of the other man's 1930 book on money. Then that man hit back at Hayek's own book. Whose book was Hayek reviewing?
answer: John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money
choices: John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money
Irving Fisher's The Purchasing Power of Money
Arthur Pigou's The Economics of Welfare
Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics
context: Hayek's two-part critique of Keynes's Treatise on Money (1930) appeared in Economica in August 1931 and February 1932. Keynes's reply attacked Prices and Production rather than defending his Treatise, and in 1932 he abandoned the debate to write what became the 1936 General Theory. Fisher, Pigou, and Marshall are all real monetary or welfare theorists of the previous generation. Source: Mises Institute, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J.M. Keynes'.

question: Rather than answer Hayek's critique of the Treatise on Money point-for-point, Keynes withdrew from the direct exchange in 1932 and spent the next four years rebuilding his monetary theory into a new book. Which book was the eventual result?
answer: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
choices: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
The Economic Consequences of the Peace
A Tract on Monetary Reform
How to Pay for the War
context: The General Theory (1936) replaced the Treatise as Keynes's monetary statement and became the founding text of Keynesian macroeconomics. The three distractors are all real Keynes works from other decades: Economic Consequences (1919), Tract (1923), How to Pay for the War (1940). Source: Mises Institute, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J.M. Keynes'.

question: In 1945 Hayek wrote a short paper. It asked how a market can use facts that no one person knows on their own. What did he call it?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
Individualism and Economic Order
The Pretence of Knowledge
context: American Economic Review 35:4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. Hayek was writing from wartime London against the Central Planning Board scheme of Oskar Lange, and he made the case that the market's own prices carry knowledge no planner ever holds. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' turns on one story. Somewhere in the world, one raw material gets scarce. Within days, every user of it saves on it. No one gives an order. Only a handful of people know the cause. Which raw material did Hayek pick?
answer: Tin
choices: Tin
Wheat
Coal
Copper
context: Hayek picked tin because it was a genuine commodity of the day whose supply chain crossed empires -- the miner in Bolivia, the smelter in Malaya, the canner in Chicago. A single rising price on the London Metal Exchange told them all what a central planner could never have compiled: use less tin. Source: FEE, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: In 1945 Hayek said most economists made the same slip. They pictured one planner who knew every fact about every worker and shop. Hayek said no planner can know all that. What word did he use for how the facts are spread out?
answer: Dispersed
choices: Dispersed
Consolidated
Public
Objective
context: Hayek's exact phrasing: the knowledge relevant to economic decisions 'never exists in concentrated or integrated form but solely as the dispersed bits of incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge which all the separate individuals possess.' The point runs through the whole essay. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Hayek's 1945 essay made a short phrase for the person who holds the local know-how: the mechanic who knows this lathe, the shopkeeper who knows these buyers, the captain who knows this port. Which three-word phrase did he coin?
answer: The man on the spot
choices: The man on the spot
The invisible hand of trade
The captain of industry
The knower behind the market
context: Hayek's argument: it is the man on the spot who has the knowledge of time and place that matters; even a perfectly benevolent central board cannot substitute for him, because his knowledge is precisely the sort that cannot be written up in a report and mailed to headquarters in time. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Hayek's 1945 essay was a direct reply. Nine years earlier, another economist claimed a Central Planning Board could 'play at markets' -- post prices, raise them when lines form, drop them when goods pile up -- and match a real market. Whose 1936 essay was Hayek answering?
answer: Oskar Lange, On the Economic Theory of Socialism
choices: Oskar Lange, On the Economic Theory of Socialism
Abba Lerner, The Economics of Control
Maurice Dobb, Political Economy and Capitalism
Joan Robinson, The Economics of Imperfect Competition
context: Lange's Part I appeared in RES in October 1936, Part II in February 1937. He famously opened with an ironic tribute to Ludwig von Mises as 'the great advocatus diaboli' of socialism. Hayek's 1945 answer was that Lange had missed the point: the market's prices aggregate knowledge that was never centrally gathered, so no board can duplicate them by trial-and-error alone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar R. Lange'.

question: The Mises 1920 calculation problem and the Hayek 1945 knowledge problem are two sides of one coin. Mises focused on what socialism lacks in tools; Hayek on what it lacks in info. Without market prices for the means of production, what did Mises say socialism has no way to do?
answer: Compare the costs of alternative production plans
choices: Compare the costs of alternative production plans
Reward its most productive workers fairly
Enforce contracts among cooperating enterprises
Distribute consumer goods on a per capita basis
context: Mises's 1920 essay Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen argued that without private ownership of the means of production there are no exchanges of them, so no prices, so no way to answer 'is it cheaper to build the railway of steel or of aluminium?' Hayek added: even if you tried to set trial-and-error prices, you would still not have the dispersed knowledge those prices normally aggregate. Source: Mises Institute, 'The End of Socialism and the Calculation Debate Revisited'.

question: In 1974 Hayek won the top prize in economics. He was known for attacking central planning. But the man who shared the prize with him had an odd trait. What was it?
answer: The co-winner held nearly opposite views on central planning
choices: The co-winner held nearly opposite views on central planning
The co-winner was Hayek's own graduate student
The co-winner had already won the same prize three times before
There was no co-winner; Hayek received it alone
context: The joint citation honoured 'pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations' and 'penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena'. Myrdal was a leading Swedish social-democratic policy intellectual; the Academy paired the two deliberately, and each spent his Nobel lecture disagreeing with the other. Source: NobelPrize.org, 'The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 1974'.

question: In 1979 American drivers waited in long lines to buy gas. Some states let you buy only on odd or even days by plate number. Using Hayek's 1945 idea, what had gone wrong at the pump?
answer: The federal ceiling on retail gasoline prices had broken the signal that would have called forth more supply
choices: The federal ceiling on retail gasoline prices had broken the signal that would have called forth more supply
The OPEC cartel had unilaterally halted all crude oil exports to the American market
The Federal Reserve had refused to expand the money supply enough to accommodate demand
The Environmental Protection Agency had banned all leaded gasoline sales without notice
context: The Emergency Petroleum Allocation Act of 1973 held domestic gasoline prices below the world price for the rest of the 1970s; the 1979 lines were the shortage the cap guaranteed. President Reagan lifted the controls in January 1981 and the queues vanished within weeks -- exactly the Hayekian prediction. Source: Institute for Energy Research, 'Price Controls and the 1970s Oil Crisis'.

question: In 1980 Thomas Sowell wrote a whole book to expand on Hayek's short 1945 essay. He took the price-signal idea into law, science, and daily life. Hayek called it the best book on economics in many a year. What was it called?
answer: Knowledge and Decisions
choices: Knowledge and Decisions
Basic Economics
Wealth, Poverty and Politics
A Conflict of Visions
context: Sowell wrote in the acknowledgements that no other single source had shaped his framework more than the 1945 Hayek essay. Knowledge and Decisions became the standard American undergraduate route into Hayekian economics, precisely because it puts the dispersed-knowledge point in terms an 18-year-old can grasp in one sitting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Austrians use Hayek's 1945 knowledge argument for more than price ceilings on goods. They point to one big hidden price control that runs through all modern finance. Which price do Austrians say is itself set by a national committee?
answer: The interest rate, set below the market-clearing rate by the central bank
choices: The interest rate, set below the market-clearing rate by the central bank
The retail price of gasoline, capped by the Department of Energy
The wage of federal contractors, floored by the Davis-Bacon Act
The exchange rate of the dollar, pegged by the Treasury
context: The Austrian argument, from Mises through Hayek to Rothbard: the interest rate is a price like any other -- the price of present goods in terms of future goods -- and when a central bank pushes it below the rate that would clear the loanable-funds market, it breaks the signal that would tell entrepreneurs whether long-lived projects can be sustained. This is the mechanism behind Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Hayek made his 1945 essay the centerpiece of a 1948 University of Chicago Press book. He paired it with his 1937 essay 'Economics and Knowledge,' first given as a talk to the London Economic Club. What was the 1948 book called?
answer: Individualism and Economic Order
choices: Individualism and Economic Order
The Counter-Revolution of Science
Studies in Philosophy, Politics and Economics
The Constitution of Liberty
context: The 1948 volume was Hayek's own bid to fix the shape of the argument for postwar economists: 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937) framed the problem, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) delivered it in a form any working economist could read in a lunch break, and the surrounding essays applied it to markets and planning. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Hayek: The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)'.

question: Two kids trade lunches. One kid's apple cost 25 cents at the store, and the other kid's sandwich cost 4 dollars. They both walk away happy after the trade. How can that be?
answer: Value depends on what each person wants, not just the price tag
choices: Value depends on what each person wants, not just the price tag
One of them was tricked
The store was wrong about the prices
The apple was actually worth 4 dollars
context: Menger (1840-1921) reported on grain and stock prices for the Lemberger Zeitung and then the Wiener Zeitung in the 1860s -- watching real traders form prices in real time is where his subjective-value instinct came from. He joined the University of Vienna law faculty in 1872 and won the economic-theory chair in 1873. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: You are dying of thirst in a desert. The FIRST bottle of water someone offers you is a lifesaver. The TENTH bottle you barely need. Why is the tenth bottle worth so much less to you than the first?
answer: Each extra one adds less value than the one before
choices: Each extra one adds less value than the one before
The tenth bottle contains less water
Water always gets cheaper over time
The desert changes the price of water
context: Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre translates literally as 'Foundations of the Theory of the National Economy,' but the standard English rendering has always been Principles of Economics -- confusingly sharing a title with Alfred Marshall's 1890 book. The English translation by James Dingwall and Bert F. Hoselitz did not appear until 1950. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: In 1871 Carl Menger wrote a book. He said the value of a good does not come from the work put into it. It comes from something else. In Menger's view, where does value come from?
answer: The usefulness the good has to the person choosing to buy it
choices: The usefulness the good has to the person choosing to buy it
The number of hours workers spent making it
The total cost of the raw materials inside it
The price the seller decides to charge for it
context: Braumueller was a mid-sized Vienna academic publisher; Menger paid for the printing himself in the hope the book would open the university door -- which it did, two years later. Duncker und Humblot was the Berlin house of Schmoller and the German Historical School; Gustav Fischer of Jena published much of the later German-language economics literature. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: In the early 1870s, three economists in three countries — Austria, England, and France — each came up with the same big idea on their own. Value comes from the extra use of the next unit, not the total. What is this cluster of discoveries called?
answer: The Marginal Revolution
choices: The Marginal Revolution
The Methodenstreit
The Keynesian Revolution
The Neoclassical Synthesis
context: William Stanley Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Switzerland reached the marginal-utility insight independently of Menger and of each other; none of the three knew the others were working on it. It stands with Darwin-Wallace natural selection (1858) and Leibniz-Newton calculus as one of history's clearest cases of parallel scientific invention. The Methodenstreit was Menger's LATER 1883 methodological quarrel with Schmoller; the Keynesian Revolution was 1936; the Neoclassical Synthesis was Samuelson's 1940s-50s fusion. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalism; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: A student asks Menger why Adam Smith and Karl Marx said a good's value comes from the work to make it. Menger says they were looking in the wrong place. Value is not in the good; it is in the mind of the buyer. A loaf is worth more to a hungry man than a full one. What is Menger's idea called?
answer: The subjective theory of value
choices: The subjective theory of value
The labor theory of value
The quantity theory of money
The comparative advantage argument
context: Menger's move was not to REFINE the labor theory but to REPLACE it. Adam Smith, David Ricardo, and Karl Marx all held labor-embodied theories in some form; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced them with subjective valuation. The quantity theory of money (Hume, Fisher, Friedman) explains price levels; comparative advantage (Ricardo 1817) explains trade -- neither is what Menger contributes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: For a long time, economists were puzzled. Diamonds cost a lot, but water, which we need to live, costs almost nothing. Menger solved the puzzle. He said do not look at the total supply. Look at what?
answer: The next specific unit a chooser is ranking
choices: The next specific unit a chooser is ranking
The average labor-hours across all producers
The total quantity supplied in a year
The moral desert of the buyer
context: A chooser never ranks 'all water' against 'all diamonds'; he ranks the NEXT glass against the NEXT stone. Water is so abundant that the marginal glass is nearly worthless; diamonds are so scarce that the marginal stone is very valuable. Total utility is enormous for water and tiny for diamonds; the MARGINAL utility is the reverse -- and price tracks the margin. Adam Smith noticed the paradox in Wealth of Nations (1776); it took Menger, Jevons, and Walras 95 years to solve it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalism.

question: The German word Grenznutzen, meaning marginal utility, is not in Menger's 1871 book. Someone else coined it. He built on an older term for marginal cost by von Thuenen. Who was he?
answer: Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Friedrich von Wieser
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Carl Menger himself
Leon Walras
context: Wieser (1851-1926), one of Menger's two most important students, coined Grenznutzen to name a concept his teacher had already articulated in prose. Boehm-Bawerk, the other great student, developed capital and interest theory instead. The English 'marginal utility' is a direct translation of Wieser's German. So the school's most famous term was named by the pupil, not the founder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Menger wrote his 1871 book in plain prose. He used no math, no graphs, no curves. He said economics is about human choice, not numbers. Boehm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, and Rothbard all kept this style. What lasting mark did that choice leave on the Austrian school?
answer: Arguing in prose rather than in mathematical models
choices: Arguing in prose rather than in mathematical models
Building large econometric models
Founding the discipline of experimental economics
Grounding claims in national statistical surveys
context: Menger's rejection of mathematical economics was not incidental; it was a claim about the SUBJECT -- since valuation is subjective and preferences are ordinal, false precision misleads more than it clarifies. Walras and Jevons, the co-inventors of marginalism, went the other way and built the mathematical tradition. Experimental economics (Vernon Smith, Nobel 2002) came a century later; large econometric models are Cowles Commission and Klein 1940s-60s; national statistical surveys are the German Historical School Menger's 1883 Methodenstreit book attacked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: Menger drafted but never published a Volume 2 of Principles, intended to cover capital and interest. The book that occupies that missing volume's place in the Austrian corpus was written by his student instead, appearing as Kapital und Kapitalzins in the 1880s. Who filled the gap?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
Fritz Machlup
context: Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) wrote Kapital und Kapitalzins (Capital and Interest) in three volumes 1884-1889 -- history and critique of interest theories, positive theory of capital, and further essays -- effectively the Volume 2 Menger never produced. Boehm-Bawerk also served three terms as Austrian finance minister and taught the young Mises. Wieser wrote on marginal utility and social economics rather than capital; Mises and Machlup were of later generations. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: Menger's 1871 Principles founded the Austrian School in German. For 79 years there was no English edition -- the tradition traveled to America through Mises's students, not through the book itself. When did James Dingwall and Bert F. Hoselitz's English translation finally reach print through the Free Press?
context: The 1950 Free Press edition, with an introduction by Frank Knight, appeared 29 years after Menger's death (1921) and only after his student Hayek had already moved to LSE (1931) and then Chicago (1950). Frank Knight -- the great Chicago economist and Milton Friedman's teacher -- wrote the introduction. The 79-year gap is a measure of how far the German-speaking Austrian tradition had traveled before English-speaking economics noticed the founding text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: The founder of the Austrian School had a son named Karl. Karl became a top mathematician, joined the Vienna Circle, ran his own math club in interwar Vienna, and later taught for decades at the Illinois Institute of Technology. Whose son was he?
answer: Son of Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian School
choices: Son of Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian School
Son of Ludwig von Mises
Nephew of Friedrich Hayek
Grandson of Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985) did not follow his father into economics; he did mathematics, contributed to dimension theory, edited the Mathematical Colloquium proceedings that included work by Kurt Goedel and John von Neumann, and belonged to the Vienna Circle. So the Menger name reaches into TWO of interwar Vienna's great intellectual traditions -- Austrian economics through the father, mathematical positivism through the son. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: A Bitcoin miner's computer tries to add a new block to the chain. It must find a special number that, when mixed with the block, gives a fingerprint starting with a set number of zeros. What is that special number called?
answer: A nonce
choices: A nonce
A hash
A seed
A salt
context: The 'nonce' (number-used-once) is what miners search for. Trillions of guesses per second per machine try different nonces until one produces a hash below the required difficulty target. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nonce.

question: A Bitcoin miner's computer has only one way to find the right code for a new block. It has to guess again and again, very fast. What everyday word do Bitcoin teachers use for this?
answer: A digital lottery
choices: A digital lottery
A digital marathon
A digital auction
A digital contract
context: Every guess is a lottery ticket; more hashing power means more tickets per second; the miner with the most tickets wins most often. First to find a valid nonce broadcasts the block and other miners immediately begin building on top of it. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: The tool Bitcoin uses to turn each try into a fingerprint was built by the US National Security Agency and set as a standard in 2001. Which hash function is it?
answer: SHA-256
choices: SHA-256
SHA-3
Scrypt
Ethash
context: SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) is a member of the SHA-2 family, published by NIST in 2001. Litecoin uses Scrypt; Ethereum used Ethash before the Merge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2.

question: The Bitcoin network changes how hard the mining puzzle is on a set schedule. This keeps blocks coming about every ten minutes. How often does the difficulty change?
answer: Every 2,016 blocks
choices: Every 2,016 blocks
Every 210,000 blocks
Every 100 blocks
Every 10,000 blocks
context: Difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks (roughly two weeks at 10-minute blocks). If blocks came faster than expected, difficulty rises; slower, it falls. This is how Bitcoin auto-regulates against changes in aggregate mining power. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Difficulty.

question: To undo old Bitcoin trades, an attacker must redo the work on every block he changes. He also has to stay ahead of all the honest miners. What share of the mining power would he need?
answer: More than half
choices: More than half
About a quarter
About one tenth
About one hundredth
context: The classic 51% attack: an attacker with more hashing power than the rest of the network combined can, in principle, rewrite recent history. The energy is what makes such an attack expensive; that is the security. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-spending.

question: The power that Bitcoin miners burn is not a side effect. It is core to keeping the network safe. In one short phrase, what role does that power play?
answer: It is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network
choices: It is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network
It is a byproduct of the transaction-processing bandwidth
It is a subsidy that pays for the developer-team infrastructure
It is the cooling cost of the servers that broadcast transactions
context: The economic barrier to attack is what real-world energy an attacker would have to burn to redo the work faster than the honest network. Defenders call this 'the energy IS the security.' Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin solved a famous computer-science puzzle: how can messengers who cannot fully trust each other still agree on one true version of a message, even if some of them are liars? What is this classic puzzle called?
answer: The Byzantine Generals Problem
choices: The Byzantine Generals Problem
The Halting Problem
The Traveling Salesman Problem
The P-versus-NP Problem
context: Byzantine Generals (Lamport, Shostak, Pease, 1982): how do untrusted, distributed parties reach agreement on a shared record without a central authority? Nakamoto Consensus is the first known solution using proof-of-work as the coordinating mechanism. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault.

question: The named consensus design that combines proof-of-work with the rule that the honest chain is the one with the most cumulative work is called after Bitcoin's pseudonymous founder. What is it called?
answer: Nakamoto Consensus
choices: Nakamoto Consensus
Byzantine Consensus
Cascade Consensus
Deterministic Consensus
context: 'Nakamoto Consensus' is the standard name in cryptography and computer-science literature for the proof-of-work + longest-chain rule Satoshi introduced with Bitcoin. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nakamoto_consensus.

question: Critics call Bitcoin mining wasteful. Defenders say normal money also burns huge energy, but it is hidden. Which set of hidden costs do they usually name?
answer: Bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the entire regulatory apparatus
choices: Bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the entire regulatory apparatus
Central bank cooling systems, satellite payment routing, and mint-vault air handling
Government subsidies to Bitcoin miners built into monetary policy operations
Federal Reserve academic research on money-supply forecasting
context: The defender's move: fiat's energy cost is spread across every branch, every armored truck, every printing plant, every ATM, every regulatory apparatus. Bitcoin makes its energy cost visible and concentrated; fiat hides its energy cost. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: A Bitcoin miner who finds a valid nonce and broadcasts a valid block collects a compound payment made of newly-issued coins plus fees on the transactions the block carries. What is the standard name for this payment?
answer: The block reward
choices: The block reward
The transaction cascade
The mining tip
The confirmation fee
context: 'Block reward' = newly-issued coins from the current issuance schedule plus fees on the transactions the miner has included in the block. Issuance falls to zero around 2140; by then miners live on fees alone. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Block_reward.

question: One kind of digital money makes computers all over the world race to solve hard puzzles. This burns a lot of power. Why would anyone build money to work this way?
answer: So no single group can easily fake or take over the money
choices: So no single group can easily fake or take over the money
So only rich people can use it
To warm up cold rooms in winter
The designers wanted to sell more electricity
context: The Merge (September 15 2022) joined Ethereum's execution layer with its already-live proof-of-stake beacon chain. Ethereum's energy consumption dropped by roughly 99.95% overnight. Source: ethereum.org/en/roadmap/merge.

question: In one type of digital money, users do not burn power. Instead they lock up a big deposit of the money. If they cheat, they lose the deposit. What is this system called?
answer: Proof-of-stake
choices: Proof-of-stake
Proof-of-work
Proof-of-effort
Proof-of-honor
context: Proof-of-stake (PoS): the right to propose the next block is assigned in proportion to staked collateral, not to burned electricity. Cardano, Solana, and most post-2018 chains launched with PoS from the start. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake.

question: On September 15, 2022 the Ethereum Merge happened. The Ethereum Foundation gave a clear number for the power savings. By about how much did power use drop that day?
answer: About 99.95 percent
choices: About 99.95 percent
About 50 percent
About 25 percent
About 10 percent
context: The Ethereum Foundation's post-Merge figure is a roughly 99.95% cut in network electricity use. That is the strongest engineering argument PoS supporters make for the switch. Source: ethereum.org/en/energy-consumption.

question: One popular blockchain lets you help run the network by locking up coins as a deposit instead of by burning electricity on puzzles. If you try to cheat, you lose your deposit. What is that idea called?
answer: Proof-of-stake
choices: Proof-of-stake
Proof-of-work
Proof-of-labor
Proof-of-trust
context: Vitalik Buterin published the Ethereum white paper in late 2013 and has argued for proof-of-stake since Ethereum's earliest design discussions. The Merge was the culmination of an eight-year design goal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalik_Buterin.

question: Bitcoin fans have a top complaint about proof-of-stake. They say it brings back a trait of old money that proof-of-work was built to reject. What trait is it?
answer: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
choices: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
Requirement of a central government treasury for issuance
Dependence on trusted third-party settlement rails
Delegation of block production to a small licensed authority
context: The Bitcoin-community argument: whoever starts with the most tokens has the most power to add blocks, entrench their position, and shape network rules, without an external check equivalent to the electricity a PoW miner must burn. Source: mises.org/library/proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake.

question: One Bitcoin critique of proof-of-stake has a name: the nothing-at-stake problem. What does the attack say can happen?
answer: Validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once, since no real-world resource is spent per signature
choices: Validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once, since no real-world resource is spent per signature
Validators can rewrite the block chain to their advantage without incurring any staking penalty
Validators can drop their staked collateral before their signatures are recorded
Validators can vote in proportion to their trading volume rather than their staked balance
context: Under PoW a miner can only mine one chain at a time (electricity is a real resource). Under naive PoS a validator can sign every fork simultaneously; the defense requires trusted checkpoints or slashing penalties that add complexity and trust assumptions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake#Attacks.

question: In 2023 the head of one US finance agency said many proof-of-stake tokens might count as investment contracts under US law. Which agency was that?
answer: The Securities and Exchange Commission
choices: The Securities and Exchange Commission
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission
The Federal Trade Commission
The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority
context: Gary Gensler, then SEC chair, made this suggestion in public testimony in 2023; the SEC's PoS-token stance has since become a running legal question for Ethereum and other PoS chains. Source: sec.gov (Gensler public testimony 2023).

question: Bitcoin remains on proof-of-work as a core design principle. In the Bitcoin-community argument, the electricity cost is not a bug but which specific kind of feature?
answer: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
choices: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
A regulatory-compliance cost that satisfies environmental disclosure rules
A liquidity provision that reduces short-run mining-fee volatility
A payment to network engineers who maintain node infrastructure
context: The Nakamoto-Consensus defense: the electricity is what makes Bitcoin's security depend on something outside the network's own token economics. Proof-of-stake keeps costs internal and depends on economic incentives among token holders. Source: mises.org/library/proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake.

question: The proof-of-work vs proof-of-stake debate is one of the largest live economic-engineering contrasts in cryptocurrency. Both sides made real bets in 2022. In one sentence, what will decide which was right?
answer: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
choices: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
Whether central banks issue their own digital currencies competing with both
Whether the SEC issues a definitive ruling on token classification
Whether major derivative exchanges list futures on both consensus mechanisms
context: The empirical verdict on PoW vs PoS security will require decades of live operation across real attacks, market crashes, and regulatory pressure. Bitcoin has fifteen years of proof-of-work data; Ethereum's proof-of-stake has three post-Merge years. Source: mises.org/library/pow-pos-empirical.

question: Two named cryptocurrencies persisted on proof-of-work well past the 2022 Merge, both technical descendants of Bitcoin. Which pair are they?
answer: Litecoin and Dogecoin
choices: Litecoin and Dogecoin
Cardano and Solana
Polkadot and Avalanche
Tron and EOS
context: Litecoin (2011, Charlie Lee) and Dogecoin (2013, Billy Markus & Jackson Palmer) are Scrypt-based PoW coins descended from Bitcoin's codebase. Cardano, Solana, Polkadot, and Avalanche all use PoS variants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litecoin.

question: For a long time, economists said bakers cared about money but leaders only cared about doing good. One school said no. Leaders want things too, like getting re-elected. What is this school called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Public finance
Monetary policy
Central planning
context: Tullock, a lawyer by training, was one of the founders of public choice theory alongside James Buchanan. Buchanan would later win the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economics for the field's development. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: In 1966 Gordon Tullock started a journal with a long name. Later it was renamed to a two-word name that stuck to the whole field. What was its first title?
answer: 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making'
choices: 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making'
'Studies in Political Economy'
'Journal of Institutional Analysis'
'Constitutional Economics Review'
context: The journal renamed itself 'Public Choice' in 1969, and the new name became the label for the whole scholarly field. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: The public choice school studies politicians and government workers as people who respond to incentives, just like anyone else. It grew up at a state university in one US state, then moved to a second school in the same state. Which state?
answer: Virginia
choices: Virginia
Massachusetts
California
New York
context: The center was originally at the University of Virginia, moved to Virginia Tech, and then followed Buchanan to George Mason in 1983 -- an unusual case of a research center migrating with its founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: Public choice is a branch of economics. It studies people in government the same way it studies anyone else. What does it assume about workers in government?
answer: They respond to incentives too, and often act in their own interest
choices: They respond to incentives too, and often act in their own interest
They ignore personal gain and always serve the public good
They act at random and cannot be predicted by economists
They only respond to what voters demand in each election
context: Founded 1965 as the Committee on Non-Market Decision Making. The society hosts an annual conference; the European Public Choice Society (1972) and Public Choice Society of Japan (1996) followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_choice.

question: Public Choice as a discipline was ratified by a specific award to one of its co-founders in 1986. What was awarded, and to whom?
answer: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
choices: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
The John Bates Clark Medal, to Gordon Tullock
The Presidential Medal of Freedom, to William Niskanen
The Manhattan Institute Hayek Prize, to Anthony de Jasay
context: The Nobel-adjacent prize (usually just called the Nobel Prize in Economics). Buchanan's citation credited his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for economic and political decision-making. Tullock never received the prize, an omission still noted by public-choice scholars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/James_M._Buchanan.

question: By 2020 Public Choice was cited across economics, political science, sociology, and law. Its early pages laid down the intellectual scaffolding of a whole field. Which cluster of concepts is characteristic of the field's contribution?
answer: Rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, expressive voting
choices: Rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, expressive voting
Aggregate demand, marginal propensity to consume, Phillips curve, IS-LM
General equilibrium, comparative statics, Walrasian auctioneer, Edgeworth box
Mean-variance optimization, capital asset pricing model, efficient markets
context: Tullock coined 'rent-seeking' in 1967 in a Public Choice paper. Niskanen 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government' (1971) worked out bureaucratic behavior. Buchanan-Tullock 'The Calculus of Consent' (1962) had already introduced constitutional political economy. All worked out first in the journal before diffusing more widely. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_choice.

question: If workers at a store go on strike, the store might lose money or even close. But if the workers at a police station went on strike, who would be hurt the most?
answer: The regular people who need protecting
choices: The regular people who need protecting
The bankers who lend to the police
Foreign countries
Other police departments
context: Franklin D. Roosevelt wrote to Luther Steward, President of the National Federation of Federal Employees, on August 16, 1937. Roosevelt considered a public-sector strike 'unthinkable and intolerable.' Source: presidency.ucsb.edu (Roosevelt letter to Steward, 1937).

question: In 1937 Franklin D. Roosevelt argued that government workers should not bargain the way private workers do. He said the person across the table is different in each case. Who sits across from workers at a private company but not at a government job?
answer: A profit-maximizing private employer
choices: A profit-maximizing private employer
A voluntary industry trade association
A regulated common carrier
A cooperatively-owned enterprise
context: In the private sector, wage demands trade off against the employer's profits and the firm's competitive survival. In the public sector, the employer is a taxpayer-funded entity whose ultimate check-writer is the same voter the union spends dues to influence. Source: Roosevelt letter (1937).
