question: In 2008 the U.S. government spent hundreds of billions of dollars to rescue big banks that had made bad bets. What is the name for the trap where knowing you will be rescued makes people take EVEN BIGGER risks next time?
answer: Moral hazard
choices: Moral hazard
Sunk cost
Free trade
Opportunity cost
context: Moral hazard: once creditors and banks expect rescue in a crisis, they demand less risk premium and take more risk, making the system more fragile for the next crisis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard.

question: In 2008 the government rescued big banks that were about to fail. The visible good was stopping a wider financial crash right then. What is the hidden long-term cost that critics of these rescues keep pointing out?
answer: Future bankers take bigger risks because they now expect a rescue when things go wrong
choices: Future bankers take bigger risks because they now expect a rescue when things go wrong
The paperwork cost of running the rescue program
The tax revenue lost on stock dividends the government received
The paperwork burden the rescue put on small community banks
context: The Bastiat UNSEEN in a bailout is not in the year of the bailout; it is in the next crisis. The rescued creditors' expectation of rescue changes behavior going forward. Source: cato.org/commentary/tarp-moral-hazard.

question: A bank kept most of its money in long-term government bonds it had bought when interest rates were very low. When rates jumped up, those bonds were worth much less. Nervous customers heard the news and rushed to pull their cash out all at once. What is that panicked mass withdrawal called?
answer: A bank run
choices: A bank run
A margin call
A short sale
A dividend cut
context: SVB failed March 10 2023 with roughly 93% of its deposits UNINSURED, mostly tech firms and venture-capital funds. Signature Bank followed days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank.

question: US bank insurance normally covers only $250,000 in any one account. In March 2023, the government said it would cover every dollar in one failed bank, even accounts far above the limit. What lesson does that send to wealthy savers?
answer: Do not worry about the limit; the government may cover you anyway
choices: Do not worry about the limit; the government may cover you anyway
Never keep more than $250,000 in any bank, ever again
Only use cash and avoid all banks completely from now on
Move all your money to foreign banks immediately
context: The joint March 12 2023 announcement invoked the systemic-risk exception; Signature Bank got the same treatment days later. Uninsured depositors -- who had chosen to keep more than $250K in a single account -- were made whole at zero cost. Source: federalreserve.gov (joint press release, March 12 2023).

question: Rich depositors had left far more than the insured amount in one bank, betting a run would never happen. The government then made them whole after the run hit. What lesson about caution does that erase for next time?
answer: Splitting your money across many banks was the safe move; the bailout hides that lesson
choices: Splitting your money across many banks was the safe move; the bailout hides that lesson
Keeping cash under your mattress is the only safe move
Only small community banks are safe; big banks are not
Buying private insurance is required by federal law
context: The market's normal signal to a depositor over the FDIC cap: split your money across banks. The 2023 SVB rescue eliminated that signal for large uninsured depositors going forward. Source: cato.org/commentary/svb-bailout-moral-hazard.

question: The classic rule for a central bank's crisis response was written by Walter Bagehot in 1873. Bagehot said the lender of last resort should lend freely, take only good collateral, and charge what sort of interest rate?
answer: A high, punishing rate
choices: A high, punishing rate
The prevailing market rate
A subsidized concessional rate
A rate fixed by statute
context: Bagehot's rule: 'lend freely, at high rates, against good collateral.' The punishing rate is the point -- banks would only draw the facility in true crisis, not because it was cheap. The 2023 SVB bailout gave uninsured depositors a FREE option instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street_(book).

question: The moral-hazard critique of federal bailouts has a Bastiat-shaped logic. One rescue in one crisis changes what every future actor expects. The real cost shows up in the next crisis the earlier bailout quietly invited. Which precedent-and-sequel pair does this ladder trace?
answer: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization
choices: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization
Continental Illinois 1984 as precedent; Long-Term Capital 1998 as institutionalization
Penn Central 1970 as precedent; Chrysler 1979 as institutionalization
Franklin National 1974 as precedent; Continental Illinois 1984 as institutionalization
context: The 2008 TARP established that the federal government would rescue major-bank creditors; the 2023 SVB action made the rescue apply to any deposit at any bank the regulators later name systemic. The UNSEEN cost of 2008 is paid in the changed behavior visible in 2023. Source: mercatus.org/publications/svb-bailout-changed-behavior.

question: Anna Schwartz co-wrote the 1963 Monetary History of the United States with Milton Friedman. Later, she offered a sharp one-line warning about the direction the Federal Reserve had taken by the 21st century. In her words, the Fed was now really in the business of doing what?
answer: Preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money
choices: Preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money
Fine-tuning the unemployment rate to a Phillips-curve target
Coordinating fiscal policy with the elected Treasury
Regulating derivatives markets under a systemic-risk mandate
context: Schwartz's warning, restated in her final years: the Fed's mission had drifted from monetary stability toward defending asset prices, and the moral hazard consequences would surface in the next crisis. Source: wsj.com/articles/anna-schwartz-1915-2012.

question: The government wants every kid to learn, so it pays for school. But does it have to run every school, or can parents take that money to any approved school they pick?
answer: Parents can take the money to any approved school
choices: Parents can take the money to any approved school
The government must run every single school itself
Only rich families should get to pick a school
Schools should have no rules or funding at all
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Government in Education,' in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest (Rutgers University Press, 1955). Friedman argued for funding pupils (via vouchers) rather than school buildings. Source: JSTOR (Solo 1955 collection).

question: A big-city teachers union goes on strike three times in ten years, closing schools for 300,000 kids each time. When workers whose paychecks come from taxes go on strike, who is left with no other choice?
answer: Families whose kids can only attend the public schools
choices: Families whose kids can only attend the public schools
Only the teachers themselves
The politicians who signed the contracts
Business owners in other states
context: The Chicago Teachers Union struck in 2012 (9 school days), 2019 (11 days), and 2022 (5 days) -- each closing schools for approximately 300,000 students, disproportionately low-income, whose parents cannot easily choose an alternative. Source: chicagotribune.com strike coverage.

question: A city sets up a program where poor families get about $10,000 a year that they can only spend on tuition at any private school they choose. What is this kind of school-choice payment called?
answer: A school voucher
choices: A school voucher
A public-school tax
A tuition loan
A federal college grant
context: The DC Opportunity Scholarship Program was enacted in the 2004 DC School Choice Incentive Act. Multi-year IES / Patrick Wolf and Anna Kisida evaluations (US Department of Education 2010, 2018) found statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for scholarship recipients. Source: ed.gov (DC OSP evaluations).

question: For years, the US Department of Education studied a DC voucher program. Patrick Wolf's team compared kids with a voucher to kids without one. What clear benefit did the voucher kids show?
answer: Higher graduation rates
choices: Higher graduation rates
Lower graduation rates
Higher rates of college non-attendance
Higher rates of school-year absence
context: The IES evaluations (2010, 2018) documented statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for DC OSP scholarship recipients. Congressional attempts to shut the program down have come repeatedly from the DC teachers-union's allies. Source: ies.ed.gov (Wolf + Kisida evaluations).

question: In a large American city, some public schools and some free 'charter' schools share the same building, teaching students from the same neighborhood. Why is this a useful test for comparing the two kinds of schools?
answer: The neighborhood and building are the same, so those cannot explain any score gap
choices: The neighborhood and building are the same, so those cannot explain any score gap
All the kids have the same last names, so it must be genetics
The kids are picked at random by the federal government each year
The kids share the same lunches, so nutrition is the reason
context: Thomas Sowell, Charter Schools and Their Enemies (Basic Books, 2020). Sowell used NYC co-location data to compare charter and district students in the same building. In every matched-building comparison, charter students outperformed. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 2020).

question: A big city fits two schools inside one building — one run by the district, one a charter — sharing hallways and gyms. What is the biggest advantage of comparing the two schools inside the same building?
answer: You can rule out the building and the neighborhood as reasons for any score gap
choices: You can rule out the building and the neighborhood as reasons for any score gap
You can force both schools to teach exactly the same lessons
You can give both schools the same teachers each school year
You can guarantee every student earns an A grade
context: NYC co-location rules place charter schools and district schools inside the same physical building, allowing direct like-for-like comparison. Sowell used this data to build his 2020 book. Source: schools.nyc.gov (co-location policy history).

question: A well-known argument in public choice studies of schools says that teachers' unions push hard for their own members' pay and job protection, sometimes at the cost of what parents want. What pattern is this in public choice?
answer: A special-interest group getting more from the system than the average voter does
choices: A special-interest group getting more from the system than the average voter does
A random side effect of holding elections every four years
A rule that automatically balances every group's power
A federal law that gives unions the final word on schools
context: Terry Moe, Special Interest: Teachers Unions and America's Public Schools (Brookings Institution, 2011). Moe applied Olson-style analysis to teachers-union political power. Source: brookings.edu (Moe 2011).

question: A state tries to pass a law giving families money to send their kids to any school they choose. The group most likely to lose from the change -- teachers in one big union -- spends about ten times more against the law than families spend for it. What does this show about who fights hardest in politics?
answer: A small group with a lot to lose fights harder than a big group with a little to gain
choices: A small group with a lot to lose fights harder than a big group with a little to gain
Big groups always beat small ones in every election
Money never changes the outcome of a vote
Voters always pick the option that helps the most people
context: The CTA spent tens of millions of dollars against Proposition 174 in 1993, outspending the pro-voucher side by roughly 10-to-1. The initiative failed. It is a textbook Olson concentrated-benefit case study. Source: California Secretary of State campaign-finance records; Moe (2011).

question: Mancur Olson's rule says a small group with a lot to gain will out-organize a large group with only a little to lose. Applied to American K-12 schools, one specific group fits that shape perfectly: it organizes members, negotiates contracts, backs candidates, and staffs school-board elections. Who is that concentrated interest?
answer: The teachers' union
choices: The teachers' union
State textbook publishers
Local chambers of commerce
Neighborhood parents' associations
context: The teachers' union is the concentrated organized beneficiary with the resources and staff to shape school-board and legislative outcomes. Parents and children are the dispersed victim class that pays higher taxes and receives worse outcomes but does not systematically organize. Source: Moe, Special Interest (Brookings 2011).

question: The K-12 education case teaches a reasoning move about how to frame the education-policy debate. What is the honest structural question a public-choice reader should press, rather than 'are teachers bad'?
answer: Which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules
choices: Which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules
Which political party spends more per capita on schools
Which state has the highest average teacher salary
Which district uses the newest textbooks
context: The Olson-Stigler applied move: individual educators are usually decent people; the rule-selection process is dominated by whichever organized interest has resources and staff. That is a structural analysis, not a moral one. Source: Olson (1965); Moe (2011).

question: Milton Friedman's 1955 essay launched the modern school-choice movement. Its main proposal was to separate two functions that governments had long combined. Which pair of functions did Friedman propose separating?
answer: Funding schooling versus producing it
choices: Funding schooling versus producing it
Testing students versus grading teachers
Recruiting teachers versus recruiting principals
Building schools versus stocking libraries
context: Friedman's move: the state may legitimately fund a service without also being the exclusive producer of that service. Vouchers fund the pupil rather than the building; private, charter, magnet, and district schools then compete for that funded pupil. Source: Friedman, 'Role of Government in Education' (1955).

question: In the U.S., the president can only be elected twice. This limit was added to the Constitution after one president won four elections in a row. What is the general name for a rule that caps how many terms a leader may serve?
answer: Term limits
choices: Term limits
The filibuster
Judicial review
An executive order
context: The 22nd Amendment (ratified February 27, 1951) limits the president to two elected terms, passed in response to FDR's four elections. Source: constitution.congress.gov (Twenty-Second Amendment).

question: In 1995 the US Supreme Court decided a 5-4 case. It said only a constitutional amendment -- not a state -- can add new rules for who can serve in Congress. So states could not set term limits for their members of Congress. What is that case called?
answer: US Term Limits Inc. v. Thornton
choices: US Term Limits Inc. v. Thornton
Powell v. McCormack
Roe v. Wade
Reynolds v. Sims
context: US Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton, 514 US 779 (1995), decided 5-4 on May 22, 1995. States cannot impose term limits on federal congressional service; only a constitutional amendment can. Source: supremecourt.gov (514 US 779).

question: For decades, polls have shown steady public support for limits on how long a member of Congress may serve. What range of support do Gallup and Pew typically find?
answer: About 75 to 83 percent
choices: About 75 to 83 percent
About 25 to 35 percent
About 40 to 50 percent
Essentially split fifty-fifty
context: Congressional term-limits polling has stayed in the ~75-83% range across decades of surveys by Gallup, Pew, and others. It has never come close to the two-thirds House and Senate majorities required to send an amendment to the states. Source: news.gallup.com (term-limits polling history).

question: In 1962, Buchanan and Tullock split politics into two levels. At the top, people agree on rules that will bind future officeholders. At the lower level, sitting officeholders resist those rules. What did the pair name these two levels?
answer: The constitutional and the post-constitutional
choices: The constitutional and the post-constitutional
The federal and the local
The judicial and the legislative
The elected and the appointed
context: The constitutional level is where rules are chosen behind a veil of uncertainty about your own future position. The post-constitutional level is choices made within the rules by known-position actors. Term limits are the paradigmatic case of a rule desired at level one, resisted at level two. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 6.

question: In November 1990, California voters passed the first US state law setting term limits for state lawmakers. What was that ballot measure called?
answer: Proposition 140
choices: Proposition 140
Proposition 13
Proposition 209
Proposition 187
context: California Proposition 140 (November 1990) established term limits on state legislators, executive-branch officials, and staff. It launched the 1990-94 wave of state-level term-limit reforms. Source: California Secretary of State (Proposition 140 official election materials).

question: After California and other states passed term limits, studies showed some big and surprising effects. Lawmakers had less time in office, and they had less know-how. Toward which groups did the power visibly shift?
answer: The executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff
choices: The executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff
The judicial branch and state constitutional officers
Political action committees only
Local school boards and city councils
context: Post-term-limits studies including Elhauge (1997) and Hansen on California pre-and-post-Proposition-140 found power shifted toward actors whose knowledge was not term-limited. The Virginia school's unintended-consequences prediction. Source: Elhauge, University of Chicago Law Review (1997).

question: A congressman who has been in office for decades brushes off calls for term limits: 'We already have term limits -- they're called elections.' Why do supporters of term limits find that answer weak?
answer: Long-serving incumbents almost always win, so real elections barely limit anyone
choices: Long-serving incumbents almost always win, so real elections barely limit anyone
Elections are held only once every twenty years
The Constitution bans all elections after age fifty
Voters never care who their representative is
context: Alan Grayson (D-FL), a two-term House member, repeatedly used the 'elections are term limits' line as the standard incumbent parry. The line captures the post-constitutional logic Buchanan predicted. Source: contemporary press coverage 2010-16.

question: Switzerland's federal executive is a seven-member Federal Council. Its presidency rotates yearly, so no single person builds up the perks of the office long enough to entrench. What does the Swiss system show?
answer: A constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start
choices: A constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start
A recent reform in the wake of a scandal
A UN treaty obligation binding on European states
A holdover from medieval papal succession rules
context: Switzerland's rotating presidency is a constitutional-level structural rule adopted at foundation, so no sitting incumbent had to vote to shorten his own tenure. It illustrates the Buchanan point about which anti-incumbent rules can actually get chosen and stick. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Council_(Switzerland).

question: Buchanan's diagnosis of the term-limits deadlock also fits other reforms with the same shape. Which reform below shares the pattern, where the people who would lose from the change are the very ones whose votes would pass it?
answer: Campaign-finance reform in the US Congress
choices: Campaign-finance reform in the US Congress
Tariff repeal by consumer initiative
Interest-rate targeting by the Fed
Sunset provisions for expiring tax cuts
context: Campaign-finance reform, redistricting reform, gerrymandering reform, and term limits all share the losers-must-enact-the-reform pattern. Buchanan's constitutional-level analysis predicts these reforms will struggle regardless of majority popular support. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Grofman + Handley on gerrymandering.

question: The term-limits case teaches a rule of thumb about certain reforms. When a reform asks current officeholders to accept a cost, and the benefits flow to future citizens or challengers, what should the analyst expect?
answer: The reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support
choices: The reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support
The reform will pass by acclamation within one session
The reform will pass automatically once polling exceeds sixty percent
The reform will pass only through executive order
context: The default is failure at the post-constitutional stage. Which is not cynicism -- it is Buchanan's constitutional-political-economy analysis of which rules survive democratic selection when the rule-writers themselves would bear the costs of the rule. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Grofman (2006).

question: Between May and July of 2022, three 'crypto' companies fell apart in a chain reaction. Tens of billions in customer funds were wiped out -- and none of it was really about Bitcoin. Of those three altcoin projects, which one fell first?

FTX

question: A company promises its coin will always trade for exactly one dollar. But it does not actually hold real dollars. Instead, a computer program trades a sister coin to keep the price steady. What can go wrong with that setup?

The coin becomes safer than the U.S. dollar

question: A digital coin promised to always equal one dollar and paid huge rewards to holders. question: A US 'crypto bank' run by Alex Mashinsky had been paying high yields on customer deposits. When Terra crashed, it set off a run on his company. On which date did that firm freeze withdrawals and later file for bankruptcy?

question: On June 12, 2022, the Celsius Network froze customer accounts and soon filed for bankruptcy. About how much customer money was trapped inside when the freeze began?

about $50 million
about $30 billion
about $500 billion

question: In 2022, a crypto lender blew up after one of its biggest borrowers, a hedge fund, could not repay hundreds of millions. What is the general word for a chain where one big failure knocks down others?
answer: Contagion
choices: Contagion
Inflation
Deflation
Speculation

Alameda Research was FTX's affiliated trading firm (later collapse); LTCM was a 1998 failure; Bridgewater is unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_Digital.

question: A crypto coin promised to always be worth exactly one dollar without any real dollars backing it -- the promise depended on trading with a partner coin using a math formula. Only governments are allowed to create crypto coins
Coins backed by trading formulas can never lose value

question: Alex Mashinsky, the head of Celsius Network, was arrested after his firm collapsed and was later convicted in a New York federal court in December 2024. What was the substance of that conviction?
answer: fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL
choices: fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL
identity theft against Celsius customers
unregistered securities offering only
money laundering only

question: In 2022, several big crypto companies -- Terra, Celsius, Voyager, and the exchange FTX -- collapsed and users lost billions. But one specific group of Bitcoin owners lost nothing in every case. What decision had they made that protected them?
answer: They held their own bitcoin themselves instead of trusting a company to hold it for them
choices: They held their own bitcoin themselves instead of trusting a company to hold it for them
They bought the failed company's own token first so they could withdraw before others
They turned on two-factor login and used a strong password on the company account
They paid a monthly fee to join the company's advertised insurance plan
context: In every 2022 collapse the customers who had moved bitcoin to their own hardware wallets were unaffected; those who had trusted a third party for a promised yield lost access. 2FA does not protect against custodian insolvency; native tokens (LUNA, CEL, FTT) collapsed alongside their issuers; insurance programs were widely absent or hollow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_bubble.

question: Looking back at 2022, a Bitcoin educator makes a point Andreas Antonopoulos has taught for years. The claim is that the failing crypto companies were built very differently from Bitcoin itself. Which version of that point does the argument press?
answer: That 'crypto' companies with an issuer or a promised-yield model can collapse, while Bitcoin held in self-custody has no counterparty to fail in the first place
choices: That 'crypto' companies with an issuer or a promised-yield model can collapse, while Bitcoin held in self-custody has no counterparty to fail in the first place
That all cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin eventually collapse in the same way through cascading market losses and customer runs on custodial services
That Bitcoin itself failed as a protocol in 2022 alongside Terra and Celsius and only survived because major exchanges chose to keep supporting it
That regulators should treat Bitcoin and 'crypto' identically in every jurisdiction since the underlying mathematics is the same across the whole industry
context: The Antonopoulos/Ammous move: Terra, Celsius, Voyager and FTX all had issuers or promised-yield structures with counterparty risk; Bitcoin held on a hardware wallet has neither. Bitcoin itself did not collapse; its price fell but the protocol continued operating; equating 'crypto' with Bitcoin is exactly the confusion the argument refuses. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.); Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: A shopkeeper's window is broken. He pays the glazier six francs to fix it. Some townsfolk say this is GOOD for the town -- the glazier now has money to spend. What did they FORGET?
answer: The six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or bread
choices: The six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or bread
Broken windows really do create brand-new wealth
The glazier will donate his fee back to the shop
The town gets richer every time something breaks
context: Bastiat (1801-1850) published the pamphlet a few months before his December 1850 death in Rome; it is his last complete work. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: The 1850 Bastiat pamphlet carries a title, in the French original, that names the whole method in five words. What is that title, in English?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
The Harmonies of Political Economy
The Law of Free Exchange
A Petition of the Merchants of Bordeaux
context: French original: Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas. Standard English editions since 1859 keep the literal title. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: The opening of Bastiat's 1850 essay lays out the whole method. Every act or law produces not just one immediate effect but a whole series of later effects that go unseen. In shorthand, what pair does he draw?
answer: Between the seen and the unseen
choices: Between the seen and the unseen
Between supply and demand
Between value and price
Between rent and profit
context: The whole essay's method is a single move: name the visible first effect, then name the invisible later effects the visible one hid. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay draws its main contrast between two kinds of economist. The bad one restricts himself to the visible effect. What does the good economist do differently?
answer: Takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen
choices: Takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen
Reports the aggregate government multiplier for each proposed policy
Consults the historical record for identical policies in prior centuries
Weighs the immediate winners against a randomly-drawn sample of losers
context: This is the essay's programmatic sentence: the good economist FORESEES the effects the bad economist misses because they haven't happened yet. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay is built as a sequence of twelve short chapters, each a worked example of the seen/unseen method applied to a specific French policy. Which chapter opens the sequence?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The candlemakers' petition
The negative railway
The Chinese and the English
context: Chapter 1 is 'The Broken Window', built around James Goodfellow's careless son and the six-franc pane; every later chapter is another worked case. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: A famous 1850 essay about a shopkeeper's broken window was written in French. It took nine years for the first English version to appear. Why does a delay like that matter for spreading ideas?
answer: Readers in other languages cannot use the idea until someone translates it
choices: Readers in other languages cannot use the idea until someone translates it
Ideas that take longer to translate are always more true
Translated ideas lose their meaning within one year
Countries reject any book more than one year old
context: William Ballantyne Hodgson (1815-1880), Scottish educational reformer and free-trader, produced the 1859 English edition; George B. de Huszar's Liberty Fund translation (1964) is the modern standard. Source: oll.libertyfund.org/titles/bastiat-selected-essays-on-political-economy.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay was kept in continuous American print starting in 1946 by a New York classical-liberal institute co-founded that same year by Leonard Read and Henry Hazlitt. Which institute kept it in print?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education
The Cato Institute
The Mises Institute
The Heritage Foundation

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay found its most famous 20th-century restatement in a short 1946 American book. question: A U.S. president in the 1980s cut the top income tax rate from 70% all the way down to 28%. Supporters said lower rates would push people to work more and start more businesses. What theory says lower rates can sometimes raise MORE total tax money?

question: At a Conservative Research Department meeting in the summer of 1975, Margaret Thatcher interrupted a speaker urging a middle way. She pulled a book from her handbag, banged it on the table, and said 'This is what we believe.' Which book did Thatcher slam on the table?

question: In April 1947, Friedrich Hayek brought 36 free-market scholars to a hotel in a Swiss mountain village. Ludwig von Mises, Milton Friedman, Karl Popper, and Lionel Robbins were among them. They founded a society that linked free-market thinkers for the next 40 years. What is it called?

The three distractors are real organisations of very different politics: the Fabian Society is British democratic socialist (founded 1884), the Bilderberg Group is a private policy conference (founded 1954), and the Trilateral Commission is a US-Europe-Japan policy body (founded 1973). question: In the 1980s, the British government sold its national phone company to the public. More than two million small savers bought shares. What is the general name for a government selling a state-owned business to private owners?

British Rail, the Post Office, and the National Coal Board all remained in public ownership through the Thatcher years -- the coal board actively so, since it was the government's opponent in the miners' strike of 1984-85. British Gas followed in 1986 with the famous 'Tell Sid' campaign; British Airways in 1987. Source: Institute for Government, 'The Privatisation of British Telecom (1984).'

question: A big coal miners' union in Britain went on strike for a whole year in the 1980s. The workers finally ran out of money and had to go back to work with no deal. What lesson does this show about strikes as a tool?

Jack Jones led the TGWU in the 1970s; Vic Feather was TUC general secretary; Rodney Bickerstaffe led NUPE and later UNISON. None led the 1984-85 miners' strike. Source: Wikipedia, 1984-1985 United Kingdom miners' strike.

question: In October 1986, Britain dropped many old rules on the London Stock Exchange. Fixed fees ended. Foreign firms could now join, and paper trading moved onto computer screens. What do we call removing rules like this to open up a market?

Source: Wikipedia, Big Bang (financial markets).

question: In 1979 the top British income tax rate was 83 percent. By 1988 it had been cut all the way down to 40 percent. What do supporters of big rate cuts argue happens when the tax rate on high earners drops sharply?

question: For most of the 20th century, big-government planning was the mainstream idea in universities. question: A former fighter pilot read a book by an Austrian economist warning that big government planning leads to tyranny. He asked the author how to fight back. The advice: don't run for office; win the war of ideas from outside by starting a think tank. Why is that strategy powerful?

The three distractors are real organisations of adjacent politics: the Adam Smith Institute (founded 1977) was a later free-market think-tank; the Centre for Policy Studies was founded by Keith Joseph and Thatcher herself in 1974; the Fabian Society is the century-old British socialist think-tank. question: The 1920s stock boom ended in a two-day panic in New York. The worst two days got nicknames using a color and a weekday. Which pair of days marked the crash?

question: The date the pre-crash Dow peak of 381 was first regained by the same index -- after the 1929 fall, the Depression years, World War II, and the postwar boom -- was a landmark for anyone who had held stocks since 1929. In what decade did the Dow finally recover to its September 1929 peak?

question: Hayek's health had been poor in the years before the 1974 prize, and friends reported the recognition genuinely reinvigorated him. His final book, published in 1988 when he was 89, is a sustained argument against socialism as an intellectual and moral system. What is the book titled?

question: After the dot-com bust, Alan Greenspan's Fed cut its main interest rate to a low level. It held the rate there for a full year, from June 2003 to June 2004. That fed the housing boom that peaked in 2006. What did Greenspan cut the rate to in June 2003?

question: After the 2008 crash, the Fed cut rates to zero and began buying huge amounts of bonds. It ran three rounds of buying from 2008 to 2012. The Fed's balance sheet grew from under $1 trillion to over $4 trillion by 2014. What is the one-phrase name for this buying program?

Investment-grade bonds -75%, corporate credit -70%, and municipal bonds -65%
context: The speculative-asset tier -- long-duration growth stocks, crypto, meme stocks -- corrected hardest as rates rose. Real estate and broad equities were stickier because Powell's 2022-23 hikes came after the peak and did not fully unwind earlier gains. Source: Grokipedia 'Everything bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: A government runs out of money. It seizes land from a big organization inside its own country and prints paper money saying 'this money is backed by that land.' What is the danger of this kind of paper money?
answer: The government can just print more whenever it wants, so the money loses value
choices: The government can just print more whenever it wants, so the money loses value
The land will always keep the money valuable
Only the organization loses out, not regular people
Paper money is always safer than gold
context: The Assembly's November 2 1789 decree nationalized the property of the Church in France to serve as backing for a new currency. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1789, the French Revolution issued a new paper money. Each note was a legal claim on Church land the state had seized. The paper money had one name. What was it called?
answer: The assignat
choices: The assignat
The livre tournois
The louis d'or
The franc
context: The name came from the French verb 'assigner' -- each note was assigned against specific land parcels for redemption. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: France's first paper money, the assignats, came out in late 1789. The first batch was 400 million livres, and the Assembly swore it would be the only one. By 1795 the total in use was a very different figure. What did the total reach?
answer: Over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit
choices: Over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit
About 2 billion livres, roughly 5 times the promised limit
About 800 million livres, roughly double the promised limit
Just under 400 million livres, exactly the promised limit
context: Every subsequent Convention and Directory added new issues to cover expenses. By late 1795 the outstanding stock exceeded 40 billion livres of face value. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: Soon, French farmers and traders refused paper money and asked for gold coin. The revolutionary state did not cut back on paper. Instead, it raised the legal penalty. What was the top penalty for treating gold as worth more than paper?
answer: Death
choices: Death
Prison for one year
A fine of 100 livres
Public flogging
context: The Convention's 1793-94 anti-hoarding laws carried capital punishment for those who refused assignats at face value or hoarded specie. Legal coercion did not restore confidence in the paper. Source: Andrew Dickson White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: By 1796 an assignat was worth about one thousandth of its face value. The Directory withdrew the currency and attempted a fresh start with a new paper money supposedly backed by the same land. What was the replacement called?
answer: The mandat territorial
choices: The mandat territorial
The new assignat
The livre revolutionary
The franc germinal
context: The mandats territoriaux were introduced in March 1796 and collapsed even faster than the assignats they replaced, losing 97% of value within months. Napoleon later restored specie-based currency with the franc germinal in 1803. Source: Grokipedia 'Mandat territorial' (2026-09-05).

question: The Assignat crash was France's second try at a national paper money in less than a hundred years. The first try ended in a 1720 crash in Paris, run by a Scottish schemer. Whose plan was that first try?
answer: John Law's Banque Royale and Mississippi Company
choices: John Law's Banque Royale and Mississippi Company
Jean-Baptiste Colbert's royal treasury
Cardinal Richelieu's tax edicts
Necker's compte rendu
context: France tried paper money in 1716-1720 under John Law, saw it collapse, and stayed off paper for the next seventy years. The Assignat was the second full experiment -- same country, same result. Source: Grokipedia 'John Law (economist)' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1912 an American historian wrote a short but strong book. It warned his own country about a French paper-money crash from more than a hundred years before. Why do writers today keep pointing back to that French story?
answer: It shows what happens when a government prints too much paper money too fast
choices: It shows what happens when a government prints too much paper money too fast
It proved that only gold coins can ever be used as money
It caused France to ban paper money worldwide
It made French bread cheaper for two full years
context: Andrew Dickson White was Cornell's co-founder and first president, and his 1912 book Fiat Money Inflation in France has been in print continuously since. Source: Grokipedia 'Andrew Dickson White' (2026-09-05).

question: Andrew Dickson White's 1912 study of the Assignat episode concluded with a line still quoted by Austrian economists. Which conclusion did he draw?
answer: No government could make paper worth as much as gold when there was more paper than the land could redeem
choices: No government could make paper worth as much as gold when there was more paper than the land could redeem
Paper money can succeed if backed by patriotic sentiment
Only unlimited legal-tender enforcement can preserve currency value
The failure of paper money in France was due to foreign interference
context: White's book documented every mechanism the Revolution used -- legal tender laws, price controls, capital punishment for speculators -- and their uniform failure once the paper supply outran the backing. Source: White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: During the French Revolution, the government printed huge amounts of paper money. When it lost value, they tried price controls, made refusing the paper illegal, and even executed 'hoarders.' Prices kept climbing. Which later inflation episode used the same playbook and failed the same way?
answer: Weimar Germany 1921-1923
choices: Weimar Germany 1921-1923
The 1944-1971 Bretton Woods system
The 1930s British sterling area
The 19th-century Latin Monetary Union
context: Every hyperinflating government reaches for the same tools: legal tender laws, wage and price controls, criminal penalties for currency skepticism. And every one fails for the same reason -- the underlying money-printing is untouched. Source: White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: Bastiat would read the Assignat episode as a case where a visible near-term gain hides a systematic destruction that shows up later. Which pairing best captures the seen-and-unseen contrast?
answer: Seen: legal-tender laws and price controls; Unseen: goods vanishing from shops and savers wiped out
choices: Seen: legal-tender laws and price controls; Unseen: goods vanishing from shops and savers wiped out
Seen: rising real wages; Unseen: falling unemployment
Seen: increased tax revenue; Unseen: lower interest rates
Seen: growing exports; Unseen: falling imports
context: Bastiat's frame: the visible policy tools look decisive; the invisible costs -- black markets, empty shelves, evaporated savings -- are the actual result. The Assignat is a textbook illustration published 40 years after Bastiat's death. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In a 1912 book on money, an Austrian economist made this claim. Money must have had some other use before it became money. If not, no one could know what it was worth on its first day. Which Austrian economist made this claim?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger
Friedrich Hayek
Murray Rothbard
context: Mises presented the Regression Theorem in 'The Theory of Money and Credit' (1912). Menger had proposed the general theory of money's emergence (1892); Hayek and Rothbard later extended Mises's work. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: In Austrian economics, Mises made an argument. He said money must have had some other use before it became money. His argument has a name. What is it called?
answer: the Regression Theorem
choices: the Regression Theorem
the Calculation Debate
the Praxeological Axiom
the Time-Preference Theorem
context: The Regression Theorem is Mises's 1912 argument. The Calculation Debate is Mises's separate 1920 case against socialism; praxeology is his general methodology; time-preference is a distinct concept in Bohm-Bawerkian capital theory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: Some Austrian economists said Bitcoin should never have caught on as money. They said money must start as a useful item first, like gold or salt. Bitcoin had no prior use. What did Bitcoin end up showing about that idea?
answer: Digital scarcity alone can give something monetary value
choices: Digital scarcity alone can give something monetary value
Money always needs a government to declare it legal
Gold is the only true form of money
Money only works if it is backed by silver
context: Frank Shostak, longtime Mises Institute scholar, argued Bitcoin failed the Regression Theorem and was therefore a bubble. Robert Murphy later took the opposite (pro-Bitcoin) side; Peter Boettke is at George Mason; Israel Kirzner works on entrepreneurship not monetary theory. Source: https://mises.org/profile/frank-shostak.

question: In the 2010s, Frank Shostak studied Bitcoin using the Regression Theorem. He drew a direct conclusion. What did he predict about Bitcoin's future?
answer: that Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that would eventually collapse
choices: that Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that would eventually collapse
that Bitcoin would become the world's dominant reserve currency by 2020
that Bitcoin should be adopted by central banks as a reserve asset
that Bitcoin's value was purely a matter of government regulation
context: Shostak's conclusion from applying the Regression Theorem as he read it: Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that must eventually collapse. He did not predict reserve-currency status, central-bank adoption, or a regulation-only explanation. Source: Shostak Mises Wire articles 2013-15.

question: Younger Austrian economists pushed back on Frank Shostak. Saifedean Ammous, Peter St Onge, and others led the reply. They said Shostak had missed something about Bitcoin's real early days. What did the Ammous side claim?
answer: that Bitcoin did have a prior non-monetary use -- a cypherpunk collectible cryptographers valued for the technical achievement itself
choices: that Bitcoin did have a prior non-monetary use -- a cypherpunk collectible cryptographers valued for the technical achievement itself
that the Regression Theorem does not apply to any digital currency by definition, so Bitcoin sits outside its scope
that Bitcoin had an implicit government-backing guarantee from the start through federal law-enforcement action
that Mises himself would have retracted the Regression Theorem if he had lived to see Bitcoin's first two years
context: The Ammous/St Onge response: in Bitcoin's earliest days it functioned as a cypherpunk collectible whose non-monetary use was the technical curiosity itself; that initial demand satisfied the theorem's requirement. The other options are not what the pro-Bitcoin Austrians argued. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8-9.

question: Ammous said Bitcoin does fit the Regression Theorem. He pointed to one deal as the moment Bitcoin went from a hobby item to real money for goods. Which deal marks that turning point?
answer: the 10,000-BTC pizza purchase of May 22, 2010
choices: the 10,000-BTC pizza purchase of May 22, 2010
the January 3, 2009 genesis block
the October 31, 2008 white paper
the January 2013 Cyprus banking crisis
context: Ammous points to Laszlo Hanyecz's May 22, 2010 pizza trade as the dateable transition point from cypherpunk collectible to medium of exchange for physical goods. The genesis block and white paper are pre-money events; the Cyprus crisis (March 2013) is later. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8.

question: By about what year did most Austrian economists agree with the Ammous side? Most now accept that Bitcoin fits the Regression Theorem when read correctly.
answer: by roughly 2018-2020
choices: by roughly 2018-2020
by roughly 2012
by roughly 2025
by roughly 2030
context: The dispute was broadly resolved in the modern Austrian community by around 2018-2020, with working economists like Ammous, Bob Murphy, Peter St Onge, Vijay Boyapati having converged on the pro-Bitcoin reading. Shostak has kept his position. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers 2015-20; Bob Murphy Show archive.

question: Some Austrian economists argue that anything used as money must have started with some other use first -- like gold, which was valued for jewelry long before it became coins. Why does Bitcoin make people debate this old rule?
answer: Bitcoin had no other use before people started trading it, yet it still became money
choices: Bitcoin had no other use before people started trading it, yet it still became money
Bitcoin can only be spent inside a single video game
Bitcoin was invented by an old French king
Bitcoin coins are actually made of solid gold
context: Robert Murphy hosts the Bob Murphy Show and has featured the Bitcoin/Regression Theorem debate extensively. Sowell is not an Austrian and does not run a Bitcoin podcast; Friedman was a monetarist, died 2006; Samuelson was a Keynesian, died 2009. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_P._Murphy.

question: One writer looked back at the Shostak-Ammous fight and said the lesson goes past Bitcoin itself. Which broader reasoning move does the story teach about how a serious school of thought should treat a new real-world case?
answer: That even a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and the resolution comes by looking harder at the historical record
choices: That even a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and the resolution comes by looking harder at the historical record
That any internal disagreement inside a school of thought discredits the whole tradition and reveals its foundational theorems as unable to survive scrutiny
That founding texts should be treated as fixed and never re-examined against new empirical cases, since re-examination undermines the tradition's authority
That new empirical cases should always be rejected if they conflict with existing theory, since preserving theoretical purity is more valuable than case-by-case revision
context: The dispute-recognition move: internal disagreement is a sign of a live tradition; the resolution came from re-examining Bitcoin's actual early history rather than reinterpreting Mises's 1912 text. The other options are opposite reasoning moves that would have prevented the resolution. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard.

question: Austrian economists spent a century arguing that governments always debase paper money, and that only a truly scarce, hard-to-counterfeit asset (once, gold) protects savers. Bitcoiners say the same case now fits a new asset. Which property of Bitcoin carries that Austrian case?
answer: Its fixed 21-million cap plus proof-of-work makes it costly to create and impossible to inflate
choices: Its fixed 21-million cap plus proof-of-work makes it costly to create and impossible to inflate
Its friendly logo makes people want to save in it rather than spend it
Its use of the internet makes it faster than paper checks in the mail
Its price rises whenever the Federal Reserve prints more dollars
context: Peter St Onge's academic writing (papers 2015 onward) is the standard bridge between the Mises-Rothbard tradition and modern Bitcoin economics. Shostak took the opposite position; Block and Hulsmann have been publicly ambivalent. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_St._Onge.

question: A bunch of banks made bad bets on bonds that lost value. To keep them from failing, the country's central bank started a program that let them borrow money using those bad bonds as collateral. What is this kind of central-bank rescue usually called?
answer: An emergency lending facility
choices: An emergency lending facility
A public works program
A stimulus check
A trust fund
context: The BTFP was announced March 12 2023 as part of the emergency response to the SVB and Signature failures. It offered one-year loans to US-chartered banks against posted collateral of Treasuries, agency debt, or MBS. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: A bank owns bonds only worth 80 cents on the dollar right now. The central bank lets the bank borrow using those bonds as collateral -- but counts them as worth the full 100 cents. Why do critics call this a hidden bailout?
answer: The central bank is pretending the bonds are worth more than the market says
choices: The central bank is pretending the bonds are worth more than the market says
The bank has to pay a huge interest rate
The government is buying the bonds outright
The bank must sell all its assets first
context: Par valuation meant a 10-year Treasury bought at 1.5% yield when 10-year yields were 4% could be pledged at 100 cents on the dollar rather than roughly 80 cents. The Fed was accepting underwater bonds at their pre-loss face value. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: When the Federal Reserve loans money to a bank, it takes bonds from the bank as collateral. Normally the Fed looks at what those bonds could actually sell for today, then trims that number a bit more for safety. What is this normal practice called?
answer: Collateral is valued at market price, typically with a haircut
choices: Collateral is valued at market price, typically with a haircut
Collateral is valued at book value with no haircut
Collateral is valued at par regardless of market conditions
Collateral is valued at whichever is lower of book or market
context: The traditional Discount Window values collateral at market minus a haircut, ensuring the Fed is over-collateralized. BTFP's departure from this norm was explicit -- and explicitly a subsidy to banks whose portfolios had lost value. Source: Grokipedia 'Discount window' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2023 the Fed lent banks money using their bonds as collateral, valued at what banks originally paid, not today's lower price. Critics said it worked just like the Fed's earlier bond-buying programs, known as quantitative easing or QE. What nickname did they give the new program?
answer: QE by another name
choices: QE by another name
The banker's discount
Stealth capital injection
The regulatory rebate
context: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, Lyn Alden, Jim Bianco and other analysts publicly called BTFP 'QE by another name.' The Fed's balance sheet was rising against the announced quantitative tightening program because banks were borrowing directly from the BTFP window. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023 the Fed set up an emergency loan program to lend cash to banks whose bond holdings had lost value after interest rates rose. Borrowing under the program grew fast. About how much had banks borrowed from it at its peak in early 2024?
answer: About $167 billion
choices: About $167 billion
About $25 billion
About $500 billion
About $1 trillion
context: BTFP borrowings peaked at roughly $167 billion in early 2024. Every dollar borrowed under BTFP was a dollar of implicit rate-cycle-loss coverage for the borrowing bank. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 releases 2024).

question: The Fed can only set up special emergency loan programs when things are very bad. That was the case in March 2020 and again in March 2023. When the Fed reaches for that power, what does it usually tell the country?
answer: Something is seriously wrong and the Fed is trying to stop a panic
choices: Something is seriously wrong and the Fed is trying to stop a panic
The economy is booming and the Fed wants to slow it down
Congress has just passed a routine yearly budget
The dollar has been officially replaced with a new currency
context: Section 13(3), dating to 1932, permits Fed lending to non-bank borrowers in 'unusual and exigent circumstances.' Its 2020 and 2023 uses established the highest cadence of invocation in the section's history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2023, after several banks failed, the Fed set up a new short-term loan program. It let banks borrow using their bonds as backup, even bonds that had lost a lot of value. Why does a new rescue like this worry critics of the Fed?
answer: Banks may take bigger risks in the future, expecting another rescue
choices: Banks may take bigger risks in the future, expecting another rescue
Emergency programs cause every bank to close down
It forces the Fed to sell off its office buildings
It makes banks raise interest rates on savings accounts
context: BTFP expired on March 11 2024, one year after its launch. Outstanding balances continued to be paid down, but no new borrowings were permitted after that date. The precedent, however, stands. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: In several crises the Fed has taken bonds from banks as loan backup at a price higher than the bonds could sell for. What is the risk when a central bank acts like shaky assets are worth more than they really are?
answer: It hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing
choices: It hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing
It doubles the value of every bond overnight
It shrinks the money supply on purpose
It forces all banks to sell their buildings
context: The 2008 Term Auction Facility (TAF) was the previous precedent for accepting collateral at above market value. BTFP was in effect a re-run of that mechanism, calibrated to bond-loss stress rather than to broader liquidity strain. Source: Grokipedia 'Term Auction Facility' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023 the Federal Reserve started a lending program (the Bank Term Funding Program, or BTFP) that let banks borrow using bonds worth less than face value -- but the Fed accepted them at full face value. Which 'seen vs unseen' reading best captures what that program really did?
answer: Seen: it steadied the banks. Unseen: it subsidized losses the Fed's own low-rate policy had caused.
choices: Seen: it steadied the banks. Unseen: it subsidized losses the Fed's own low-rate policy had caused.
Seen: rising interest rates. Unseen: falling exports.
Seen: growing employment. Unseen: shrinking productivity.
Seen: a broad recovery. Unseen: a narrow crisis in one region.
context: The banks had bought long bonds at low rates because the Fed's earlier policy made them attractive. When the same Fed's tightening exposed those bonds to loss, the BTFP quietly reimbursed the losses. The whole cycle -- create the incentive, expose the loss, cover the loss -- was internal to Fed choices. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: The Federal Reserve's 2023 emergency lending program (the Bank Term Funding Program, or BTFP) formally ended in March 2024. Why do critics say ending the program does not undo the precedent it set?
answer: Every bank now knows the Fed will lend against bad bond portfolios in the next crisis too
choices: Every bank now knows the Fed will lend against bad bond portfolios in the next crisis too
The Fed announced it will never offer another emergency loan to any commercial bank
Interest rates will never rise again, so bank bond losses cannot recur
Ending the program proves the Fed has given up on all rescue tools forever
context: The BTFP ran its course but its precedent is now baked into every bank's implicit risk framework. Duration mismatch is less risky when the central bank has demonstrated willingness to cover the loss. Moral hazard accumulates one precedent at a time. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: The government starts giving every college student $10,000 in aid to help with tuition. What tends to happen to tuition prices in the years after?
answer: Tuition prices go up by about the same amount
choices: Tuition prices go up by about the same amount
Tuition prices fall because students have more money
Tuition prices stay exactly the same forever
Colleges refund the extra aid to families
context: William Bennett was Reagan's Secretary of Education (1985-88). His 1987 NYT essay 'Our Greedy Colleges' launched what came to be called the Bennett Hypothesis. Source: nytimes.com/1987/02/18 (Bennett op-ed).

question: In 1987, William Bennett made a claim. It now bears his name as a hypothesis. He said extra federal college aid mostly flows to which group?
answer: Colleges, through higher tuition
choices: Colleges, through higher tuition
Students, through lower net cost
Federal loan servicers, through fees
State governments, through matching grants
context: The Bennett Hypothesis: subsidies to a demand-side party (student) can be substantially captured by the supply-side party (college) when supply is constrained and demand is inelastic. Source: Bennett, NYT (1987).

question: US federal student loan debt grew a lot from the early 1990s through 2023. About what dollar total does it stand at in the mid-2020s?
answer: About $1.7 trillion
choices: About $1.7 trillion
About $170 billion
About $17 trillion
About $170 million
context: Total federal student loan debt grew from ~$100B in the 1990s to ~$1.7T in the early-to-mid 2020s. The debt is largely the mirror image of the tuition inflation the Bennett Hypothesis predicts. Source: newyorkfed.org (Household Debt and Credit Report).

question: From 1978 to 2018, US public four-year college tuition rose about 213% in real terms. Private four-year tuition rose about 129%. This growth matched steady rises in one type of federal money. Which type?
answer: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
choices: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
Federal defense procurement contracts
Federal highway trust fund grants
Federal agriculture price supports
context: The tuition rise tracks federal aid expansion tightly -- the 1965 Higher Education Act reauthorizations, the 1992 direct-loan program, and the 2010 elimination of private-lender intermediation each expanded federal aid. Source: nces.ed.gov (tuition historical series); collegeboard.org (Trends in Student Aid).

question: A 2015 New York Fed study looked at what happens when the government hands out more student loans. When federal loans went up by a dollar, what did the researchers find happened to college sticker tuition?
answer: A $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition
choices: A $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition
A $1 increase in loans led to about a $0.05 decrease in tuition
A $1 increase in loans led to about a $2 decrease in net cost
A $1 increase in loans produced no measurable tuition change
context: Lucca + Nadauld + Shen, New York Fed Staff Report 733 (2015, revised 2019). The 60-cent tuition pass-through is a direct market-mechanism confirmation of the Bennett Hypothesis using discontinuities in loan-limit rules. Source: newyorkfed.org (staff report 733).

question: Two economists built a computer model of US college tuition from 1987 to 2010. They tested how much of the huge tuition rise came from Washington making more student aid money available. Roughly what share did their model blame on the aid expansion?
answer: Essentially all of it
choices: Essentially all of it
About one-quarter
About half
None of it
context: Gordon + Hedlund's model attribution was approximately 106% of the observed rise -- essentially all of it, with a slight overshoot other model features offset. Note the model dependency in interpreting the exact number. Source: NBER Working Paper 21967 (Gordon + Hedlund 2016).

question: Colleges spent a lot of the new loan money on more staff, not more teachers. From 1987 to 2011 the number of US college students grew by 50%. Administrative staff grew by about what share?
answer: About 87 percent
choices: About 87 percent
About 15 percent
About 200 percent
About 5 percent
context: The Delta Cost Project and GAO documented administrative-staff growth of ~87% from 1987 to 2011, well ahead of the ~50% student-enrollment rise. The aid revenue built bureaucracy rather than classrooms. Source: deltacostproject.org (Trends in College Spending reports).

question: For decades the price of college in America has risen far faster than most other prices. What is the most common explanation critics give for the runaway costs?
answer: Cheap government-backed student loans let colleges keep raising tuition
choices: Cheap government-backed student loans let colleges keep raising tuition
Fewer people wanting to attend college each year
Falling wages for professors and staff
A shortage of paper for printing textbooks
context: Richard Vedder, Going Broke by Degree: Why College Costs Too Much (AEI Press, 2004). Vedder's book presented the tuition-inflation / administrative-bloat pattern years before the Lucca and Gordon-Hedlund quantitative work. Source: aei.org (Vedder 2004).

question: The Bennett Hypothesis pattern shows up in more than college costs. Where else does the same idea show up in US policy: a subsidy to buyers that gets eaten by tight supply?
answer: Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets
choices: Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets
Federal wildlife-refuge acquisitions
National Park entrance fees
Federal snow-plowing grants
context: Section 8 vouchers substantially raise landlord rent capture in constrained markets. Similar mechanisms operate in health-insurance subsidies (premium inflation) and the 2008-10 first-time homebuyer credit (largely captured in seller prices). Source: Collinson + Ganong on Section 8; Zwick + Malani on homebuyer credit.

question: The Bennett Hypothesis gives an analyst a check to run before any new buyer-side subsidy is approved. What question should the analyst ask about the supply side?
answer: Who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity
choices: Who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity
Whether the supplier's headquarters is unionized
Whether the supplier accepts credit cards
Whether the supplier files its taxes electronically
context: The reasoning move: when a subsidy is proposed, ask whether the supply side is constrained and whether the specific suppliers have pricing power. If yes, expect substantial subsidy capture through prices. Source: Bennett (1987); Lucca + Nadauld + Shen (2015).

question: The three ways the Bennett Hypothesis works in college can fit in one sentence. Which sentence best captures what federal student aid does overall?
answer: It builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity
choices: It builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity
It reduces the total price paid per credit hour
It shifts students into cheaper community colleges
It eliminates the need for private philanthropy
context: The three-part mechanism: demand-side pricing effect, administrative expansion of aid-funded revenue, and amenity-competition arms race in place of price competition. All three point in the same direction. Source: Gordon + Hedlund (2016); Vedder (2004); Delta Cost Project reports.

question: One night in 1961, the East German government sealed the line between East and West Berlin. First they used barbed wire. Then they put up a concrete wall that stood for 28 years. What did they build?
answer: The Berlin Wall
choices: The Berlin Wall
The Iron Curtain
The Elbe Line
The Warsaw Line
context: Walter Ulbricht's East German government built the initial barrier overnight August 12-13, 1961. It grew into a concrete wall encircling West Berlin, standing until November 9, 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: The Berlin Wall ran for a substantial distance around West Berlin. Roughly how long was the full barrier?
answer: About 155 kilometers
choices: About 155 kilometers
About 15 kilometers
About 1,550 kilometers
About 500 kilometers
context: The Wall was roughly 155 km (96 miles) long, encircling West Berlin -- not running along the East-West German border. It included concrete, watchtowers, a 'death strip', anti-vehicle trenches, and patrol roads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: The Berlin Wall in East Germany was built during the Cold War. Its watchtower guns did not point west toward the free countries. They pointed the other way. Which direction did the guns actually point?
answer: East, at East Germans
choices: East, at East Germans
West, toward free Berlin
Straight up, at aircraft
Both directions equally
context: The Wall's fortifications faced INWARD -- guns and mines directed at East Germans trying to leave, not westward at any invading force. The design fact is the argument: the state had to wall its own citizens in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: East Germany built the Wall in 1961 because its people had been walking out. Between 1949 and 1961 many East Germans left for the West through open Berlin — more than a fifth of the country. About how many had left?
answer: About 3.5 million
choices: About 3.5 million
About 350,000
About 35 million
About 35,000
context: About 3.5 million East Germans left through Berlin between 1949 and August 1961 -- roughly a fifth of the country's population. The Wall was built to stop the flow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: During the 28 years the Wall stood, people died trying to cross it. What is the Berlin Wall Memorial's documented figure for confirmed deaths at the Wall itself?
answer: About 140
choices: About 140
About 14
About 1,400
Over 14,000
context: The Berlin Wall Memorial documents about 140 confirmed deaths at the Wall itself; several hundred more died at the wider inter-German border. The first was Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961); the last was Chris Gueffroy (February 5, 1989). Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: East Germany's communist government ran a huge secret police. It had one officer for every 180 citizens, plus twice as many unpaid spies. What does that huge amount of spying tell us about how the rulers held on?
answer: It had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control
choices: It had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control
Most citizens loved the government and rarely needed watching
The police mainly caught foreign spies from the West
The system worked because everyone freely volunteered to inform
context: Ministerium fuer Staatssicherheit -- Ministry for State Security -- gave East Germany the highest surveillance-to-population ratio of any modern state. Source: bstu.de (Stasi Records Archive).

question: The Berlin Wall split communist East Berlin from the free West for nearly 30 years. Within days of its being built, people started dying trying to escape -- some by jumping from apartment windows in the border zone. What does that very first escape death show?
answer: People were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside
choices: People were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside
Escape attempts were actually very rare from the start
The wall was quietly popular with most East Berliners
The wall stopped nobody from crossing in either direction
context: Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961) died jumping from her fourth-floor Bernauer Strasse apartment on the border. She is the first of the Berlin Wall Memorial's documented victims. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: The Berlin Wall was built and guarded to stop people from moving in one direction only. In February 1989, just months before the Wall fell, guards shot the last person killed trying to cross. In which direction were people trying to escape?
answer: From communist East Berlin to free West Berlin
choices: From communist East Berlin to free West Berlin
From free West Berlin into communist East Berlin
From East Berlin north into Denmark
In both directions about equally at all times
context: Chris Gueffroy (February 5, 1989) was shot trying to cross to West Berlin. His death drew international protest and East German policy shifted; his was the last shooting fatality at the Wall. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: After East Germany fell in 1990, ordinary East Germans got the right to read the secret files their old government's spies had kept about them. Why does opening files like this matter after a police state falls?
answer: It lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known
choices: It lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known
It makes the old spies work harder in the future
It automatically arrests everyone named in the files
It hides the truth so the country can move on faster
context: The Stasi Unterlagen Gesetz (Stasi Records Act, December 1991) established the office administering the archive and gave individuals the right to read their own files. The former ministry headquarters at Normannenstrasse is now the Stasi Museum. Source: bstu.de.

question: The Wall physically illustrated one core Austrian argument about the calculation debate. Which argument does 3.5 million pre-1961 East German exits and the inward-facing wall demonstrate at physical scale?
answer: When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in
choices: When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in
The market side always subsidizes the planned side
Planning works well as long as walls are built early
Cold War rivalry drove all migration flows
context: The argument is exit-as-verdict: given free comparison across an open border for twelve years, the population had voted with its feet. The Wall's inward-facing design is the calculation-debate answer made physical. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: The Wall's construction and dismantling frame the exact 28-year interval when Berlin was a divided city. In what years did the Wall stand?
context: The Wall was built August 12-13, 1961 and fell November 9, 1989 -- 28 years and 3 months. The demolition was completed by the early 1990s; small segments remain as memorials, and a double-cobblestone line traces the former path across the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: Around 2019 a short three-word meme took over Bitcoin Twitter. It became the standard reply to any headline about a bank freeze, a money-printing binge, or a currency crash. Which phrase?
answer: 'Bitcoin fixes this'
choices: 'Bitcoin fixes this'
'To the moon'
'Diamond hands'
'When Lambo?'
context: Popularized by Michael Saylor and thousands of others. Half meme, half genuine argument that most modern financial pathologies trace to monetary debasement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: Bitcoin fans often say they want nothing to do with a much bigger online scene full of thousands of copycat coins and scams. What broader label do they try to distance Bitcoin from?
answer: 'Crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins
choices: 'Crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins
The traditional-finance industry
The federal-reserve academic literature
Central-bank digital currencies
context: Bitcoin advocates argue Bitcoin is monetary infrastructure with a specific design; altcoins are, in their view, mostly speculative tokens or venture-capital exit vehicles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A 'sat' or satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest divisible unit. How many satoshis make up one Bitcoin?
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC. Named after Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto. Naming the smallest unit for the creator is analogous to naming a small currency unit for a founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Satoshi_(unit).

question: Some Bitcoin fans buy a small fixed amount on a regular schedule, like every week or every month, no matter what the current price is doing. Bitcoin community members use a slang phrase for this steady buying habit. What is it commonly called?
answer: Stacking sats
choices: Stacking sats
Rebalancing the portfolio
Hedging the position
Rolling the futures
context: Formally this is dollar-cost averaging. The community identity built around stacking emphasizes the discipline of not trying to time the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: In Bitcoin online communities there is a dismissive slogan aimed at people who refuse to buy any Bitcoin at all: 'Have fun staying poor.' What is the slogan's core claim about people who hold only regular dollars?
answer: Inflation slowly eats dollar savings, so refusing Bitcoin leaves them poorer over time
choices: Inflation slowly eats dollar savings, so refusing Bitcoin leaves them poorer over time
Bitcoin owners are legally required to give money to skeptics
The government pays Bitcoin owners a monthly bonus
Only rich people are allowed to buy Bitcoin
context: Cobie is the pseudonym of Jordan Fish, a British Bitcoin and altcoin trader who co-hosts the UpOnly podcast. The slogan expresses the impatience of holders who have watched skeptics predict Bitcoin's death for years while the network keeps functioning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: The Bitcoin community has its own habits and rituals: stacking sats, running nodes, going to meetups, holding conferences. A Nobel-winning economist would call this a modern example of one idea he defined. Which idea?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order
choices: Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order
John Maynard Keynes's animal spirits
Milton Friedman's permanent-income hypothesis
Paul Samuelson's revealed preference
context: Spontaneous order is Hayek's term for shared norms and institutions -- like language, common law, and open-source software -- that arise without any central planner. Bitcoin culture emerged with no central architect. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: Big Bitcoin conferences in Nashville, Miami, Prague, and Riga attract tens of thousands each year. They feel very different from a typical Wall Street investment conference. What subject dominates the keynote talks on the main stage?
answer: Talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips
choices: Talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips
Presentations of specific-price Bitcoin forecasts by regulated broker-dealers
Panels on hedge-fund short-selling strategies
Endorsements of specific altcoins by government regulators
context: The culture's emphasis on long time preference (deferring consumption today for a stronger monetary position later) and monetary-history education distinguishes the Bitcoin conference circuit from the mainstream investment-conference culture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_conference.

question: In May 2010, a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz offered 10,000 bitcoins to anyone who would send him a meal. What simple food did he ask for?
answer: two large pizzas
choices: two large pizzas
