answer: A digital file can be copied and spent twice
choices: A digital file can be copied and spent twice
Digital files are too heavy to move
Computers cannot count money
Nobody wants online money
context: David Chaum founded DigiCash in Amsterdam in 1989 to license his 1982 blind-signatures work as an anonymous digital cash system. PayPal (1998, Confinity) was e-mail money for eBay; Silk Road (2011) was a Tor darknet market; Coinbase (2012) is a modern Bitcoin exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In November 1998 a Chinese-American coder on the cypherpunk mailing list posted a two-page plan. It described digital cash with no bank, where every user kept their own copy of the ledger. What was the plan called?
answer: b-money
choices: b-money
Hashcash
bit gold
e-gold
context: Wei Dai posted 'b-money' to the cypherpunk list in November 1998. Hashcash (Adam Back, 1997) is a separate proof-of-work anti-spam scheme; bit gold (Nick Szabo, 1998) is a different cypherpunk digital-scarcity design; e-gold (Douglas Jackson, 1996) was a centralized gold-backed online payment system, not a cypherpunk proposal. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: In 1997, a British programmer proposed a simple rule. Before your computer can send any email, it must first solve a small math puzzle. The puzzle takes about half a second, and a normal person barely notices the delay. What happens to spammers who try to send a million emails a day?
answer: The puzzles would take days, so spamming stops paying
choices: The puzzles would take days, so spamming stops paying
Their emails would arrive faster than normal
The rule would only slow small senders
Spammers would ignore the rule and win anyway
context: Adam Back proposed Hashcash in 1997 as an anti-spam measure imposing a small proof-of-work stamp on each email. SpamAssassin is a Bayesian mail filter; PGP is Phil Zimmermann's email-encryption tool; bit gold is Nick Szabo's separate 1998 currency-design essay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: Adam Back built Hashcash in 1997 to fight email spam. It had one key trick that Bitcoin would later put to a new use ten years later. Which computer property did Hashcash prove could work?
answer: solving one puzzle is expensive but verifying a solution is instant
choices: solving one puzzle is expensive but verifying a solution is instant
solving is cheap but verifying is expensive
puzzles chain into a tree structure with logarithmic verification
puzzles require a trusted authority to issue
context: Hashcash proof-of-work is asymmetric: brute-force hash search is costly, but anyone can hash the answer once to check it. Satoshi adopted the same primitive as Bitcoin's mining puzzle. Tree-structured verification (Merkle trees) is a separate 1979 technique also used in Bitcoin; PoW explicitly needs no trusted authority. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: In 1998 a coder and legal scholar, who had coined the term 'smart contracts' two years earlier, posted a new design. It used chained proof-of-work puzzles to make scarce digital tokens, with no issuer setting the supply. Which cypherpunk plan was this?
answer: bit gold
choices: bit gold
b-money
DigiCash
Hashcash
context: Nick Szabo drafted bit gold in 1998 (blog post 2005); the design chained PoW puzzles into scarce digital tokens. He coined 'smart contracts' in 1996. b-money is Wei Dai's separate 1998 proposal; DigiCash is Chaum's 1989 company; Hashcash is Adam Back's 1997 anti-spam PoW. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: David Chaum's DigiCash was private and hard to fake in the early 1990s. By 1998 the company had gone bankrupt. Later cypherpunk designs tried to fix one big flaw in it. What was the flaw?
answer: the money still had to be issued by a trusted bank that could be shut down
choices: the money still had to be issued by a trusted bank that could be shut down
the cryptography relied on hash functions that were later broken
the anonymity technique required government registration of every user
the transaction fees were higher than credit-card fees
context: DigiCash's blind signatures made spending anonymous, but coins still had to be issued by a partner bank; without one, no money. That single trusted issuer became the choke point. b-money, bit gold, and later Bitcoin all specifically eliminated the trusted issuer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In 1998, Wei Dai wrote a paper describing a system called b-money. Every user kept a copy of the ledger, transactions were broadcast to the whole network, and new money came from proof-of-work. Dai openly identified two pieces he had not fully solved. Which technical gap did b-money leave open that Bitcoin's 2008 design later closed?
answer: how to reach network consensus when different users see different transaction orderings
choices: how to reach network consensus when different users see different transaction orderings
how to compress the ledger onto a single hard drive
how to convert existing dollars into b-money
how to encrypt individual transactions so third parties cannot read them
context: b-money left consensus and honesty-enforcement unsolved. Satoshi's proof-of-work plus longest-chain rule was specifically designed to resolve exactly those two problems. Ledger compression, dollar conversion, and payload encryption are separate matters. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Bitcoin's 2008 white paper is best understood as a synthesis of four earlier cypherpunk digital-cash proposals. But only two of them are cited directly in Satoshi's reference list. Which pair of proposals appears in the paper's references?
answer: b-money and Hashcash
choices: b-money and Hashcash
DigiCash and bit gold
DigiCash and Hashcash
bit gold and b-money
context: Satoshi's 2008 white paper cites Wei Dai's b-money as reference 1 and Adam Back's Hashcash as reference 6. It does not cite DigiCash (Chaum) or bit gold (Szabo) directly, though the intellectual debt is widely acknowledged. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In March 1993, cryptographer Eric Hughes wrote a founding essay for the cypherpunk mailing list. Its opening line is often quoted as the philosophical anchor of the whole cypherpunk lineage that eventually led to Bitcoin. Which sentence opens that manifesto?
answer: 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.'
choices: 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.'
'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
'Cypherpunks write code.'
'The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it.'
context: Hughes opens 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' (March 9, 1993) with this line. The 'specter' opener is Tim May's 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto; 'Cypherpunks write code' appears later within Hughes's essay as the operative motto; the routing-around-censorship line is John Gilmore's aphorism. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: In the 1990s a small group of coders started meeting. They wanted regular people to keep their messages private from big companies and the government. What tool did they push people to use?
answer: Cryptography (scrambling messages with a code)
choices: Cryptography (scrambling messages with a code)
Just ignoring the internet
Waiting for a new law
Only writing letters on paper
context: Eric Hughes hosted the fall 1992 Oakland meetings in his house. Timothy May was the retired Intel physicist; John Gilmore was Sun's fifth employee. Adam Back is a British cryptographer who joined the broader mailing list later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Back in the 1990s, some coders made secret codes to hide messages from the government. Why did they say this was so important?
answer: A government that can read all your messages can control you
choices: A government that can read all your messages can control you
Because messages take up too much room
Because computers were too slow
Because letters are cheaper than emails
context: Jude Milhon (aka 'St Jude'), Mondo 2000 writer and hacker, coined the name 'cypherpunks' at one of the early meetings. William Gibson coined 'cyberpunk' but not 'cypherpunks'; May and Hughes were among those meeting but did not coin the name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: In the early 1990s a group of code fans near San Francisco started a mailing list. They wanted strong codes to give regular people privacy from big governments and companies. What did they call themselves?
answer: The cypherpunks
choices: The cypherpunks
The hackers union
The open-source movement
The free-software foundation
context: John Gilmore hosted the cypherpunk mailing list on toad.com from his personal server. Hughes and May co-founded the community but did not host the list; Zimmermann is the PGP author. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Timothy May made enough on stock options to retire in his thirties. Then he became a full-time thinker. Where had he worked on the alpha-particle memory chip problem in the late 1970s?
answer: Intel
choices: Intel
Motorola
Texas Instruments
IBM
context: Timothy May worked at Intel; he helped solve alpha-particle contamination in DRAM chips in the late 1970s. Motorola, TI, and IBM were competitors on other semiconductor problems. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: In the 1990s, an online mailing list called the cypherpunks gathered coders, hackers, and privacy activists. They said strong encryption was the key to online freedom. What big idea did they push?
answer: Ordinary people should be able to use unbreakable codes without asking permission
choices: Ordinary people should be able to use unbreakable codes without asking permission
Only governments and militaries should be trusted with strong codes
Encryption should be banned so police can read every message
Only large banks should be allowed to use private codes
context: Julian Assange (later WikiLeaks founder) was part of the cypherpunk mailing list in the 1990s. Jobs, Berners-Lee, and Brin were building different projects and were not on the cypherpunk list. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: The cypherpunk mailing list had a short three-word motto, coined by Eric Hughes in March 1993. It drew a sharp line: only shipping real software counted, not just talk. Which motto captured that rule?
answer: 'Cypherpunks write code.'
choices: 'Cypherpunks write code.'
'Privacy above all.'
'Encrypt or die.'
'Freedom through math.'
context: 'Cypherpunks write code' comes from Hughes's March 9, 1993 A Cypherpunk's Manifesto and became the operative motto: writing working software was the only thing that mattered. The other slogans circulate in adjacent movements but are not the specific line. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: The founding cypherpunk meetings happened in Oakland for a reason. Two of the world's best cryptography programs were within driving distance. Which two universities were those?
answer: Stanford and Berkeley
choices: Stanford and Berkeley
Harvard and MIT
Caltech and UCLA
Princeton and Yale
context: Stanford (home of Diffie-Hellman and Hellman) and Berkeley (Hughes's own graduate department) were the two Bay Area cryptography centers within reach of the Oakland meetings. Harvard/MIT, Caltech/UCLA, and Princeton/Yale are in other regions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Some cypherpunk list members from the 1990s later became important to Bitcoin's technical design. Which group of four had all joined the list by the late 1990s?
answer: Adam Back, Wei Dai, Hal Finney, and Nick Szabo
choices: Adam Back, Wei Dai, Hal Finney, and Nick Szabo
Vitalik Buterin and Charlie Lee
Michael Saylor and Peter Schiff
Do Kwon and Sam Bankman-Fried
context: The mid-1990s cypherpunk list included Back (Hashcash), Dai (b-money), Finney (RPOW), and Szabo (bit gold). Buterin and Lee are 2010s crypto figures; Saylor and Schiff are separate 2000s+ figures; Kwon and SBF are 2020s crypto collapses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Fifteen years after the Oakland meetings, in October 2008, someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto posted a nine-page paper to a cryptography mailing list whose lineage traced directly back to the toad.com list. Which specific technical class of paper did Satoshi post in that message?
answer: a Bitcoin white paper describing a peer-to-peer electronic cash system with proof-of-work consensus
choices: a Bitcoin white paper describing a peer-to-peer electronic cash system with proof-of-work consensus
a proposal for a new US securities regulation covering internet-based investment platforms
an academic paper on the mathematics of prime-number distribution and the Riemann hypothesis
an anti-spam framework for consumer email extending the Hashcash and DomainKeys approaches
context: Satoshi's October 31, 2008 posting was 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' to a cryptography mailing list descended from toad.com. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: A cypherpunk historian looking back at Bitcoin's 2008 emergence from the toad.com lineage argues that the community's fifteen-year bet on one specific proposition had finally paid off in the largest possible way. Which reasoning move does the argument credit the movement for making at the founding meetings?
answer: That mathematics and code could give ordinary people privacy the government could not take away
choices: That mathematics and code could give ordinary people privacy the government could not take away
That academic conferences alone could deliver privacy without any working software
That legislative advocacy was the only viable path for privacy technology
That corporate partnerships were the correct model for delivering cryptography
context: The cypherpunk founding bet: math + code could deliver ordinary-user privacy without state permission. Bitcoin's launch is the largest single realization of that bet. Academic-conference-only, legislative, and corporate-partnership paths are exactly what the community rejected. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: A US law says a farmer cannot cut trees or build on any land where a rare animal is found. The government does not pay him for the lost value. What might a farmer do the moment he spots that rare animal on his own land?
answer: Shoot, shovel, and shut up -- so no one knows the animal was there
choices: Shoot, shovel, and shut up -- so no one knows the animal was there
Call the government right away to report it
Charge visitors money to see the animal
Move to a different state
context: The Endangered Species Act of 1973 was signed by Nixon on December 28, 1973. Uncompensated use-restriction on private land is the structural feature that generates the perverse-incentive problem discussed in this ladder. Source: fws.gov (ESA history).

question: Some rural landowners fear finding an endangered species on their land, since the rules can lock up the land. They have a folk phrase for how to react: shoot it, bury it, tell no one. What three-verb phrase names this?
answer: Shoot, shovel, and shut up
choices: Shoot, shovel, and shut up
Trap, tag, and turn in
Hide, haul, and hope
Sell, sign, and settle
context: 'Shoot, shovel, and shut up' is the widely-reported folk phrase among landowners whose properties are threatened with ESA designation. It captures the rational response to the statute's concentrated-cost structure. Source: nyt.com and reason.com coverage of ESA critiques.

question: In North Carolina, some landowners cut down their pine trees young and fast when a rare bird moved in nearby. They feared the government would lock up their land to protect the bird's home. A 2003 study spotted the pattern. Which bird was it about?
answer: The red-cockaded woodpecker
choices: The red-cockaded woodpecker
The spotted owl
The sage grouse
The whooping crane
context: Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael, 'Preemptive Habitat Destruction Under the Endangered Species Act' (Journal of Law and Economics, 2003), documented preemptive pine harvest near red-cockaded woodpecker colonies. Source: jstor.org (Lueck + Michael 2003).

question: A US law restricts what landowners can do near active nests of rare birds. Near rare woodpeckers, researchers found owners often did the opposite of what the law hoped for. What did the rule actually produce?
answer: Destruction of mature pines before the birds could arrive
choices: Destruction of mature pines before the birds could arrive
Widespread planting of new pine seedlings
Voluntary conservation easements on new tracts
Nesting-box installation programs by landowners
context: The rational landowner destroys suitable habitat BEFORE a listed species arrives, so the property does not become subject to ESA restrictions. The statute causes the habitat destruction it was designed to prevent. Source: Lueck + Michael, Journal of Law and Economics (2003).

question: A US law protects rare animals on private property, restricting what an owner can do on his own land. All Americans get a small benefit from the protection, but a handful of landowners pay very heavy costs. What is that pattern called?
answer: Concentrated costs combined with dispersed benefits
choices: Concentrated costs combined with dispersed benefits
Concentrated costs combined with concentrated benefits
Dispersed costs combined with dispersed benefits
Symmetric costs and benefits on all parties
context: The specific landowner who draws the unlucky species-discovery outcome bears a concentrated cost; species-preservation benefits are shared by everyone in dispersed form. Both this mirror and Olson's original pattern produce systematic political-economy failures. Source: Adler, 'Money or Nothing' (Boston College Law Review 2008).

question: A US law often bans landowners from using parts of their own property to protect a rare species, without paying them a cent. One reform proposal says the government should instead pay owners for the lost usage rights. What is the general name for such a paid agreement?
answer: A conservation easement
choices: A conservation easement
A property seizure order
A zoning fine
An eminent domain lawsuit
context: Jonathan Adler, 'Money or Nothing: The Adverse Environmental Consequences of Uncompensated Land-Use Controls' (Boston College Law Review, 2008). Adler argues compensation aligns landowner incentives with actual habitat preservation. Source: bc.edu/lawreview.

question: Elinor Ostrom studied how groups protect shared resources. For saving endangered species on private land, what kind of setup does her work favor?
answer: Local landowner cooperatives with genuine ownership of the conservation problem
choices: Local landowner cooperatives with genuine ownership of the conservation problem
A single federal super-agency with global jurisdiction
Pure private-property regimes with no conservation role at all
State-owned nationalized wildlife reserves replacing all private land
context: Ostrom's polycentric design principles (Governing the Commons, 1990) apply directly: local user groups with clearly defined boundaries and shared stake outperform top-down uncompensated federal listing regimes. Source: Ostrom (1990); Anderson + Leal, Free Market Environmentalism (Palgrave 2001).

question: The 'shoot, shovel, and shut up' behavior is one example of a broader class of policy failure. A regulation aims at one outcome but produces the opposite. In political-economy language, what is this class of failure called?
answer: Perverse incentives
choices: Perverse incentives
Distributional coalitions
Regulatory capture
Rent-seeking
context: Perverse-incentive failures occur when a rule creates individual incentives whose aggregate effect defeats the rule's stated purpose. The Delhi Cobra Effect, Mexico City license-plate driving restrictions, and ethanol mandates on feedstocks are related cases. Source: Sowell, Applied Economics (Basic 2007).

question: One U.S. law forbids harming certain rare animals and lets the government freeze what a private landowner can do with land where one is found -- with no payment. In real cases, owners quietly cleared their trees before a survey could find the animal. What is the public-choice lesson?
answer: If you put the whole cost of a rule on one person, they will act to avoid the rule before it hits
choices: If you put the whole cost of a rule on one person, they will act to avoid the rule before it hits
The government should ban all private ownership of land near listed species
Wildlife rules never need to consider what landowners might do next
Only the federal government should own any land where wildlife lives
context: The Adler-Lueck synthesis: uncompensated concentrated-cost regulations attract preemptive destructive behavior. Compensation aligns landowner incentives with the regulation's stated purpose. Australia's Bush Heritage Trust operates on this model. Source: Adler (2008); Lueck + Michael (2003).

question: A US law requires gasoline to contain a certain amount of fuel made from corn. Millions of acres of American corn now go into car engines, not into food. What does this rule tend to do to the price of corn as food?
answer: It makes food-corn more expensive because so much corn is used as fuel
choices: It makes food-corn more expensive because so much corn is used as fuel
It has no effect on corn prices
It makes food-corn free for shoppers
It only affects the price of gasoline
context: Abbreviated RFS. Its stated purposes were reducing dependence on imported oil and lowering greenhouse-gas emissions. Its principal beneficiaries were US corn growers and ethanol blenders (ADM, POET). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Renewable_Fuel_Standard_(United_States).

question: The Renewable Fuel Standard passed in 2005. It made growers turn a lot of corn into ethanol for fuel. By 2011, about how much of the US corn crop was going into fuel instead of food or feed?
answer: About 40 percent
choices: About 40 percent
About 5 percent
About 10 percent
About 80 percent
context: The diversion converted roughly two-fifths of the country's largest single field crop into motor-fuel input. World corn prices roughly doubled between 2006 and 2013 as a direct consequence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ethanol_fuel_in_the_United_States.

question: In January 2007 tens of thousands of people protested in a Latin American capital because the price of a staple food had roughly doubled in months. What was the staple, and where did the protests happen?
answer: Maize tortillas, in Mexico City
choices: Maize tortillas, in Mexico City
Rice, in San Salvador
Wheat bread, in Buenos Aires
Cassava flour, in Caracas
context: The Mexican tortilla-price spike tracked the US corn-price spike almost exactly. Similar food-price protests broke out in Egypt, Haiti, and other importing countries through 2007-2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: The World Bank estimated that the 2007-2008 global food-price rise pushed a specific approximate number of people back into extreme poverty. What was that number?
answer: More than 100 million
choices: More than 100 million
About 500,000
About 2 million
About 1 billion
context: The World Bank's own calculations identified more than 100 million pushed below the extreme-poverty line, mostly in food-importing countries in Africa and Asia. The scale of the international spillover is why the ethanol mandate is a Bastiat case at planetary scale. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: In 2008 an internal World Bank memo by economist Donald Mitchell attributed a large share of the 2002-2008 global food-price rise to a specific policy category. Which one?
answer: Biofuel mandates diverting food crops to fuel
choices: Biofuel mandates diverting food crops to fuel
Drought caused by anthropogenic climate change
Chinese state grain stockpiling
Panama Canal shipping bottlenecks
context: Mitchell's memo (later leaked to the press) estimated biofuel demand accounted for a large share of the price rise. Drought and oil prices also mattered; but biofuel demand was the largest policy-driven contributor and could have been reversed by legislative action alone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: A high-school student asks a Bastiatian economist how a US law about GASOLINE could cause tortilla-price riots in Mexico City. The economist points to a specific reasoning move. Which is it?
answer: Seen-versus-unseen at planetary scale: US corn diverted to fuel raises world corn prices, and food-importing countries pay the invisible cost
choices: Seen-versus-unseen at planetary scale: US corn diverted to fuel raises world corn prices, and food-importing countries pay the invisible cost
The Laffer curve applied to Mexican maize tariff revenue
The Coase theorem applied to farmer-consumer negotiations at the border
The Phillips curve applied to Mexican unemployment
context: Applied Bastiat: seen is US energy-independence talking points and Iowa corn-farm prosperity; unseen is the Guatemalan or Mexican family whose staple food now costs twice as much because of a US law about motor fuel. The dispersed costs cross national borders. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: An airplane maker's biggest rival brings out a plane that burns less fuel. Airlines start ordering the rival's plane instead of the old one. What is this kind of competitive pressure most likely to push the first company to do?
answer: Redesign its own plane to be more fuel-efficient
choices: Redesign its own plane to be more fuel-efficient
Stop making planes altogether
Raise its prices to make more money
Ignore the rival completely
context: The Airbus A320neo (New Engine Option) launched in December 2010, forcing Boeing to respond quickly with the 737 MAX derivative rather than a clean-sheet replacement. The MAX entered service in May 2017. Source: boeing.com; airbus.com.

question: An airplane company rushes out a new plane to beat a competitor. To avoid the expense of retraining pilots, it hides the redesign with a piece of software. Two planes crash and hundreds die. What does this show about cutting corners?
answer: Cutting corners to save money can cost lives
choices: Cutting corners to save money can cost lives
Software always fixes hardware problems
Pilots never need any training
Bigger engines are always safer
context: MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) was designed to compensate for the MAX's altered high-angle-of-attack pitch behavior. Its single-sensor design and hidden nature became the central certification issue. Source: House T&I Report on 737 MAX (September 2020).

question: Boeing's 737 Max jet crashed twice in five months. One went down off Indonesia in 2018 and one in Ethiopia in 2019. How many people died in the two crashes?
context: Lion Air 610 killed 189; Ethiopian 302 killed 157. Combined toll 346. Both crashes involved MCAS activation from erroneous angle-of-attack readings, with pilots unable to recover the automatic nose-down trim. Source: NTSB, KNKT (Indonesia), and ECAA (Ethiopia) final reports.

question: After two Boeing 737 Max airplane crashes in 2018 and 2019, this model of plane was banned from flying worldwide. Roughly how long did that worldwide grounding last before the plane was cleared to fly passengers again?
answer: About 20 months
choices: About 20 months
About 2 months
About 5 years
About 3 days
context: The 737 MAX was grounded worldwide from March 13, 2019 to November 18, 2020 -- approximately 20 months. Return-to-service required software revisions, additional training, and independent FAA re-certification. Source: faa.gov (737 MAX ungrounding record).

question: For 20 years before the Boeing 737 Max crashes, the FAA let Boeing's own workers sign off on safety checks for Boeing planes. What is the deep problem with a company checking its own product for the regulator?
answer: The reviewer's paycheck depends on the product passing
choices: The reviewer's paycheck depends on the product passing
The reviewer will always end up much too strict
The regulator will always ignore the results anyway
The reviewer will not understand the product being tested
context: The Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program authorized manufacturer engineers to act as FAA designees for certain certification tasks. The critical MCAS single-sensor decision and manual-omission call were made under ODA authority without independent FAA review. Source: faa.gov (ODA program history).

question: Two Boeing 737 Max planes crashed and 346 people died. A US House committee spent months looking at how the flight-control problem was hidden from regulators and airlines. What two-word phrase did the final report use to name Boeing's behavior?
answer: A culture of concealment
choices: A culture of concealment
An engineering triumph
A safety renaissance
A regulatory partnership
context: The House T&I Final Committee Report (September 16, 2020) documented what it called a 'grossly insufficient' certification process and 'a culture of concealment' at Boeing. Source: transportation.house.gov (Final 737 MAX Committee Report).

question: In 2021, the plane maker Boeing paid a large federal settlement for lying to safety regulators about its 737 Max jet. About how big was that settlement?
answer: About $2.5 billion
choices: About $2.5 billion
About $250 million
About $25 million
About $25 billion
context: Boeing agreed to a $2.5B deferred prosecution agreement with the DOJ in January 2021 for fraud on the FAA. It is one of the largest such settlements in aviation history and is treated as close to a legal admission of the regulatory-capture pattern. Source: justice.gov (Boeing DPA January 2021).

question: In January 2024 a plug-door blew out of a Boeing 737 jet in flight over Oregon. Nobody died, but the scary event renewed a specific worry about the company. Which worry was that?
answer: That cost cutting had undermined factory quality control
choices: That cost cutting had undermined factory quality control
That pilots were being paid too much money
That jet fuel prices were rising too quickly
That airport security lines were too long
context: Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 lost a plug-door in flight on January 5, 2024. The NTSB investigation revealed missing bolts and highlighted Boeing quality-control problems distinct from but adjacent to the 737 MAX certification story. Source: ntsb.gov (Flight 1282 preliminary report 2024).

question: After two 737 MAX airliner crashes, investigators found that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had let Boeing itself sign off on safety of the new plane. Public-choice writers called this a 'structural' failure, not a bribery scandal. What does 'structural' mean here?
answer: The people who actually know enough to check the design work for the company being checked
choices: The people who actually know enough to check the design work for the company being checked
Specific FAA workers were paid cash bribes by Boeing officials
Congress had banned the FAA from ever reviewing the new plane's flight software
Boeing's chief executive personally overturned FAA decisions
context: The Stigler capture prediction meets its structural limit case in aviation certification: the FAA regulates aircraft manufactured by very few US companies, and the depth of engineering knowledge required to certify a modern airliner exists overwhelmingly inside the manufacturer. ODA formalized this asymmetry. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Levine + Forrence (1990).

question: After the 737 MAX airliner crashes revealed that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had let the manufacturer sign off on its own safety review, Congress passed a reform law in late 2020. Which specific reform did that law require?
answer: Stronger independent FAA review of a manufacturer's own safety sign-offs
choices: Stronger independent FAA review of a manufacturer's own safety sign-offs
A complete ban on the FAA reviewing any commercial airliner design
A rule that the FAA must publish every safety complaint within 24 hours
A rule that only the president can approve any new plane design
context: The Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act (December 2020) reformed the ODA program, required additional whistleblower protections, and imposed new manufacturer-notification and FAA-oversight duties. Source: congress.gov (Public Law 116-260, Division V).

question: The US Farm Bill is a very large federal law renewed roughly every five years. Its combined ten-year budget was scored at about $1.5 trillion. What is the largest single component of that spending?
answer: SNAP (formerly food stamps)
choices: SNAP (formerly food stamps)
Crop insurance
Direct commodity subsidies
Conservation reserves
context: SNAP consumed approximately 76% of 2018 Farm Bill projected ten-year spending. Farm commodity programs were ~7%; crop insurance ~9%; conservation ~7%. The vast majority of the 'Farm Bill' is nutrition assistance, not farm spending. Source: cbo.gov (2018 Farm Bill scoring).

question: A senator wants a new bridge for her state. Another senator wants a new army base for his. Neither bill would pass alone, so they combine the two into one big bill and vote for each other's project. What is this vote-trading trick called?
answer: Logrolling
choices: Logrolling
Filibustering
Gerrymandering
Caucusing
context: Logrolling is the vote-trading mechanism Buchanan + Tullock analyzed as a defining feature of majority-rule legislative bodies. Each side votes for the other side's priorities to secure its own. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 10.

question: The US farm bill ties food-stamp money to farm subsidies. This deal started in 1973 with two senators from opposite parties -- a Republican from Kansas and a Democrat from South Dakota. Who were they?
answer: Bob Dole and George McGovern
choices: Bob Dole and George McGovern
Barry Goldwater and Hubert Humphrey
Charles Percy and Edmund Muskie
Robert Taft and Estes Kefauver
context: Robert Dole (R-KS) and George McGovern (D-SD) architected the ongoing bundling of nutrition assistance and farm programs beginning with the 1973 Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act. Every farm-bill reauthorization since has kept the bundle. Source: Grokipedia 'Farm bill'; Guenther, 'Robert Dole' (2018).

question: The Farm Bill mixes two programs in one law: food stamps for poor city families, and cash for farmers. Which team of lawmakers keeps this bundle glued together year after year?
answer: Urban Democrats plus rural Republicans
choices: Urban Democrats plus rural Republicans
Urban Republicans plus rural Democrats
Coastal libertarians plus midwestern socialists
Southern populists plus Rocky Mountain progressives
context: Urban and suburban Democrats have the votes for SNAP but not for farm subsidies; rural Republicans have the votes for farm subsidies but not for SNAP. Bundled in a single bill, each side votes for the other's priorities to secure its own. Source: Grokipedia 'Farm bill'; Sheingate, The Rise of the Agricultural Welfare State (Princeton 2001).

question: In 2013 the US House voted to split food-stamp aid out of the farm bill and pass it as a separate law. Farm-state and city-state members of Congress had long voted together by keeping the two bundled. What happened to that split when the House and Senate wrote the final law?
answer: The split failed and the two programs were bundled back together
choices: The split failed and the two programs were bundled back together
The split became law right after the House vote
The president vetoed the split and Congress overrode him
The Senate approved the split by unanimous consent
context: The 2013 House vote to separate SNAP from the farm bill passed on party lines but failed in conference. The final 2014 Farm Bill reconstituted the historical bundle. The pattern held: separation destroys the bipartisan coalition each half needs. Source: congress.gov (2013 farm bill legislative history).

question: The federal food-stamp program helps low-income Americans buy groceries each month. Its full name is the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. As of 2023, about how many people were getting this help?
answer: About 42 million
choices: About 42 million
About 4 million
About 200 million
About 420,000
context: SNAP covered approximately 42 million recipients as of 2023, mostly in urban and suburban households. The urban-suburban geographic base is what gives Democratic legislators the personal stake in preserving the bundle. Source: fns.usda.gov (SNAP data).

question: The 1996 Line-Item Veto Act would have let a president strike individual provisions of a bundled bill without vetoing the whole thing. It was struck down in a June 25, 1998 Supreme Court decision. What is that case called?
answer: Clinton v. City of New York
choices: Clinton v. City of New York
INS v. Chadha
US v. Nixon
Bowsher v. Synar
context: Clinton v. City of New York, 524 US 417 (1998), struck down the 1996 Line-Item Veto Act as unconstitutional. Bundled bills therefore remain a device Congress can protect through the presentment clause. Source: supremecourt.gov (524 US 417).

question: A Senator wants a special favor for his home state. He knows one big bill about the military passes every year no matter what. So he quietly attaches his favor to that bill. What is that legislative trick called?
answer: A rider
choices: A rider
A veto
A filibuster
A caucus
context: The NDAA is 'must-pass' annual legislation, so unrelated riders often ride on it. The same logrolling mechanism operates: riders that could not pass alone secure passage attached to a bill neither party wants to be seen voting against. Source: crsreports.congress.gov (NDAA analysis).

question: For decades, the U.S. Farm Bill has bundled farm subsidies together with food-stamp help for poor families in cities (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP). Rural and urban senators vote yes together. What is the general public-choice reason for this kind of odd bundling?
answer: Each half alone could not get a majority, so bundling them creates one
choices: Each half alone could not get a majority, so bundling them creates one
Congress does not have enough paper to print two separate bills
Bundling hides all federal spending from ordinary voters forever
Bundling is required to prevent the president from vetoing the bill
context: Buchanan-Tullock logrolling operating as designed. The diagnostic question: what happens to the voting coalition if you unbundle? If it collapses, the bundle is the reason both halves pass. This is not corruption -- it is coalition mechanics. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962), Chapter 10.

question: The Buchanan-Tullock 'logrolling' theory predicts a clear pattern for laws bundled together to build a voting coalition. What happens to such a bundle if you try to separate its parts?
answer: The voting coalition collapses and neither half passes
choices: The voting coalition collapses and neither half passes
Both halves pass separately by even larger majorities
Only the more expensive half survives
Only the cheaper half survives
context: The unbundling test: if the bundle exists for coalition mechanics, separation removes the vote-trade that makes each half viable. This is why the 2013 House SNAP separation attempt failed in conference. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); the 2013 farm bill legislative history.

question: An old economist wrote his last book to argue against socialism. His main point was that no small group of planners, however smart, can know enough to actually run a whole economy. Why not?
answer: The information is spread across millions of people making their own choices
choices: The information is spread across millions of people making their own choices
Planners work too slowly
Socialism is too expensive to try
Planners never went to school
context: 'The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism' appeared in 1988 as Volume 1 of the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek, published by the University of Chicago Press, edited by W. W. Bartley III. Hayek was 89 and died in 1992. Source: Wikipedia article on The Fatal Conceit (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fatal_Conceit).

question: An economist wrote a book calling socialism a 'fatal conceit' -- a deadly kind of pride. What did he say was so proud about central planners?
answer: They thought a small group could plan what millions of people need
choices: They thought a small group could plan what millions of people need
They believed they were smarter than any king
They wore fancy clothes and lived in palaces
They spoke more languages than anyone else
context: The Fatal Conceit was Volume 1 of the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. The multi-decade Chicago project is now edited by Bruce Caldwell. Source: University of Chicago Press catalog page (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/F/bo3643985.html).

question: In his 1988 book, Hayek refused to call the market 'capitalism.' He gave his own name to a system that lets strangers trade across a whole continent, using rules no committee ever wrote. What does Hayek call it?
answer: The extended order of human cooperation
choices: The extended order of human cooperation
The spontaneous market equilibrium
The great division of intellectual labor
The self-regulating price mechanism
context: Hayek: 'our civilization depends, not only for its origin but also for its preservation, on what can be precisely described only as the extended order of human cooperation, an order more commonly, if somewhat misleadingly, known as capitalism.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Extended order' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_order).

question: Hayek's book 'The Fatal Conceit' (1988) opens with his big claim about morals. Morals, he says, are a third kind of guide, sitting between two others: raw instinct on one side and pure reason on the other. What is that opening chapter called?
answer: Between Instinct and Reason
choices: Between Instinct and Reason
The Origins of Liberty, Property and Justice
The Extended Order and Population Growth
The Errors of Socialism
context: The opening chapter of The Fatal Conceit is 'Between Instinct and Reason.' Hayek: morals 'are not a creation of man's reason but a distinct second endowment conferred on him by cultural evolution.' Source: Reason magazine review 'The Moral Glue' (December 1988) (https://reason.com/1988/12/01/the-moral-glue1/).

question: In 'The Fatal Conceit,' Hayek says socialism rests on a big mistake. People who could design factories and planes thought they could design a whole society the same way. What claim about knowledge does Hayek use to call that a mistake?
answer: That the market uses more dispersed knowledge than any single mind or committee could hold
choices: That the market uses more dispersed knowledge than any single mind or committee could hold
That workers under socialism systematically consume less than under a market economy
That central planning tends to produce insufficient consumer choice at the retail level
That the state's monopoly on currency causes long-run inflation on a predictable lag
context: Hayek: the extended order 'constitutes an information gathering process, able to call up, and put to use, widely dispersed information that no central planning agency, let alone any individual, could know as a whole.' The fatal conceit is imagining a designed replacement could hold that knowledge. Source: Wikipedia, 'Extended order.'

question: A 1700s Scottish philosopher wrote: "the rules of morality are not the conclusions of our reason." He meant that right and wrong grow out of long tradition and shared habits, not out of one clever person's arguments. Which broader claim does that idea support?
answer: Long-tested traditions can be wiser than any single clever planner
choices: Long-tested traditions can be wiser than any single clever planner
A small expert group can design a better morality from scratch
Old rules should always be replaced by newer ones
Morality means whatever the government says it means today
context: Hayek opens with David Hume's line 'the rules of morality are not the conclusions of our reason,' anchoring the book in the Scottish Enlightenment view (Hume, Ferguson, Smith, Mandeville) that a working society uses evolved rules its members did not invent. Source: Andrew J. Oliet substack review (https://andrewjoliet.substack.com/p/navigating-dual-moralities).

question: Hayek says the rules that let people cooperate at huge scale -- private property, honest trade, keeping contracts, the family -- were not designed by anyone. They spread like natural selection, but on customs and habits instead of on genes. What does Hayek call this process?
answer: Cultural evolution
choices: Cultural evolution
Rational reconstruction
Institutional consent
Democratic revision
context: Hayek's mechanism: cultural evolution -- the extended order 'arose from unintentionally conforming to certain traditional and largely moral practices, which spread by means of an evolutionary selection.' Source: Reason Papers essay on Hayek's extended order (https://reasonpapers.com/pdf/23/rp_23_3.pdf).

question: In his final book, The Fatal Conceit, the economist Friedrich Hayek argued that no single planner can ever know enough to run a whole economy. What is the name for that Hayek idea?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The efficient market
The paradox of thrift
The invisible hand
context: William Warren Bartley III took over preparation of the manuscript after Hayek fell ill in 1985. Bruce Caldwell (editor of the Collected Works) has argued the evidence points to the finished book being 'a product more of [Bartley's] pen than of Hayek's,' though the core argument is unmistakably Hayek's. Ronald Hamowy edited the Definitive Edition of Constitution of Liberty, a different book. Source: Wikipedia, The Fatal Conceit.

question: Hayek's 'The Fatal Conceit' aims at Soviet planning. But in the book he warns about a milder Western version too. Even friendly Keynesian management, he says, still assumes a designer's grasp of an order built on scattered knowledge no planner can hold. What single move ties his critique of Soviet planning to his critique of Western technocracy?
answer: Both treat the evolved order as though a rational designer could grasp and improve on the knowledge it embodies
choices: Both treat the evolved order as though a rational designer could grasp and improve on the knowledge it embodies
Both underestimate the aggregate demand generated by public investment in physical infrastructure
Both fail to enforce the sound-money discipline that only a gold standard can supply
Both misread Adam Smith as a laissez-faire absolutist rather than a moral philosopher
context: Hayek's target in The Fatal Conceit is not only Soviet planning (visibly collapsing as he wrote) but also Western Keynesian macroeconomic management as a milder form of the same category mistake -- the fatal conceit is that any planner can hold the dispersed knowledge the extended order embodies. Source: Wikipedia, The Fatal Conceit; Cato Regulation 'Against Tribal Instincts' (https://www.cato.org/regulation/spring-2018/fatal-conceit).

question: When 'The Fatal Conceit' appeared in 1988, some passages struck careful readers as written in a diction unlike Hayek's earlier work. Bruce Caldwell -- the editor now overseeing the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek -- has argued from textual evidence that the manuscript was reworked more heavily than a normal editing pass, though the core argument remains unmistakably Hayek's. Which reasoning move about textual sources does the Caldwell caution press?
answer: That a heavily rewritten manuscript should be read as a joint editor-author work, with specific passages flagged as uncertain
choices: That a heavily rewritten manuscript should be read as a joint editor-author work, with specific passages flagged as uncertain
That the entire book should be treated as a posthumous forgery and removed from the Collected Works
That the book's central arguments are refuted by the manuscript-editing anomalies alone
That Hayek's earlier books should be re-read as similarly rewritten by unnamed editors
context: Bruce Caldwell has argued textual evidence points to 'a product more of [Bartley's] pen than of Hayek's' -- so scholars should treat specific passages as uncertain while acknowledging the core argument (extended order, cultural evolution, fatal conceit) is unmistakably Hayek's mature synthesis. The book remains Volume 1 of the Collected Works. Source: Wikipedia; Alan Ebenstein biography review (https://www.independent.org/tir/2001-fall/friedrich-hayek/).

question: President Woodrow Wilson signed the law that created the modern US central bank. He signed it two days before Christmas. In what year?
context: The Federal Reserve Act was signed on December 23, 1913, after most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/federal_reserve_act_signed.

question: In 1913, the US created its own central bank. It decides how much money exists and where interest rates go. What is this US central bank called?
answer: The Federal Reserve
choices: The Federal Reserve
The World Bank
The Treasury Department
The Bank of America
context: Wilson (Democrat, 28th president 1913-21) signed the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, ten months into his first term. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: The 1913 Act set up a group of regional Reserve Banks instead of one big bank in one city. This split kept banking power from being packed into a single place. How many regional Reserve Banks did the Act create?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
One
Fifty
Six
context: Twelve regional Reserve Banks: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Richmond, Atlanta, Chicago, St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Dallas, San Francisco. Each was owned by its member commercial banks, not by the federal government. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-banks.htm.

question: The 1913 Federal Reserve Act made a new central bank. It alone could print the paper money Americans still carry today. What are these notes formally called?
answer: Federal Reserve Notes
choices: Federal Reserve Notes
Treasury Notes
United States Notes
National Bank Notes
context: The dollar bills in circulation are Federal Reserve Notes, backed by the Fed's assets rather than by gold. Before 1913, national banks issued their own notes backed by Treasury bonds. Source: federalreserve.gov/faqs/currency.htm.

question: In 1913, one congressman warned that the new Fed would become 'the invisible government by the money power.' What was he warning about?
answer: That control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes
choices: That control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes
That paper money would replace gold coins in daily use
That most private banks would go out of business quickly
That the federal government would soon take over all factories
context: Rep. Charles Lindbergh Sr. (R-MN) opposed the bill from the House floor in December 1913, warning it would create 'the most gigantic trust on earth'. His son the aviator was 11 years old at the time. Source: Congressional Record, House, December 22, 1913.

question: A country creates a huge new central bank that will lend money to other banks in an emergency. The plan is designed at a private meeting on an island with only a handful of rich bankers invited. What is the biggest worry with a plan made that way?
answer: The bank might quietly serve those few insiders more than ordinary people
choices: The bank might quietly serve those few insiders more than ordinary people
The bank cannot legally exist without a public vote first
The public will refuse to spend the new money at all
The bank will forget to hire anyone to run it
context: The Jekyll Island meeting (November 1910) at the private hunting club of J.P. Morgan and other Wall Street bankers produced the Aldrich Plan, whose essential mechanisms were adopted (with Democratic rebranding) as the Federal Reserve Act. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jekyll_Island.

question: The 1913 Federal Reserve Act got its short name from its two main sponsors: a senator from Oklahoma and a House member from Virginia. What were their last names?
answer: Owen and Glass
choices: Owen and Glass
Aldrich and Vreeland
Sherman and McKinley
Bland and Allison
context: Senator Robert Owen (D-OK) chaired Senate Banking; Representative Carter Glass (D-VA) chaired House Banking. The Act is sometimes called the Owen-Glass Act. Glass later co-sponsored the 1933 Banking Act (Glass-Steagall). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, adds money to or drains money from the banking system by buying and selling one main type of security. Which securities does it use?
answer: Treasury securities
choices: Treasury securities
Corporate bonds
Mortgage-backed securities
Foreign-currency reserves
context: Open-market operations are the Fed's day-to-day tool: buying Treasuries adds reserves and pushes rates down; selling Treasuries drains reserves and pushes rates up. The NY Fed desk executes them. In 2008-09 the Fed extended purchases to mortgage-backed securities under emergency authority. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

question: The 1913 Act was signed on December 23 -- unusually late in the calendar year for such a substantive bill. Historians note this timing was politically deliberate. What was the practical effect of scheduling the signing so close to Christmas?
answer: Most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays
choices: Most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays
The stock exchanges were closed for holiday trading
European banks could not open new gold accounts
The federal budget deadline forced an immediate signature
context: The Senate passed the bill December 19; the conference report was finalized December 22; Wilson signed December 23. Many members had already headed home. Critics like Lindbergh treated the timing as evidence that debate had been foreshortened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: A widely shared 'deathbed regret' quotation about the Federal Reserve is often attributed to Woodrow Wilson. The sourcing has serious problems, however. Which best describes its actual status?
answer: The 'unwittingly ruined my country' portion has no verified primary source and is likely apocryphal
choices: The 'unwittingly ruined my country' portion has no verified primary source and is likely apocryphal
The full quote is documented in Wilson's collected papers at Princeton
The quote was published in the New York Times the week Wilson died
The quote comes from Wilson's 1913 book 'The New Freedom'
context: Historians (including Wilson biographer John Milton Cooper) have been unable to locate the 'unwittingly ruined' language in Wilson's papers. A separate passage about 'the invisible government by the money power' is authentic and appears in Wilson's pre-signing 1913 book 'The New Freedom'. Honesty rail: cite only what is verifiable. Source: princeton.edu/~mudd (Wilson papers).

question: The 1913 law creating the Federal Reserve gave it no specific number goals -- only vague language about 'furnishing an elastic currency.' Congress did not add explicit goals until 1978. Which two goals did that later law tell the Fed to pursue at the same time?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Zero inflation and the abolition of paper money
Full public ownership of every commercial bank
A fixed exchange rate with the British pound
context: The 1978 Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act added the explicit dual-mandate language (maximum employment plus stable prices) to the Federal Reserve Act. Before 1978 the Fed's goals were essentially self-defined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey%E2%80%93Hawkins_Full_Employment_Act.

question: A 1978 US law gave the Fed two goals at once -- one about jobs and one about the value of the dollar. What is this pair usually called?
answer: The dual mandate
choices: The dual mandate
The single mandate
The gold anchor
The Bretton Woods rule
context: The Fed's 'dual mandate' is a shorthand for maximum employment plus stable prices, established by the Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/section2a.htm.

question: A 1978 US law told the Fed to do two things at once: keep prices steady and keep as many people working as it can. What is a problem with giving one group two goals?
answer: The two goals can pull against each other, so the bank has to choose
choices: The two goals can pull against each other, so the bank has to choose
Neither goal really matters at all
One agency should have many more goals
The bank always ignores both goals
context: Full title: Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978; sponsors Senator Hubert Humphrey (D-MN) and Representative Augustus Hawkins (D-CA). Humphrey died in January 1978 and the Act was named in his honor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey%E2%80%93Hawkins_Full_Employment_Act.

question: The two policy goals assigned to the Fed by the 1978 law are usually stated as a pair. What are the two goals in the pair?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Maximum growth and low taxes
Trade balance and currency reserves
Balanced budget and low national debt
context: The Federal Reserve Act (as amended in 1978) directs the Fed to 'promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates'. The third goal is treated as derivative. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/section2a.htm.

question: The Federal Reserve in America has two main goals: keep prices steady and keep jobs up. Europe's central bank was set up with only one main goal. What is that one goal?
answer: Keep prices steady
choices: Keep prices steady
Get everyone a job
Hold lots of gold
Grow the economy fast
context: Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union makes price stability the ECB's primary objective; other goals may be supported only 'without prejudice' to it. This single-mandate design was influenced by the German Bundesbank's inflation-fighting record. Source: ecb.europa.eu/mopo/intro/objective.

question: In 1967-68, Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps showed that any long-run trade-off between inflation and jobs would break down. Once workers learn to expect higher prices, they adjust. Then in 1978 Congress passed the dual-mandate law. What was awkward about the timing?
answer: The trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation
choices: The trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation
The trade-off had just been confirmed by a decade of Keynesian success
The natural-rate concept had not yet been proposed
The Phillips curve was a brand-new discovery
context: By 1978 stagflation (simultaneous high inflation and unemployment) had made the naive Phillips-curve trade-off untenable. The dual mandate embedded the trade-off in statute at the very moment academic economics was walking away from it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_curve.

question: Austrian economists say a central bank with two goals faces a steady political pull toward one side. Which side does the Austrian critique say tends to win in practice?
answer: The employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not
choices: The employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not
The price side, because inflation directly hurts bond markets that lobby the Fed
Both sides equally, since the mandate is symmetric on paper
Neither side, since the Fed is technically independent of politics
context: The Austrian public-choice reading: unemployment produces immediate political pressure; a couple of extra points of inflation is diffuse and delayed. A Fed with both goals therefore leans easy over time, producing persistent low-grade inflation and asset-price booms. Source: mises.org/library/case-100-percent-gold-dollar.

question: The Fed's official price-stability target uses a specific consumer inflation index, not asset prices like housing or stocks. Which measure does the Fed track for its 2 percent target?
answer: The core PCE price index
choices: The core PCE price index
The Case-Shiller housing price index
The S&P 500 total return
The M2 money supply
context: The Fed's 2% target is stated on core Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation. Austrian critics note that this leaves asset-price inflation (housing bubbles, stock booms) formally uncounted -- a lever the employment side of the mandate exploits. Source: federalreserve.gov/faqs/economy_14400.htm.

question: In 2021 the Fed kept calling fast-rising prices 'transitory' for months. Then in 2022 it had to raise interest rates sharply. For Austrian critics of the Fed's dual mandate, what pattern did this show?
answer: The employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error
choices: The employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error
The unusually rapid market response to Fed guidance
The success of forward-guidance communication tools
The dominance of monetary versus fiscal policy in modern practice
context: Fed leadership held rates near zero through most of 2021 while inflation ran above 5 percent, using the labor-market recovery as reason to delay. When the pivot came in March 2022, the Fed had to tighten unusually fast. Austrians treat this as the mandate's incentive structure playing out on schedule. Source: federalreserve.gov press releases 2021-22.

question: As a rules-based alternative to Fed discretion, Milton Friedman long argued the central bank should not choose an interest rate at all but should be bound to a mechanical rule. What was Friedman's proposed rule?
answer: A constant money-supply growth rate
choices: A constant money-supply growth rate
A constant unemployment target
A constant real wage index
A constant nominal exchange rate
context: Friedman's 'k-percent rule' would have set money-supply growth at a low, constant percentage annually, removing Fed discretion over the employment-inflation trade-off entirely. Rothbard argued Friedman's rule was still fiat and preferred a gold-anchored money. Source: Friedman, A Program for Monetary Stability (1960).

question: The 1978 U.S. law that gave the Federal Reserve its 'dual mandate' -- maximum employment and stable prices -- was named after a senator who died before it passed. Austrian critics argue those two goals often clash directly. Which clash do they point to?
answer: Printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable
choices: Printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable
Lower taxes always cause both goals to fail together
Full employment automatically causes deflation, which raises prices
Stable prices are always achieved without any change in employment
context: Hubert Humphrey (D-MN, former Vice President under Johnson and 1968 Democratic presidential nominee) died January 13, 1978. Augustus Hawkins (D-CA), the House co-sponsor, lived until 2007. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey.

question: Thomas Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (1980) extended F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay on scattered knowledge well beyond the price system. Three years later Hayek reviewed the book in Reason magazine. What did Hayek say about it?
answer: That it was the best book on general economics in years
choices: That it was the best book on general economics in years
That it restated his own argument and added nothing new
That its examples were American and would not travel
That it belonged to sociology rather than to economics
context: Hayek's 1983 Reason review said the book expanded admirably on his own concepts and made them clear to lay readers through real-world examples. Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) also took the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Thomas Sowell says people who fight over one law after another are not really arguing about the laws. Deep down, they hold different views of one thing. Different views of what?
answer: What human beings are capable of
choices: What human beings are capable of
Who ought to hold political power
How wealth ought to be divided up
Which rights the law must protect
context: Sowell's constrained vision treats human capacities as permanently limited by flaws, scarcity and incomplete knowledge, so every arrangement buys one thing by giving up another. The unconstrained vision treats those limits as artifacts of bad institutions that clear-sighted people could redesign away. Sowell's most quoted sentence belongs to the first: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A newspaper column says a new program is working. Its proof is three interviews with people who say the program changed their lives. Which of Sowell's five standing questions does the column invite?
answer: What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
choices: What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
context: Sowell's complaint in The Vision of the Anointed is that a claim gets accepted 'even though evidence is seldom asked or given'. Three people who feel helped tell you nothing about the people the programme missed, harmed, or would have helped anyway -- and those are the ones no reporter interviews.

question: A city says its housing program built 4,000 apartments and moved 4,000 families in. Every number counts what the program made. Not one counts what it used up or pushed aside. Which of Sowell's five questions was skipped?
answer: At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
choices: At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
context: The money, the land, the timber and the builders' hours all had other employments, and those employments are now gone. Sowell's point is that a benefit figure standing alone is not analysis -- it is advertising. The cost is real whether or not anybody publishes it.

question: A writer lists real failures at a private insurer -- claims denied, customers stranded -- and says the state should take over. Sowell replies that the insurer is real, but the state in the writer's head is not. Which of Sowell's five questions is he pressing?
answer: Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
choices: Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
context: This is the move at the heart of Knowledge and Decisions: markets and governments are both ways of deciding, and both are staffed by real people with limited knowledge. Comparing a real market with an ideal government is not a comparison at all. Sowell's question does not settle who wins -- it insists that both contestants show up.

question: A state caps the rent a landlord may charge. In the first year the tenants in those flats pay less, exactly as promised, and the cap is declared a success on that evidence. Landlords, builders and would-be tenants have not yet had time to do anything about it. Which of Sowell's five questions has been skipped?
answer: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
choices: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
context: Applied Economics carries the subtitle Thinking Beyond Stage One for exactly this reason. A landlord who cannot raise the rent can still stop maintaining, convert the building, or sell it; a builder can put his capital somewhere else entirely. None of that shows up in year one, and all of it lands on the tenants the cap was written for.

question: A candidate promises to end homelessness for good, with no downside for anyone. Sowell denies that any such plan can exist -- not because this one is flawed, but because of what policy always is. Which of his five questions does he press?
answer: What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
choices: What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
context: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' -- A Conflict of Visions (1987). The trade-off question is not the same as the cost question: cost asks what the resources gave up, trade-offs asks which problems you have agreed to accept in exchange for the ones you are removing. A programme with no downside is not a bargain a human being can strike.

question: Thomas Sowell's Applied Economics (2003) draws a line between the way a politician evaluates a policy and the way an economist does. His charge is not that politicians are stupid; it is that their analysis reliably halts at one particular point. Where does it halt?
answer: At the policy's first, immediate result
choices: At the policy's first, immediate result
At the point where the money runs out
At the next general election in the cycle
At the boundary of their own department
context: Hence the subtitle: Thinking Beyond Stage One. Sowell's chapters run housing, medical care, discrimination and national development through the later repercussions, which he says are often very different from the immediate effects and much longer lasting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One'.

question: Hayek's 1945 essay showed how prices carry scattered knowledge to strangers. Sowell agrees. He then asks a further question about every institution -- markets, courts, firms, families, and legislatures. What further question does he ask?
answer: How each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken
choices: How each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken
How each one distributes the gains among the people taking part
How much each one costs the taxpayer to administer in a year
How quickly each one can be replaced when the public turns on it
context: This is Sowell's extension of Hayek and the reason 'compared to what?' is an institutional question rather than a debating trick. A firm that misjudges its customers loses money and has to change; an agency that misjudges its clients may get a larger budget. Both make mistakes. What separates them is what happens next. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: A government proposes to cancel all outstanding student debt. Thomas Sowell would grant that the first effect is exactly what its authors promise: today's borrowers stop owing. His fifth question asks what follows. Which second-round effect does it put first?
answer: Colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation
choices: Colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation
Banks tighten lending to every borrower who is not at a college
Graduates who repaid early petition Congress for equal treatment
States cut their own university funding by the amount forgiven
context: All four are second-round effects worth tracing; Sowell's question puts the incentive change first because it is the one that alters what people do from now on, rather than redistributing what has already happened. Note what the question does not do: it does not tell you the policy is wrong. It tells you which column of the ledger the proposal has left blank.

question: A student learns Sowell's five questions and runs them on rent control, tariffs and the minimum wage -- and ends up disagreeing with Sowell about all three. The questions have still done their work. What is it that the five questions actually deliver?
answer: An account of what a policy costs and causes, which you then weigh yourself
choices: An account of what a policy costs and causes, which you then weigh yourself
A ranking of policies from the most harmful down to the least harmful
A test that every sound policy passes and every unsound one fails
A method for predicting which policies a legislature will adopt
context: The five-question distillation -- trade-offs, at what cost, compared to what, what hard evidence, and then what happens -- is a reader's compression rather than a list Sowell packaged in one book; the questions appear across A Conflict of Visions, Knowledge and Decisions, The Vision of the Anointed, Applied Economics and dozens of columns. They yield a full account and no verdict. Two people can run all five honestly on the same policy and still weigh the answers differently, because what a society should trade for what is not an economic question.  (Legend.)

question: Inside the Federal Reserve, one committee votes to raise, lower, or hold the target interest rate. What four-letter name is that committee known by?
answer: FOMC
choices: FOMC
OCC
FDIC
CFPB
context: The Federal Open Market Committee sets the Fed funds rate target and directs open-market operations. Every 6-8 weeks its policy statement is the market-moving output. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: The US central bank's rate-setting group holds a set number of regular meetings each year. About how many meetings does it hold?
answer: Eight
choices: Eight
Two
Twenty
Fifty
context: The FOMC meets eight times a year on a published calendar, roughly every 6-8 weeks. Each meeting yields a policy statement, a chair press conference, and minutes released three weeks later. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm.

question: The Federal Open Market Committee sets US interest rates. Its voters come from two Fed groups. How many voting seats are there at each meeting?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
Seven
Five
Nineteen
context: Twelve voting seats: seven Board of Governors members in Washington plus five regional Reserve Bank presidents. Nineteen officials attend and speak, but only twelve vote. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: The Fed has twelve regional banks. Most take turns voting on rates. But one bank votes at every meeting. It sits in the country's biggest money city. Which city is that?
answer: New York
choices: New York
Chicago
San Francisco
Dallas
context: The New York Reserve Bank president holds a permanent FOMC vote; the other 11 regional presidents rotate through four voting seats on annual cycles. NY's permanent seat dates to the 1913 founding when it was the largest district. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: The Fed has seven Board members in Washington. The President picks them and the Senate approves them. Each term is very long — much longer than the President's. How long is one term?
answer: Fourteen years
choices: Fourteen years
Four years
Six years
Life
context: Fourteen-year non-renewable terms are the longest fixed terms of any federal position other than Supreme Court justices (who have life tenure). The length is set by the Federal Reserve Act to insulate governors from short-term political pressure. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-board.htm.

question: A central banker has a habit. Every time stocks drop hard, he cuts rates to save the investors. After years of this, how do big investors act?
answer: They take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out
choices: They take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out
They stop investing entirely and buy only gold coins
They lend only to farmers and small shops
They demand higher interest rates on every loan
context: Greenspan chaired the Fed 1987-2006 across the Black Monday 1987 crash, the 1998 LTCM rescue, the 2000 dot-com bust and the 2004-06 rate cycle. His dominance of FOMC agenda-setting became a case study in chair-driven committee dynamics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Greenspan.

question: A central bank does not directly set every interest rate in the country. Instead it picks one key rate — the overnight rate banks charge each other to borrow — and pushes markets toward that target. What is this key rate called?
answer: The federal funds rate
choices: The federal funds rate
The mortgage rate
The credit card rate
The savings account rate
context: The FOMC votes a target range for the federal funds rate -- the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to each other. The New York Desk then conducts open-market operations to keep the effective rate in that range. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' makes a point Austrian critics apply to central banks that set rates. No group, however smart, can gather up the scattered facts held by billions of borrowers, savers, and firms. What is this move usually called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The free-rider problem
The principal-agent problem
The tragedy of the commons
context: Hayek argued that the price system distributes knowledge no central board could gather in time -- the 'knowledge problem'. Applied to the FOMC: twelve people cannot know the 'correct' interest rate for an economy of hundreds of millions. Source: Hayek, American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: The Senate does not vote on regional Fed presidents. Instead, private banks in that Fed district pick them. Which group actually chooses each regional bank president?
answer: The Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank
choices: The Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank
The Senate Banking Committee
The full Board of Governors alone
The President of the United States
context: Each regional bank has nine directors (three classes); the non-banker directors (Class B and C) select the regional president, with Board of Governors sign-off. There is no Senate confirmation. Public-choice critics call this a governance gap. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-banks.htm.

question: Traders read every Fed statement so closely that changing one word can move markets by billions. What nickname do we give the reporters and analysts who do this close reading?
answer: Fed watchers
choices: Fed watchers
Reserve auditors
Rate scouts
Balance-sheet analysts
