question: A famous 1850 French pamphlet argues that when a government uses the law itself to take from one group and give to another, it is committing what the author calls 'legal plunder.' What is the pamphlet's main claim about the proper job of law?
answer: Law exists to protect life, liberty, and property, not to redistribute them
choices: Law exists to protect life, liberty, and property, not to redistribute them
Law exists mainly to redistribute wealth from rich to poor
Law should set every price and wage in the economy
Law should force every citizen to work in state-run jobs
context: Paul's Liberty Defined (2011) cites The Law as the single best entry point; the pamphlet is, by wide margin, the first Austrian-adjacent text most American libertarian teenagers ever read. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Defined.

question: For most of the 1900s, English readers of Bastiat had only three short translations. All three came from one liberty group in New York. Which one put them out?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
The Cato Institute
The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Mont Pelerin Society
context: FEE was founded 1946 by Leonard Read in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Its editions were excellent for their day but covered only a fraction of Bastiat's actual output; most of his correspondence, journalism, and Assembly speeches had never been translated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: A rich businessman starts a private foundation. Its mission is to reprint and hand out old books by dead economists who defended free markets, so students in future centuries can still read them. What is this an example of?
answer: Private funding keeping ideas alive across generations
choices: Private funding keeping ideas alive across generations
A government-run textbook program
A public library system paid by taxes
A university tenure system
context: Liberty Fund's Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat is projected to run to six volumes. Goodrich, an Indiana lawyer and businessman, endowed the foundation specifically to sustain the classical-liberal scholarly tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: A shopkeeper's window is broken by a stray rock. He pays a glazier to fix it. A crowd says the accident was actually good for the town because it gave the glazier work. What is the crowd missing?
answer: The shopkeeper cannot now spend that money on something else
choices: The shopkeeper cannot now spend that money on something else
The glazier will refuse to accept the payment
The window was actually fine and did not need fixing
The shopkeeper will get his money back from the town
context: Hart works alongside general editors Jacques de Guenin and Jean-Claude Paul-Dejean. He also maintains the Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org), a free online archive of classical-liberal texts that includes all the Bastiat volumes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: Volume 3 of the Liberty Fund Collected Works of Bastiat came out in 2017. It includes his most famous 1850 essay on hidden versus visible effects. What is that essay called?
answer: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
choices: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
'The General Theory'
'The Wealth of Nations'
'Das Kapital'
context: 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas' (1850). Volume 3 also contains the Economic Sophisms, Bastiat's satirical essays including the Petition of the Candlemakers demanding a law against the sun. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat's most famous essay talks about a shopkeeper whose window is smashed by a boy. Neighbors say 'well, at least the glazier gets work.' What does Bastiat say the neighbors are missing?
answer: The shopkeeper would have spent that money on something else, so nothing new is created
choices: The shopkeeper would have spent that money on something else, so nothing new is created
The glazier will hire more workers, so the town is truly richer
Breaking things is a hidden way to grow the economy
Insurance companies cover the loss, so nobody is really hurt
context: The Liberty Fund Collected Works (7 volumes, 2011-) added scholarly apparatus the earlier FEE translations lacked: introductions locating each essay in 1840s French political context, glossaries of French figures, and modern translations that restored passages 19th-century English editions had toned down. Source: Grokipedia 'Frederic Bastiat' + Liberty Fund catalog.

question: David M. Hart, the Liberty Fund's English editor for the Bastiat Collected Works, has also built and maintained a free online resource that makes the whole Bastiat corpus (and hundreds of other classical-liberal texts) available at zero cost to any 21st-century reader with internet access. What is the resource called?
answer: The Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org)
choices: The Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org)
The Ludwig von Mises Institute online archive
The Cato Institute policy library
The Federal Reserve archival collection
context: Any curious kid with internet access can now read every essay Bastiat ever wrote, in modern English, on a free website funded by a classical-liberal foundation. The tradition is being actively cultivated, not just preserved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: Money spent on US federal lobbying has grown a lot since 1998. About how much did federal lobbying cost in 2023?
answer: About $4.1 billion
choices: About $4.1 billion
About $410 million
About $41 billion
About $41 million
context: Federal lobbying spending grew from ~$1.44B in 1998 to ~$4.1B in 2023 per opensecrets.org (Center for Responsive Politics). Registered federal lobbyists number ~11,000-14,000. Source: opensecrets.org (Lobbying Data).

question: People spend money to chase favors from the government. They pay for lobbying, campaign gifts, and lawsuits to change rules. What kind of loss is this called?
answer: Deadweight loss
choices: Deadweight loss
Sunk cost
Transfer payment
Opportunity income
context: Tullock's move: resources burned in the competition for privilege produce no goods or services; they only reshuffle existing wealth. The whole rectangle of resources burned is deadweight loss to society. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (June 1967).

question: In 2023 one industry spent about $385 million on lobbying the US federal government -- more than any other. Which industry led the list?
answer: Pharmaceuticals and health products
choices: Pharmaceuticals and health products
Defense contractors
Motion pictures and television
Iron and steel
context: Pharmaceuticals/health products led at ~$385M in 2023, followed by electronics manufacturing and equipment (~$228M) and insurance (~$164M). Source: opensecrets.org (Top Industries 2023).

question: One group has been the biggest single spender on US federal lobbying most recent years. In 2023 it spent about $68 million. Which group is it?
answer: The US Chamber of Commerce
choices: The US Chamber of Commerce
The National Rifle Association
The American Bar Association
The American Legion
context: The US Chamber of Commerce has been the largest single-organization federal lobbying spender for most recent years -- ~$68M in 2023. National Association of Realtors (~$52M) and Meta Platforms (~$20M) round out the top individual spenders. Source: opensecrets.org (Top Organizations 2023).

question: In a 2014 paper, three economists -- Bertrand, Bombardini, and Trebbi -- asked whether lobbying works through knowledge or through personal ties. Their paper had a memorable title. What was it?
answer: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
choices: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
The Price of Access
Do Lobbyists Matter?
Money and Influence
context: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi, 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? An Empirical Assessment of the Lobbying Process' (American Economic Review, December 2014). Answer: mostly whom. Source: aeaweb.org (Bertrand et al. 2014).

question: Members of Congress and top staff who leave for lobbying often earn many times their old federal pay. Which range best fits the pay bump they usually get?
answer: 500 to 1000 percent
choices: 500 to 1000 percent
10 to 25 percent
0 to 5 percent
Pay cuts of 30 to 50 percent
context: Ex-Members and ex-senior staffers who become lobbyists command salary premiums of ~500-1000% over their government pay, consistent with a market pricing their capture-value. Source: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi (2014); Blanes i Vidal + Draca + Fons-Rosen, American Economic Review (2012).

question: A 1938 US law makes people report when they lobby for foreign governments or companies trying to sway US opinion and policy. What short name is that law known by?
answer: FARA
choices: FARA
FLDA
USRA
FIDA
context: The Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), passed 1938, requires disclosure of foreign-government-directed lobbying. FARA disclosures in recent years total ~$500M/year, on top of the ~$4B/year in domestic-lobbying disclosure. Source: justice.gov/nsd-fara.

question: In Washington DC many lobbying firms and trade groups have their offices along one downtown street. The street's name has become shorthand for the whole lobbying industry. What does that shorthand teach about how policy gets made?
answer: Lobbyists cluster near power because access to lawmakers is valuable
choices: Lobbyists cluster near power because access to lawmakers is valuable
Lobbying firms are legally required to share one office building
Lobbyists usually prefer to work far from all elected officials
The federal government owns all the offices near Congress
context: K Street NW in downtown Washington DC hosts many of the largest lobbying firms and trade associations. 'K Street' has become synonymous with the lobbying industry as an American shorthand. Source: Grokipedia 'K Street (Washington, D.C.)'.

question: Tullock's 1967 paper and today's lobbying totals point to the same story about the $4 billion a year spent on federal lobbying. Which sentence best fits Tullock's view?
answer: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
choices: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
Money is spent purely to educate legislators about general policy tradeoffs
Money is spent on ceremonial political events with no material effect
Money is spent solely to comply with existing legal disclosures
context: Tullock's rent-seeking framework: $4B/year is not being spent to persuade Congress of general truths. It is being spent to capture concrete, industry-specific policy outcomes. The stated purpose (democratic participation) is not always false; the aggregate spending is not consistent with it either. Source: Tullock (1967); opensecrets.org.

question: When a complex new law targets one industry, the lobbying pattern gives you a useful habit of mind. What should a careful policy watcher suspect by default?
answer: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
choices: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
The beneficiaries are always the retail voters who elected the sponsors
The statute is copied verbatim from a Nordic model
The statute was drafted overnight by a single ideologue
context: When a proposed statute is complex, industry-specific, and heavily lobbied, the Tullock-Olson default is that the concentrated organized interests are the primary beneficiaries. The First Amendment protects petition; the ladder analyzes the aggregate incentive structure. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: You are dying of thirst in a desert. Someone offers you a glass of water and you would trade almost anything for it. But if they offer you a fifth glass after four, you barely care. Why does the fifth glass feel less valuable than the first?
answer: You need it much less than the first one
choices: You need it much less than the first one
The water changes chemistry after four glasses
The seller has to lower the price by law
The government taxes extra glasses
context: Menger's Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre insisted that value is subjective, ranked by an individual chooser, and always applies to a specific additional unit rather than to a good as a class. That single move dissolved a hundred years of classical puzzles. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger and the Sesquicentennial Founding of the Austrian School'.

question: Two people find identical gold coins on the beach. One is a rich collector who already has thousands of them. The other is a poor kid who needs bus fare home. Who values that one coin more?
answer: The poor kid, because he needs it more right now
choices: The poor kid, because he needs it more right now
The rich collector, because he understands gold
They value it equally because it is the same coin
Neither, because gold has no real value
context: Jevons's The Theory of Political Economy appeared in London in 1871, the same year as Menger's Grundsaetze. Marshall would not publish his Principles until 1890; Mill and Senior belonged to the earlier classical generation. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: In 1871 an English economist argued that a thing's value depends not on the whole pile you own, but on how useful one more unit would be to you right now. If you have zero apples, one more is huge; if you have twenty, one more is small. What is this idea called?
answer: Marginal utility
choices: Marginal utility
Labor theory of value
Cost of production
Fair market price
context: Jevons was Professor of Political Economy at Owens College, Manchester -- the institution that later became the University of Manchester. He wrote The Theory of Political Economy while holding that chair. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: In the 1870s one economist went further than the others. He built a math model where every price in every market is set at the same time, all linked together, like one giant system of equations. What is this idea called?
answer: General equilibrium
choices: General equilibrium
Partial equilibrium
The gold standard
Central planning
context: Walras published in Lausanne, using the French word 'rarete' for what English readers called marginal utility. Cournot preceded him with 1838 mathematical duopoly; Pareto succeeded him in the Lausanne chair after 1893; Bastiat was of an older generation and no marginalist. Source: Britannica, 'Leon Walras'.

question: Some economists try to model a whole economy at once, with every price and every buyer tied into one huge system of equations. What is the biggest real-world problem with this?
answer: Real people change their minds and new products appear every day
choices: Real people change their minds and new products appear every day
Computers today are still too slow to add up any prices
There is a law against writing equations about markets
Economists refuse to share their equations with each other
context: Walras held the chair of political economy at the Academie de Lausanne (later the University of Lausanne) from 1870; his book was printed there in 1874. The Lausanne School of general equilibrium takes its name from the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leon Walras'.

question: Between 1871 and 1874, three economists in three countries -- Menger, Jevons, and Walras -- each landed on the same new idea. Historians of economic thought call it one of the tightest cases of parallel invention ever. What name do they give this cluster?
answer: The marginal revolution
choices: The marginal revolution
The neoclassical synthesis
The Methodenstreit
The Keynesian revolution
context: The Methodenstreit was the later Menger-Schmoller quarrel over historicist versus analytic method; the neoclassical synthesis was the mid-twentieth-century Samuelson fusion of Keynes and Walras; the Keynesian revolution was the 1930s reversal against neoclassical orthodoxy. Only the 1871-1874 cluster is called the marginal revolution. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: In the 1870s three economists in three different countries came up with the same idea at almost the same time. The value of one more slice of pizza depends on how many slices you have already eaten. What do economists call this idea?
answer: Marginal utility
choices: Marginal utility
The labor theory of value
The invisible hand
Comparative advantage
context: Marshall married Jevons's marginal-utility insight to partial-equilibrium supply-and-demand diagrams, adding elasticity of demand, consumer surplus and the representative firm. The Cambridge School he founded dominated English-speaking economics for the next half century. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alfred Marshall'.

question: Carl Menger thought Walras's plan -- modeling the whole economy as one big system of equations -- was wrong at the deepest level, not just as a matter of technique. What was Menger's objection?
answer: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
choices: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
The mathematics of 1874 was not yet advanced enough for the task
General-equilibrium models understate the importance of labour-time in value
Walras had rejected marginal utility in favour of pure cost-of-production
context: Menger accepted the marginal-utility insight the three founders shared; his disagreement was about method. This methodological gap between the Austrian and Lausanne roads persists to the present day and underlies the Austrian critique of modern DSGE modelling. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: The idea that each extra unit of a good is worth less than the one before was written down by a German scholar. He put it on paper years before famous economists caught on. What does that earlier discovery show about big economic ideas?
answer: Big ideas often show up in more than one place before the world is ready to hear them
choices: Big ideas often show up in more than one place before the world is ready to hear them
Only one person can ever discover any economic idea
Economic ideas always come first from the most famous universities
Nobody thought about value at all before the year 1870
context: Gossen's 1854 Entwickelung der Gesetze des menschlichen Verkehrs laid down what are still called Gossen's Laws of diminishing marginal utility and equimarginal allocation. Robert Adamson of Manchester found the surviving copy in 1878 and Jevons publicly acknowledged Gossen's priority in the second edition of his own book. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gossen's laws'.

question: Once the marginal-unit move was on the table, an entire class of classical value theories collapsed at one stroke. Which theory did it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
choices: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
The quantity theory of money later revived by Milton Friedman
The theory of comparative advantage stated by David Ricardo
The Malthusian population principle
context: Every rung of the labour-theory chain assumed value was a property of the good, fixed by its cost or labour input. The marginalist move denies the assumption: value is a ranking of the next unit by a specific chooser. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus were unaffected -- each addressed a different question. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: Three economists in three countries hit the same core insight within three years. That suggests the marginal idea was ripe by 1870. But the three roads split sharply into the Austrian, Cambridge, and Lausanne schools -- with different methods, styles, and reach. What does that split suggest about economics?
answer: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
choices: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
It is primarily an empirical laboratory science like chemistry
It is settled by mathematical proof once its axioms are stated
It has no genuine intellectual disagreements after 1874
context: The Austrian, Cambridge and Lausanne schools agreed on the marginal-utility insight but disagreed sharply about whether economics should be prose-based praxeology, partial-equilibrium diagrams, or systems of simultaneous equations. Those methodological choices still divide the profession. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: In the 1800s some economists said the only way to know the economy was to gather piles of history and numbers from one country. Austrians said no. What did the Austrians say you also need?
answer: Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country
choices: Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country
The exact weight of every coin in circulation
A list of every farmer's birthday
A map of every road in the country
context: The book was Untersuchungen ueber die Methode der Socialwissenschaften (Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences, with Special Reference to Political Economics), 1883. Schmoller held the chair at the University of Berlin from 1882 and led what economists call the 'younger' German Historical School. Ricardo was 60 years dead; the physiocrats a century earlier; Veblen and the American institutionalists would come after 1899. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: A kid watches her older brother argue with their parents on twenty different days. Every single time, when he raises his voice, the argument gets worse. She decides: "Raising your voice makes arguments worse." What kind of reasoning did she use?
answer: Inductive
choices: Inductive
Deductive
Circular
Random
context: Induction moves from cases to a general rule; deduction moves from general premises to specific conclusions (like geometry proving a theorem from axioms). The German Historical School was inductive-first; Menger's Austrians were deductive-first. This deductive-vs-inductive split is what a 'method-war' -- a Methodenstreit -- is FOUGHT OVER. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: In the 1880s, economists in Germany and Austria fought a long, bitter argument. One side said the way to do economics was pure abstract theory. The other side said only close study of history and real cases. What was the fight really about?
answer: The right method for doing economics
choices: The right method for doing economics
How high tariffs on grain should be
Whether to abolish paper money
Whether workers should form unions
context: Methodenstreit literally means 'method-fight' or 'quarrel over method' -- Streit is the German for a dispute or fight. Kulturkampf was Bismarck's 1870s fight with the Catholic Church; Klassenkampf is Marx's class struggle; Vernunftstreit is not a standard historical term. The word Methodenstreit is now used by historians for any deep methodological quarrel, but by default it means THIS ONE. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: In 1883, Menger said economics is like geometry. It has laws that hold in every time and place. You start from a few simple truths about how people choose. Then you reason down to the rest. From which base does a geometry-like science reason?
answer: From general first principles down to specific cases
choices: From general first principles down to specific cases
From specific cases up to tentative rules
From surveys of the general population
From statistical patterns in historical data
context: This is deduction: axioms first, theorems derived. Menger's atom was the individual acting to satisfy a want; from that atom he derived subjective value, marginal ranking, price formation. Ludwig von Mises would later name the method PRAXEOLOGY (Human Action, 1949). The Historical School's method -- from cases up to tentative rules -- is induction; surveys and statistical patterns are its tools. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: In the late 1800s, a German professor sneered at a small group of economists based in Vienna, calling them a Vienna sect. The insult stuck, and the group proudly kept the label. What is this school of economic thought called today, named after the country its founders lived in?
answer: The Austrian School
choices: The Austrian School
The Chicago School
The Cambridge School
The Berlin School
context: The very name 'Austrian School' was invented by an opponent as a put-down and adopted by the accused as a name of honor. The Manchester School was the free-trade movement around Cobden and Bright (1830s-60s); the Lausanne School was Walras and Pareto's mathematical-equilibrium tradition; the Cambridge School was Alfred Marshall's neoclassical mainstream. Schmoller's slur is now the name of a Nobel-decorated tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: In 1884, Menger wrote a short, angry book to answer Schmoller's review. It came as a set of open letters to a friend. The title was 'The Errors of Historicism in German Economics.' Which reasoning move did Menger press against the Historical School?
answer: That economic laws are universal and hold in every time and place, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them
choices: That economic laws are universal and hold in every time and place, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them
That economic laws depend entirely on the historical period, so no universal science of economics is possible
That only mathematical models can settle economic questions
That government must collect national statistics before any economic argument is legitimate
context: Hayek later said Menger 'ruthlessly demolished Schmoller's position' in the 1884 pamphlet. The point is exact: a scarce means will still be economized in ancient Rome and in modern Vienna; a chooser will rank in every century. History is DATA, not the SOURCE. Menger did not reject historical study; he denied it could replace theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Schmoller led German economics from his professor's chair at the University of Berlin. He publicly declared that Vienna-school thinkers were unfit for German university appointments. What concrete consequence did that declaration have across Germany?
answer: A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments
choices: A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments
An immediate ban on Menger's Principles being sold in Germany
Menger's removal from his chair at the University of Vienna
The dissolution of the Verein fuer Socialpolitik
context: Schmoller controlled Prussian academic appointments through his Berlin chair, his editorship of the leading journal, and his chairmanship of the Verein fuer Socialpolitik. His public verdict effectively closed the German academic market to Austrians well into the 1900s -- a professional freeze, not a book ban. Menger kept his Vienna chair; the Verein continued and Schmoller kept chairing it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: After 1884, Menger's students kept fighting Schmoller. They defended the Austrian method of reasoning from first principles. Which pair of Menger's Vienna pupils carried the school forward?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
Fritz Machlup and Gottfried Haberler
John Maynard Keynes and Joan Robinson
context: Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) and Wieser (1851-1926) were Menger's direct pupils and the school's second generation. Mises and Hayek were the THIRD generation (Mises studied under Boehm-Bawerk; Hayek under Wieser and then Mises). Machlup and Haberler were the fourth. Keynes and Joan Robinson were the Cambridge tradition Austrians would fight NEXT. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: The personal quarrel ended when Schmoller died in 1917. But the method split it started stayed permanent. Which lasting divide in twentieth-century economics still traces back to Berlin in 1883?
answer: Methodological individualism versus historical-institutional analysis
choices: Methodological individualism versus historical-institutional analysis
Free trade versus protectionism
Gold standard versus fiat currency
Micro versus macro economics
context: The Austrian line (Menger, Boehm-Bawerk, Wieser, Mises, Hayek) kept methodological individualism -- the individual choosing actor as the atom of analysis. The descendants of the German Historical School (Veblen, Commons, and later institutional, behavioural, and evolutionary economics) kept the historical-institutional focus on how rules, habits, and organizations shape choice. Both traditions still argue the 1883 quarrel every generation. Free trade vs protectionism, gold vs fiat, and micro vs macro are separate debates. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: The Methodenstreit gave the Austrian School its name. But it did not hand the school every one of its famous ideas. Which pillar of Austrian economics was not born in the 1883 method quarrel, but was developed later by the school's successors?
answer: The socialist calculation critique of central planning
choices: The socialist calculation critique of central planning
The rejection of the labor theory of value
The claim that value is subjective
The insistence on universal deductive laws
context: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' -- the argument that without market prices no rational allocation is possible -- came in 1920, thirty-seven years after Menger's method book. Subjective value, the rejection of labor value, and universal deductive laws were all Menger 1871 and 1883 -- the founding moves. The calculation critique is the DAUGHTER of the founding method, not the mother. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: From 1920 to 1934, a group of Vienna scholars met every other Friday night in a small office. They argued for three hours about economics, history, and more. No fees, no exams, no degree. Whose private seminar was it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Joseph Schumpeter
context: Mises (1881-1973) worked at the Handelskammer -- the Austrian Chamber of Commerce -- as an economic policy adviser from 1909 onwards, and used his office there as the meeting room. The seminar is remembered as the Mises-Kreis or the Privatseminar. Menger had retired in 1903 and died in 1921; Boehm-Bawerk died in 1914; Schumpeter had left Austria for Bonn and would soon leave for Harvard. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/ludwig-mises-and-the-vienna-private-archive/.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises taught that no small group of experts in a capital city can plan a whole economy well. Why not?
answer: Millions of people have information the planners never see
choices: Millions of people have information the planners never see
The experts do not have enough calculators
The people refuse to obey any rules
The experts always lie about their plans
context: Privatseminar (private + seminar) marks its outside-the-university status; Hauptseminar means main university seminar; Kolloquium is a formal academic colloquium (Karl Menger the younger ran a Mathematical Colloquium in the same Vienna years); Lehrstuhl means academic chair. The Privatseminar had no institutional home -- that was the point. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: Two of the regulars at Mises's Vienna office in the 1920s went on to top-tier fame in economics. One won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1974. The other helped start a whole new field of analysis in 1944. Which pair fits?
answer: Friedrich Hayek and Oskar Morgenstern
choices: Friedrich Hayek and Oskar Morgenstern
Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard
John Maynard Keynes and Joan Robinson
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
context: Hayek shared the 1974 Nobel with Gunnar Myrdal for his work on money and business cycles. Morgenstern co-authored Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with John von Neumann in 1944 -- the founding book of game theory. Both cut their teeth in Mises's Vienna office in the 1920s. Rothbard was Mises's New York student decades later; Keynes and Robinson were the Cambridge tradition; Friedman and Schwartz met at NBER in America. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: Mises worked as a policy adviser at a place in Vienna. His famous Privatseminar met in the same building. Which place was it?
answer: The Austrian Chamber of Commerce (Handelskammer)
choices: The Austrian Chamber of Commerce (Handelskammer)
The University of Vienna Faculty of Law
The Austrian National Bank
The Ministry of Finance
context: Mises never held a paid university chair in Vienna; the Faculty of Law let him teach as an unsalaried Privatdozent, but his day job -- and the seminar's meeting room -- was at the Handelskammer. The Austrian National Bank and the Ministry of Finance were separate institutions Mises advised as an outside expert. The choice of the Chamber of Commerce, not the university, was itself an emblem of the seminar's independent, non-academic character. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: A London professor visits a private seminar in Vienna. He is so impressed by one young economist that he invites him back to London to teach. That single invitation carries a whole school of economic thought to England. What lesson does this show?
answer: Personal contact and one open door can carry ideas across borders
choices: Personal contact and one open door can carry ideas across borders
Ideas only travel through best-selling published books
Universities never share professors across national borders
Governments must approve every new economic theory first
context: Robbins was head of the LSE economics department and the author of An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science (1932), which carried strong Austrian influence. His invitation brought Hayek to LSE in 1931 and set up the famous Hayek-Keynes debates of the 1930s. Keynes was at Cambridge, not LSE; Pigou held the Cambridge chair; Beveridge was LSE Director but not the economist who spotted Hayek. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In the 1920s a Vienna economist held a small seminar at home. Guests included economists, philosophers, and sociologists. Why can a mix of fields help an economist think better?
answer: Other fields ask questions economics alone would never think to ask
choices: Other fields ask questions economics alone would never think to ask
Economists cannot count above ten without a philosopher's help
Sociologists always agree with whatever an economist says
Only philosophers are allowed to publish economic papers
context: Schuetz (1899-1959) worked days as a bank lawyer and joined the Privatseminar in the 1920s; his book The Phenomenology of the Social World (1932) argued that economics rests on the meanings actors give their own actions -- a philosophical fit with Mises's methodological individualism. He escaped to New York in 1939. Popper, Neurath, and Schlick belonged to the neighboring Vienna Circle of logical positivists, not the Mises Kreis. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: In 1920s Vienna, a Mathematical Colloquium met apart from the Privatseminar. Kurt Goedel and John von Neumann joined. Its host was also in the Vienna Circle. His father helped found the Austrian School. Who was the host?
answer: Karl Menger the younger
choices: Karl Menger the younger
Rudolf Carnap
Hans Hahn
Philipp Frank
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985), son of Carl Menger the economist, did dimension theory in mathematics, edited the proceedings of his Mathematical Colloquium (which included Goedel's incompleteness results and von Neumann's work), and sat in the Vienna Circle. The Menger name reaches into TWO of interwar Vienna's most consequential intellectual gatherings -- his father founded one tradition, and Karl the younger crossed into the other. Carnap, Hahn, and Frank were Vienna Circle members but not sons of the Austrian School's founder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: In spring 1934 Mises took a chair at the Graduate Institute in a Swiss city. The Vienna Privatseminar ended. Four years later the Nazis took Austria. As a Jew and a liberal, leaving Vienna likely saved his life. Which city did he move to?
answer: Geneva
choices: Geneva
Basel
Zurich
Bern
context: The Graduate Institute of International Studies (Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales) is in Geneva. Mises taught there as professor of international economic relations until 1940, then emigrated to New York when the German army approached Switzerland's borders. The Anschluss came in March 1938. Basel, Zurich, and Bern all have universities but not the Graduate Institute. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Between 1931 and 1940, the Vienna economists left Austria. They ended up at Harvard, Princeton, New York, and other schools. Why did the whole seminar break up?
answer: Its members were Jews or liberals who had to flee Central Europe as the Nazis rose
choices: Its members were Jews or liberals who had to flee Central Europe as the Nazis rose
The Rockefeller Foundation ordered them all to come to the United States
The Austrian government paid for their emigration
They were all fired from their Vienna university positions in 1934
context: The Anschluss of March 1938 made staying impossible for the Jewish and liberal members; Mises had left in 1934 and Hayek in 1931 -- both jumps early enough that they moved as scholars, not as refugees. Machlup was on Rockefeller in America when the Anschluss happened and stayed; Morgenstern was visiting Princeton and chose to stay; Haberler was already at Harvard by 1936. The Rockefeller Foundation funded some fellowships but did not order anyone; the Austrian government did not pay; most of them never held salaried Vienna chairs to be fired from. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Machlup; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Morgenstern; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Fritz Machlup left Vienna in 1933 on a Rockefeller fellowship. He never came back. Over the next forty years he held chairs at three American schools. He pioneered the economics of knowledge and information. Which three schools were they?
answer: Johns Hopkins, Princeton, and New York University
choices: Johns Hopkins, Princeton, and New York University
Harvard, Yale, and Columbia
Chicago, Stanford, and Berkeley
MIT, Cornell, and Brown
context: Machlup was Hutzler Professor at Johns Hopkins 1947-1960, Walker Professor at Princeton 1960-1971, and professor at NYU 1971-1983. His 1962 book The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States is a founding text of information economics. Haberler went to Harvard; Morgenstern to Princeton; Hayek to LSE and later Chicago and Freiburg. Machlup's specific triangle -- Hopkins, Princeton, NYU -- is his own. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Machlup.

question: A politician promises free college, free health care, and better pay. He says the rich will pay for it all. But the rich cannot pay that much. Who pays the rest?

question: The main US group tied to today's democratic-socialist wave grew fast. It went from about 6,000 members in 2014 to around 92,000 by 2021. What is the group called?

question: Today's democratic socialists often push a $15 minimum wage, rent control, government-set drug prices, and one big health plan run by the state. What is the short name for the health plan?

question: The same tools apply no matter what a policy is called. Suppose a $30-an-hour minimum wage is set above the market rate. Which classical reasoning move fits best?
answer: Seen-versus-unseen -- the worker priced out of the labor market is the hidden cost

question: The same tools apply to rent control. Critics from Friedman and Stigler in 1946 down to today's Austrian writers press one move hardest. Which one?
answer: The knowledge-problem and supply-response mechanism -- fewer apartments over time

question: In his 1920 essay on socialist planning, Mises did not attack socialism on politics. What kind of argument did he make?

A theological argument about property

question: The bank's teach-recognition-not-verdict move on this ladder means the kid learns to run one specific analytical chain. Which chain?
answer: Identify the reasoning move a specific critic would press, without demanding the kid share the critic's verdict
choices: Identify the reasoning move a specific critic would press, without demanding the kid share the critic's verdict
Automatically oppose any government policy
Automatically support any market-based approach
Reject any moral evaluation of policy
context: The Recognition-not-verdict move: the answer names the CRITIC'S move (Friedman on minimum wage, Hayek on drug pricing, Buchanan on deficit); the answer never names 'the policy is bad' or 'socialism is wrong'. Source: bank_pipeline framing rules.

question: There is a real gap between 2020s American democratic socialism and Soviet-style planning. What key difference does the bank highlight?

It DOES propose replacing market prices with government-set ones in labor, housing, healthcare, education, energy. The reasoning moves against Gosplan apply less catastrophically in scale but by the same mechanism. Source: dsausa.org platform.

question: The bank teaches the kid to run the reasoning chain but leaves the political verdict to the kid. What is the classical reasoning move that applies to government-negotiated drug pricing (as in Medicare price-setting)?

question: The ladder has one main rule. It is about political labels and the reasoning moves under them. What is the rule?

The reasoning moves apply to any policy that suppresses a price signal, regardless of whether the label is 'socialism', 'progressive reform', 'social democracy', or 'consumer protection'. Source: bank framework rules.

question: A town wants a law. Every train on a new line between two big cities must stop there for a whole day. Local workers get paid to unload and reload each crate. Who wins and who loses if the law passes?

question: In Bastiat's 'negative railway' story, a Bordeaux lawmaker says the train should stop at his city. That break would make work for three local trades. Which three?

question: In 'Economic Sophisms,' Bastiat's 'negative railway' joke targets a real plan for a railway between two capitals. Which two cities was it going to link?

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' joke, taken all the way, calls for a break at every stop on the line. What do you end up with?

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' joke has a twin. The twin mocks the same make-work idea, but from destruction instead of friction. Which twin joke is it?

question: Someone argues that adding extra stops and toll booths along a train line will boost the economy, because more towns will get to serve travelers. A French writer used this to expose a broken argument. What is wrong with treating delays as a benefit?

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' is the classic reply to any claim that a labor-saving machine 'destroys jobs.' If breaking a rail line to give porters work were a real gain, we would also have to smash two ancient labor-saving tools. Which two?

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' idea shows up today in a scare about a new kind of software. The software makes text and images. Which scare uses the same shape?

question: A town has a broken bridge fixed quickly by a new machine, freeing the workers to build a new school. question: One Sunday night in August 1971, President Nixon cut into TV shows with a big speech. He announced huge changes to the economy. He also cut the last link between the dollar and gold for foreign central banks. What is that speech usually called?

question: The Nixon shock was really three moves at once, not one. One shut the gold window. Another was a move at home -- the first peacetime price controls in US history. What was that move?

About 15 years
More than 100 years
context: From August 15, 1971 to 2026 is 54-55 years -- longer than any earlier pure-fiat regime in US peacetime history. The 1862-79 greenback interruption during and after the Civil War lasted 17 years. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends.

question: The timing of the Nixon shock was simple politics. Nixon was up for re-election the next year. He wanted the pain of the dollar fix to fall on foreigners, not on voters. What year was that election?
context: Nixon won re-election in November 1972 carrying 49 states. Wage-price controls kept CPI appearances calm through the campaign; inflation exploded in 1973-74 after the controls unravelled. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_presidential_election.

question: Nixon-era fiscal recklessness that Bretton Woods could not accommodate had two main sources: costly domestic social programs and a foreign war. Which pair does the Austrian critique name as the load Bretton Woods buckled under?
answer: The Great Society and the Vietnam War
choices: The Great Society and the Vietnam War
The New Deal and the Korean War
The New Frontier and the Cold War arms race
The Fair Deal and the Marshall Plan
context: The Johnson-Nixon combination of Great Society spending and Vietnam War financing pushed the fiscal deficit into what could no longer be paid in gold at $35/oz. Nixon's 1971 announcement made the failure formal. Source: mises.org/library/nixon-shock.

question: Bitcoin fans see the Bitcoin white paper as an answer to the money problem born from the Nixon shock. The paper came out in October 2008. About how long after August 15, 1971 did it appear?
answer: Thirty-seven years
choices: Thirty-seven years
Eight years
Ninety years
Fifty-five years
context: August 1971 to October 2008 is 37 years. The Bitcoin white paper proposed a fixed-supply digital money as an alternative to central-bank-managed fiat -- an answer, in its authors' framing, to the political-money problem that Nixon inaugurated. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: A city passes a law. Only 12,000 taxis can work here. You need a special license to drive one. No new licenses will be made. What will most likely happen over the next 20 years?
answer: The price of a license rises very high because new ones cannot be made
choices: The price of a license rises very high because new ones cannot be made
The price of a license drops close to zero
Anyone can start driving a taxi anytime
Nothing changes because taxis do not matter
context: The Haas Act of 1937 created the New York City taxi-medallion system. The cap made each medallion an artificially scarce property right that would eventually trade for over a million dollars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: In New York City by 2014 there was a legal limit on how many yellow taxis could exist -- about 11,700 total. To drive one, you had to buy a government license called a "medallion." Roughly what did one medallion cost at the peak?
answer: $1.3 million
choices: $1.3 million
$13 million
context: The NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission auction records show medallion prices rising from $2,500 in 1947 to $200,000 in 1997 to about $1.3 million in 2013-14. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: In 2011, a San Francisco startup launched a phone-based ride app in New York City. It signed up as a 'black car' service, not as a taxi. Which company was it?
answer: Uber
choices: Uber
Lyft
Curb
Via
context: Uber's NYC launch in 2011 categorized each driver as a for-hire vehicle (FHV) rather than a taxi, bypassing the yellow-cab medallion cap entirely and letting supply expand to meet demand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Uber.

question: For decades a New York City taxi driver had to own a metal disc called a medallion to drive a yellow cab. In 2013 one medallion sold for about $1.3 million. Then Uber came in and by 2019 the price had crashed about 92 percent. Roughly what price was left?
choices: $1 million
context: Medallion auction prices tracked the collapse: about $1.3M (2013) to about $700K (2016) to about $100K (2019). Many owners had borrowed against medallions as collateral. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: A city limits the number of taxi permits, so only a small fixed number of cabs are allowed on the streets. This helps existing drivers earn more. A French writer's method asks: who is the hidden loser no one immediately sees?
answer: The riders who cannot find a cab and walk, wait, or drive drunk
choices: The riders who cannot find a cab and walk, wait, or drive drunk
The bookkeepers who record the taxi companies' profits
The mechanics who service each yellow cab already on the road
The city clerks who publish the auction results each year
context: Bastiat's move from That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (1850): the visible medallion owners were rich; the invisible losers were the would-be riders denied service and the would-be drivers blocked by the cap. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: Before ride apps, New York yellow cabs skipped some parts of the city where street pickups paid less. Which neighborhoods were the best-known example?
answer: The outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens
choices: The outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens
The Financial District and Midtown Manhattan
LaGuardia and JFK airport terminals
Times Square and Rockefeller Center
context: Yellow-cab economics depended on street hails, so drivers concentrated in Manhattan; the app-hail model let for-hire vehicles serve outer-borough demand that had gone unserved for decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_and_Limousine_Commission_(New_York_City).

question: In May 2019, two New York Times reporters ran a Pulitzer-finalist series on the taxi medallion crash. It tracked about 950 owner bankruptcies and 8 driver suicides. What was the series's headline focus?
answer: How reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers
choices: How reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers
How Uber built a monopoly in New York City
How the Haas Act created New York's first cab rules
How the NYC Taxi Commission was reformed in 2019
context: Emma Fitzsimmons and Brian Rosenthal's NYT series showed that many owner-drivers had bought medallions at peak prices using loans they could not repay after the collapse. Source: nytimes.com/2019/05/19/nyregion/nyc-taxis-medallions-suicides.html.

question: Bastiat's method reads the 2013-19 medallion collapse as more than a loss for medallion owners. On his accounting, what was the collapse actually revealing about the seven-decade run of the cap?
answer: The capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting from riders and blocked drivers for 76 years
choices: The capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting from riders and blocked drivers for 76 years
A one-time market crash unrelated to earlier medallion prices
Uber's illegal subsidies temporarily undercutting a fair market
A currency-inflation effect on New York asset prices
context: Bastiat's move: the medallion price had capitalized the transfer FROM riders and blocked drivers TO cap-protected owners; the collapse reversed a transfer that had run one way since 1937. Painful for owners, but a reversal. Source: bastiat.org (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen, 1850).

question: Ludwig von Mises said that when a government prints lots of new money, prices go up. Who tends to be hurt the most by rising prices?
answer: People with savings and people on fixed incomes
choices: People with savings and people on fixed incomes
Only foreign travelers
Only the very rich
Nobody; printing money is free
context: Mises's NYU seminar met on Thursday evenings for twenty-four years, in the Graduate School of Business Administration on Trinity Place and later on Washington Square. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: A famous economist said: 'You cannot run a whole economy from one office. The people in charge cannot know what every family and business needs.' What is this idea called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The math problem
The luck problem
The weather problem
context: NYU paid Mises nothing; his salary was covered by outside donors. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In the 1940s, a famous free-market economist could not land a paid teaching job at any big US school. His ideas were out of fashion. A private group had to pay his salary at New York University so he could still teach. Why did a private group have to step in?
answer: Universities would not hire scholars whose ideas they disliked
choices: Universities would not hire scholars whose ideas they disliked
The scholar refused to teach any students
The government had banned him from teaching
He asked for a huge salary no school would pay
context: The William Volker Fund of Kansas City funded much of the mid-century Austrian revival in America. Source: grokipedia.com/page/William_Volker_Fund.

question: In the 1940s, most schools ignored a famous economist. His free-market ideas were unpopular. Fans of his books quietly chipped in to keep his classes going for years. What does this show about ideas?
answer: Even unpopular ideas can survive if some people value them
choices: Even unpopular ideas can survive if some people value them
Only ideas the government approves can survive
Only ideas that make money in the short run survive
All ideas that survive must be true
context: Lawrence Fertig, a Madison Avenue advertising executive who admired Mises's work, personally supplemented Mises's NYU salary and endowed a lecture hall named after him. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: One economist wrote a giant 1962 textbook that started with a single person alone on an island, then built up trade, prices, and money step by step. Why start economics from one person alone?
answer: To show that every trade and price begins with individual choices
choices: To show that every trade and price begins with individual choices
Because groups of people are illegal in economic theory
Because Robinson Crusoe was the first real economist
Because islands are the only place markets ever exist
context: Rothbard attended the NYU seminar from 1949 and remained through the 1960s. His subsequent writing carried the seminar's tradition to a wider American audience. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: One economist said an entrepreneur is a person who spots a chance others have missed. It is like seeing a wrong price on a shelf. What does this view say drives new firms and better prices?
answer: Alertness to opportunities other people have overlooked
choices: Alertness to opportunities other people have overlooked
A government official approving each new business idea
Random luck with no skill or noticing involved at all
Copying exactly what every other seller is already doing
context: Israel Kirzner's NYU PhD under Mises produced Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago, 1973), the foundational modern statement of Austrian entrepreneurship theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Israel_Kirzner.

question: Ludwig von Mises taught his first American doctoral student in New York in the 1950s. That student later spent his career teaching Austrian economics at a small liberal-arts college. What was the effect on Austrian economics in America?
answer: Austrian ideas kept a foothold in a few colleges even when mainstream departments ignored them
choices: Austrian ideas kept a foothold in a few colleges even when mainstream departments ignored them
Every US university started teaching Austrian economics by 1970
Austrian economics survived only in Europe and never reached the US
Mainstream US departments quickly adopted the Austrian view of banking
context: Hans Sennholz taught for decades at Grove City College, where he trained a generation of Austrian-friendly American economists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Sennholz.

question: In the 1930s and 40s many top Austrian economists fled Europe. Several kept teaching in American schools into the late 1960s. Why did their long American teaching careers matter for economics?
answer: They carried Austrian ideas into a whole new generation of English-speaking students
choices: They carried Austrian ideas into a whole new generation of English-speaking students
They proved Austrian ideas only worked inside Austria
They ended all study of Austrian economics forever
They replaced all American economics teaching with Marxist teaching
context: Mises's last seminar was December 1969; he died in October 1973 at age 92. The seminar ended without a successor; the American Austrian tradition would not have another dedicated graduate program until Auburn (1982) and George Mason. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In 1907 the United States had NO central bank. When several big New York banks began to fail, the federal government could not stop the panic. Who ended up organizing the rescue?
answer: A group of wealthy private bankers, using their own money
choices: A group of wealthy private bankers, using their own money
Congress, by passing an emergency bill overnight
The US Army, by seizing all the banks
The state of New York, by declaring war on Wall Street
context: J.P. Morgan (70 years old in 1907) coordinated the private rescue, summoning bank and trust presidents to his personal library and pooling their capital. It was the last major US financial rescue conducted by a private individual acting as de facto central bank. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: The 1907 New York banking panic is also called the Knickerbocker Crisis. It got that name from the one place whose fall started the big run. What kind of place was Knickerbocker?
answer: A trust company
choices: A trust company
A commercial bank
A stock exchange
An insurance company
context: The Knickerbocker Trust Company was the third-largest trust in New York. Trust companies held bank-like deposits but faced looser reserve rules than national banks. When Knickerbocker's president was linked to the Heinze copper-corner scheme, depositors fled. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knickerbocker_Trust_Company.

question: The 1907 panic began when two brothers tried to corner shares of one mining firm. They failed. Which brothers ran the failed corner?
answer: Otto and Augustus Heinze
choices: Otto and Augustus Heinze
Frederick and Charles Barney
James and John Stillman
Nelson and Winthrop Aldrich
context: The Heinze brothers tried to squeeze short-sellers of United Copper Company stock. When the squeeze collapsed on October 16, 1907, depositors at banks associated with the Heinzes started pulling funds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: During the crisis, Morgan called rival bank and trust chiefs to one spot in his own house. He locked them in until they put up rescue money. Where were they held?
answer: His personal library at 219 Madison Avenue
choices: His personal library at 219 Madison Avenue
The floor of the New York Stock Exchange
The board room of the Bank of New York
The White House Cabinet Room
context: The building is now the Morgan Library and Museum. The 'locked in the library' detail comes from Morgan's son-in-law Herbert Satterlee's 1939 biography and is well-attested in period accounts. Source: themorgan.org/about.

question: The 1907 crisis showed a gap in the American money system. Reformers spent the next six years arguing to fill it. What key thing did the country lack?
answer: A lender of last resort
choices: A lender of last resort
A federal income tax
A national stock exchange
A commercial-bank deposit insurer
context: Without a central bank, panics required ad-hoc rescues by private figures. The 1907 crisis made the political argument that the country needed a permanent institution able to supply liquidity in a run -- an argument that produced the Federal Reserve six years later. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/panic-of-1907.

question: During the rescue, Morgan told the head of the New York Stock Exchange that closing it 'would be too great a shock.' He then got a big sum from bank chiefs in his library. Roughly how much did he raise, and how fast?
answer: About $25 million in 15 minutes
choices: About $25 million in 15 minutes
About $250 million in an hour
About $1 billion in a day
About $2 million in 15 minutes
context: Morgan raised roughly $25 million from bank presidents assembled in his library in about 15 minutes to keep the NYSE open. Adjusted for the era, this was the operative moment of the private rescue. Source: Satterlee, J. Pierpont Morgan: An Intimate Portrait (1939).

question: Morgan decided to let the Knickerbocker Trust fail but organized the rescue of another major trust he judged to be solvent. Which trust did he save?
answer: Trust Company of America
choices: Trust Company of America
Bankers Trust
United States Trust
Manhattan Trust
context: Trust Company of America was hit by a run in the days after Knickerbocker's failure. Morgan judged it solvent, arranged a private syndicate to backstop its deposits, and it survived. This is the earliest well-documented case of a private banker distinguishing solvent from insolvent institutions in a panic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: During the 1907 New York banking panic, the U.S. Treasury moved $35 million of federal money into New York banks to try to stop the panic. What is a modern name for this kind of rescue?
answer: A bailout
choices: A bailout
A tariff
A stimulus check
A gold-standard reset
context: George Cortelyou (Treasury 1907-09) added federal deposits to New York national banks during the crisis. This gave Morgan's private effort a substantial fiscal complement -- an early example of Treasury-Fed style coordination before the Fed existed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_B._Cortelyou.

question: After the 1907 banking panic, Congress created a special study group that worked for four years to design a permanent central bank for the US. Why did lawmakers say they wanted one?
answer: So there would be a lender of last resort during future bank panics
choices: So there would be a lender of last resort during future bank panics
So the US government could stop printing all paper money forever
So banks could stop paying any interest to depositors
So Americans would only use gold coins again
context: Senator Nelson Aldrich chaired the Commission, which studied European central banks and produced the Aldrich Plan of 1911 -- the structural blueprint behind the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Monetary_Commission.

question: Historian Charles Kindleberger said Morgan's rescue could not be done again. Leaving future panics to one aging private banker was no long-term plan. What did he say the rescue was 'the last time' any single person did?
answer: Acted as a central bank in a major crisis
choices: Acted as a central bank in a major crisis
Owned a majority stake in a Wall Street trust
Held gold reserves for the US Treasury
Personally set discount rates for member banks
context: Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes uses the Morgan 1907 episode as the pivot case -- the last time an individual performed the lender-of-last-resort function that permanent central banks now provide. Source: Kindleberger + Aliber, Manias, Panics, and Crashes.

question: After a major American banking panic in 1907, Congress worked for six years and then passed a law in 1913 that created a national central bank meant to prevent future panics. What was that 1913 law called?
answer: The Federal Reserve Act
choices: The Federal Reserve Act
The Sherman Antitrust Act
The Glass-Steagall Act
The Securities Exchange Act
context: Signed December 23, 1913, the Federal Reserve Act created the permanent lender-of-last-resort infrastructure the 1907 crisis had shown the country lacked. Its structural design came out of the Aldrich Plan and the Jekyll Island meeting of November 1910. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/federal_reserve_act_signed.

question: Adam Smith opened Book 1, Chapter 4 of his 1776 book with a puzzle he could not solve. One common thing is very useful, he said, but you can buy almost nothing with it. Another thing is almost useless, yet you can trade a lot for it. Which two things did he compare?
answer: Water and diamonds
choices: Water and diamonds
Bread and gold
Iron and silver
Salt and pearls
context: The passage runs 'Nothing is more useful than water: but it will purchase scarce any thing; scarce any thing can be had in exchange for it. A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' It is the founding statement of the paradox of value. Source: Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations Book 1 Ch 4, via geolib.com.

question: Adam Smith saw the water-and-diamonds puzzle. He did not solve it. He split the word 'value' into two senses and moved on. Which two senses did he name?
answer: Value in use and value in exchange
choices: Value in use and value in exchange
Natural price and market price
Real value and nominal value
Absolute value and relative value
context: Real / nominal and natural / market are also genuine Smith distinctions but they belong to different chapters; the paradox-of-value passage explicitly opens with value-in-use and value-in-exchange as the two senses of the word. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paradox of value'.

question: After Adam Smith, many economists tried to say a thing's value came from how much work went into making it. This is called the labor theory of value. Which two thinkers pushed it hardest, in books from 1817 and 1867?
answer: David Ricardo and Karl Marx
choices: David Ricardo and Karl Marx
Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill
Jean-Baptiste Say and Frederic Bastiat
Nassau Senior and John Elliott Cairnes
context: Ricardo's Principles of Political Economy and Taxation appeared in 1817; Marx's Capital appeared in German in 1867. Both took embodied labour to be the objective source of value -- Marx developed it into a theory of surplus value and exploitation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Labor theory of value'.

question: The 1871 Grundsaetze of Carl Menger dissolved Smith's puzzle by rejecting the whole search for an objective property of a good. Where, according to Menger, does the value of a good actually reside?
answer: In the ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against alternative uses
choices: In the ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against alternative uses
In the average number of labour-hours embodied in producing it
In the objective usefulness of the substance to human survival
In the political power of the class that produces it
context: Menger's move was that no chooser ever compares 'water as a class' with 'diamonds as a class'; a chooser always compares one more unit of a good, given current holdings, against the next-best alternative use of the same effort or money. Source: Wikipedia, 'Principles of Economics (Menger book)'.

question: Menger tells this story. A farmer has five sacks of grain. He uses them for his bread, his animals, seed, brewing, and feeding parrots. If he loses one sack, which use does he give up first? And what does that set?
answer: The parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
choices: The parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
His own bread -- and the most-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
Every use loses equally -- so the value is the average of the five uses
The bread and the seed together -- because they are the productive uses
context: Menger's insight is that a rational chooser losing one unit will drop the least-urgent use first; therefore the value of any one interchangeable unit equals the importance of the marginal use, not the peak use. This is diminishing marginal utility stated at the level of a specific person's ranking. Source: Libertarianism.org, 'Menger's Principles of Economics: The Marginal Revolution'.

question: Menger's method solves the old diamond-water puzzle. In a city with plumbing, why does one more glass of water rank so low while one more diamond ranks so high?
answer: Water is abundant so the marginal glass serves only a trivial use; diamond stock is near zero so the marginal stone serves a top-ranked use
choices: Water is abundant so the marginal glass serves only a trivial use; diamond stock is near zero so the marginal stone serves a top-ranked use
Water is a public good and diamonds are a private good, so only diamonds carry value
Diamonds embody more labour-hours per unit than water does
The government sets the price of water below its true value
context: Once value is a ranking of the marginal unit, high total utility and high marginal utility come apart. Water's total utility is enormous but its marginal utility to a plumbed household is nearly zero; a first diamond's marginal utility to someone who has never owned one is large. Source: Study.com, 'Diamond-Water Paradox'.

question: The best test of Menger's answer is to reverse the scarcities. Put a traveller in the middle of a desert with one canteen of water and pockets full of diamonds. According to the marginal-unit move, what should happen to his ranking of the next glass versus the next stone?
answer: The ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond
choices: The ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond
The ranking stays the same -- diamonds always outrank water because they always cost more to make
Both goods have equal marginal value in any setting
The ranking depends on the traveller's political beliefs, not on his holdings
context: That the ranking reverses on the reverse scarcities is the diagnostic test of the marginal-unit move: value was never a property of the good, it was a ranking that depended on how much of each the chooser already held. Source: Adam Smith Works, 'Three Ways of Looking at the Water-Diamond Paradox'.

question: Once Menger's move is on the table, an entire class of nineteenth-century value theories collapses in the same stroke. Which of these theories does it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value, because it assumed value was a property of the good rather than of a chooser's ranking
choices: The labour theory of value, because it assumed value was a property of the good rather than of a chooser's ranking
The quantity theory of money, because it treated the money supply as exogenous
The theory of comparative advantage, because it depended on labour cost differences
The Malthusian theory of population, because it assumed diminishing returns in agriculture
context: Every step of the labour-theory chain -- Smith on embodied labour, Ricardo's refinement, Marx's socially necessary labour -- assumed value belonged to the good. Denying the assumption denies the whole chain. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus depend on other assumptions and are unaffected. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginalism'.

question: Water is enormously useful when you have none at all, since you would die without it, but if you already have plenty of water, one more glass barely matters to you. Textbooks use two matched terms for these two very different values. What are they?
answer: Total utility and marginal utility
choices: Total utility and marginal utility
Real value and nominal value
Objective utility and subjective utility
Gross utility and net utility
context: Textbooks separate total utility (the whole stack of satisfactions from all units held) from marginal utility (the added satisfaction from one more unit given current holdings). Menger's water-and-diamonds resolution is the classic teaching case for the distinction. Source: Study.com, 'Diamond-Water Paradox'.

question: The marginal-unit fix goes beyond diamonds and water. Value is a chooser's ranking of one more unit against the next-best use. Once you accept that, older ways to talk about value break down. Which older project becomes hopeless?
answer: The whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good itself
choices: The whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good itself
The project of measuring prices in a common unit of account
The project of studying international trade patterns
The project of writing economic history
context: Menger, Jevons and Walras converged on the same conclusion in the 1871-1874 marginal revolution: value is not IN the good, it is a ranking of the next unit by a chooser. Once that move is made, cost-of-production and labour-embodied theories lose their footing. Prices, trade patterns and economic history remain perfectly good subjects of study. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginalism'.

question: In 1908 Colonel Willoughby Verner wrote to The Times about the hedges along English country roads, which had been cut back so drivers could see much farther ahead. He wrote to describe what the clear sightlines had done. What did he report?
answer: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common
choices: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common
Drivers took to the lanes, and horse traffic vanished
Drivers kept to main roads, and village trade collapsed
Drivers slowed at bends, and crashes became rarer
context: Grokipedia's Risk compensation article records Verner's 1908 letter to The Times as the earliest documented observation of the pattern: improving the road did not buy the safety the improvement promised, because drivers spent part of it on speed. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: In 1965, Ralph Nader wrote a book saying Detroit cared more about power and style than about surviving a crash. The next year, Senate hearings showed what General Motors had done to Nader. The news swung public opinion behind the first federal auto-safety law. What had General Motors done?
answer: Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader
choices: Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader
Quietly recalled the model Nader had singled out for attack
Bought his publisher and cancelled the second print run
Paid a rival engineer to write and publish a rebuttal book
context: President Lyndon Johnson signed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act on September 9, 1966, with Nader among roughly 200 people at the Rose Garden ceremony. The Act produced the first mandatory federal vehicle standards, effective with the 1968 model year. Sources: Wikipedia, 'National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act'; Wikipedia, 'Ralph Nader'.

question: American football teams swapped leather headgear for rigid plastic-shell helmets in the late 1940s. Skull fractures fell, as the designers expected. But cervical-spine injuries rose, and researchers traced the rise to a change in how players now hit each other. What did players start doing?
answer: Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet
choices: Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet
Gripping the facemask to swing an opponent down
Driving the helmet into the opponent's front knee
Locking both arms around the opponent's waist
context: The leather helmet made spearing too painful to attempt; the plastic shell made it survivable for the tackler, so the technique spread and the neck paid for it. The protection was real, and the behaviour moved to consume part of it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: From 1968, the U.S. made every new car have seat belts, padded dashboards, and safer steering columns. In a 1975 paper, Sam Peltzman found that deaths per crash dropped as the engineers had promised. But total highway deaths did not fall. What did his data show that closed the gap?
answer: Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent
choices: Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent
Rear-seat passenger deaths rose faster than front-seat deaths
Belts were fitted in the cars but almost no driver buckled them
New highway building pushed traffic onto narrow rural roads
context: Peltzman, 'The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation', Journal of Political Economy 83(4), 677-725, August 1975. The crash-test literature implied annual highway deaths would be about 20 percent greater without the mandated devices; Peltzman argued the offsets were close to complete, with lives saved inside the car paid for by deaths outside it and by more accidents overall. Source: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/260352

question: A city wants to require bike helmets. It points to lab tests showing how much a helmet cuts head injuries in a crash. A Chicago-school economist tells the council the lab number is the wrong one to plan on. What is his objection?
answer: That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain
choices: That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain
That the council cannot know which streets its cyclists actually fear most
That the helmet makers will end up writing the standard the council adopts
That the cost falls on cyclists while the credit goes to the councillors
context: The three rejected choices are real reasoning moves aimed elsewhere: Hayek's knowledge problem, George Stigler's regulatory capture (1971), and Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits with dispersed costs (1965). The move being made here is incentive recognition -- the engineering estimate describes the device, not the person using it.

question: In 1972 the FDA ordered child-safe caps on aspirin and some other drug bottles. W. Kip Viscusi later checked the poisoning data. Aspirin poisonings had not dropped. Poisonings from other painkillers had gone up. What did Viscusi say parents were doing?
answer: Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach
choices: Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach
Buying larger bottles because the safe caps cost more per pack
Switching to painkillers the new rule did not yet cover
Storing several drugs together in one unmarked kitchen jar
context: Viscusi named it the 'lulling effect': a cap that is hard for an adult to open gets left loose, and a cap advertised as child proof invites a parent to relax the precaution the child actually depended on. W. Kip Viscusi, 'The Lulling Effect: The Impact of Child-Resistant Packaging on Aspirin and Analgesic Ingestions', American Economic Review 74(2), 324-327, May 1984.

question: Airbags and antilock brakes reach drivers through the market, not through a law. Safety-minded drivers buy them first. In a 2006 study, Winston, Maheshri, and Mannering tested crash data on this. What did they find the two devices had done to crashes and injuries?
answer: Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed
choices: Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed
