answer: The socialist calculation problem
choices: The socialist calculation problem
The overproduction paradox
The trade-deficit puzzle
The wage-lag effect
context: Published by George Routledge & Sons in London in 1935, with Hayek's own introductory essay 'The Nature and History of the Problem' and Barone's 'Ministry of Production in the Collectivist State' as an appendix. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: Hayek's most famous essay said the facts you need to run an economy live in millions of minds. The tin miner's local rock, the shopper's list, the machinist spotting a faster tool. Prices, he said, pull all of it together on their own. Which journal ran the September 1945 essay?
answer: The American Economic Review
choices: Economica
The American Economic Review
The Quarterly Journal of Economics
The Journal of Political Economy
context: 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' ran in AER volume 35, number 4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. It was written as a direct rebuttal of Oskar Lange's market-socialist proposal, reframing the argument from prices to knowledge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society.

question: In his 1945 essay, Hayek gave Lange one point. A planning board might make its own guess-and-check work. But Hayek said this misses what markets can do and planners cannot do at all. Which ability did Hayek give to markets alone?
answer: Aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
choices: Aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
Enforcing binding property rights against politically-connected insiders
Predicting long-run structural shifts in industry composition
Maintaining stable purchasing power across the business cycle
context: The market process is not primarily a calculating device; it is a knowledge-discovery device. The 'knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- who has a spare truck, which mine seam thinned out, which customer is ready to try a substitute -- exists only in the heads of the people on the spot. Prices summarise it. Source: fee.org/articles/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/.

question: An Austrian economist who fled Vienna for New York wrote a big 1949 book restating a key argument: without real market prices, no central planner can figure out how much of each good the country should make. What is the core problem he named?
answer: The economic calculation problem
choices: The economic calculation problem
The tax revenue problem
The population growth problem
The trade deficit problem
context: 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics' (Yale, 1949) devoted a full section to the impossibility of economic calculation under socialism, drawing on the twenty-nine years of debate since 1920. Hayek's parallel restatement came in 'Individualism and Economic Order' (1948). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: For decades, mainstream economists thought Lange's guess-and-check board had beaten Mises on paper. Austrian economists said no, but had to wait on history. What single event in November 1989 made even friendly mainstream economists reopen the question?
answer: The fall of the Berlin Wall
choices: The signing of the Maastricht Treaty
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The Plaza Accord devaluation of the dollar
The passage of the Single European Act
context: On November 9 1989 East German official Guenter Schabowski, at a press conference, mistakenly announced immediate opening of the border; the wall was breached that night. Within two years every planned economy in Eastern Europe had collapsed and begun a market transition. Source: www.archives.gov/news/topics/berlin-wall-anniversary.

question: After the Soviet Union fell in the early 1990s, one long-time socialist economist wrote an essay. He had spent decades defending planning. But he admitted the free-market side of the 1920 planning debate had turned out to be right. What does this admission show?
answer: Even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions
choices: Even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions
Socialist economists never admit anything, no matter what happens in the world
The 1920 debate about planning was never actually settled by any evidence
Central planning worked well and only the Soviet version of it failed
context: The line was: 'It turns out, of course, that Mises was right.' Heilbroner (1919-2005) had held the Norman Thomas chair at the New School and had, in the 1953 first edition of 'The Worldly Philosophers', omitted Mises, Hayek and Friedman entirely. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right.

question: One Austrian economist argued central planners could not calculate real prices without markets. A second Austrian economist pushed the point deeper: even if planners had every price already, they still could not gather all the local knowledge that ordinary people use every day. What did the second thinker add to the first?
answer: The knowledge problem, that no central office can collect all the scattered facts guiding daily choices
choices: The knowledge problem, that no central office can collect all the scattered facts guiding daily choices
The tax problem, that planners cannot collect enough taxes
The voting problem, that planners cannot count votes accurately
The transport problem, that planners cannot ship goods on time
context: Don Lavoie (1951-2001) coined the modern phrase 'the knowledge problem' in this book and its companion 'National Economic Planning: What Is Left?' (both 1985). Peter Boettke and Virgil Storr edited the 2016 reissue. Source: www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning.

question: The Soviet Union used a huge system of forced-labor camps from 1930 to the mid-1950s. Prisoners worked in freezing mines and forests, and millions died. What Russian word is the name for this camp system?
answer: Gulag
choices: Gulag
Kolkhoz
Duma
Politburo
context: Glavnoye Upravleniye Lagerei (Main Camp Administration) ran the Soviet camp system. At peak it comprised over 400 camps and held several million prisoners at any given moment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag.

question: A famous Russian writer had been a prisoner in the Soviet forced-labor camps. He secretly wrote a huge book about the camps while still inside the USSR, then had friends smuggle the pages out on tiny film. What did his book give the world?
answer: The truth about the Soviet camps
choices: The truth about the Soviet camps
A love story from wartime Russia
A guide to Russian cooking
The plans of the Soviet space program
context: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (1918-2008) spent eight years in the camps (1945-53) after his arrest for a private letter mocking Stalin. His The Gulag Archipelago was published in Paris in three volumes 1973-75. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Solzhenitsyn.

question: In 1973 a Russian writer who had spent years inside the Soviet labor camps published a huge three-volume book in Paris exposing the whole camp system. His book broke the West's belief that the camps were a small problem. What did the book mostly reveal?
answer: The vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings
choices: The vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings
That the camps were actually schools of arts and crafts
That the camps held only convicted violent criminals
That Stalin had personally freed most of the prisoners
context: The Gulag Archipelago combined Solzhenitsyn's own experience with hundreds of survivor accounts he had collected. English translation appeared 1974-78 in three volumes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago.

question: In December 1973, the first book of The Gulag Archipelago came out. Two months later, the Soviet state hit back at Solzhenitsyn. What did they do?
answer: Stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt
choices: Stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt
Sentenced him to a new 15-year camp term
Placed him under indefinite house arrest in Moscow
Sent him to internal exile in Kazakhstan
context: Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the USSR on February 13, 1974. He lived in Vermont from 1976 to 1994 and returned to Russia in May 1994 after the USSR's fall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Solzhenitsyn.

question: In the late 1930s, the Soviet ruler ordered mass arrests, show trials, and killings of anyone he thought disloyal. Soviet records later showed roughly how many people this campaign killed?
answer: Well over a million people
choices: Well over a million people
Only a few hundred people at most
About ten thousand people in total
Zero people, since the trials were peaceful
context: Robert Conquest's The Great Terror (Macmillan, 1968) was pioneering. A 1990 revised edition (Oxford UP) folded in the archival numbers. Conquest reportedly suggested titling the new edition 'I Told You So, You... Fools' (an expletive softened for a family bank). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Terror.

question: The Soviet government sent millions of people to forced-labor camps. Many were charged with political crimes. The camps spread across Siberia and other cold places. What was this camp system called?
answer: The Gulag
choices: The Gulag
The Peace Corps
The Marshall Plan
The Warsaw Pact
context: Anne Applebaum's Gulag: A History (Doubleday, 2003) drew on newly opened Soviet archives. Her later work includes Iron Curtain (2012) on postwar Eastern Europe and Red Famine (2017) on Ukraine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag:_A_History.

question: Anne Applebaum's book Gulag counted the prisoners who passed through the Soviet camps from 1930 to 1953. What was her figure?
answer: About 18 million
choices: About 18 million
About 1.8 million
About 180,000
About 180 million
context: About 18 million prisoners passed through the Gulag between 1930 and 1953, with roughly 1.5-1.7 million documented camp deaths. Further mortality in the deportation-settlement system for kulaks and deported peoples adds to the associated total. Source: Applebaum, Gulag: A History (2003).

question: Solzhenitsyn was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in a specific year but could not travel to accept it because he feared being denied re-entry to the USSR. In what year did he win?
context: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1970 cited 'the ethical force with which he has pursued the indispensable traditions of Russian literature'. Solzhenitsyn could not travel to accept in Stockholm and finally received the medal at the 1974 Nobel ceremony after his expulsion. Source: nobelprize.org (Solzhenitsyn 1970).

question: In 1974, The Gulag Archipelago came out. It hit the French left with real moral force. A group of former Maoists broke with communism. What was this group called?
answer: The Nouveaux Philosophes
choices: The Nouveaux Philosophes
The New Left
The Frankfurt School
The Situationists
context: The Nouveaux Philosophes (New Philosophers) -- Andre Glucksmann, Bernard-Henri Levy, and others -- publicly renounced Marxism partly under the impact of Solzhenitsyn's book. The moment marked the French intellectual left's break with communist theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouveaux_philosophes.

question: The Soviet archives opened after 1991. They confirmed the high death toll a Western historian had estimated back in 1968. Many critics had called his number wildly too high. It turned out he was right. What does this show?
answer: Honest outside estimates can be closer to the truth than a closed regime's official numbers
choices: Honest outside estimates can be closer to the truth than a closed regime's official numbers
Historians outside a country can never estimate that country's deaths accurately
Soviet official statistics on the Terror were always accurate all along
The Great Terror actually caused very few deaths
context: The editor did not use the suggested title -- the 1990 revised edition was still called The Great Terror -- but the anecdote captured the intellectual settlement. Sovietologists who had dismissed Conquest's 1968 count as Cold War inflation found the archives confirmed his numbers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Conquest. (Original quote used an expletive; softened for a family bank.)

question: In 1995 Thomas Sowell wrote a book attacking a group he called 'the anointed.' These are people in schools, media, and government who treat their own good intentions as proof a program worked. The subtitle named the habit outright. What was it?
answer: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
choices: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
Ideological Origins of Political Struggles
A Common Sense Guide to the Economy
The Decline, the Deception, the Dogmas
context: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (Basic Books, 1995). The three rejected subtitles are also Sowell's own: A Conflict of Visions (1987), Basic Economics, and Inside American Education. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell).

question: In 1999 Thomas Sowell wrote a book about two ideas of fairness. One says everyone plays by the same rules. The other says: fix the unfair hands life deals so outcomes come out even. What did Sowell call the book?
answer: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
choices: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
Discrimination and Disparities
A Conflict of Visions
Knowledge and Decisions
context: Published by the Free Press in 1999, with sections titled 'The Mirage of Equality', 'The Tyranny of Visions' and 'The Quiet Repeal of the American Revolution'. Sowell's word 'cosmic' is doing real work: the second standard is what someone would choose if he were designing the universe from scratch, and it is therefore not a standard any human institution can be held to. Source: Simon and Schuster publisher page (https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Quest-for-Cosmic-Justice/Thomas-Sowell/9780684864631).

question: Thomas Sowell's 2010 book on intellectuals opens by refusing the everyday meaning of the word. He does not mean a clever person, and he does not mean a person with degrees. His definition is narrower than that, and turns on the job itself. Whom does Sowell count as an intellectual?
answer: Someone whose occupational output is ideas themselves
choices: Someone whose occupational output is ideas themselves
Someone who holds a university post in the humanities
Someone who advises governments on questions of policy
Someone whose writing reaches a large popular audience
context: Sowell's phrase is that 'an intellectual's work begins and ends with ideas, not the practical application of ideas to real world problems.' The narrowness is deliberate and load-bearing: it is what lets him make the accountability argument later in the book, and it is why a surgeon or an engineer, however brilliant, is not an intellectual while doing his own job. Intellectuals and Society (Basic Books, January 5, 2010); a Revised and Expanded Edition followed in 2011.

question: In The Vision of the Anointed Thomas Sowell set out a four-stage pattern he says repeats through social policy. Stage one: a situation is proclaimed a crisis. Stage two: the anointed propose a remedy promising result A, while critics warn it will produce result Z. Stage three: result Z arrives. What does Sowell say stage four looks like?
answer: The remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause
choices: The remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause
The remedy is quietly repealed and its authors move on to a fresh crisis
Congress commissions an independent review that settles the disagreement
The critics are invited to draft the replacement legislation themselves
context: Sowell's line on stage four: 'No burden of proof whatever is put on those who had so confidently predicted improvement.' The champions may also argue that things would have been worse still without the remedy -- a claim that cannot be checked, and is not offered to be checked. Source: Mises Institute, 'How The Vision of the Anointed Explains Every Crisis in America' (https://mises.org/power-market/how-vision-anointed-explains-every-crisis-america).

question: A campaign wants to pay back every group for past wrongs so outcomes finally come out even. In The Quest for Cosmic Justice, Thomas Sowell says the wish is decent, but he still objects. Which objection does he press?
answer: That nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice
choices: That nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice
That voters would never approve the taxes such a programme has to raise
That the agencies running the programme would capture most of the money
That courts, not legislatures, must settle questions of historical wrong
context: This is Hayek's knowledge problem carried into the moral realm: redressing disadvantage across ethnicities, generations and geographies would require knowing what every group's circumstances actually were and what each owes the others -- knowledge that is scattered, contested and in most cases gone. The rejected choices are real objections too (public choice, regulatory capture, constitutional), but they are not Sowell's move here.

question: Sowell compares the intellectual to a surgeon, an engineer, and a battle commander. A commander who fails at the wrong moment can pay with his own life. Sowell says the intellectual's work is judged by a very different test. Whose vote decides if an intellectual has done well?
answer: The peers who read the work and praise it
choices: The peers who read the work and praise it
The voters who elect politicians who adopt it
The publishers and editors who paid for it
The students who are taught it at university
context: Sowell's point is not that intellectuals are stupid or wicked; it is that the feedback loop that disciplines a surgeon or a bridge-builder is missing. Ideas are judged by whether they sound good to other people in the same trade. Whether they 'make life better or worse for others', Sowell writes, 'is another question entirely.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Intellectuals and Society'.

question: The first stage of Sowell's four-stage pattern is the proclaimed crisis, and his complaint about it is not that the situation described is pleasant. It is that one particular check almost never gets run before a crisis is declared. Which check?
answer: Whether the trouble had already been getting better for years
choices: Whether the trouble had already been getting better for years
Whether a foreign country has already tried the proposed remedy
Whether the people affected were ever asked what they wanted
Whether the money to pay for the remedy exists anywhere at all
context: Sowell's wording: such a situation is 'routinely characterized as a crisis, even though all human situations have negative aspects, and even though evidence is seldom asked or given to show how the situation at hand is either uniquely bad or threatening to get worse. Sometimes the situation described as a crisis has in fact already been getting better for years.' A remedy introduced onto an improving trend can then claim credit for the trend.

question: Thomas Sowell's charge that intellectuals pay no price for being wrong leans on historical cases, and the one he presses hardest concerns Britain between the wars. British intellectuals of the 1930s campaigned hard on a question of national defence, and the country paid for their position within the decade. What did they campaign for?
answer: Against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed
choices: Against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed
For handing the navy's budget to the new air force
For a defence union with France and the Low Countries
Against keeping a garrison east of the Suez Canal
context: Sowell's wider claim in Intellectuals and Society is that during the twentieth century intellectuals 'have on balance made the world a worse and more dangerous place', often lending support to dictators. The interwar British case is his cleanest illustration of the accountability gap: none of the writers who argued against rearming lost their standing when the war came. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intellectuals and Society'.

question: Sowell's definition is narrow enough to exclude people commonly filed under the label. An engineer who publishes brilliant papers on bridge design is not, by Sowell's test, working as an intellectual when he designs bridges. Why not?
answer: Because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls
choices: Because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls
Because he is paid by a firm rather than by a university
Because bridge design rests on physics rather than argument
Because he publishes for other engineers, not for the public
context: The test is not the subject matter, the employer or the audience -- it is whether the work terminates in ideas or in something the world can break. This is why Sowell's definition matters for the argument: the same person can be an intellectual on Tuesday, writing on social policy, and not one on Wednesday, signing off a span.

question: A campaigner defends a proposal by saying that the experts agree with it. Sowell's whole argument about idea-workers turns that sentence into a question the listener ought to ask back. What is the question?
answer: Which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong?
choices: Which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong?
Which experts, and who paid for the studies they are citing?
How many experts disagree, and where has their work appeared?
How long have the experts held this view, and what changed it?
context: The rejected questions are worth asking too -- funding, dissent, and the history of a consensus all bear on it. But Sowell's specific contribution is the accountability question, because it sorts experts by the one variable his definition isolates: whether being wrong costs them anything. An epidemiologist, an actuary and a bridge engineer answer it very differently.

question: Sowell's 1995 book describes what policy elites do; his 2010 book asks why they can keep doing it, decade after decade, without the pattern ever breaking. The explanation he gives is structural rather than a claim about anyone's character. What is it?
answer: Nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false
choices: Nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false
Their credentials shield them from having to argue with outsiders
The press shares their politics and declines to report the failures
Voters forget quickly and rarely reopen an argument about old policy
context: This is the spine of the trilogy: The Vision of the Anointed (1995) records the pattern, The Quest for Cosmic Justice (1999) examines the standard that licenses it, and Intellectuals and Society (2010) supplies the mechanism. Note what the argument does not claim -- not that the anointed are dishonest, and not that their conclusions are always wrong. It claims that the occupation carries no cost for being wrong, so nothing in it corrects the error. A reader can accept the mechanism and still disagree with Sowell about any particular policy.

question: A French writer in the 1840s wrote short funny essays defending free trade. His most famous point: when the government does something, you SEE the visible result, but you must also think about the hidden costs you don't see. What did he call this?
answer: The seen and the unseen
choices: The seen and the unseen
Supply and demand
The invisible hand
The gold standard
context: Bastiat was elected to the Constituent Assembly on April 23, 1848 as one of seven deputies from Landes, served on the finance committee, and generally voted with the center-left; his term ran until his death on December 24, 1850. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: A famous French writer defined the government this way: 'a big story where everyone tries to live at the cost of everyone else.' What was his point?
answer: Every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else
choices: Every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else
Government can print free money for everyone
Government workers pay their own salaries
Government spending never requires taxes
context: The essay 'The State' (L'Etat) appeared in near-final form in the Journal des Debats on September 25, 1848 after a shorter draft had run in Bastiat's own revolutionary paper Jacques Bonhomme in June. It was reprinted as a booklet by Guillaumin later the same year. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: Bastiat's 1848 essay 'The State' contains the single most-quoted line he ever wrote: a compact one-sentence definition of what a government actually is. Fill in the blank: 'The state is the great ______ by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else.'
answer: fiction
choices: fiction
leviathan
machine
market
context: The French original reads 'L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde.' The Dean Russell English translation renders 'grande fiction' as 'great fictitious entity,' but 'great fiction' is the version that circulates in almost every 20th-century classical-liberal citation. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/quotes/frederic-bastiat-on-the-state-as-the-great-fiction-by-which-everyone-seeks-to-live-at-the-expense-of-everyone-else-1848.

question: Bastiat's 1848 essay 'The State' opened with a joke prize. Not five hundred francs, but a million, plus crowns, crosses, and ribbons. It was for anyone who could clearly define what one word? Then he gave his own famous one-line entry.
answer: The word 'the State'
choices: The word 'the State'
The word 'liberty'
The word 'property'
The word 'the People'
context: The essay opens: 'I would like to see a prize founded, not of five hundred francs, but of a million, with crowns, crosses and ribbons, for the person who gives a good, simple and intelligible definition of this word: the State.' The mock contest was rhetorical -- Bastiat never had to pay out because, as he framed it, no non-mystical definition could avoid collapsing into the transfer-shape his own line named. Source: https://www.panarchy.org/bastiat/state.1848.html.

question: A French economist in the 1840s summed up bad government with a warning: it is 'the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else.' What key insight is he pointing at?
answer: Voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors
choices: Voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors
Voters can lower taxes just by voting for more spending
Governments always spend money on exactly the right things
Every citizen already produces enough to fund all programs
context: Jacques Bonhomme was Bastiat's short-lived revolutionary paper founded during the 1848 Paris moment; a draft of 'The State' ran there in June 1848 before the fuller version appeared in the Journal des Debats on September 25. 'Jacques Bonhomme' is the traditional French nickname for the rural common man -- the audience Bastiat pitched the essay to. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: In an 1850 pamphlet, Frederic Bastiat warned about a trick. Pass a law that makes taking from your neighbor legal. Then it even looks fine. What did he call this trick?
answer: Legal plunder
choices: Legal plunder
Free exchange
Voluntary trade
Simple charity
context: The Law (La Loi) was published in June 1850. It repeats and sharpens the 'great fiction' insight of the 1848 essay, casting the same claim as a critique of the perversion of legal force. Bastiat died on December 24, 1850. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat put his 1848 essay 'The State' in the Journal des Debats, a top Paris daily. Who read that paper -- the readers he wanted his 'great fiction' line to reach?
answer: The liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership
choices: The liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership
The Bonapartist Catholic peasantry
The Marxist Parisian workers' clubs
The Legitimist rural nobility
context: The Journal des Debats was historically the paper of liberal-Orleanist bourgeois opinion under Louis-Philippe and remained an influential centrist daily under the Second Republic. Bastiat chose it deliberately -- his target reader was the propertied liberal, not the barricade fighter. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: In 1986 an American economist won the Nobel Prize. He built a whole school on one point. Voters and politicians use government power to help themselves. They respond to incentives like anyone else. What is this field called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Labor economics
Behavioral finance
Game theory
context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for his work founding public choice theory -- the formal analysis of politics using economic tools -- with his 1962 book The Calculus of Consent, co-authored with Gordon Tullock, as the flagship text. Buchanan repeatedly cited Bastiat as the classical statement of the same insight. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/frederic-bastiat-government.

question: Two French essays published within eleven days in September 1848 both attacked the Provisional Government's promises. One was Bastiat's 'The State,' with its 'great fiction' line. The other, published in the same paper, was an article by Alexis de Tocqueville. The two men held one seat between them on the same committee of the Constituent Assembly that autumn. Which committee was that?
answer: The finance committee
choices: The finance committee
The judiciary committee
The military committee
The colonial committee
context: Bastiat served on the Constituent Assembly's finance committee through 1848-1849 -- the committee handling the tax and spending questions his 'great fiction' line directly framed. Tocqueville, elected the same April, served in the Assembly as well and would soon join the government as foreign minister. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat's 'great fiction' line is quoted often by free-market thinkers. But the real payoff for a reader today is the reasoning move it names. Which move does the line press?
answer: That every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen
choices: That every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen
That any government is a criminal conspiracy against its own population
That representative democracy is preferable to monarchy on efficiency grounds
That the free market always produces the best possible distribution of wealth
context: The 'great fiction' Bastiat is naming is the illusion that the state has some independent fund of wealth of its own; the reasoning move is that every promised benefit must in fact come from someone -- the tax-payer, the money-holder, the excluded competitor. The reader can accept or reject Bastiat's evaluation; the MOVE is the transfer-recognition. James Buchanan's public choice theory, honored with the 1986 Nobel, formalized the same insight. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/frederic-bastiat-government.

question: For a long time people thought a thing's price should equal the hours of work put into making it -- ten hours of work = twice the price of five. Then economists noticed something different. Where does a thing's value actually come from?
answer: From how much the person choosing it wants it right now
choices: From how much the person choosing it wants it right now
From how many hours the worker spent making it
From how much the raw materials cost
From the average price it usually sells for
context: Menger's move was to relocate value from the OBJECT to the SUBJECT: the same loaf of bread ranks high to a hungry man and low to a full one, so value is not a property of the loaf. The labor theory (Smith 1776, Ricardo 1817, Marx 1867) had made value inhere in the good; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced it in 1871-1874 with subjective valuation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book); mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: A farmer has 5 sacks of grain and no way to buy or trade for more. He uses sack 1 for food, sack 2 for extra food, sack 3 for chickens, sack 4 for whisky, sack 5 for his pet parrots. Robbers steal ONE sack. Which use does he drop first?
answer: The least important one -- parrot feed
choices: The least important one -- parrot feed
The most important one -- basic food
He splits the loss across every use equally
The oldest use -- whisky-brewing
context: Menger's core marginal move is right here: the value of ONE sack is not the average across all uses and not the most important use, it is the LEAST important use the farmer would sacrifice on losing one. This is why the SAME grain is worth different amounts to a well-supplied farmer and a starving one -- their marginal uses differ. The example is from Book 3 of the 1871 Grundsaetze. Source: ecaef.org/carl-menger-and-the-idea-that-broke-economics-open/.

question: Adam Smith noticed a strange puzzle in 1776. Water is needed for life yet almost free. Another substance is not needed for life at all yet sells for a fortune. This puzzle took about 95 years to solve. Which substance was the expensive one in Smith's puzzle?
answer: Diamonds
choices: Diamonds
Salt
Tulips
Silk
context: Smith wrote: 'Nothing is more useful than water, but it will purchase scarce anything... A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' Smith moved on rather than solving it; the resolution waited for the 1871 Marginal Revolution. Salt was famously scarce in some ancient economies but not Smith's example; the tulip mania (1637) is a bubble story, not the paradox; silk was expensive but not paradoxically so. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_value.

question: In the early 1870s, three different economists in three different countries all figured out the same idea about how value works, each on their own within a few years. Historians gave the whole cluster of discoveries a name. What is it called?
answer: The Marginal Revolution
choices: The Marginal Revolution
The Keynesian Revolution
The Industrial Revolution
The Neoclassical Synthesis
context: William Stanley Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Switzerland reached the marginal-utility insight independently of Menger and of each other; none knew the others were working on it. It stands with Darwin-Wallace natural selection and Leibniz-Newton calculus as one of the clearest cases of parallel discovery in intellectual history. The Methodenstreit was Menger's later 1883 quarrel over method with the German Historical School; the Keynesian Revolution was 1936; the Neoclassical Synthesis was Paul Samuelson's 1940s-50s fusion. Source: economicsandhistory.substack.com/p/the-marginal-revolution-and-neoclassical.

question: How can water, which we need to live, be nearly free while diamonds cost a fortune? An economist named Menger said the puzzle disappears once you stop comparing all the water in the world with all the diamonds. What is a person actually ranking when they choose?
answer: The next unit added to what they already have
choices: The next unit added to what they already have
The average price over the last ten years
The total amount produced worldwide each year
The moral worth of the person who wants it
context: A city-dweller with a full tap ranks the NEXT glass of water near-zero -- his thirst is already met; the NEXT diamond added to a collection nobody has still ranks high because it is scarce. Total utility of water is enormous and of diamonds tiny; the MARGINAL utility is the reverse, and price tracks the margin. This is Menger's founding move: value is set at the margin, not by the class. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_value.

question: Menger said things in unlimited supply -- like mountain air and seawater -- meet wants but are not 'economic goods'. Something must be true of a good before a chooser has to rank one unit against another. What does Menger require?
answer: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
choices: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
The good must have taken labor to produce
The good must be legally recognized as property
The good must have a market price above zero
context: For Menger, an unlimited good has utility but no VALUE, because no chooser is ever forced to give up one use to serve another -- there is no ranking at the margin. Only when the good is scarce relative to the wants it could satisfy does a chooser have to rank the marginal unit, and only then does the subjective theory generate a price. Labor-cost, legal recognition, and positive market price are consequences of scarcity, not its cause. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: The Austrian School's most famous German term -- Grenznutzen, 'edge-usefulness' -- appears nowhere in Menger's 1871 Principles. It was coined thirteen years later, in an 1884 book by one of Menger's two great pupils. When the term was translated back into English, it became the phrase every economics textbook now teaches. Who coined Grenznutzen?
answer: Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Friedrich von Wieser
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Carl Menger himself
Leon Walras
context: Wieser (1851-1926) coined Grenznutzen in his 1884 Uber den Ursprung und die Hauptgesetze des wirtschaftlichen Werthes to name a concept his teacher had already articulated in prose. English 'marginal utility' is a direct back-translation of Wieser's coinage. Boehm-Bawerk, Menger's other great pupil, developed capital and interest theory; Menger wrote before the term existed; Walras wrote in French. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A tailor spends 10 hours making a badly-cut, badly-sewn suit that hangs poorly. A second tailor spends 5 hours making a well-cut, well-sewn suit that fits beautifully. On the labor theory of value the first suit should be worth about twice the second. On the subjective theory that Menger pressed against the classical tradition, which comparison actually holds?
answer: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth MORE, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
choices: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth MORE, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
The two suits are worth the same, because labor is labor
The 10-hour suit is still worth more, because it embodies more work
Neither suit has any value until a market price is quoted
context: This is the sharp edge of Menger's move against the labor theory: labor-hours cannot GENERATE value if a chooser ranks the badly-made product lower. Value flows one way only, from the ranking down to the price; labor spent producing something no one ranks highly is labor wasted, not value created. If the labor theory cannot survive this simple case, then Marx's entire theory of surplus value and exploitation -- built on the labor theory -- has no floor to stand on. Source: mises.org/articles-interest/subjective-theory-value.

question: David Ricardo's 1817 Principles said the value of a good comes from the labor put into it. Fifty years later, a German exile in London built a whole theory of capitalist exploitation on that base. He said 'socially needed labor time' was the source of every good's value, and the gap between that value and the worker's wage was surplus taken by the boss. Menger's subjective theory tears the whole thing apart by showing labor cannot make value at all. Whose 1867 book carries the exploitation argument the subjective theory undoes?
answer: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
choices: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
John Stuart Mill, in Principles of Political Economy
Thomas Malthus, in An Essay on the Principle of Population
Jean-Baptiste Say, in A Treatise on Political Economy
context: Marx's 1867 Das Kapital vol. 1 inherits Ricardo's labor theory and refines it as 'socially necessary labor time'; the entire theory of surplus value, exploitation, and the falling rate of profit depends on labor being the source of value. If Menger's subjective account is right, this foundation is gone: value comes from the chooser's ranking, not from labor-hours. Boehm-Bawerk drove the point home explicitly in Karl Marx and the Close of His System (1896). Mill (1848), Malthus (1798), and Say (1803) all predate Marx and do not carry the exploitation theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_theory_of_value.

question: In the subjective theory of value, the price a buyer will pay for the next unit lives in his own head. It is set by how he ranks that unit against other uses only he knows. A central board trying to set a rational price hits a wall no dataset can fix, because the key fact is not in any dataset. Which later Austrian argument does this feed straight into?
answer: Mises's socialist calculation argument
choices: Mises's socialist calculation argument
Ricardo's comparative advantage argument
Friedman's monetarist quantity theory
Coase's transaction-cost theorem
context: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth runs directly out of subjective value: if value lives in individual choosers' rankings, then a central planning board without market prices has no way to know how to allocate scarce means -- the information it would need is dispersed across millions of heads and revealed only through the choices those choosers actually make. Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' extends the same point. Ricardo, Friedman, and Coase pressed unrelated arguments. Source: mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: Menger's 1871 Principles started the German-speaking Marginal Revolution. But no one put it into English for 79 years. The ideas reached America through Mises's students, not through the book itself. In what year did the English edition finally come out?
context: The 1950 Free Press edition appeared 29 years after Menger's death (1921), 79 years after the German original (1871), and only after Menger's pupil Hayek had already moved from Vienna to LSE (1931) and then Chicago (1950). Frank Knight -- Milton Friedman's teacher at Chicago -- wrote the introduction. The gap is a measure of how far the Austrian tradition had traveled inside German-speaking economics before English-speaking economics noticed the founding text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: In 1912, a 31-year-old economist in Vienna wrote his first big book. He also handed it in as the thesis he needed to be allowed to teach at the University of Vienna. The book founded Austrian money theory. Who was the young author?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Carl Menger
Ludwig von Mises
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Friedrich Hayek
context: Ludwig von Mises (born Sep 29 1881) was 31 when 'Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel' appeared. He submitted it as his Habilitationsschrift to obtain the venia legendi, the license to lecture at university level. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises; mises.org/library/book/theorie-des-geldes-und-der-umlaufsmittel.

question: Ludwig von Mises wrote a book about money in German in 1912. In English it is called 'The Theory of Money and Credit'. What was the German title?
answer: Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen
Menschliches Handeln
context: 'Umlaufsmittel' literally means 'means of circulation'; Batson translated it as 'fiduciary media' inside the text, but the publisher chose the cleaner 'Money and Credit' for the English title. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: A shopkeeper asks: why does a silver coin have any value at all? People say, because it buys stuff today. But it only buys stuff today because it bought stuff yesterday, and the day before, and back and back. If you keep going back in time, what did the coin's value first come from?
answer: A time when silver itself was a useful thing people wanted for jewelry, tools, and trade
choices: A time when silver itself was a useful thing people wanted for jewelry, tools, and trade
A government law that ordered everyone to accept it
A magic property built into the coin at the mint
A promise from a bank to trade it for something else
context: Mises's move: today's demand rests on yesterday's known purchasing power, and you can trace the chain back through time until you reach a moment when the money-good had a non-monetary use (gold as jewelry, silver as ornament, cattle as food). The circularity dissolves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: Economists in the early 1900s noticed a pattern. When a central bank makes loans very cheap, businesses build lots of new factories and houses. A few years later, many of those projects turn out to be losers and shut down. What did the economists call this up-then-down cycle?
answer: The boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit
choices: The boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit
The natural rhythm of the seasons
The result of workers asking for higher pay
A punishment sent by foreign competitors
context: Hayek's LSE lectures 'Prices and Production' (1931) built the roundabout-production capital theory of Boehm-Bawerk together with Mises's monetary seed into the full ABCT: artificially low interest rates from bank credit expansion distort the structure of production, generating an unsustainable boom that must end in a bust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: In 1912 Ludwig von Mises had to solve Menger's 1871 puzzle about money. He traced money demand back in time, one day at a time. It had to land on a moment where the chain could close. What kind of moment was that?
answer: A day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use
choices: A day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use
A day when a sovereign first stamped his image on a coin and decreed its face value
A day when a chartered private bank first issued notes payable to bearer on demand
A day when a joint-stock company first offered redeemable shares in a public market
context: Gold jewelry and dentistry, silver ornament, cattle used for food and traction, salt for preservation. Once the chain lands on a real barter-good with real demand for its own sake, the value it later carries as money is grounded in something outside the circular loop. Source: mises.org/online-book/man-economy-and-state-power-and-market/5-marginal-utility-money/b-money-regression.

question: In 1912 Ludwig von Mises wrote a book on money. He said that when a central bank makes a lot of new money, prices don't rise evenly. Who gets hurt first and worst by this?
answer: Savers and people on fixed incomes
choices: Savers and people on fixed incomes
Bankers who receive the new money first
Government officials who set the policy
Owners of gold and silver mines
context: The 1953 Yale edition added Part Four -- Mises's direct response to the Keynesian orthodoxy that had swept postwar Anglo-American economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: In a short 1963 book titled 'What Has Government Done to Our Money?', an Austrian economist explained that governments over history often shave down the metal in coins or print extra paper. What is that practice called?
answer: Currency debasement
choices: Currency debasement
Free banking
The gold standard
A trade surplus
context: Rothbard packed the case for commodity money and against government-run currency into a booklet aimed at the general reader. Fifty years on it remains the standard introduction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Has_Government_Done_to_Our_Money%3F.

question: In January 2009 a new digital money called Bitcoin was mined for the first time. It was only digital. No state backed it. It had never traded as anything else. Some Austrians said Mises had ruled it out. They pointed to one part of his 1912 argument. Which part did they use against Bitcoin?
answer: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
choices: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
The quantity theory's requirement of stable velocity of circulation
The state theory's requirement of tax-driven acceptance
The real-bills doctrine's requirement of short-term commercial backing
context: The debate raged in Austrian circles from about 2011. Critics argued Bitcoin was born as pure money and therefore was ruled out on Misesian grounds; defenders had to find the prior demand Mises's chain required. Source: mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bitcoin-regression-theorem-and-emergence-new-medium-exchange.

question: In 2013 Konrad Graf answered an Austrian objection to Bitcoin. Critics said Bitcoin broke Mises's 1912 rule that money must grow from a prior use. Graf said the earliest users already valued Bitcoin for a real use. What use did he point to?
answer: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
choices: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
Its use as a store of value with a predictably fixed twenty-one-million supply cap
Its use as a settlement layer for high-frequency exchange trading
Its use as programmable collateral for decentralised lending contracts
context: The first buyers wanted the tokens because the underlying protocol did something no other technology could -- move digital value across a network without a trusted third party. That utility, present before any market price, was the non-monetary demand the regression theorem required. Source: www.konradsgraf.com/blog1/2013/2/27/in-depth-bitcoins-the-regression-theorem-and-that-curious-bu.html.

question: Not every Austrian thought Mises's regression theorem needed defending against Bitcoin. Robert Murphy and Silas Barta split from Konrad Graf and Peter Surda. They refused to hunt for a prior non-money use at all. They said Mises's 1912 argument answered a different question than Bitcoin poses. How did they read the reach of the theorem?
answer: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
choices: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
As overturned by Milton Friedman's 1956 restatement of the quantity theory
As applying only to commodities Menger's 1892 essay classified as saleable
As already refuted by Georg Knapp's 1905 state theory of money
context: Murphy and Barta treated the theorem as a historical explanation of how commodity monies emerged, not a constraint on future ones. Konrad Graf, Peter Surda, and Jeffrey Tucker took the other route -- accept the theorem, find the prior non-monetary demand. Source: stephankinsella.com/2025/07/austrians-bitcoin-impossible/.

question: A Wall Street bank boss becomes the Treasury Secretary (top government money job) for a few years, then quits and goes right back to Wall Street as a top-paid banker. Later his bank gets in trouble and the government bails it out. What is this move called?
answer: The revolving door between government and Wall Street
choices: The revolving door between government and Wall Street
An arm's-length transaction
A pure free market
A public works project
context: Robert Rubin, Goldman Sachs 1966-1992, Treasury Secretary 1995-99 under Clinton, Citigroup executive committee 1999-2009. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rubin.

question: In late 2008, US banks were about to fail. The Treasury Secretary rushed a rescue plan through Congress. What do we call it when the government uses tax money to save a private business?
answer: A bailout
choices: A bailout
A tariff
A tax cut
A stimulus check
context: Henry 'Hank' Paulson joined Goldman in 1974, became CEO in 1999, and served as Treasury Secretary July 2006 to January 2009. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Paulson.

question: In 2008 a giant insurance company was about to fail. The US Treasury rescued it, and much of the rescue money then flowed straight to the big banks that had done business with it. What is the worry when the government rescues big banks like this?
answer: Banks will take even bigger risks next time, since they expect another rescue
choices: Banks will take even bigger risks next time, since they expect another rescue
Small savers will suddenly earn much higher interest
Ordinary shoppers will pay less for groceries
Banks will start refusing to lend to anyone at all
context: Goldman received approximately $12.9B as an AIG counterparty via the ~$182B AIG rescue. The AIG-Goldman payments became a focal point of revolving-door criticism of the 2008 crisis response. Source: fcic.gov (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report, 2011).

question: Timothy Geithner led the New York Fed from 2003 to 2009. He then served as Obama's Treasury Secretary from 2009 to 2013. After he left Treasury, what kind of firm did he join as president?
answer: A private-equity firm
choices: A private-equity firm
A hedge fund
A public university
A commercial airline
context: Geithner joined the private-equity firm Warburg Pincus as president in March 2014. His 2014 memoir Stress Test explicitly defends the 2008-09 bailouts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Geithner; warburgpincus.com.

question: After Janet Yellen left the Fed in 2018, she earned about $7 million giving speeches before she joined Biden's cabinet in 2021. Who paid most of that money?
answer: Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs
choices: Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs
European central banks
US public school districts
Nonprofit advocacy groups
context: Yellen's financial disclosures documented approximately $7M in Wall Street speaking fees over the two-year interval. The pattern -- top financial-regulator role followed by high-fee industry advisory -- matches the earlier three Treasury secretaries. Source: US Office of Government Ethics disclosures 2020-21.

question: In 2009 a former economist at the International Monetary Fund gave a warning. Big US banks had so much power that they helped write the rules meant to control them. What is this pattern called?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Free-market competition
Proof-of-work mining
Voluntary exchange
context: Simon Johnson, 'The Quiet Coup' (The Atlantic, May 2009). Johnson, MIT professor and former IMF chief economist, applied his IMF-era capture-diagnosis toolkit to the US financial-crisis response. Source: theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2009/05.

question: In 2012 Chicago economist Luigi Zingales wrote a book. He said America's finance world had drifted from free markets to what he called crony capitalism, and he asked for reforms. What was the book called?
answer: A Capitalism for the People
choices: A Capitalism for the People
The Wealth of Nations Revisited
The Bailout State
Free Markets Under Fire
context: Luigi Zingales, A Capitalism for the People: Recapturing the Lost Genius of American Prosperity (Basic Books, 2012). Zingales -- Italian-born, teaching at Chicago Booth -- became a mainstream-economics voice against financial-sector regulatory capture. Source: basicbooks.com (Zingales 2012).

question: In 2019 the head of a US agency that regulates drug companies stepped down. Soon after, he took a paid seat on the board of a big drug company he had just been regulating. What is this pattern of moving between regulator and regulated industry called?
answer: The revolving door
choices: The revolving door
Insider trading
A market corner
A public buyback
context: Scott Gottlieb, FDA Commissioner 2017-19, joined the Pfizer board in June 2019. It is a parallel modern case of the pattern documented across finance, defense, and pharmaceutical regulation. Source: pfizer.com (board announcement June 2019).

question: Simon Johnson and Luigi Zingales both see the revolving door between industry and government as a form of regulatory capture. What feature makes the capture work?
answer: The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it
choices: The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it
Regulators are secretly bribed with cash payments
Federal law requires all regulators to work in industry first
The industry has hidden veto authority over hiring decisions
context: The Stigler-capture-via-revolving-door mechanism: the career incentives of every serving official partly align with the industry regardless of individual character, because the qualified pool has this shape by construction. This is institutional-incentive selection, not corruption. Source: Johnson (2009); Zingales (2012); Stigler (1971).

question: The four Treasury secretaries' Wall-Street-to-Treasury pattern illustrates a general reasoning move applied to top financial regulation. The move is NOT that these individuals were personally corrupt. What is the actual claim?
answer: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
choices: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
The pattern is criminal conspiracy prosecutable under federal statute
The pattern is entirely random and requires no explanation
The pattern is imposed by international treaty obligations
context: Each of the four served legally and by presidential appointment. The critique targets the STRUCTURAL pattern that produces the pattern: the pool of qualified candidates comes from and returns to the industry. Source: Zingales (2012); Johnson (2009); Stigler (1971).

question: A 2014 paper by Bertrand, Bombardini, and Trebbi put a price on the revolving door. It looked at former Members of Congress and senior staffers who became lobbyists. What pay jump over their old government salary does the research usually find?
answer: 500 to 1000 percent premiums over their government pay
choices: 500 to 1000 percent premiums over their government pay
10 to 20 percent premiums
Essentially no premium over public pay
Pay cuts of 30 to 50 percent
context: The Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi 2014 AER paper 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?' documented substantial premiums for connected lobbyists, consistent with a market pricing capture-value. Source: aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.104.12.3885.

question: Some 1800s thinkers like Antoine Cournot wrote in heavy math. Bastiat wrote very differently. What kind of writing did he choose?
answer: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
choices: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
Formal mathematical proofs
Latin scholastic disputation
Long-form academic treatises
context: Bastiat wrote so that a French farmer could follow the argument, deliberately unlike Cournot's 1838 Recherches that used calculus to model demand curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Antoine_Augustin_Cournot.

question: Bastiat's essays usually start by giving the reader something to picture. It might be a broken shop window, a new railway, or a French chamber debate. What is this opening move called?
answer: Starting with a concrete scene
choices: Starting with a concrete scene
Starting with a mathematical equation
Starting with a historical statute
Starting with a syllogism
context: Part one of the Bastiat method: put a scene in front of the reader before you make the argument. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The Bastiat method has a second rule. Before you answer an argument, you must first state it in a certain form. In what form must you state the other side?
answer: In its strongest form
choices: In its strongest form
In its weakest form
In caricature form
In its shortest form
context: Part two: state the opposing view sympathetically and at its strongest. This is Bastiat's 'ineptly defended' discipline, later renamed 'steelmanning' in 21st-century rationalist writing. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The third and final part of the Bastiat method surfaces what the opposing view has hidden. What does the third step trace?
answer: The unseen consequences
choices: The unseen consequences
The historical antecedents
The mathematical proof
The alternative equilibrium
context: Part three: trace the unseen -- the tailor whose sale was lost when the shopkeeper repaired his broken window, the worker priced out by the minimum wage, the consumer who paid more for domestic goods. Source: bastiat.org.

question: A 1946 Harper book by an American journalist used Bastiat's method on New Deal policies, chapter by chapter. It became the most-read popular Austrian book in English. What is the book's title?
answer: Economics in One Lesson
choices: Economics in One Lesson
Basic Economics
Free to Choose
The Wealth of Nations
context: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946) is a chapter-by-chapter application of the seen/unseen method to mid-20th-century American policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: A 1980 book by Thomas Sowell used the same seen/unseen method on modern policy. It tested policy claims by looking at everyday choices. What is the book's title?
answer: Knowledge and Decisions
choices: Knowledge and Decisions
A Conflict of Visions
Basic Economics
The Vision of the Anointed
context: Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) is the most sustained modern application of the classical-liberal knowledge-and-decision framework to policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Bastiat's method is powerful but has limits. Which classical-liberal topic does it not by itself give the tools for?
answer: Monetary theory and business-cycle analysis
choices: Monetary theory and business-cycle analysis
Public-facing argument about tariffs
Public-facing argument about make-work schemes
Public-facing argument about the broken window
context: For monetary theory the tradition needs Menger, Mises, and Hayek; for capital theory Bohm-Bawerk; for public choice Buchanan and Tullock. Bastiat's method is the first tool, not the only one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Almost the whole of Bastiat's published output was compressed into the last few years before his 1850 death. Roughly how many years did his major writing career span?
answer: Five
choices: Five
Twenty-five
Fifteen
Two
context: Bastiat farmed at Mugron in the Landes for most of his adult life, publishing his first major essays in 1844-1845 and dying December 24, 1850. The pamphlets, sophisms, and Harmonies were all produced in that five-year window. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: For many years a US law has kept the price of one common food at about twice the world price. It does this by limiting imports and giving loans to growers. Which food is it?
answer: Sugar
choices: Sugar
Coffee
Cocoa
Vanilla
context: The US Sugar Program, established by the Sugar Act 1934, still runs under each Farm Bill; typical US price in the 2010s was about 35 cents per pound against a world price of about 17 cents. Source: gao.gov/products/rced-00-126.

question: The US government puts a big tax on sugar brought in from other countries. Because of that, sugar in America costs about twice the world price. Who is hurt most?
answer: American shoppers -- they pay more for candy, soda, and food
choices: American shoppers -- they pay more for candy, soda, and food
American sugar farmers -- they lose sales
Foreign sugar growers -- they gain a bigger market
No one -- everyone pays the same price
context: The Sugar Act 1934 first structured the quota, loan, and allotment system that still supports US sugar prices today under the 2018 Farm Bill's re-authorization. Source: grokipedia.com/page/United_States_Sugar_Program.

question: In 2003 the maker of a famous ring-shaped candy shut its Michigan factory. It moved to a city in Canada. US sugar cost about twice as much as Canadian sugar. Why was American sugar so pricey?
answer: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more
choices: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more
American sugar tastes different from Canadian sugar
Sugar cannot grow anywhere in the United States
The US mint uses sugar to make coins
context: Kraft Foods moved Life Savers production from Holland, Michigan to Montreal in 2003 because Canadian sugar was about half the US price under the US Sugar Program. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Life_Savers.

question: Two Chicago-area candy makers moved much of their work overseas in the 2000s. They said US sugar prices were too high. Which pair moved?
answer: Ferrara Pan and Brach's
choices: Ferrara Pan and Brach's
Hershey and Mars
Wrigley and Tootsie Roll
See's and Ghirardelli
context: Ferrara Pan Candy Company moved much of its Chicago-area production to Mexico in the 2000s; Brach's Confections closed its Chicago plant in 2003 and moved to Mexico. Both cited US sugar prices. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ferrara_Candy_Company.

question: The US Sugar Program passes every Farm Bill, even though hundreds of millions of shoppers pay more for candy, soda, and baked goods. Which idea best explains why it keeps winning?
answer: Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
choices: Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
John Rawls's veil of ignorance
Ronald Coase's transaction-cost bargaining
John Kenneth Galbraith's countervailing power
context: Olson's The Logic of Collective Action (1965): about 4,000 sugar farms get large concentrated payoffs and organize politically; about 330 million consumers each pay a few dollars extra a year and do not. The smaller organized group wins. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: US sugar lobbyists often say the local industry needs to be shielded from cheaper foreign sugar. Bastiat wrote a famous 1845 satire that mocks that argument. What is the satire called?
answer: The Petition of the Candlemakers
choices: The Petition of the Candlemakers
The Broken Window fallacy
The Negative Railway argument
The Petition of the Vintners
context: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat's Petition of the Candlemakers had French makers of candles and lamps demand a law blocking sunlight to protect them from unfair sun-powered competition. Source: bastiat.org/en/petition.html.

question: Bastiat's method points at the DOWNSTREAM industries that use sugar as an input. What outcome does his method predict for those industries when a domestic law doubles their input cost against the world price?
answer: They move production to where sugar is cheap
choices: They move production to where sugar is cheap
They automate away all remaining sugar workers
They keep US production and absorb the input cost
They petition congress to raise consumer prices further
context: The predicted move played out in 2003 when Life Savers relocated from Michigan to Montreal, in the 2000s when Ferrara Pan and Brach's moved much production to Mexico. Higher US input costs pushed candy jobs across the border. Source: trade.gov/employment-changes-us-food-manufacturing-impact-sugar-prices.

question: One Florida family gets most of the gains from the US Sugar Program. They own Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals. What is the family's name?
answer: The Fanjul family
choices: The Fanjul family
The Hershey family
The Mars family
The Coca-Cola Candler family
context: The Fanjul brothers of Florida own Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals; they are the paradigm case of a small, politically-organized beneficiary group that has kept the Sugar Program in every Farm Bill. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fanjul_brothers.

question: No single person in a country knows where every apple is, how many nails a factory needs, or what shoe size Aunt Judy prefers. That knowledge is spread across millions of people. What tool lets all of that hidden knowledge get used, without any boss having to know it?
answer: Prices in a free market
choices: Prices in a free market
A government planning committee
A national computer running the whole economy
A single wise king
context: F. A. Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4, September 1945, pages 519-530 -- eleven pages that became one of the most-cited economics papers of the 20th century. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society).

question: Hayek's most-cited paper came out in 1945. It ran in the top journal of the American Economic Association. Which one?
answer: The American Economic Review
choices: The American Economic Review
The Journal of Political Economy
The Economic Journal
Econometrica
context: The essay appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. Hayek was writing from wartime London (LSE had by then returned from its Cambridge evacuation). Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In 1945, F. A. Hayek wrote an essay about the real problem of running an economy. He said it is not just how to share out things we already have. Blackboard planners in the 1930s had been solving that. So what did Hayek say the real problem is?
answer: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
choices: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
How to equalize the marginal productivity of capital across all industries
How to compute the aggregate demand curve for a whole national economy
How to eliminate the fluctuations of the business cycle through fiscal policy
context: Hayek's reframing was the essay's central move: the socialist-calculation debate was not about better arithmetic; it was about the unavailability of the underlying data to any single mind or committee. The knowledge that a market uses to allocate resources is scattered across millions of heads and cannot be gathered up to a central board in usable time. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago hosted PDF (https://home.uchicago.edu/~vlima/courses/econ200/spring01/hayek.pdf).

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay draws a sharp line between two kinds of knowledge. On one side is the scientific knowledge in textbooks that a central board could in principle collect. On the other side is a different kind of knowledge -- inherently dispersed, held by individuals about their particular jobs, ships, warehouses, and customers. What does Hayek call this second, load-bearing kind of knowledge?
answer: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
choices: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
The general theory of aggregate demand and supply
The rational expectations of forward-looking agents
The universal grammar of market institutions
context: Hayek's phrase: the important knowledge in an economy is 'the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- that a certain ship is half-empty, that a warehouse has a surplus, that a foreman on the third shift has spotted a way to save two hours. This knowledge is inherently local and inherently dispersed. Source: Hayek 1945, Econlib version (https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html).

question: Hayek's 1945 essay used one metal as a running example. When a new use pops up or a mine closes, its price rises. Every user then cuts back, even if they do not know why. Which metal did he use?
answer: Tin
choices: Tin
Copper
Iron
Silver
context: The tin example on page 526 of the American Economic Review version is the paragraph everyone quotes. Hayek's point: a single number -- the tin price -- carries the whole world's changing knowledge about tin (mine closures, new uses, war coming) to every user of tin, without any user needing to know the underlying cause. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF.

question: In 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' F. A. Hayek gave a famous metaphor for the price system: it works like a piece of machinery for registering change, a system where each producer watches only the movement of a few pointers. To which modern technology did Hayek compare the price system?
answer: A system of telecommunications
choices: A system of telecommunications
A national railway timetable
A wartime radar screen
A newspaper printing press
context: Hayek's phrase: the price system is 'a kind of machinery for registering change, or a system of telecommunications which enables individual producers to watch merely the movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might watch the hands of a few dials.' Prices carry knowledge no single mind holds. Source: Western Sydney Pressbooks critical-analysis version (https://westernsydney.pressbooks.pub/criticalanalysis/chapter/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/).

question: Mises said that without market prices, planners cannot figure out what to make. A younger Austrian added a sharper point: even trying hard, planners cannot gather all the little bits of local know-how that markets pull together every day. What is this idea called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The tax collection problem
The public goods problem
The population problem
context: Mises 1920 said no exchange, no prices, no rational allocation. Hayek 1945 added: even if a benevolent, honest planner had perfect intentions, the dispersed knowledge that market prices summarize is not gatherable in usable time by any central agency. The Austrian critique of planning is not about will or motive -- it is about knowability. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF; Mises Institute critical commentary.

question: Hayek's famous 1945 essay was reprinted in a 1948 book of his essays from the University of Chicago. The book covers individualism, spontaneous order, and the socialist calculation debate. What is the book called?
answer: Individualism and Economic Order
choices: Individualism and Economic Order
The Constitution of Liberty
Studies in Philosophy Politics and Economics
The Counter-Revolution of Science
context: Individualism and Economic Order (University of Chicago Press, 1948) collected Hayek's essays from the 1930s and 1940s including 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937), and 'The Meaning of Competition.' The Constitution of Liberty (1960), Studies (1967), and The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) are all real Hayek works of later or different focus. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In December 1974 F. A. Hayek delivered the Nobel Memorial Prize lecture in Stockholm on the failures of the mathematical macroeconomics of the day. The title of the lecture was a direct descendant of the 1945 essay's argument about what a central mind cannot hold. What was the title?
answer: The Pretense of Knowledge
choices: The Pretense of Knowledge
The Fatal Conceit
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture 'The Pretense of Knowledge' argued that the postwar economics profession had adopted the manner of the physical sciences while imitating something it could not actually deliver -- the pretense that macroeconomic aggregates and models could substitute for the dispersed knowledge the price system aggregates. The lecture is the direct descendant of the 1945 essay. Source: Econlib version of Hayek 1945.

question: The reasoning move at the heart of Hayek's 1945 essay is one a critic of central planning can carry into any policy debate -- rent control, minimum wages, wage-price controls, ration schemes. It is NOT a moral verdict; it is a claim about knowability. Which move does the essay actually press?
answer: That the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board
choices: That the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board
That central planners are always corrupt and always self-interested
That a planned economy must eventually generate hyperinflation of the consumer price index
That workers in planned economies are forbidden from changing jobs by law
context: The essay's argument is a claim about the STRUCTURE of economic knowledge, not a moral or motive claim. Even a saintly, brilliant planner cannot hold the knowledge the price system aggregates because that knowledge lives in millions of individual heads about local circumstances. The student can accept or reject the move, but the essay actually presses this reasoning move, not the corruption or hyperinflation charges. Source: Hayek 1945.

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay closes with a striking image of what a market economy accomplishes: without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause of a raw-material scarcity, tens of thousands of people are made to use the material more sparingly. What one word from the essay best names this achievement Hayek was praising?
answer: A marvel
choices: A marvel
A miracle
A machine
A market
context: Hayek writes: 'The marvel is that in a case like that of a scarcity of one raw material, without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' The word MARVEL carries the essay's astonishment -- that a system no one designed does what no committee could. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In Vienna in the late 1920s, Ludwig von Mises ran a private seminar. Many young Austrian economists went. Friedrich von Hayek was the first to leave. Which British school asked him in 1931 to give four lectures that led to a permanent chair?
answer: The London School of Economics
choices: The London School of Economics
The University of Cambridge
The University of Oxford
The University of Edinburgh
context: Lionel Robbins, then rebuilding LSE's economics department, brought Hayek over from 27 to 30 January 1931 to give the lectures published later that year as Prices and Production. The talks landed so well that LSE offered Hayek the Tooke Chair the following year. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Hayek stayed at the London School of Economics for almost twenty years after his 1931 invitation. Which chair did he hold from 1932 until he left for Chicago in 1950?
answer: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
choices: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
The Cassel Chair of Economics
The Drummond Chair of Political Economy
The Marshall Chair of Political Economy
context: Named for the 19th-century monetary theorist Thomas Tooke, the Tooke Chair was LSE's senior economics professorship. Hayek held it from 1932, became a British subject in 1938, and finally left in 1950 for a position in Chicago's Committee on Social Thought. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.
