question: Fritz Machlup had studied under Ludwig von Mises in 1920s Vienna. In 1933 he took a grant that carried him to Columbia, Harvard, Chicago and Stanford. In 1935 he settled into an American teaching job for the next twelve years. Where?
answer: The University of Buffalo
choices: The University of Buffalo
The University of Chicago
Princeton University
Cornell University
context: Machlup held his Buffalo chair from 1935 to 1947, later moving to Johns Hopkins and then Princeton. He was one of the first of Mises's Vienna circle to make a fully American career. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fritz Machlup'.

question: Gottfried Haberler was another Austrian economist trained by Mises. From 1934 to 1936 he worked for an international body based on Lake Geneva. That job led to his book 'Prosperity and Depression'. Which body hired him?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
The Bank for International Settlements
The International Chamber of Commerce
The International Labour Office
context: Haberler served in the economic administration of the League of Nations in Geneva from 1934 to 1936. In autumn 1936 he moved to a Harvard professorship that lasted until his 1971 retirement. Source: Britannica, 'Gottfried von Haberler'.

question: Oskar Morgenstern ran the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research and joined the Mises seminar. He was out of Europe when German troops entered Austria on March 13, 1938. Where was he, and what did he do?
answer: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
choices: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
In Zurich on sabbatical; he returned home the following month
In London consulting for the Bank of England; he moved on to Cambridge
In Stockholm at a conference; he stayed and took a Riksbank post
context: Morgenstern was travelling in America as a Carnegie Visiting Professor when the Anschluss occurred. From six invitations he chose a three-year appointment as Class of 1913 Lecturer in Political Economy at Princeton, and simply did not return home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar Morgenstern'.

question: Ludwig von Mises himself left Vienna in 1934 for a paid chair he had never been offered in his own city. Which foreign institution did he move to, where he taught for the next six years?
answer: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
choices: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
The London School of Economics
The Sorbonne in Paris
The University of Zurich
context: Vienna had recognised Mises with only an unpaid Privatdozent title. The Geneva institute (Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales) gave him his first paid professorship. He held the chair from 1934 until 1940. Source: Mises Institute, 'Ludwig von Mises: The Logician of Freedom'.

question: In July 1940, Ludwig von Mises and his wife Margit fled Geneva as the Germans took France. Spain turned them back three times before they got a visa at Toulouse. They crossed Spain and boarded a ship for America. From which port did they sail?
answer: Lisbon
choices: Lisbon
Bilbao
Barcelona
Vigo
context: Portugal's neutrality made Lisbon the great escape port for European refugees in 1940. Mises and Margit sailed from there and docked in New Jersey on 2 August 1940, where their Viennese friend Alfred Schutz met them on the pier. Source: Future of Freedom Foundation, 'Celebrating the Arrival of Ludwig von Mises in America'.

question: When Ludwig von Mises stepped off the ship in New Jersey on August 2, 1940, many already saw him as one of the great economists of his time. How old was he, and what US university chair awaited him?
answer: Fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life
choices: Fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life
Forty-four, and a full Harvard professorship awaited him
Sixty-seven, and a Yale endowed chair had been arranged in advance
Fifty-two, and a Chicago professorship followed within the year
context: Mises was born on 29 September 1881. He turned 59 the month after his arrival. From 1945 to 1969 he taught at New York University as an unpaid Visiting Professor; the William Volker Fund paid his stipend until 1962, and a consortium including the businessman Lawrence Fertig, who sat on the NYU board, took over afterwards. Source: FEE, 'Ludwig von Mises: A Prophet Without Honor in His Own Land'.

question: Karl Menger was a mathematician and the son of the founder of the Austrian School. He left Vienna a full year before the Anschluss for a visiting job at an American Catholic university. He then resigned his Vienna chair in March 1938. Which US university took him in?
answer: The University of Notre Dame
choices: The University of Notre Dame
Georgetown University
Fordham University
The Catholic University of America
context: Menger arrived in South Bend, Indiana in autumn 1937 and stayed until 1946. His father Carl Menger had founded the Austrian School with the 1871 Grundsaetze; the son carried the family name into American mathematics. Source: MacTutor, 'Karl Menger'.

question: Seven years after the Nazis fell, a small group of scholars met on a mountain above Lake Geneva. They wanted to see if classical liberal thought could be rebuilt after the war. Hayek called the meeting on 10 April 1947. Thirty-six came, including Mises, Machlup, Friedman, Stigler, Popper and Robbins. What group was founded there?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Cato Institute
The Institute of Economic Affairs
The Foundation for Economic Education
context: The Mont Pelerin Society took its name from the hotel above Lake Geneva where the founding meeting was held. Hayek served as its first President until 1961. Half a dozen of the founders were direct veterans of Mises's old Vienna Privatseminar. Source: montpelerin.org, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: In 1974 the Nobel Prize in Economics went to a former member of Mises's Vienna seminar. He shared it with the Swedish social-democrat Gunnar Myrdal. Which Vienna emigre won?
answer: Friedrich von Hayek
choices: Friedrich von Hayek
Fritz Machlup
Gottfried Haberler
Oskar Morgenstern
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel citation named his work on money, credit and interdependence between economic, social and institutional phenomena. Machlup, Haberler and Morgenstern each made major contributions in America but Hayek alone of the Vienna diaspora was Nobel-honoured. Source: Britannica, 'F. A. Hayek'.

question: In 1920s Vienna a group of economists argued that no small committee -- no matter how smart -- could plan a whole country's economy. Why not?
answer: No committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth
choices: No committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth
Committees are always lazy
Committees don't have enough computers
Committees never agree with each other
context: The Vienna Circle of logical positivists, gathered around Moritz Schlick and Rudolf Carnap, was the leading interwar philosophy-of-science movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: In the 1930s a math whiz proved that no math system can prove every true fact inside it. Austrian economists made a like point about the economy. What did they say?
answer: No small group can ever plan a whole economy -- they can't know enough
choices: No small group can ever plan a whole economy -- they can't know enough
The economy runs on pure luck
Only the smartest person should set every price
Math cannot describe money
context: Kurt Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorems were presented partly through Menger's Vienna colloquium, one of the most famous mathematical results of the 20th century. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Godel%27s_incompleteness_theorems.

question: In early 1900s Vienna, Ludwig von Mises argued against those who wanted the state to plan the whole economy. He said no planner can copy one key tool. What everyday thing helps millions of people work together?
answer: Market prices
choices: Market prices
Government orders
Newspaper editorials
Weather reports
context: Moritz Schlick was shot dead by Johann Nelbock on the University of Vienna's Philosophenstiege on June 22, 1936, an early hammer-blow to the interwar Vienna intellectual scene. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Moritz_Schlick.

question: The Vienna Circle stood against Mises's free-market group. Its leading thinker, Otto Neurath, is tied to which political tradition?
answer: Socialism
choices: Socialism
Classical liberalism
Traditional conservatism
Anarcho-capitalism
context: Otto Neurath combined logical-positivist philosophy with Austro-Marxist socialism; the Vienna Circle formally endorsed physicalism and rejected metaphysics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Rudolf Carnap left Vienna in 1935 for a US school. It became a main home of logical positivism in North America. Which school did he join?
answer: The University of Chicago
choices: The University of Chicago
Harvard University
the University of California, Berkeley
Columbia University
context: Carnap took a chair at the University of Chicago in 1935 and taught there until 1952 before moving to UCLA. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Kurt Godel fled Vienna in 1940 by an odd route across Asia. He then joined an American institute and stayed there the rest of his life. Where did he end up?
answer: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
choices: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
MIT
Harvard University
the University of Chicago
context: Godel fled via the Trans-Siberian Railway and Japan in 1940, arriving at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he became a colleague of Einstein and von Neumann. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Kurt_Godel.

question: In 1938 Vienna's great scene of coffeehouse thinkers, math whizzes, and writers was scattered almost overnight. What kind of political change usually makes free thinkers flee a country?
answer: A dictator takes over and shuts down free debate
choices: A dictator takes over and shuts down free debate
The country holds a peaceful election
The country lowers its taxes
A new stock exchange opens for business
context: The March 1938 Anschluss brought Nazi Germany into Austria and expelled Jewish intellectuals from Vienna's universities. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anschluss.

question: In 1934 a Viennese philosopher proposed a simple test for whether an idea should count as real science: it has to be possible to state what evidence would prove the idea wrong. What is the name of this test?
answer: Falsifiability
choices: Falsifiability
Verification
Consensus
Repeatability
context: Karl Popper's Logik der Forschung (1934) put falsifiability at the center of scientific method, in opposition to Vienna Circle verificationism. He shared the classical-liberal politics of Mises without belonging to the Circle. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Popper.

question: Two kids trade lunch: your apple for their cookie. Both walk away happier. Why did the trade make both of you better off?
answer: Each of you valued what you got more than what you gave up
choices: Each of you valued what you got more than what you gave up
One of you must have tricked the other
The apple and cookie cost exactly the same to make
Trading always makes one person lose
context: Menger took the chair in 1873 in the Faculty of Law and Political Economy (economics was then taught inside the law faculty) and held it for thirty years, until 1903. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Carl_Menger.

question: You have five dollars. You can spend it on a comic book OR on ice cream, but not both. If you pick the comic, the ice cream you gave up is called the ___ of your choice.
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Sunk cost
Marginal cost
Fixed cost
context: Wieser held the Vienna chair from 1903 to 1922. He also served as Austro-Hungarian Minister of Commerce in 1917-1918. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Menger's other big first-generation student took a Vienna chair in 1904. He had just quit as Austria-Hungary's Finance Minister. He taught there until his death in 1914. Who was he?
answer: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
Karl Menger the younger
context: Bohm-Bawerk held a parallel Vienna chair from 1904 until his death in 1914, giving Vienna both leading Menger students teaching side by side for a decade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: In 1900s Vienna, one famous seminar taught students who later split apart on politics. Some grew up to defend free markets. Others grew up to lead socialists. What big question did the two sides argue about?
answer: Whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well
choices: Whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well
Whether numbers should be written left to right or right to left
Whether spring or fall is a better time to sow wheat
Whether German or French makes a better first language
context: The 1905-1914 Bohm-Bawerk seminar had the future greatest Austrian liberal (Mises), the future Austrian Social Democrat foreign minister (Otto Bauer), and the future Marxist finance minister of Weimar Germany (Hilferding) sitting together. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: Ludwig von Mises said a small group of central planners can never run a whole country's economy the way a family plans its weekly budget. Why not?
answer: They lack the millions of local price signals that markets produce
choices: They lack the millions of local price signals that markets produce
Central planners always cheat and steal from ordinary citizens
Central planners refuse to work more than four hours a day
Central planners are not allowed to use computers
context: Mises took his Vienna doctorate in 1906 and habilitated in 1913 as a Privatdozent -- an unpaid lecturer with the right to teach -- while working full-time for the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: A country ends its markets and lets a state committee set every price by rule. Austrian economists say one tool for guiding what gets made and how much then vanishes. What tool is lost?
answer: Prices that reveal what people really want
choices: Prices that reveal what people really want
The postal service and its mail carriers
The alphabet used to write down new laws
The soldiers who patrol the country's border
context: Hans Mayer held the Vienna chair from 1922 to 1938; the paid chair thus passed out of the front-rank Austrian tradition just as the private-seminar tradition became the school's main institutional home. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Mayer_(economist).

question: In the 1920s a Marxist economist served as Finance Minister of Germany. During that period the government printed huge amounts of new money to pay its debts. What happens to prices in a country that prints a lot of new money very fast?
answer: Prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value
choices: Prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value
Prices fall because there is more money to spend
Prices stay the same because printing is invisible
Prices only rise on goods brought in from abroad
context: Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910) was a leading Marxist analysis of banking; he later served twice as Finance Minister of Weimar Germany. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rudolf_Hilferding.

question: Vienna's role as the home of Austrian economics ended for one clear political reason in one year. The last school members had to emigrate. Which event ended it?
answer: The 1938 Anschluss with Nazi Germany
choices: The 1938 Anschluss with Nazi Germany
The 1919 Treaty of Saint-Germain
The 1927 July Revolt
The 1934 Austrian Civil War
context: Mises had already left Vienna for Geneva in 1934. The 1938 Anschluss ended the Vienna institutional tradition; the remaining figures (Hayek at LSE from 1931; Haberler at Harvard 1936; Morgenstern at Princeton 1938; Machlup in America 1933) had all emigrated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto posted the Bitcoin white paper to a cypherpunk email list on October 31, 2008. For a math paper it is short. About how long is it, not counting the notes?
answer: About nine pages
choices: About nine pages
About one page
About fifty pages
About two hundred pages
context: Nine pages of body text, organized into twelve numbered sections plus an abstract and references. That is the length of a typical computer-science conference paper of its era. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin white paper opens with a specific abstract sentence about the problem the paper is trying to solve. Which of these is the actual opening line?
answer: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
choices: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
'Money is a social construct that will be replaced by decentralized applications.'
'The Federal Reserve is the enemy of every honest saver.'
'This paper introduces a new consensus mechanism called proof-of-stake.'
context: The opening sentence identifies the trusted-third-party dependency as the problem to eliminate. The rest of the paper explains the peer-to-peer solution. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: To add a new block of transactions to the Bitcoin chain, a computer must first solve a very hard math puzzle that eats real electricity. This design makes cheating very expensive. What is the name of this security method?
answer: Proof-of-Work
choices: Proof-of-Work
Proof-of-stake
Free banking
Legal tender
context: Section 3 introduces the timestamped chain concept; Section 4 shows how to secure it. The section explicitly cites Adam Back's Hashcash as prior art. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin white paper cites specific prior work in cryptography and digital cash. Which pair of predecessors does the reference list name?
answer: Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money
choices: Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money
David Chaum's DigiCash and Nick Szabo's bit gold
Vitalik Buterin's Ethereum and Charlie Lee's Litecoin
Ralph Nader's Public Citizen and Milton Friedman's Free to Choose
context: Both Hashcash and b-money were cypherpunk-lineage proposals from the 1990s that Satoshi combined and extended. DigiCash and bit gold are historically related but are not cited in the paper's references. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Section 7 of the Bitcoin paper adds a data trick. It lets old spent records be trimmed from the chain while still proving the chain's history. What is the structure called?
answer: A Merkle tree
choices: A Merkle tree
A linked list
A hash table
A relational database
context: Named for Ralph Merkle, who patented the structure in 1979. Each block header commits to the Merkle root of its transactions, so nodes can discard old bodies and keep only proofs. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin paper describes a way for a phone wallet to check that a payment happened without downloading the whole history of every transaction. Instead the wallet keeps only tiny summary headers of each block. What is the point of this shortcut?
answer: A small device can verify payments without running a full node
choices: A small device can verify payments without running a full node
It makes every bitcoin transaction completely private
It removes the need for any miners at all
It changes bitcoin's fixed supply cap
context: SPV enables phone-and-laptop wallets to check that a payment is in the longest chain by requesting Merkle proofs from full nodes. It is what made mobile Bitcoin wallets practical. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The white paper's twelfth section is unusually short for a technical paper -- just a brief summary of the coin-as-chain-of-signatures and proof-of-work security argument. Which title does the twelfth section carry, and how long is it?
answer: Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs
choices: Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs
Discussion, roughly two pages
Bibliography, roughly one page
Appendix A, roughly three pages
context: The paper is famously terse. Satoshi said what needed saying and stopped. The Conclusion recaps the peer-to-peer solution and the assumption that honest miners hold more hashing power than any attacker. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: An American economist likes to say: 'There are no solutions, only trade-offs.' What does he mean?
answer: Every choice gives up something else -- you can't get all good and no cost
choices: Every choice gives up something else -- you can't get all good and no cost
Smart leaders can fix every problem at zero cost
Only the government can solve real problems
If you try hard enough, no one has to lose anything
context: Thomas Sowell (born June 30, 1930, Gastonia, North Carolina) was adopted and raised by his great-aunt Molly and her two adult daughters after his father died shortly before his birth and his mother died a few years later; the family moved to Harlem when he was nine. Walter Williams taught at George Mason, Glenn Loury at Brown, and W. Arthur Lewis won the 1979 Nobel Prize. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell grew up poor in a wooden house in North Carolina. His family had no electricity and no running water. In his memoir, he told about one ordinary thing he had simply never learned as a boy. What was it?
answer: That blond was a hair color
choices: That blond was a hair color
That milk came from cows
That the ocean was salt water
That radios carried live music
context: Sowell wrote in A Personal Odyssey (Free Press, 2000) that his childhood encounters with white people were so limited that he did not know blond was a hair color. He recalled a small wooden house in Charlotte on an unpaved street with no electricity or running water. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell', citing A Personal Odyssey.

question: Thomas Sowell won a spot at Stuyvesant, a top New York school. He was the first in his family to study past sixth grade. At seventeen, short on money and living in a home that fought, he quit and went to work. Which job did he take?
answer: Delivering telegrams for Western Union
choices: Delivering telegrams for Western Union
Sorting mail at the main post office
Loading freight on the Brooklyn docks
Running an elevator in a midtown tower
context: Sowell dropped out of Stuyvesant at 17 because of financial difficulties and family quarreling, then worked long hours in a machine shop and as a delivery man for Western Union. He also tried out for the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1948. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell later became a famous economist. One of his best-known points is about a rule that sounds nice but ends up hurting the very people it's supposed to help: a minimum wage set higher than what a beginner's work is worth. Who does he say gets hurt most?
answer: Young workers with no experience, who can no longer get their first job
choices: Young workers with no experience, who can no longer get their first job
Rich business owners who lose most of their money
Older workers who have been employed for decades
Farmers who grow food for city customers
context: After basic training in South Carolina, Sowell was sent to a photography school in Florida and served as a Marine photographer; he was discharged in 1952 and never rose above private first class. Photography remained his lifelong hobby. Sources: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A young man rode the bus home each day from downtown, past rich stores, past a concert hall, past comfortable blocks, then over a bridge to his poor tenement. The contrast puzzled him. In his early twenties, which thinker did he first turn to for an answer?
answer: Karl Marx
choices: Karl Marx
Adam Smith
Frederick Douglass
Benjamin Franklin
context: Sowell has said he was a Marxist through his twenties. Of the bus ride he wrote: 'The contrast between that and what I'd been seeing most of the trip really baffled me. And Marx seemed to explain it.' He wrote a Harvard senior thesis on Marxian economics and a Columbia master's thesis on Marxian business cycle theory. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: In 1959, young Thomas Sowell moved to the University of Chicago. He went to study with a famous economist there. The Chicago school taught that one tool guides the economy better than any state plan. What tool did they mean?
answer: The price of goods and labor in a free market
choices: The price of goods and labor in a free market
A list of quotas set by lawmakers
A yearly government printout of who should produce what
A vote every month on what should cost how much
context: Sowell chose Columbia in order to study under George Stigler, later a Nobel laureate; on learning Stigler had moved to Chicago he followed him there in the fall of 1959 and took his PhD at Chicago in 1968, with a dissertation on Say's Law and the general glut controversy. Friedman, Knight and Becker were all Chicago economists. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: In 1980 Thomas Sowell left teaching to write books and columns full time. He joined a research group that studies public policy from a free-market view. What is such a group called?
answer: A policy think tank
choices: A policy think tank
A trade union
A stock exchange
A credit union
context: Sowell joined the Hoover Institution at Stanford as a fellow in April 1977 and became a senior fellow in September 1980, holding the title Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow on Public Policy. He had earlier been at the Urban Institute (1972-74) and the American Enterprise Institute (1975-76), which is why those are live answers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: In the summer of 1960 Thomas Sowell, whose first year of graduate school at Chicago had left his politics untouched, took a summer job at the U.S. Department of Labor studying Puerto Rico's sugar industry, where Washington set the wage floor. He saw that as that floor rose, the sugar payrolls shrank. He brought the finding to the office he had joined. What would his colleagues not do?
answer: Test whether the law was helping the workers
choices: Test whether the law was helping the workers
Release the employment figures he had assembled
Compare Puerto Rico with mainland sugar growers
Let an intern brief the division chief directly
context: Sowell has said his colleagues were surprised by his questioning and that 'they certainly weren't going to engage in any scrutiny of the law' -- their job was to enforce it, not to check it. He called this 'the beginning of the erosion of my faith in government programs.' Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Britannica 'Thomas Sowell'; New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell reached Harvard by an unlikely road -- dropout, Marine, night classes at Howard -- and graduated magna cum laude in 1958. Asked long afterwards to name the best thing about having gone there, he gave an answer that had nothing to do with the teaching. What did he say?
answer: That you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
choices: That you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
That nobody there ever asked where you had gone to high school
That you learn how fast a reputation starts doing your arguing for you
That it teaches you to distrust every credential, beginning with your own
context: Sowell's line: 'One of the best things about going to Harvard is that, for the rest of your life, you are neither intimidated nor impressed by people who went to Harvard.' He finished high school by equivalency after the Marines, took a civil service job in Washington and studied nights at Howard University before transferring. Source: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell was asked to teach a course on the Soviet economy. Prepping it finally made Hayek's 1945 essay click. He saw why Soviet plans failed, and he put it in one line about who held what. Which line?
answer: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
choices: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
Those who wrote the plans never had to live under the plans they wrote
Those who owned nothing were told every day that they owned everything
Those who waited longest in the queue were always served last
context: Sowell: 'There was a knowledge problem that was inherent in that system. In a nutshell, those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power.' Hayek's essay is 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Knowledge and Decisions (1980) is the book where Thomas Sowell carried Hayek's idea about scattered information into real courts, firms, schools, and lawmaking. He traded graphs for real places a reader could picture. Hayek reviewed it himself, and his title was not modest. What did Hayek call it?
answer: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year
choices: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year
A Worthy Successor to The Road to Serfdom
An American Answer to the Planners
The Case Against Expertise, Made at Last
context: Hayek titled his review of Knowledge and Decisions 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'; the book also won the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. Sowell has called it a book-length application of Hayek's 1945 essay to specific American institutions. Sources: Wikipedia 'Knowledge and Decisions'; FEE, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; New Criterion.

question: Thomas Sowell has said the summer of 1960 began the erosion of his faith in government programs -- not because the sugar numbers alone convinced him, but because of how the people around him received the numbers. He compressed that summer into one sentence he has been applying to institutions ever since. Which sentence?
answer: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
choices: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
That good intentions and good results are different things, and only results can be counted
That every program grows until it costs more than the problem it was built to solve
That the people a program is meant to help are the last whose interests anyone counts
context: Sowell's own words: 'It forced me to realize that government agencies have their own self-interest to look after, regardless of those for whom a program has been set up.' This is public-choice reasoning arrived at by observation, before Sowell had read the public-choice literature. Option two is close to Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions', a genuinely different move. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: In the 1990s a group called the cypherpunks said normal people should be able to send notes, and later money, that no bank or state could read or block. What tool made that possible?
answer: Strong encryption -- math that scrambles the message
choices: Strong encryption -- math that scrambles the message
Louder microphones
Faster mail trucks
Better paper envelopes
context: Timothy C. May was the retired Intel physicist. Gilmore was Sun's fifth employee; Hughes was a Berkeley mathematician; Chaum was an American cryptographer at a different company. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: In 1988 a computer scientist made a bold guess. If normal people got strong code to scramble their notes, no state could spy on their letters or block private money. What did he think would grow?
answer: Private communication and private trade between strangers
choices: Private communication and private trade between strangers
Only more junk mail
Nothing -- people wouldn't care
Bigger post offices
context: May's 1988 essay is 'The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto'. 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' was Eric Hughes's separate March 1993 essay; 'The Cyphernomicon' was May's later 1994 book-length FAQ; 'The Sovereign Individual' is a 1997 book by Davidson and Rees-Mogg. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: In 1988, Timothy May wrote the Crypto Anarchist Manifesto. It starts with a line copied from a famous 1800s text. Which line did May borrow?
answer: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
choices: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
'We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.'
'Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent...'
'When in the course of human events, it becomes necessary for one people...'
context: May's opening deliberately echoes the 1848 Communist Manifesto's 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism.' The other openings are Declaration of Independence (1776) and Gettysburg Address (1863). Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's 1988 essay warned that a 'specter' would soon haunt the political world. It stood for a set of powers he said strong codes would give people. Which powers did he predict?
answer: communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government
choices: communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government
cheap global manufacturing and rapid international logistics for goods moving across every continent
solar power and unlimited clean energy sufficient to end civilization's fossil-fuel dependence permanently
artificial intelligence sophisticated enough to replace most human labor across every category of employment
context: May's specter was strong cryptography enabling anonymous communication, contracting, and trade beyond state surveillance. The other categories are separate technological forecasts May did not centrally address in the manifesto. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's 1988 manifesto has one line about what people would soon be able to do together in secret. Which prediction does he make about anonymous action?
answer: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
choices: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
'The internet will soon make all of human knowledge free of charge and instantly available to every person on the planet regardless of their nation.'
'Computers will one day think and feel as humans do, and will eventually claim rights of their own from the human governments that built them.'
'Every citizen of every industrial nation will one day own a personal computer more powerful than anything a national laboratory possesses today.'
context: The exact quote from May's manifesto. The other statements are broadly attributed to different figures (Stallman on knowledge freedom, Minsky/Kurzweil on AI, various early PC forecasts). Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's 1988 essay named several tools he thought the math would soon make possible. Cypherpunks went on to build most of them over the next thirty years. Which tools did May sketch?
answer: anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments
choices: anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments
smartphones, social media, video streaming, and cloud storage
gene therapy, artificial hearts, brain implants, and space elevators
hydrogen fuel cells, fusion power, and orbital solar arrays
context: May specifically anticipated remailers, pseudonyms, smart contracts, and untraceable payments -- all built between 1990 and 2010. The other technology lists are unrelated. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May did not name Bitcoin in his 1988 essay, but he predicted the shape of something that showed up twenty years later. Which 2008 event most directly matched his untraceable-payments idea?
answer: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008
choices: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008
the Federal Reserve's 2008 quantitative easing program
the launch of Facebook in 2004
the introduction of chip-and-PIN credit cards
context: Bitcoin's 2008 white paper realized in engineering form the untraceable-payments capability May had forecast in 1988. QE, Facebook, and chip-and-PIN cards are unrelated technologies. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In the early 1990s a group of programmers, cryptographers, and privacy activists called themselves cypherpunks. They shared one core belief about what ordinary people should be able to use freely. What did they think ordinary people needed?
answer: Strong encryption for private messages and digital cash
choices: Strong encryption for private messages and digital cash
Only government-approved chat apps
Only paper money, never any digital money
Only bank-issued forms of communication
context: 'The Cyphernomicon' (1994) by Timothy May is a book-length FAQ. 'The Crypto Handbook' is a fabrication; 'The Anarchist Cookbook' (William Powell, 1971) is a separate unrelated pamphlet; 'A Cypherpunk's Grimoire' does not exist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: A modern cypherpunk historian says Timothy May's 1988 essay is best read not as a report on what already existed -- there was no code, no working system -- but as a special kind of intellectual work. How does the historian describe it?
answer: a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software
choices: a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software
a summary of already-shipping cryptographic tools that had reached ordinary consumers by the late 1980s
a proposal for a specific new company that May intended to found using his Intel stock-option wealth
a legal brief prepared for a specific US court case involving the export of cryptographic software
context: The essay was pure forecast in 1988 -- no working code, no infrastructure. Every specific technology May named would be built over the next thirty years by the movement he named. It was not a shipping summary, corporate proposal, or legal brief. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: When Timothy May died in 2018, his obituary in the crypto press gave him one clear role in the chain of ideas that led to Bitcoin. Which role did the crypto world give him at his death?
answer: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
choices: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
the actual person behind the Satoshi pseudonym
the founder of the Bitcoin Foundation
the CEO of the first Bitcoin exchange
context: May's 2018 obituaries credited him as a co-founder of the cypherpunk movement from which Satoshi wrote. He never claimed the Satoshi identity, did not found the Bitcoin Foundation, and did not run an exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: A child is offered one cookie today or two cookies tomorrow, and grabs the one today. A lender is offered $100 back today or $100 back next year, and asks for $105 for the wait. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk gave a name to this plain fact in his 1889 book. What did he call it?
answer: Time preference
choices: Time preference
Marginal utility
Opportunity cost
The endowment effect
context: Boehm-Bawerk's time preference is the ranking every chooser puts on a present good above the SAME good in the future -- two apples today over two apples next year, dinner tonight over dinner tomorrow. Marginal utility (Menger 1871, Wieser 1884) is a different concept about the LAST unit; opportunity cost (Wieser again) is about the next-best forgone use; the endowment effect (Thaler 1980) is a modern behavioural finding about ownership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: If someone offers you one candy bar TODAY or two candy bars a WHOLE YEAR from now, most people pick today. What is this preference for stuff-sooner over stuff-later called?
answer: Time preference
choices: Time preference
Inflation
A tariff
A subsidy
context: Mises attended Boehm-Bawerk's celebrated Vienna seminar 1905-1913 and inherited both the time-preference framework and the general Austrian method. Hayek was Mises's own student at Vienna in the 1920s (Boehm-Bawerk died in 1914 when Hayek was 15); Rothbard was Mises's American student in the 1950s at NYU; Kirzner was another Mises student at NYU. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: A hedge-fund analyst asks a plain question: WHY should anyone pay interest? If I lend you $100 for a year and you give me back exactly $100, I'm no worse off -- I got my money back. Boehm-Bawerk's time-preference account says the lender IS worse off, because being made whole after a wait is not being made whole at all. What has the lender given up that must be compensated?
answer: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
choices: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
The labor-hours he spent earning the money
The physical wear on the coins from being handled
The cost of writing up the loan contract
context: This is the pure time-preference theory of interest in its cleanest form: interest is the price of WAITING, not a payment for risk or wear or paperwork. The lender defers a year of spending; only a promise of MORE than the original sum next year compensates him for that deferral. Mises would call the pure-time-preference component 'originary interest' in Human Action (1949); Rothbard would build his entire interest theory on this alone in Man, Economy, and State (1962). Source: econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html.

question: Time preference varies wildly between choosers. A child grabs the cookie NOW. A monk under vows may live indifferent to whether the meal comes today or next week. A grandmother forgoes a cruise to leave money for a grandchild who will spend it decades from now. What does the Austrian tradition say every chooser -- however patient -- still has some of?
answer: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
choices: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
A precise numerical discount rate they can state on request
A moral obligation to prefer later over sooner
A market-determined interest rate identical to everyone else's
context: Even the patient monk still prefers a good NOW to the same good in the infinite future -- a promise of an apple in a thousand years is worth zero today to anyone who will not be alive to eat it. Time preference is positive for every actor with a finite horizon; only the SIZE varies. The child has a very high time preference (cookie now); the grandmother has a very low one; both have some. Source: mises.org/library/brief-defense-misess-conception-time-preference-and-his-pure-time-preference-theory-interest.

question: In Human Action (1949), Ludwig von Mises argued that time preference is not a quirk some people have and others do not. It is built into every human choice, because we always rank sooner against later. Mises gave a special name to the interest that comes from pure time preference. Which name?
answer: Originary interest
choices: Originary interest
Nominal interest
Compound interest
Marginal interest
context: Mises separated three components in market interest: (1) originary interest, the pure time-preference core; (2) an entrepreneurial component covering business risk; (3) a price premium covering expected inflation. Only the originary interest is praxeological -- built into human action itself -- and would remain in Mises's evenly rotating economy where risk and inflation are removed by assumption. Nominal, compound, and marginal are unrelated finance terms. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: A famous economist stripped interest rates down to their bones. Business risk and expected inflation add extra pieces on top, he said, but the base rate before those add-ons comes from just one thing. What does he say sets that base rate?
answer: How much people prefer having money now over later
choices: How much people prefer having money now over later
How productive machines and factories currently are
How much new gold is dug out of the ground each year
How high wages get pushed by big labor unions
context: Rothbard's is a Pure Time-Preference Theory of interest (PTPT) -- the productivity-of-capital account (going back to Boehm-Bawerk's own THIRD reason for interest, and to Fisher) is rejected as confused; risk and inflation get modelled as separate premiums added on top. The market rate you actually see is time preferences plus those premiums. Frank Fetter's 1904 Principles gave the pure account first; Mises and Rothbard both credit him. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf.

question: Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 book pushed a next step. A people who save more, on the whole, can build things a spend-it-all people cannot. They can support long work chains, tools that make tools, and projects that take a decade. A people who eat what they make as fast as they make it cannot. What did he call these long chains where saved goods are patiently rearranged to make more later?
answer: Roundabout production
choices: Roundabout production
Comparative advantage
Aggregate demand
Full employment equilibrium
context: Roundabout production is Boehm-Bawerk's central capital-theory concept: instead of catching fish with bare hands, first make a net; instead of walking, first build a car factory; instead of a car factory, first build a machine-tool industry to build the factory. Each step adds waiting time and requires deferred consumption. Comparative advantage is Ricardo 1817 on trade; aggregate demand and full employment are Keynesian macroeconomic constructs from the 1930s. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: Two countries start with the same people and resources. Country A saves hard and puts off spending for a generation. Country B spends every dollar right away and borrows to spend more. Boehm-Bawerk's time-preference theory says which country ends up with the more capital-heavy economy?
answer: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
choices: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
Society B -- higher spending drives more investment
Both equally -- time preferences do not affect capital structure
Society B -- consumption is what stimulates growth
context: Deferred consumption is what FREES real resources for long-term projects: workers and materials not consumed today can be used to build tools, factories, and infrastructure whose payoff comes years out. Society B's aggressive present consumption leaves nothing for the long projects. This is why Austrians (Boehm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek) argue that SAVING -- not spending -- is the engine of a capital-intensive economy, directly against the Keynesian priority given to aggregate demand. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: A central bank pushes short-term interest rates well below the rate that would balance actual saving against actual borrowing. Entrepreneurs looking at the low rate start long-term projects -- factories, subdivisions, mining operations -- on the reading that lots of long-term saving is available. But consumers have not in fact deferred any consumption; the low rate was a policy choice, not a signal from real saving. Which Austrian move names what the low rate has done?
answer: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
choices: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
It efficiently reallocates resources to their highest-value use
It cures the shortage of aggregate demand
It permanently raises the economy's growth rate
context: This is the time-preference core of Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1929-1931): when the central-bank rate is held below the market-clearing rate, entrepreneurs get a false signal that consumers have saved more than they have. Long projects get started that cannot in fact be finished with the real resources available. The bust is the market discovering the truth -- capital gets written down, malinvested projects are liquidated, workers laid off, and the economy returns to a structure the real time preferences will support. The other three options describe Keynesian, Chicago-neoclassical, and stimulus-permanence claims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: A critic of modern democracy argues that politicians only serve short terms, so they promise big spending now and leave the bills for later leaders and future kids. Over generations, what does this critic say the short-term thinking produces?
answer: Rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking
choices: Rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking
A permanent rise in the standard of living
A stable long-run balance in the political system
A gradual return to hereditary monarchy
context: Hoppe's central thesis links rising time preference to decivilization: short-horizon political incentives crowd out long-horizon private planning, borrowing-against-the-future replaces saving, and the visible symptoms are rising crime, degenerating standards, and swelling public debt. The book is controversial and Brandon's bank presents it as one named critic's argument. Time preference is Hoppe's master variable; the argument runs straight out of Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Boehm-Bawerk gave three reasons for positive interest in his 1889 book: (1) future goods will be more plentiful; (2) people undervalue future needs from carelessness; (3) present goods work better for starting production. Frank Fetter, Mises, and Rothbard later said only one of these truly belongs to the pure interest rate. The other two are separate effects. Which reason is the pure-time-preference core?
answer: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
choices: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
The greater physical productivity of tools made today
The larger future supply of goods
The scarcity of gold-based money
context: The Fetter-Mises-Rothbard purification argues that Boehm-Bawerk's first reason (larger future supply) collapses back into the second (it works only via preferences), and the third (productivity of present goods) is a productivity effect, not a time-preference effect. What is left as the ROOT of interest is the pure ranking of present over future -- reason two, in Boehm-Bawerk's numbering. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: Prices start rising fast across a country. Instead of fixing the cause (too much printed money), the top officials keep telling everyone 'don't worry, it will pass on its own.' What ONE-WORD label do they usually stick on the rising prices?
answer: Transitory
choices: Transitory
Permanent
Explosive
Runaway
context: Jerome Powell, Janet Yellen, and most Federal Open Market Committee members publicly called the 2021 inflation 'transitory' at press conferences and hearings from April through November. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank. It can create new dollars out of nothing and lend them to big banks. When it creates a LOT of new dollars fast, what usually happens to the prices YOU pay in stores?
answer: Prices go up -- your money buys less
choices: Prices go up -- your money buys less
Prices go down -- your money buys more
Prices stay exactly the same
Only rich people's prices go up
context: Powell was appointed by President Trump and reappointed by President Biden. He led the FOMC through the pandemic response, the transitory-inflation call, and the 2022-23 tightening cycle. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2021 claim that inflation would fade quickly rested on three ideas: pandemic base effects, supply-chain snarls, and one more claim about the US job market. What was the third support?
answer: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
choices: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
Higher productivity would offset any wage pressure
Immigration would keep wage growth low
Automation would eventually replace scarce workers
context: The 'transitory' case argued that with unemployment still elevated, workers lacked bargaining power for the wage gains that would sustain price inflation. Critics pointed out that a 25%+ expansion in the M2 money supply is not absorbed by labor-market slack. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: In February 2021, a well-known Democratic economist warned that a huge new spending bill could push prices up sharply. Within a year, food, gas, and rent were rising at the fastest rate in about 40 years. What was he warning about?
answer: Inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods
choices: Inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods
A sudden shortage of paper for printing books
A drop in the number of people going to college
A rise in the price of internet service alone
context: Summers's February 4 2021 Washington Post op-ed argued that the size of the Biden fiscal package created substantial inflation risk. Fed officials publicly dismissed the warning. He was largely proven right within twelve months. Source: Washington Post (February 4 2021).

question: In 2021 the US central bank kept calling the rising prices 'transitory,' meaning the problem would fade on its own soon. Prices climbed all year anyway. What lesson do many critics draw from that episode?
answer: Officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it
choices: Officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it
Central banks always predict inflation perfectly ahead of time
Prices only rise when the weather is unusually bad
Rising prices are always the fault of everyday shoppers
context: Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on November 30 2021: 'I think it's probably a good time to retire that word.' CPI was already at 6.8% year-over-year that month. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: Six months after the Fed chair retired the transitory framing, US year-over-year consumer price inflation reached its cycle peak in a specific month. What did that peak reading come in at?
answer: 9.1% in June 2022
choices: 9.1% in June 2022
5.4% in June 2021
12.3% in September 2022
6.8% in November 2021
context: The June 2022 CPI print of 9.1% was the highest US year-over-year inflation since November 1981. It came six months after the transitory framing was abandoned and marked the peak that Powell then aggressively tightened to reverse. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: After a huge burst of new money printing, the government said prices were only rising because of supply-chain trouble that would soon pass. Critics said the real cause was different. What was their main point?
answer: When the money supply grows a lot, prices eventually rise no matter what supply chains do
choices: When the money supply grows a lot, prices eventually rise no matter what supply chains do
Supply-chain trouble only affects services, never physical goods
Higher interest rates were already fixing the problem quickly
Prices always fall three months after any shock
context: The monetarist point: transitory factors resolve, but a large one-time expansion in the money supply flows through prices over a lag of 12-24 months. The Fed was staring at the monetary cause and offering a supply-side explanation. Source: Steve Hanke, Johns Hopkins Money and Growth papers (2021).

question: By late 2021 US prices were rising over 6 percent a year. The Federal Reserve kept interest rates at zero and kept buying assets anyway. Critics said this was still too loose. What term describes keeping money cheap while prices are already rising?
answer: Easy money
choices: Easy money
Tight money
Neutral money
Balanced money
context: The Fed maintained QE and zero rates through November 2021 despite inflation already at 6.2%. The critique: the Fed was pouring gasoline on the very fire it was calling a mirage. Source: federalreserve.gov (FOMC statements November 3 2021).

question: The transitory story is now cited as the modern Fed's worst forecasting error. What lesson does the Austrian tradition draw from it about how central banks predict inflation?
answer: Central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them
choices: Central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them
Central banks always over-tighten in response to inflation forecasts
Central bank models correctly predict inflation trajectories within two years
Central bank forecasts are unbiased on average and only occasionally wrong
context: The transitory episode is a case study in institutional motivated reasoning: the Fed had run enormous QE and preferred an explanation that did not implicate its own actions. A recognition move about how central banks talk about inflation. Source: George Selgin, Cato Institute commentary (2022-23).

question: Before the big 2021-2022 inflation hit, an economist who backed hard money was nominated to the Federal Reserve's board but rejected by the Senate. Critics said she was too skeptical of easy money. What does that rejection show about how the Fed picks its leaders?
answer: Nominees who challenge the Federal Reserve's usual easy-money views often fail confirmation
choices: Nominees who challenge the Federal Reserve's usual easy-money views often fail confirmation
Only nominees who oppose all Federal Reserve policy ever get confirmed
Nominees are picked at random from a lottery of American economists
The Senate rubber-stamps every Federal Reserve nominee without a hearing
context: Shelton's 1994 book Money Meltdown and later writings argued that unrestrained Fed discretion produced asset inflation and currency debasement. Her November 2020 Senate cloture defeat is often cited by Austrian analysts as a lost hard-money oversight opportunity. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1920s and 30s, some economists asked a hard question. Could a full socialist economy really work if a state committee had to set the price for every good? What did they say?
answer: No -- without market prices, planners are flying blind
choices: No -- without market prices, planners are flying blind
Yes -- committees always know best
Yes, if the committee has enough computers
Yes, as long as the leader is smart
context: Hoff (1895-1982) took his doctorate at the University of Oslo. Ohlin, Frisch, and Myrdal were other Nordic economists of the same generation but on different sides of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff's 1938 Norwegian doctoral dissertation on the calculation debate was translated to English 11 years later in 1949 by M. A. Michael and published by William Hodge of London. What was the English title?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
The Constitution of Liberty
The Road to Serfdom
Human Action
context: The Norwegian original was 'Okonomisk kalkulasjon i socialistiske samfund.' The 1949 English edition brought Hoff's argument to a wider audience just as Human Action was appearing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff's 1938 book surveyed the state of the calculation debate as of the late 1930s. Which literatures did it draw on?
answer: German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together
choices: German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together
The German Marxist literature alone
The Anglo-American Marshallian tradition alone
The French general-equilibrium school alone
context: Hoff defended Mises against Oskar Lange in careful detail, marshalling the German, English, and Soviet evidence. The book was in a real sense the definitive 1938 statement of the Austrian side of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff was not primarily an academic; he was a businessman and magazine editor. During World War II he suffered a specific consequence of his other career. What was it?
answer: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
choices: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
He fled to neutral Sweden and taught at Stockholm University for the duration
He served as economic advisor to the Norwegian government-in-exile in London
He worked as a translator for the Allied forces in Iceland
context: Hoff edited the anti-Nazi magazine Farmand. Nazi occupation authorities arrested him for the editorship. He survived; after the war Farmand became a leading Nordic classical-liberal publication and Hoff a major figure in the small postwar European liberal revival. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: In April 1947, Hayek called together 39 scholars at a Swiss mountain resort. They founded a group to defend classical liberal ideas. Trygve Hoff was one of the founders. What was the group called?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Chicago School Society
The Vienna Circle
The Fabian Society
context: Named for Mont Pelerin above Vevey, Switzerland, where the founding meeting was held April 1-10, 1947. Hoff joined Mises, Hayek, Friedman, Ropke, Rustow, Robbins, Popper, Polanyi, Stigler, Machlup, and Knight in the founding cohort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: In 1981, an American group reprinted Trygve Hoff's 1938 book. Another economist wrote a new foreword, giving it new life for a new age. Which group brought it back?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Cato Institute
The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
The Bank for International Settlements
context: The foreword was written by Karl Brunner, the Swiss-born monetarist. The reprint made Hoff's careful pre-Hayek-1945 defense of Mises available to modern Austrian scholars for the first time in decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: In 1967, Gordon Tullock wrote a nine-page paper in a small journal. He argued that the usual textbook cost of monopoly was way too small. What did he title the paper?
answer: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
choices: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
The Political Economy of Redistribution
The Vote-Trading Machinery of Congress
The Calculus of Public Choice
context: Gordon Tullock, 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' (Western Economic Journal, June 1967, later renamed Economic Inquiry). It was initially rejected by more prestigious journals before finding a home. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Tullock 1967).

question: A firm sees Congress about to grant it a $100-million-a-year tariff. Tullock in 1967 asked: how much will the firm spend on lawyers, gifts, and lobbying to win it?
answer: Up to $100 million per year
choices: Up to $100 million per year
About $1 million per year
About $10 million per year
Whatever the median firm spends
context: Tullock's insight: firms will burn real resources on the competition for privilege up to the full value of the privilege sought. If competing firms fight the tariff, they will burn resources on the other side. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: A monopolist earns big profits. Rival companies and lobbyists know those profits are up for grabs. So they spend huge amounts of time and money lobbying politicians, filing lawsuits, and running ads to either grab the monopoly or defend it. What does an economist call this waste?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Fair competition
Consumer surplus
Cost-benefit balance
context: The 'Tullock rectangle': resources spent competing for the monopoly rent equal in expectation to the full monopoly-profit rectangle. Later scholars named it after him. Source: Posner, Journal of Political Economy (1975) formalized the Tullock rectangle.

question: Tullock illustrated his rectangle argument with a homespun example. What did he argue was the TRUE social cost of theft in a society?
answer: The resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools
choices: The resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools
The dollar value of stolen goods
The lost tax revenue from unreported income
The cost of judicial trials for accused thieves
context: Tullock's illustration: theft merely TRANSFERS wealth from victim to thief -- the total is unchanged. The real deadweight loss is the whole edifice of prevention and preparation on both sides. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967), section on theft.

question: A company hires expensive lobbyists to push for a new government rule that blocks its rivals. It spends millions in Washington instead of on better products. What is the general economics name for this pattern?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Regulatory capture
Moral hazard
Adverse selection
context: Tullock originated the concept in 1967; Krueger's 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' (American Economic Review, June 1974) coined the phrase 'rent-seeking' and cemented the term. Source: jstor.org (Krueger 1974).

question: Anne Krueger's 1974 paper used Tullock's idea on one developing country. Its licenses were worth huge sums, and firms spent huge amounts on lobbying to get them. Which country did she study?
answer: India
choices: India
Brazil
Turkey
Egypt
context: Krueger studied India's License Raj -- the elaborate system of import and industrial licenses that allocated the right to operate certain businesses. Her estimates suggested rent-seeking losses of a large percentage of Indian GNP. Source: Krueger, American Economic Review (1974).

question: Tullock's paper put monopoly, tariffs, and theft under one common analysis. What shared feature makes all three of them create his larger deadweight loss?
answer: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
choices: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
Each involves foreign parties competing with domestic firms
Each requires central-bank money-printing to sustain
Each is prohibited by the US Constitution
context: Whenever there is a REDISTRIBUTIVE prize on offer -- a rent -- real economic inputs get burned competing for the prize rather than producing value. The productive economy loses those inputs. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: An economist studied jobs that pay well and take real skill but do not actually produce anything new. Instead they help one group grab money from another group by working the rules of government. Which job is the classic example of this pattern?
answer: Lobbyists
choices: Lobbyists
Farmers
Teachers
Truck drivers
context: Tullock argued that talented lawyers and lobbyists whose entire work was securing regulatory privilege were engaged in a socially wasteful zero-sum contest. The productive economy loses their talent. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Baumol, Journal of Political Economy (1990) on productive vs unproductive entrepreneurship.

question: Tullock's argument leans on a strong claim about what firms do when they compete for a government-granted rent. What does he say the competition uses up, on average?
answer: The full value of the rent being sought
choices: The full value of the rent being sought
Half the value of the rent being sought
Only a small fraction of the rent
None of the rent, since competition is impossible
context: Under free entry into the competition for rents and constant returns to lobbying, expected dissipation equals the full rent. Later scholarship (Posner 1975, Rogerson 1982) explored conditions under which dissipation is less than full. Source: Tullock 1967; Posner, Journal of Political Economy (1975).

question: Tullock's 1967 paper is now widely regarded as the founding text of a whole subfield of political economy. What single sentence best captures its enduring reasoning move?
answer: Every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it
choices: Every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it
Monopoly profits are always immediately competed away
Foreign tariffs impose no domestic welfare cost
Theft has no social cost because it merely transfers wealth
context: The rent-seeking move: whenever a redistributive prize is on offer, real economic resources will be burned competing for it, and society loses the value of those resources. This is a general result, not a partisan claim. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Buchanan + Tollison + Tullock, Toward a Theory of the Rent-Seeking Society (Texas A&M 1980).

question: Rent-seeking is when a company spends money lobbying government for a special favor instead of making better products for customers. Which kind of policy design tends to reduce this kind of waste the most?
answer: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
choices: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
Elaborate industry-specific carve-outs and case-by-case licenses
Discretionary agency waivers granted by senior political appointees
Rotating tax preferences renegotiated each Congress
context: Broad rules leave nothing worth lobbying over; carve-outs and discretion create rents. This is why constitutional political economy favors general rules and why Buchanan named 'generality' as a core principle. Source: Buchanan + Congleton, Politics by Principle, Not Interest (Cambridge 1998).

question: Instead of many welfare plans, one economist said this: if you earn less than a set amount, the tax office sends you money. What is that kind of tax called?
answer: A negative income tax
choices: A negative income tax
A luxury tax
A sales tax
A tariff
context: Friedman's motivation was administrative simplification and preservation of work incentives via a gradual known phase-out. It differed structurally from the modern UBI concept, which typically adds a universal payment on top of the existing safety net. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: Milton Friedman's Negative Income Tax idea was tested in big trials in the US and Canada from 1968 to 1979. What was the main finding on work hours?
answer: Modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted
choices: Modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted
A total 80 percent reduction in work hours across all recipients
No measurable change in work hours in any subgroup
A doubling of work hours as recipients gained financial security to seek new jobs
context: The New Jersey/Pennsylvania (1968-72) and Seattle/Denver (1970-77) US experiments and the Manitoba MINCOME (1974-79) Canadian experiment all found modest work-hour declines with substantial administrative-cost savings over the multi-program comparison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: A US presidential candidate wanted to give every adult American one thousand dollars a month, with no strings attached. He would pay for it partly with a new sales tax. What is the general name for this kind of policy?
answer: Universal basic income
choices: Universal basic income
A progressive income tax
Payroll tax withholding
A tariff on imports
context: Yang, a tech entrepreneur, made UBI the signature of his campaign. His proposal was a universal flat payment with no income phase-out, structurally different from Friedman's NIT. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Andrew_Yang.

question: The largest recent US trial of no-strings cash transfers was funded by Sam Altman's OpenResearch. It gave $1,000 a month to 1,000 people in Illinois and Texas for three years. When results came out in August 2024, what did the study find about work hours?
answer: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
choices: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
Recipients doubled their work hours on average
Recipients quit the labor force entirely at a rate of 80 percent
Recipients showed no change in work hours whatsoever
context: The study also found modest health improvements and no clear positive employment outcomes despite proponent hopes. The findings largely echoed the 1970s NIT experiments' pattern of moderate labor-supply reductions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Two plans send everyone a monthly cash check. One older plan cancels all other welfare programs first, so the check is the whole safety net. A newer plan usually keeps every existing program and adds the cash on top. What is the key difference?
answer: The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them
choices: The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them
One is paid weekly and the other is paid once a year
One is funded by tariffs and the other by property taxes
One is only for citizens and the other includes tourists
context: Friedman would have supported replacing programs with an NIT and opposed adding a UBI on top of them. The two proposals share a label but have opposite structural implications for the state's role and for the effective marginal tax rate facing the recipient as income rises. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: A libertarian scholar proposed sending every adult American 10,000 dollars per year. His plan would end nearly every existing welfare program and use that money instead. What makes this different from an add-on plan?
answer: It replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment
choices: It replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment
It adds monthly payments on top of the existing programs
It applies only to people over 65 years of age
It is paid in food stamps rather than cash
context: The Murray design is a UBI in label but an NIT in structure -- a flat universal payment that eliminates the existing multi-program stack. Same-label proposals with different phase-out and replacement structures produce very different outcomes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: One American state has paid every one of its residents an annual share of state oil-royalty money, often around one to two thousand dollars a year per person, every year since 1982. Which state runs this longest-standing cash-dividend program?
answer: Alaska (the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend)
choices: Alaska (the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend)
Texas (the Texas Oil Trust Distribution)
California (the California Resident Dividend)
Wyoming (the Wyoming Mineral Royalty Payout)
context: The Alaska Permanent Fund was created in 1976 and the Dividend program began payouts in 1982. Every Alaskan resident (regardless of income) receives the annual share. It is the closest real-world US analogue of a UBI. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Alaska_Permanent_Fund.

question: A student asks an economist whether a Universal Basic Income, meaning a monthly government check to every adult, is 'obviously a good idea.' The economist refuses to say yes or no and instead points at a reasoning move. Which move is he pressing?
answer: Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results
choices: Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results
Any cash transfer to households below the middle income is always good
Any cash transfer to households above the middle income is always harmful
Policy details never matter because people never change their behavior
context: This is Sowell's 'there are no solutions, only tradeoffs' at the policy-design level. A UBI on top of existing programs has different effects from an NIT that replaces them. The kid learns to look under the label at the actual mechanism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Since the Agricultural Act of 1949, the US government has run a price-support program for one farm product. It even buys extra when there is a surplus and stores or dumps it. Which product?
answer: Milk (and derivative dairy products)
choices: Milk (and derivative dairy products)
Wheat only
Corn only
Soybeans only
context: The federal purchases were made largely as butter and processed cheese, which stored better than fluid milk. The program has been renamed and modified many times but the above-market-support core has persisted for 75+ years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: By 1981, after years of the federal dairy price-support buying up extra milk, the US government owned a huge pile of one dairy product. It sat in caves and warehouses across the country. Which item, and roughly how much?
answer: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese

About 10,000 pounds of yogurt
About 5 million pounds of ice cream
About 100 million pounds of powdered milk only

question: In 1981, the Reagan team gave out big blocks of the government's extra cheese to food banks. Those cheese loaves gave a new phrase to American speech. What did the phrase become?
answer: 'Government cheese'
choices: 'Government cheese'
